days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: Free cash flow to the firm and to equity: construction, leverage effects and multistage valuation
days.headline_hint: Apple's $118 billion of operating cash flow is not the number you discount
days.focus: FCFF and FCFE built from net income, EBIT, EBITDA and operating cash flow, the leverage assumption that separates them, growth as reinvestment rate times return on new capital, two-stage and fading models with an exit-multiple cross-check, and the bridge from enterprise value to a per-share value through net debt, pensions, leases, minorities and unvested stock. Assumes day 80's DCF and lesson 5's cash-flow reconciliation and lesson 11's WACC. Afterwards the reader can value any company from its 10-K by both routes and reconcile the two to the cent.
parts: Two cash flows, two discount rates: why FCFF at WACC and FCFE at the cost of equity must agree
Building FCFF from net income, EBIT, EBITDA and CFO — four routes, one answer
FCFE and net borrowing: the leverage assumption that changes the value without changing the business
Forecasting the pieces: reinvestment rate, return on new capital, and growth as their product
Two-stage and fading models: the terminal value's share and the exit-multiple cross-check
From enterprise value to equity value: net debt, minorities, pensions, leases and unvested stock
worked_examples: Apple FY2024 10-K: net income $93.7 billion, D&A $11.4 billion, capex $9.4 billion, operating cash flow $118.3 billion, term-debt repayments of $10.0 billion and the working-capital change — FCFE and FCFF by all four routes, and a two-stage per-share value against the market price.

Microsoft FY2024: FCFF from operating income of $109.4 billion, an 18% tax rate, D&A and $44.5 billion of property and equipment additions — growth as reinvestment rate times ROIC, and the terminal value at the WACC from lesson 11.

Nvidia FY2025 (year ended 26 January 2025): operating cash flow of $64.1 billion and free cash flow of about $60.9 billion, a growth fade from 30% to 4% over ten years, and the per-share value range across reinvestment assumptions.

Ford Motor Company: the bridge from enterprise value to equity value when automotive net cash sits beside Ford Credit's debt — why the last step is the hardest for a company with a captive finance arm.

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: Residual income, economic value added and the clean-surplus relation
days.headline_hint: JPMorgan trades at two and a half times book, and the ratio is a forecast of one number
days.focus: Valuation from the balance sheet forward: residual income and EVA as profit after the charge for equity, the clean-surplus identity, the model's lower sensitivity to terminal assumptions, Ohlson's persistence parameter and continuing residual income, the justified price-to-book for banks, and the adjustments when clean surplus fails — OCI, buybacks above book, goodwill. Assumes day 7's double entry, day 12's book value and day 66's cost of equity, plus lessons 17 and 18. Afterwards the reader can value a bank from ROE, book value and a cost of equity, and reconcile the answer to the dividend and cash-flow models.
parts: Profit after the cost of equity: residual income, EVA, and why accounting earnings are not enough
Clean surplus: the identity that turns dividends into book value and residual income
The model: value equals book plus the present value of residual income — and why the terminal value matters less
Persistence: Ohlson's omega, continuing residual income, and the fade of returns to the cost of capital
Banks and price-to-book: ROE minus r, and the multiple it justifies
Violations of clean surplus and the adjustments: OCI, buybacks above book, goodwill
worked_examples: JPMorgan Chase 2024: net income $58.5 billion, ROTCE 22%, tangible book value per share $97.30, and the year-end price — the price-to-tangible-book the model justifies at a 10% cost of equity, and the persistence factor the market price implies.
Home Depot FY2024: EVA from NOPAT and invested capital against HD's own disclosed ROIC of 31.3% and a WACC from lesson 11.
Coca-Cola in a single-stage residual-income model on its latest 10-K book value and ROE, set beside lesson 17's dividend-model value — why the two agree only if clean surplus holds.
A clean-surplus violation in the wild: Berkshire Hathaway's 2022 swings in net income and other comprehensive income, and what they do to a residual-income series.

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: Relative valuation: justified multiples, comparables done properly, and private company valuation
days.headline_hint: How SpaceX was worth $350 billion, then $800 billion, then $1.77 trillion, without changing its rockets
days.focus: Every multiple derived from the models that precede it — justified P/E, P/B, P/S and EV/EBITDA from fundamentals — then comparables done properly: peer selection, the harmonic mean, cross-sectional regressions, forward versus trailing and normalised earnings; and finally the company with no price: guideline public companies, guideline transactions, the income approach with a build-up rate, and the discounts for control and marketability with the evidence behind them. Assumes day 75's multiples and day 123's liquidity, plus lessons 17–19. Afterwards the reader can defend a multiple from first principles and value a private stake to the standard an appraiser or a 409A report must meet.
parts: Every multiple is a discount model in disguise: justified P/E, P/B, P/S and EV/EBITDA from fundamentals
Comparables that compare: choosing peers, the harmonic mean, and cross-sectional regressions
Forward vs trailing, normalised earnings, and the PEG ratio's arithmetic problem
Private companies: guideline public companies, guideline transactions, and the income approach
Discounts and premiums: control, marketability, and the restricted-stock evidence behind DLOM
Standards of value: fair market value, fair value, investment value — and the 409A and estate-tax settings that set the rules
worked_examples: Justified P/E for Coca-Cola from lesson 17's payout, growth and cost of equity against its trailing multiple; justified price-to-book for JPMorgan from lesson 19's ROE, growth and cost of equity against the traded ratio.
Arithmetic versus harmonic mean P/E across the S&P 500 constituents, after Baker & Ruback (1999): the index's own P/E as the harmonic case, and the upward bias a simple average introduces.

SpaceX's price ladder before it had one: the December 2024 insider tender at $185 a share (about $350 billion), the mid-2025 tender near $400 billion, the December 2025 tender near $800 billion, and the 12 June 2026 IPO at $135 a share ($1.77 trillion, first close $160.95, Nasdaq: SPCX) — split-adjusted, what marketability discount each tender implied against the price the public market finally set.

A build-up discount rate for a private manufacturer: a ten-year Treasury, a 5% equity risk premium, Kroll's tenth-decile size premium and a company-specific premium, then a marketability discount from the restricted-stock studies applied under Revenue Ruling 59-60's factors.

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: The term structure: spot, forward, par and the models behind them
days.headline_hint: Every yield curve is three curves, and the market only shows you one
days.focus: Bootstrapping spot and forward curves from the Treasury set at professional depth; the par–spot–forward identities and where they break (the coupon effect, on-the-run specialness); Nelson–Siegel–Svensson fitting as the Fed publishes it; decomposing the ten-year yield into expected short rates and a term premium (ACM, Kim–Wright); and the one-factor short-rate models (Vasicek, CIR, Hull–White) that are the machinery behind every later lesson's 'arbitrage-free' claim. Graduate level: the mathematics is done. Afterwards the reader can build a discount curve from live Treasury quotes, reproduce the Fed's NSS curve from its parameters, and say what a term-premium estimate is and is not.
parts: Three curves, one market: why par, spot and forward cannot disagree
Bootstrapping is easy until the bonds refuse to cooperate
What the ten-year yield is made of: expected policy and the term premium
A random walk with a leash: Vasicek, CIR and Hull–White
Why 'arbitrage-free' is a promise about the tree, not about the world
worked_examples: Bootstrap a zero curve from the Treasury's daily par yield curve on the run date (1-month to 30-year) and price the 4.375% note due 15 May 2036 off the spot curve versus its quoted yield, showing the coupon effect in basis points
Read the Fed's Gürkaynak–Sack–Wright NSS parameters (β0–β3, τ1, τ2) for the run date and reproduce the 2-, 5-, 10- and 30-year zero yields to the basis point

Compute the 2-year rate two years forward from the bootstrapped curve, then use the New York Fed's ACM ten-year term premium for the run date to split the ten-year yield into a policy-expectations part and a premium
Price a 10-year zero under Vasicek with κ = 0.2, θ = 4%, σ = 1% and r0 equal to run-date SOFR, and show what halving κ does to the 30-year zero and to the model's implied term premium

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: Interest-rate risk at depth: DV01, key-rate durations and convexity
days.headline_hint: The number that tells you where on the curve it will hurt
days.focus: DV01 and its relatives on real bonds; effective versus modified duration; key-rate durations as partial derivatives along the curve, and why a barbell and a bullet of equal duration behave differently; convexity — its price, when it is worth paying for, and why it dominates the long end; hedge ratios with cash Treasuries and with Treasury futures at the level year one taught them (day 90), with the futures' delivery mechanics deferred to day 6 of this block; P&L attribution into level, slope and curvature by principal components. Afterwards the reader can compute the key-rate profile of a portfolio, build a curve-neutral hedge, and read a day's bond P&L into its factors.
parts: One number is not enough: DV01, duration and where they come apart
Key-rate durations: the curve as a vector of shocks
Barbells, bullets and the convexity you are paying for
Hedging a bond book: matching DV01, then matching the shape
Convexity at the long end: the 5% of 2056 and the price of a rally
Attribution: turning a day's P&L into level, slope and curvature

Key-rate profile (2-, 5-, 10-, 30-year keys) of a barbell in the on-the-run 2-year and the 5.125% bond due August 2056 versus a bullet in the 4.375% May 2036 of equal DV01, and their P&L under a 20 bp 2s10s steepening

Hedging $100 million of the Apple 3.85% notes due 2043 with 10-year (ZN) and Ultra Bond (UB) futures, contract DV01 taken from the cheapest-to-deliver as given until day 6, and the residual key-rate exposure that remains
Principal components of one month of daily Treasury par-yield changes: the first three factors, the variance each explains, and the loadings that make them level, slope and curvature

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: Bonds with options inside: the arbitrage-free tree and option-adjusted spread
days.headline_hint: The bond that pays you back early, and how to price the option you sold without noticing
days.focus: One topic taught to the bottom: valuing cash flows that depend on the path of rates. The binomial interest-rate tree calibrated to the run-date spot curve at a stated volatility, and backward induction as conditional expectation under the risk-neutral measure; callable and putable bonds — the issuer's option and the investor's — priced on the tree; option-adjusted spread against Z-spread, and why OAS falls as the volatility assumption rises; effective duration and effective convexity from the tree, the duration that shrinks in a rally and the negative convexity of a callable; then the mortgage pass-through as the worked example rather than a subject of its own — the homeowner's prepayment option expressed as a PSA speed, cash flows at 100 PSA, and negative convexity shown numerically when the speed responds to the rate shift. CMO structuring, burnout and Monte Carlo OAS along rate paths are left out deliberately; the lesson says what they are for and no more. Afterwards the reader can calibrate a small tree, price a callable and read its OAS, turn a PSA speed into cash flows, and show in numbers why the MBS index has negative convexity.
parts: Calibrating a tree to the curve so that nothing inside it can be arbitraged
Backward induction: the value of a cash flow that depends on where rates went
Callable and putable: the issuer's option, the investor's option and the OAS
Z-spread against OAS, the volatility assumption and the duration that shrinks in a rally
The homeowner's option: a pass-through on the same tree, and negative convexity by the numbers
worked_examples: Build a four-period lognormal tree calibrated to the run-date Treasury spot curve from day 1's bootstrap at 15% rate volatility, and check it by pricing the option-free 4.375% note due 15 May 2036 on the tree back to its spot-curve price to the cent

Price a Fannie Mae callable benchmark note quoted on the run date (par call after its lockout) on the same tree: its value, OAS at the quoted price, effective duration and effective convexity, beside an option-free bullet of the same coupon and maturity

The same callable on trees built at 10% and 20% volatility: the OAS at each, why it falls as volatility rises and the Z-spread that does not move; then the putable version of the same bond and the effective duration that lengthens in a sell-off

Cash flows of a $100 million Fannie Mae 30-year 5.5% pass-through at 100 PSA (0.2% CPR ramp to 6% at month 30) priced on the tree, then effective duration and convexity from ±50 bp shifts with the speed stepping to 250 PSA in the rally and 75 PSA in the sell-off — the pool's negative convexity set beside the option-free bullet's positive number
sources: Tuckman & Serrat, Fixed Income Securities: Tools for Today's Markets, 4th ed. (Wiley, 2022), term-structure models and the chapters on fixed income options and mortgages
Kalotay, Williams & Fabozzi (1993), "A Model for Valuing Bonds and Embedded Options", Financial Analysts Journal 49(3)

days.topic: Credit analysis: default, recovery and the price of a promise
days.headline_hint: What a spread pays you for, and how little of it is actually default
days.focus: Structural models (Merton's distance to default, the KMV expected default frequency) and reduced-form models (hazard rates, Jarrow–Turnbull, Duffie–Singleton) done properly; what rating agencies actually do and what the default and recovery record says; the credit triangle and the decomposition of a spread into expected loss, risk premium and liquidity; Z-, I- and G-spreads and OAS on corporates; the credit curve and the cycle in the series the paper prints every day (ICE BofA high-yield OAS). days.topic: Beyond Black–Scholes: trees, the volatility surface and the exotics priced off it
days.headline_hint: The smile is the market telling you the model is wrong, and exactly how
days.focus: Cox–Ross–Rubinstein trees and American early exercise with discrete dividends; why the surface exists (1987, jumps, stochastic volatility); local volatility (Dupire) as the unique diffusion that fits every vanilla, and its inverse problem; stochastic volatility (Heston) and what a second factor buys; SVI parameterisation with the calendar and butterfly no-arbitrage constraints; sticky-strike and sticky-delta regimes and the term structure of skew; exotics priced off the surface — digitals as call-spread limits, barriers by reflection, Asians, autocallables — and the retail structured-product market built on them. days.topic: Private equity: the LBO model, waterfalls and what the returns really are
days.headline_hint: An IRR is a story about timing; a multiple is a story about money
days.focus: The limited partnership from commitment to wind-down: capital calls, the J-curve, management fees on committed versus invested capital, the distribution waterfall (European and American, hurdle, catch-up, clawback); the LBO model, which this block owns — sources and uses, the debt stack (revolver, term loan B, senior and subordinated notes), the debt schedule with its mandatory amortisation and excess-cash sweep, the exit at a multiple and the returns bridge into deleveraging, EBITDA growth and multiple change — built in full and checked against a real deal; why IRR misleads (subscription lines, early wins, the reinvestment assumption) and the alternatives (MOIC, DPI/RVPI/TVPI, Kaplan–Schoar PME, Direct Alpha); the evidence on performance and persistence; the marking of unlisted holdings and the smoothing it induces; secondaries, continuation vehicles and NAV loans. Afterwards the reader can build a sources-and-uses table and a debt schedule for a buyout, run a waterfall, compute a PME from a fund's cash flows, and read a public pension's PE performance table critically.

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: Risk management at depth: VaR, expected shortfall, backtests and stress
days.headline_hint: Ninety-nine days out of a hundred is a promise about the hundredth
days.focus: The four VaR engines (parametric delta-normal and delta-gamma, historical, filtered historical, Monte Carlo) and expected shortfall, all computed on the same real portfolio; coherence (Artzner) and why regulators moved to expected shortfall at 97.5% (FRTB); backtesting a VaR (Kupiec, Christoffersen) and the traffic-light regime; extreme-value tails and what they change; stress testing as the Fed runs it — the 2026 severely adverse scenario applied to a book — and reverse stress tests; risk budgeting and Euler contributions; liquidity-adjusted risk and March 2020. Afterwards the reader can compute and backtest VaR and ES on a real portfolio, apply a supervisory scenario to it, and decompose its risk by contribution.

Expected shortfall: the coherent measure and the Basel move to 97.5%
Backtesting a VaR: exceptions, independence and the traffic light
The tail is not normal: extreme-value theory and what it changes
Stress tests: the Fed's 2026 scenario applied to your book, and reverse stress
Risk budgets, Euler contributions and the liquidity you forgot to price

The Federal Reserve's 2026 severely adverse scenario (unemployment up 5.9 points to about 10%, house prices −30%, commercial real estate −39%, a sharp BBB-spread widening and a higher-for-longer VIX path) applied to a portfolio of the S&P 500, the Bloomberg Aggregate, the Apple 3.85% notes due 2043 and a REIT sleeve, with the loss attributed by shock

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: Performance measurement, attribution and GIPS
days.headline_hint: The return you earned, the return the client got and the return you may advertise are three different numbers
days.focus: Time-weighted versus money-weighted returns and when each is the honest one; Brinson–Fachler attribution with multi-period linking; factor-based attribution from a risk model; fixed-income attribution (carry, curve, spread, selection); risk-adjusted measures and their pitfalls (Sharpe, information ratio, appraisal ratio, M², the fundamental law); manager evaluation and the SPIVA record; GIPS 2020 — firm definition, composites, pooled funds, the calculation rules and what compliance asserts — and the SEC Marketing Rule's net-of-fee requirement. Afterwards the reader can attribute a real fund's active return, build a GIPS-compliant composite return, and read a performance presentation for what it hides.

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: The investor's constraints: taxes, liquidity and behaviour in allocation
days.headline_hint: After tax, after the lock-up and after the investor's own nerves, the frontier moves
days.focus: The private-wealth constraints at Level III depth, for a Pennsylvania resident: tax drag (Jeffrey–Arnott) under accrual, deferred and exempt taxation, asset location across taxable, traditional and Roth accounts (Dammon–Spatt–Zhang), the true value of tax-loss harvesting and its decay, the wash-sale and stepped-up-basis rules that bound it (IRC §1091, §1014), qualified dividends and the net investment income tax as inputs to after-tax return, and municipal tax-equivalent yields at federal plus Pennsylvania rates; liquidity budgeting for illiquid sleeves (Ang–Papanikolaou–Westerfield, the endowment model, the 2022 denominator effect); and the behavioural evidence that shows up in portfolios — the disposition effect, overtrading, home bias, the behaviour gap — with the remedies that survive scrutiny, taking the theory as year one's day 140 taught it. The retirement-account decisions (Roth conversions, distributions), death taxes and the statutory computations behind them belong to the Accounting and Wealth Management courses later in the year and are not taught here. Tax figures are stated for the run year and checked against the IRS that morning. Afterwards the reader can locate assets across account types, compute a fund's tax drag and a Pennsylvania tax-equivalent yield, size an illiquid sleeve, and quantify the behaviour gap in a fund.
parts: Tax drag: the alpha you need just to break even
Asset location: which account each asset belongs in, and why the answer is not obvious
Harvesting, wash sales and the step-up: what §1091 and §1014 do to an allocation
Municipal bonds and the after-tax return: the Pennsylvania tax-equivalent yield
Liquidity budgeting: how much illiquidity a portfolio can afford
The behaviour gap: what investors measurably do to their own returns, and what helps
worked_examples: Tax-equivalent yield of a Pennsylvania general-obligation municipal bond at its run-date yield for a Bridgeville resident in the 24% and 32% federal brackets plus Pennsylvania's 3.07% (PA-exempt), with the 3.8% net investment income tax where it applies, all figures for the run year

Asset location of a $1 million 60/40 across taxable, traditional IRA and Roth accounts: after-tax terminal wealth over twenty years with a 5% bond yield taxed as ordinary income against a 2% qualified-dividend, 5% growth equity sleeve

Tax drag on $1 million in a US large-cap fund with 50% annual turnover realising gains at the run-year 15% and 20% capital-gains rates plus the 3.8% net investment income tax, against an index fund realising almost none, over twenty years at 8% pre-tax: the after-tax terminal wealth, the pre-tax alpha the active fund needs to break even (Jeffrey–Arnott), and a harvested loss disallowed under §1091 by a repurchase inside 30 days

Liquidity budget for a $500 million endowment with 40% in private funds, a 5% payout and a 2008-style 30% drawdown with capital calls of 8% of unfunded commitments per year; Morningstar's latest 'Mind the Gap' investor-return gap for US equity funds

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: The CFA Standards and the Asset Manager Code: what the duty costs, and the economics of breach
days.headline_hint: Loyalty, prudence and care are measured in basis points, and the enforcement record says what a breach costs
days.focus: The profession's own rulebook, applied to a desk: the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and the seven Standards of Professional Conduct through the 12th-edition Standards of Practice Handbook (2024) — knowledge of the law, independence and objectivity, the new Competence standard, material nonpublic information and the mosaic theory, market manipulation, loyalty–prudence–care, fair dealing, suitability, performance presentation, diligence and reasonable basis, record retention, avoiding or disclosing conflicts, priority of transactions, referral fees — each read as a case, the handbook's way; the Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct, its six principles and what a firm's claim of compliance asserts; then the economics of breach: soft dollars and the Exchange Act §28(e) safe harbour after the SEC's 2006 guidance and MiFID II's unbundling, best execution as the fiduciary duty inside every trade, conflicts with a price (share classes, 12b-1 fees, revenue sharing), and the enforcement record's numbers — the Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative, the Robinhood best-execution order, SAC and Martoma, the 2020 JPMorgan spoofing resolution. The statute and regulation of advice — the Advisers Act, Reg BI, ERISA, the DOL rule, Form ADV — are the Wealth Management course's to teach later in the year; this lesson takes the profession's standards and what they cost. Written with the paper's political neutrality. Afterwards the reader can classify a fact pattern under the Standard it falls under, price a soft-dollar arrangement in basis points, and put a dollar figure on a conflict.
parts: The Code and the seven Standards: how the 12th-edition handbook reads a case
Integrity of capital markets: material nonpublic information, the mosaic theory and manipulation
Duties to clients: loyalty, prudence and care, fair dealing, suitability and the honest track record
Diligence, conflicts and the Asset Manager Code: what a firm's claim of compliance asserts
Soft dollars and best execution: the fiduciary duty inside every trade, and the §28(e) safe harbour
Conflicts with a price: share classes, 12b-1 fees and the enforcement record in dollars
worked_examples: Dollar cost of a 0.25% 12b-1 fee and a 0.75% higher-cost share class on a $250,000 account over 25 years at 7%, set against the SEC Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative's roughly $139 million returned to investors by the 95 self-reporting advisers (2018–2020)

Soft dollars under §28(e): a $500 million equity account turning over 60% a year at an average $60 share price, paying a bundled 2.5 cents a share against 0.75 cents execution-only — the commission dollars, the research the safe harbour lets the manager buy with them, and the cost in basis points of client assets a year, set against the same account under MiFID II unbundling with research paid from the manager's own P&L

Standard II(A) at its limit: the Elan–Wyeth bapineuzumab trades of July 2008 — the $276 million in profits and avoided losses the government attributed to Mathew Martoma's information, the nine-year sentence, SAC Capital's $1.8 billion 2013 resolution — sorted into what the mosaic theory would have permitted and what it would not

Best execution as a duty: the SEC's December 2020 Robinhood order — a $65 million penalty and the finding that inferior execution prices cost customers $34.1 million net of the commissions they saved — with the price-improvement arithmetic that produced the number, and the Standard III(A) reading of the same facts

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: Market microstructure and execution: venues, order types, algorithms and the cost of a trade
days.headline_hint: The spread is the price of being wrong about who is on the other side
days.focus: The models that explain the spread — Roll's estimator, Glosten–Milgrom adverse selection, Kyle's lambda — and the empirical measures (quoted, effective and realised spreads, price impact); the US equity market's plumbing under Regulation NMS: the order protection rule and the NBBO, the exchanges and ATSs, payment for order flow, the closing auction, the 2024 tick-size and access-fee amendments and their status on the run date; order types and what each reveals; the Treasury market's different structure and the clearing mandate (cash trades from 31 December 2026, repo from 30 June 2027); then execution — implementation shortfall, the square-root impact law, Almgren–Chriss optimal schedules, the VWAP/TWAP/POV/IS algorithm families, transaction-cost analysis and the pre-trade estimate a portfolio manager should demand. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can estimate a stock's lambda, cost a large order pre-trade, choose an algorithm with reasons, and read a TCA report.

Measuring it: quoted, effective and realised spreads, and price impact from the tape
Regulation NMS and the plumbing: protected quotes, payment for order flow, the close and the half-penny tick
Order types as signals, and the Treasury market's different rules
Implementation shortfall and the square-root law: what a big order costs
Almgren–Chriss, the algorithm families and how to read a TCA report

days.subject: Finance & Markets
days.topic: Systematic strategy design: regimes, backtests and the pathologies that survive them
days.headline_hint: A backtest is an experiment run on the only history there is, and it knows you were watching
days.focus: The capstone: a systematic strategy from signal to execution, built and judged with everything in the block. Regime detection done properly — Hamilton's Markov-switching model and its filter, hidden Markov models on returns and volatility (the linear-Gaussian state-space model and the Kalman filter are the Mathematics block's, later in the year, and are not taught here) — and what the paper's daily Regime call is and is not; regime-conditional behaviour of trend, carry and value and trend-following's crisis alpha; the pathologies at research depth — multiple testing and the deflated Sharpe ratio, combinatorial purged cross-validation, walk-forward tests and parameter plateaus, survivorship-free universes and point-in-time data, cost realism and capacity — and the McLean–Pontiff decay; a full strategy worked end to end with honest numbers. Practitioner level. Afterwards the reader can fit a regime model, compute a deflated Sharpe ratio, run a purged cross-validation, and write a research note that would survive a sceptical reader.
parts: Regimes exist, and they are hard to see in time: Hamilton's filter and the hidden Markov model
What the Regime chip in the paper is actually estimating
Trend, carry and value across regimes: crisis alpha and its cost
The pathologies at depth: multiple testing, the deflated Sharpe ratio and purged cross-validation
Data that does not lie: survivorship-free universes, point-in-time fundamentals and cost realism
A strategy built end to end, and the research note that defends it

Time-series momentum across twelve CME and ICE futures (equity, bond, currency and commodity) from 2000 to the run date: gross returns, net of the day-19 square-root cost model, and the McLean–Pontiff 26% in-sample and 58% post-publication decay applied as a haircut

Combinatorial purged cross-validation (six groups, two test groups, a one-month embargo) against plain k-fold on a 12-1 momentum signal in the S&P 500 universe with CRSP delisting returns, reporting the probability of backtest overfitting

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Consumer and producer theory with duality
days.headline_hint: The Cost of Living Has a Dual, and the CPI Is Not Quite It
days.focus: The utility-maximisation and expenditure-minimisation problems as a dual pair; indirect utility and the expenditure function; Roy's identity, Shephard's lemma, the Slutsky equation and integrability; compensating and equivalent variation; revealed preference and Afriat's theorem; then the producer side: cost and profit functions, Hotelling's lemma and flexible functional forms. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can derive a demand system from an expenditure function, compute exact welfare measures for a price change, and say precisely how the CPI's Laspeyres formula departs from a cost-of-living index.

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: General equilibrium and the welfare theorems
days.headline_hint: The Invisible Hand Has a Proof, and the Proof Has Fine Print

Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can solve a small Walrasian economy by hand, price an Arrow security, and state which welfare theorem a policy argument is silently invoking.

Sonnenschein–Mantel–Debreu: why aggregate demand need not slope down, and what that costs

Harberger's (1962) two-sector model of the corporate income tax as the first applied general-equilibrium calculation, and a published computable-general-equilibrium estimate of the 2025 US tariff increases (the Yale Budget Lab's tariff series or a PIIE working paper), read for the assumptions that generate its price and GDP numbers

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Game theory: Nash, subgame perfection and repeated games
days.headline_hint: Why Cartels Hold for Years and Break in a Week
days.focus: Normal- and extensive-form games, Nash equilibrium and its existence, mixed strategies tested on real penalty kicks, subgame perfection and backward induction, Rubinstein's alternating-offers bargaining, Bayesian games and sequential equilibrium, and repeated games: the folk theorem, grim trigger, Green–Porter price wars under imperfect monitoring and Abreu's optimal punishments. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can compute the critical discount factor for any collusive arrangement, solve a bargaining game with outside options, and read an oil-price war as an equilibrium rather than a mistake.

Subgame perfection and backward induction: credible threats and the chain-store paradox
Rubinstein bargaining: patience is bargaining power, and the strike as a costly delay

The folk theorem: what repetition makes possible, and the discount factor that decides it

days.topic: Information economics: adverse selection, moral hazard and signalling
days.headline_hint: The Bad Drive Out the Good: Akerlof's Lemons, Fifty Years of Evidence Later
days.focus: Adverse selection in Akerlof's market and its unravelling, Spence signalling with separating and pooling equilibria and the intuitive criterion, Rothschild–Stiglitz screening in insurance and the possible non-existence of equilibrium, moral hazard and the principal–agent problem with Holmström's informativeness principle, credit rationing, and the modern empirical tests: positive correlation, the Einav–Finkelstein cost curves and the welfare cost of selection. days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Mechanism design and auctions
days.headline_hint: How to Sell a Thing Whose Value You Do Not Know: The Mathematics of the Auction
days.focus: The revelation principle, incentive compatibility and the envelope characterisation of payments; Vickrey and first-price auctions under independent private values, revenue equivalence, Myerson's optimal auction and the reserve price; affiliated values, the winner's curse and the linkage principle; VCG and the Myerson–Satterthwaite impossibility; then the auctions that matter: Treasury auctions, the FCC's 2017 incentive auction and sponsored search. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can derive equilibrium bidding for a given value distribution, compute an optimal reserve, and read a Treasury auction's tail and bid-to-cover as an auction theorist would.

Bidding in first-price and second-price auctions, and why they raise the same revenue
Myerson's optimal auction: virtual values, the reserve price and the seller who wants revenue
Common values: the winner's curse in the OCS oil leases and Milgrom–Weber's linkage principle
VCG, Myerson–Satterthwaite and the limits of efficient trade
Auctions at scale: a Treasury note, the FCC's 2017 incentive auction and Google's ad exchange

A named recent 10-year Treasury note auction from the TreasuryDirect results release: the high yield against the when-issued yield (the tail), the bid-to-cover ratio, and the primary-dealer, direct and indirect shares, read as a uniform-price auction with the Treasury's 35% award limit

The 2017 FCC broadcast incentive auction (Leyton-Brown, Milgrom and Segal 2017): the descending reverse-auction clock, the clearing target falling from 126 MHz to 84 MHz over four stages, $10.05bn paid to 175 stations, $19.8bn gross forward-auction proceeds and T-Mobile's roughly $8bn

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Econometrics for causal inference: IV, diff-in-diff, RDD
days.headline_hint: Correlation Was Never Enough: How Economists Learned to Find a Cause
days.focus: The potential-outcomes framework and the selection problem; instrumental variables with LATE, weak-instrument diagnostics and the draft lottery; difference-in-differences from Card–Krueger's 2×2 to staggered-adoption event studies and the Goodman-Bacon decomposition; regression discontinuity with bandwidth choice and the McCrary test; synthetic control; and the macro variants (narrative shocks, high-frequency identification, local projections). Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can compute a Wald estimate, set up a DiD with a pre-trends check, run an RDD by hand at a threshold, and say what each design identifies and for whom. This is the year's single treatment of the toolkit: Political Science (block 7), the AI block and Wealth Management assume it rather than re-teach it. Lee's close-election discontinuity is left for Political Science to apply on its own ground, so today's regression discontinuity runs on the minimum drinking age instead.

Instruments: the draft lottery, the Wald estimator, LATE and what a weak first stage does
Difference-in-differences: Card and Krueger's four numbers, parallel trends and the event study
Staggered adoption: why two-way fixed effects can get the sign wrong, and the Callaway–Sant'Anna fix
Regression discontinuity: the jump at the twenty-first birthday, bandwidths and the density test
Synthetic control and macro identification: California's Proposition 99, Romer–Romer and local projections

Angrist's (1990) draft lottery as an instrument: the first stage (lottery number → veteran status), the reduced form (lottery number → earnings) and the Wald ratio that gives the roughly 15% earnings penalty for white veterans

Carpenter and Dobkin's (2009) minimum-drinking-age discontinuity: NHIS days-drinking and NCHS mortality for 19-to-22-year-olds by age relative to the 21st birthday, the roughly 21% jump in days on which people drink and the about 9% jump in all-cause mortality (near nine deaths per 100,000 person-years, led by motor-vehicle accidents, suicide and alcohol-coded deaths), estimated with a local linear fit and a Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik bandwidth — then McCrary's density test run where it bites, on Urquiola and Verhoogen's (2009) Chilean class-size cap, where schools bunch enrolment just below the 45-pupil threshold

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Industrial organization and antitrust economics
days.headline_hint: Two Numbers Decide Whether a Merger Is Blocked, and Both Come From a Demand Curve
days.focus: Cournot, Bertrand and Stackelberg with the Lerner–HHI relation; product differentiation (Hotelling, Salop) and the logit demand systems behind merger simulation; entry and market structure (Bresnahan–Reiss thresholds, Sutton's endogenous sunk costs); demand estimation (BLP, Nevo); merger analysis under the 2023 Guidelines with HHI and upward pricing pressure; monopolisation and platforms (US v. Google, Ohio v. American Express); the markup evidence. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can compute HHI, ΔHHI and UPP for a live merger, simulate a Cournot merger's price effect, and read a complaint or an opinion for the economics it turns on. Finance & Markets I (block 1, day 16) already measured structure — HHI as concentration, moats as ROIC-minus-WACC spreads, the five forces with numbers; this lesson is the theory beneath those numbers, cited there and derived here, and it does not redo the industry-analysis method.

Differentiation: Hotelling's beach, Salop's circle and the logit demand curve
Entry and structure: Bresnahan–Reiss thresholds and Sutton's sunk costs
Estimating demand: BLP, Nevo's cereals and the markup a court can believe
Merger review: the 2023 Guidelines, HHI presumptions, upward pricing pressure and diversion
Monopolisation and platforms: US v. Google's two rulings, American Express and the markup debate

Google (D.D.C.): the 5 August 2024 liability opinion's finding of monopoly in general search (about 90% share) and the 2 September 2025 remedies ruling (a ban on exclusive distribution contracts, data-sharing with qualified competitors, no Chrome divestiture), read for the market definition and the foreclosure economics

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Behavioural economics at depth
days.headline_hint: Losses Loom Larger by a Factor of 2.25: Prospect Theory Measured, Not Just Named
days.focus: Cumulative prospect theory with its estimated parameters and probability weighting; Rabin's calibration theorem; reference dependence (Kőszegi–Rabin); present bias in the β–δ model with sophisticates and naifs; mental accounting and the disposition effect; myopic loss aversion and the equity premium; the field evidence (gym memberships, defaults, Save More Tomorrow, tax salience); and the welfare economics of nudges including their effect sizes at scale. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can compute a prospect-theory valuation, calibrate a β–δ agent to observed procrastination, and read a nudge evaluation for what it actually measures. Descriptive throughout — what people are measured to do and what it costs them — and it is the theory and evidence two later lessons assume: the normative side (Savage's axioms, the Allais and Ellsberg paradoxes as challenges to expected utility, Newcomb's problem) belongs to Philosophy (block 5, day 10), and the advisor's practice — risk-tolerance instruments, the behaviour gap, the drawdown conversation — to Wealth Management (block 12, day 2); neither is taught here.
parts: Cumulative prospect theory: the value function, the weighting function and the 1992 parameters
Rabin's calibration: why expected utility cannot explain small-stakes risk aversion
Time: β–δ discounting, sophisticates, naifs and the gym membership that proves it
Reference points and mental accounts: the disposition effect in 10,000 brokerage accounts
Myopic loss aversion and the equity premium: Benartzi–Thaler's one-year horizon
Nudges: defaults, Save More Tomorrow, Opower, and the effect that shrank when scaled
worked_examples: Cumulative prospect theory with Tversky and Kahneman's (1992) parameters (α = β = 0.88, λ = 2.25, γ = 0.61, δ = 0.69): the value of a 50/50 gamble to win $200 or lose $100, against its expected value and against CRRA utility

Rabin's (2000) theorem: an expected-utility maximiser who turns down a 50/50 lose-$100/gain-$110 bet at every wealth level must turn down lose-$1,000/gain-any-amount; the arithmetic of the marginal-utility chain

DellaVigna and Malmendier (2006): members paying over $70 a month attend about 4.3 times, roughly $17 a visit against a $10 pay-per-visit option, and the β–δ parameters that rationalise it; Madrian and Shea's (2001) 401(k) participation rising from 37% to 86% under automatic enrolment

Odean's (1998) proportion of gains realised (0.148) against losses realised (0.098); Thaler and Benartzi's (2004) Save More Tomorrow contribution rate rising from 3.5% to 13.6% over four pay raises; DellaVigna and Linos's (2022) 8.7-point average effect in academic nudge papers against 1.4 points across two government nudge units

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Public economics: optimal taxation and incidence
days.headline_hint: The Top Tax Rate Is a Formula With Two Parameters, and Both Are Measured
days.focus: Tax incidence in partial and general equilibrium (Harberger's corporate tax, the payroll tax, excise pass-through); deadweight loss and the elasticity of taxable income as a sufficient statistic (Feldstein, Chetty); Ramsey commodity taxation and Diamond–Mirrlees production efficiency; Mirrlees's nonlinear income tax and Saez's elasticity formulas for the top rate; capital taxation from Chamley–Judd to Straub–Werning; and the marginal value of public funds as the modern welfare accounting. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can compute the optimal top rate from a Pareto parameter and an ETI, decompose who bears a corporate tax, and read a tax bill for its incidence rather than its statutory target.

Harberger's corporate tax in general equilibrium, and the modern answer from state tax changes
Deadweight loss and the elasticity of taxable income: Feldstein's shortcut and Chetty's caveat
Ramsey and Diamond–Mirrlees: inverse elasticities and why intermediate goods go untaxed
Mirrlees and Saez: the optimal top rate as 1/(1 + a·e)
Capital taxation and the MVPF: Chamley–Judd overturned, and how to rank policies by welfare per dollar

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Market design
days.headline_hint: The Economist as Engineer: Some Markets Have to Be Built Before They Can Clear

Strategy-proofness, the rural hospitals theorem and what the receiving side can still manipulate
The Match: Roth–Peranson's 1998 redesign, couples and the year the algorithm changed
School choice: Boston's mechanism, New York's 2003 redesign and the 30,000 who used to go unassigned
Trading without prices: top trading cycles, kidney exchange and the chains that run through strangers
Designing the exchange itself: frequent batch auctions and the arms race they end

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Growth accounting and Solow/Romer
days.headline_hint: Most of Growth Is the Residual, and the Residual Is Getting Harder to Find
days.focus: The Solow model solved properly (steady state, transition dynamics, the speed-of-convergence formula), the growth-accounting identity applied to the BLS total-factor-productivity data, then Romer's ideas-based growth and Jones's semi-endogenous correction tested against research-effort data. Graduate level: the differential equations are solved, not described. Afterwards the reader can decompose any country's growth into capital deepening, labour and TFP, calibrate a Solow steady state from published shares, and say why 'ideas are getting harder to find' is a claim about an exponent. Growth accounting's factor shares are day 1's producer duality under competitive pricing, and Romer's intermediate-goods sector is day 7's monopolistic competition; both are assumed, not rebuilt.
parts: Log-differentiate the production function and growth becomes an accounting identity
Solow's steady state, and why capital cannot carry growth forever
Transition dynamics: the two-percent convergence speed and what Mankiw, Romer and Weil found
Romer's non-rivalry: ideas as the input that does not run out
Jones's correction and the evidence that ideas are getting harder to find
Fifty years of the American residual: Fernald's series and the 1995–2004 burst

Calibrating the Solow steady state with s = 0.20, δ = 0.05, n + g = 0.02 and α = 1/3: k*, y*, and the convergence speed λ = (1 − α)(n + g + δ) ≈ 2% a year, then checking the implied half-life against Barro and Sala-i-Martin's cross-state estimates
China, Japan and the US 1990–2019 from Penn World Table 10.01 (rgdpo, rnna, emp, hc): how much of each country's growth is capital deepening, how much human capital, how much TFP

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Consumption and investment theory
days.headline_hint: The Cheque Arrives: What the Euler Equation Said Would Happen, and What Did
days.focus: Permanent-income and life-cycle consumption derived from the intertemporal problem, Hall's random-walk result and its rejection, precautionary and buffer-stock saving, liquidity constraints and the measured marginal propensity to consume out of stimulus payments; then investment: the Hall–Jorgenson user cost, Tobin's q with Hayashi's equivalence, and adjustment costs. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can write and estimate a consumption Euler equation on FRED data, compute a user cost of capital from a bond yield and a tax code, and read Tobin's q off the Financial Accounts. The intertemporal problem is day 1's expenditure-minimisation problem with dates as goods, so the Euler equation arrives as a first-order condition the reader has already met.

Hall's random walk: consumption should be unforecastable, and the excess-sensitivity puzzle says it is not
Precautionary saving, buffer stocks and the hand-to-mouth: why marginal propensities are heterogeneous
Investment I: the user cost of capital, and what a tax bill does to it
Investment II: Tobin's q, Hayashi's theorem and adjustment costs
The equity premium as a consumption fact: Mehra–Prescott's puzzle in the Euler equation's own terms

Tobin's q for US nonfinancial corporations from the Fed's Financial Accounts (Z.1 table B.103: market value of equity over net worth at replacement cost) and the Mehra–Prescott calculation with consumption growth mean 1.8%, s.d. 3.6% and a 6.2% equity premium

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: The New Keynesian model and Phillips-curve dynamics
days.headline_hint: Three Equations Run the Fed's Model, and One of Them Has a Slope Nobody Can Agree On
days.focus: The canonical three-equation New Keynesian model built from Calvo pricing: the dynamic IS curve, the New Keynesian Phillips curve with its derived slope κ, and the interest-rate rule; determinacy via Blanchard–Kahn and the Taylor principle; the empirical Phillips curve from Phillips's 1958 scatter to the 2021–23 nonlinearity. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can solve the log-linearised model with Galí's calibration, compute impulse responses to a policy shock, and read a Phillips-curve slope estimate for what it identifies. Calvo's price-setters are day 7's monopolistic competitors facing Dixit–Stiglitz demand of elasticity ε, and the IS curve is day 12's Euler equation written in gaps; the model is assembled from parts already built.
parts: Households and the dynamic IS curve: the Euler equation rewritten in gaps
Calvo pricing and the New Keynesian Phillips curve: deriving κ from θ, β and the labour supply
Closing the model with a rule: Blanchard–Kahn, determinacy and the Taylor principle
A monetary shock through the model: solving the impulse responses with Galí's numbers
The empirical Phillips curve: from Phillips's 1958 scatter to Hazell et al.'s regional identification
The 2021–23 surge and the return of the nonlinear curve: Benigno–Eggertsson's kink

Checking determinacy: the eigenvalues of the system at φ_π = 0.8 (Clarida–Galí–Gertler's pre-Volcker estimate) versus 2.15 (post-Volcker), and why the first admits sunspot equilibria

The Phillips scatter on FRED: core PCE inflation (PCEPILFE) against unemployment (UNRATE) and against the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio (JTSJOL/UNEMPLOY), 2000–2019 versus 2021–2024, reproducing the flat-then-steep shape Benigno and Eggertsson (2023) document
Hazell, Herreño, Nakamura and Steinsson's (2022) state-level slope estimate and the unemployment cost of a one-point disinflation it implies

Hazell, Herreño, Nakamura and Steinsson (2022) QJE; Benigno and Eggertsson (2023) NBER WP 31197; McLeay and Tenreyro (2020) NBER Macroeconomics Annual

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Monetary policy rules and transmission
days.headline_hint: A Rule Written in 1993 Still Tells You Where the Funds Rate Should Be, If You Know r-star
days.focus: Taylor rules as the Fed itself reports them, the estimation of r-star (Holston–Laubach–Williams) and its uncertainty, the transmission mechanism through the term structure, credit and the exchange rate with identified evidence (Romer–Romer, Gertler–Karadi), and the balance sheet: QE's term-premium channel, QT, the ample-reserves floor system and the Fed's own income. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can compute the Monetary Policy Report's rule prescriptions from FRED for any quarter, read the H.4.1, and say which channel a given policy move works through. The identification — Romer–Romer narratives, the thirty-minute window — is day 6's toolkit in its macro form.
parts: Taylor's rule and its descendants in the Monetary Policy Report
r-star: the Holston–Laubach–Williams filter, its standard error and why the Fed steers by a star it cannot see
Identifying the effect of a rate change: Romer–Romer narratives and the thirty-minute window
Transmission: the term structure, mortgage rates, bank lending and the dollar
The balance sheet: how QE moves the term premium, what QT undoes and where the losses sit
Operating in an ample-reserves regime: IORB, ON RRP and the floor
worked_examples: Computing the Taylor (1993), balanced-approach and first-difference prescriptions from FRED for a named recent quarter: core PCE inflation (PCEPILFE), the CBO output gap (GDPC1 against GDPPOT) and the New York Fed's current HLW r-star estimate, against the actual effective funds rate (DFF)

Gertler and Karadi's (2015) high-frequency surprise: the change in the fed funds futures price in the thirty minutes around a named FOMC statement, and the same-day response of the 2-year and 10-year yields (DGS2, DGS10)

QE's term-premium effect: the Krishnamurthy–Vissing-Jorgensen and Gagnon et al. estimates (roughly 30–100 basis points on the 10-year for the first programme) against the ACM term-premium series around the March 2009 and March 2020 announcements

The Fed's balance sheet from the H.4.1: total assets (WALCL), reserves (WRESBAL), the ON RRP facility (RRPONTSYD) and the deferred asset from suspended Treasury remittances, and what the 2022 runoff caps ($60bn Treasuries, $35bn MBS a month) did to the asset side by 2024
sources: Taylor (1993) Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series; Federal Reserve Board, Monetary Policy Report, the 'Monetary policy rules' box
Holston, Laubach and Williams (2017) Journal of International Economics; Federal Reserve Bank of New York, r-star estimates

Bernanke (2020) AER Presidential Address, 'The New Tools of Monetary Policy'; Gertler and Karadi (2015) AEJ: Macroeconomics; Romer and Romer (2004) AER; Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen (2011) BPEA
FOMC, 'Plans for Reducing the Size of the Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet' (May 2022) and subsequent statements; Federal Reserve H.4.1 statistical release

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Fiscal policy and debt dynamics
days.headline_hint: Debt Is Sustainable Right Up Until r Crosses g
days.focus: The government budget constraint and the law of motion for debt-to-GDP, the primary balance that stabilises it, Blanchard's r < g argument and its critics, Ricardian equivalence and where it fails, fiscal multipliers from cross-sectional and narrative evidence, the fiscal theory of the price level, and market discipline as seen in the 2022 gilt episode. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can run the CBO's long-term arithmetic himself, state the stabilising primary balance for any r, g and b, and read a multiplier estimate for its identification.
parts: The law of motion: Δb = (r − g)/(1 + g) · b − pb, and everything it hides
Blanchard's case: when r < g the debt rolls over, and when it does not
Ricardian equivalence, Barro's theorem and the households who do not behave that way
Multipliers: Nakamura–Steinsson's states, Ramey's narratives and the state-dependence debate
The fiscal theory of the price level: debt as a claim on surpluses
When the market decides: the gilt crisis of September 2022 and what sustainability looks like in a price
worked_examples: Rebuilding the CBO Long-Term Budget Outlook's debt path from its own assumptions (average interest rate on debt, nominal GDP growth, primary deficit) with FRED GFDEGDQ188S as the starting point, and computing the primary surplus needed to hold debt at its current ratio
Federal interest payments as a share of GDP (FRED A091RC1Q027SBEA over GDP) 1990–present, and the Furman–Summers real-interest test applied to the current path

Nakamura and Steinsson's (2014) open-economy relative multiplier of about 1.5 from state military procurement, against Ramey's (2019) survey range of roughly 0.6–1.0 for aggregate multipliers, and why the two answer different questions

The 23 September 2022 UK mini-budget: the 30-year gilt yield's move over four trading days, the LDI margin calls, and the Bank of England's 28 September purchase programme — r rising faster than any g could
sources: Blanchard (2019) AER Presidential Address, 'Public Debt and Low Interest Rates'; Furman and Summers (2020), 'A Reconsideration of Fiscal Policy in the Era of Low Interest Rates'; Mian, Straub and Sufi (2022) 'A Goldilocks Theory of Fiscal Deficits'
Ramey (2019) JEP; Nakamura and Steinsson (2014) AER; Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012) AEJ: Economic Policy; Barro (1974) JPE
Cochrane, The Fiscal Theory of the Price Level (Princeton, 2023), chs. 1–3
CBO, The Long-Term Budget Outlook (latest edition); Bank of England, Financial Stability Report, December 2022, on the LDI episode

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: The open economy
days.headline_hint: You May Have Any Two: The Trilemma the Swiss Franc Proved in Fifteen Minutes
days.focus: Mundell–Fleming with perfect capital mobility under fixed and floating rates, the policy trilemma, Dornbusch overshooting with sticky prices, covered and uncovered interest parity and the carry-trade evidence against UIP, exchange-rate regime classification, capital flows, sudden stops and Rey's global financial cycle. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can solve for the overshooting path, test UIP on FRED exchange-rate data, and classify a country's de facto regime and the policy options it leaves.
parts: Mundell–Fleming: fiscal and monetary policy under fixed and floating rates
The trilemma as a theorem, and the SNB's 15 January 2015 as its proof
Dornbusch overshooting: sticky prices make the exchange rate jump past its destination
Interest parity: covered holds, uncovered does not, and the carry trade lives in the gap
Regimes de jure and de facto: Ilzetzki, Reinhart and Rogoff's classification and the dollar's anchor
Capital flows, sudden stops and the global financial cycle: dilemma, not trilemma
worked_examples: Dornbusch overshooting for a 1% permanent money-supply increase with a money-demand semi-elasticity of 0.5 and a price-adjustment speed of 0.25 a quarter: the initial jump, the overshoot and the return path

A Fama regression for the yen: monthly changes in DEXJPUS on the 3-month US–Japan rate differential, 1990–2024, the negative slope, and the August 2024 unwind (the Bank of Japan's 31 July hike, the Nikkei's 12.4% fall on 5 August)

The SNB's removal of the 1.20 EUR/CHF floor on 15 January 2015: the intraday move, a balance sheet that had grown to roughly four-fifths of Swiss GDP defending it, and the trilemma written as a balance-sheet constraint
Hong Kong's 7.75–7.85 convertibility band from the HKMA's monthly statistics: how the aggregate balance moves when the peg is defended, and what that does to HIBOR
sources: Obstfeld and Rogoff, Foundations of International Macroeconomics (MIT Press, 1996), chs. 8–9
Mundell (1963) Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science; Fleming (1962) IMF Staff Papers; Dornbusch (1976) JPE; Fama (1984) JME
Ilzetzki, Reinhart and Rogoff (2019) QJE; Rey (2013) Jackson Hole, 'Dilemma not Trilemma'; Calvo (1998) Journal of Applied Economics; Gopinath et al. (2020) AER
IMF, Annual Report on Exchange Arrangements and Exchange Restrictions; Swiss National Bank press release of 15 January 2015

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Labour markets: search, matching and the Beveridge curve
days.headline_hint: Unemployment Is a Queue, and the Beveridge Curve Measures How Fast It Moves
days.focus: The Diamond–Mortensen–Pissarides model built from the matching function, the value equations for jobs and workers, Nash-bargained wages, free entry and the equilibrium tightness; the Hosios efficiency condition; Shimer's volatility puzzle; the Beveridge curve in JOLTS data and Michaillat–Saez's u* = √(uv). Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can solve the DMP steady state, estimate a matching-function elasticity from JOLTS, and compute the full-employment unemployment rate from the month's release.
parts: The matching function: Cobb–Douglas in unemployed and vacancies, and what the elasticity measures
Bellman equations for jobs and workers, and the wage that Nash bargaining sets
Free entry closes the model: solving for tightness, unemployment and vacancies
Hosios and efficiency: when the market's tightness is the right one, and u* = √(uv)
Shimer's puzzle: productivity shocks are too small for the unemployment they must explain
The Beveridge curve 2001–2024: shifts, loops and the soft-landing argument
worked_examples: Estimating the matching-function elasticity from JOLTS: log hires (JTSHIL) on log job openings (JTSJOL) and log unemployed (UNEMPLOY), 2001–2024, compared with Petrongolo and Pissarides's survey range of 0.5–0.7
Michaillat–Saez's full-employment rate for named months: April 2022 (u = 3.6%, v ≈ 7.0%, so u* ≈ 5.0%) against August 2024 (u = 4.2%, v = 4.6%, so u* = 4.4%), and the 1930–2024 average of 4.1%

The DMP steady state with Shimer's (2005) calibration (monthly separation rate 0.034, job-finding rate 0.45, matching elasticity 0.72, bargaining power 0.72, unemployment income 0.4 of productivity): solving for θ and the unemployment rate, then the elasticity of θ to productivity that produces the puzzle
Blanchard, Domash and Summers (2022) and Figura and Waller (2022) on the same JOLTS data: two readings of the 2022 Beveridge curve and what each implied for the unemployment cost of disinflation
sources: Pissarides, Equilibrium Unemployment Theory, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2000), chs. 1–2
Mortensen and Pissarides (1994) REStud; Hosios (1990) REStud; Shimer (2005) AER; Hagedorn and Manovskii (2008) AER; Petrongolo and Pissarides (2001) JEL
Michaillat and Saez (2024) BPEA Fall, 'u* = √uv: The Full-Employment Rate of Unemployment in the United States'; Blanchard, Domash and Summers (2022) PIIE WP 22-7; Figura and Waller (2022) FEDS Notes
BLS, Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) and the Employment Situation release

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Financial frictions and crises
days.headline_hint: Forty-Two Billion Dollars Left in a Day, and a 1983 Paper Had Already Written the Script
days.focus: Bank runs as multiple equilibria in Diamond–Dybvig, deposit insurance and its limits; the financial accelerator (Bernanke–Gertler–Gilchrist) and collateral constraints (Kiyotaki–Moore) as amplifiers; Minsky's hedge, speculative and Ponzi taxonomy formalised; leverage cycles and the run on repo; the credit-boom predictor in 150 years of data; Silicon Valley Bank as the worked case. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can compute an external finance premium, run the Kiyotaki–Moore amplification arithmetic, and read a bank's uninsured-deposit and unrealised-loss figures as run risk.
parts: Diamond–Dybvig: why a solvent bank can fail, and what deposit insurance buys
The external finance premium: the financial accelerator's mechanism and the spread that measures it
Kiyotaki–Moore: collateral, land prices and the multiplier on a small shock
Minsky formalised: hedge, speculative and Ponzi units, and the moment named after him
Leverage cycles and the run on repo: Adrian–Shin and Gorton–Metrick on 2007–08
Silicon Valley Bank, March 2023: duration, uninsured deposits and a run at the speed of a phone
worked_examples: Diamond–Dybvig with SVB's balance sheet (SVB Financial Group Form 10-K, FY2022): uninsured deposits as reported, held-to-maturity securities at amortised cost versus fair value, the unrealised loss against tangible equity, and the Fed's Barr review figures of $42bn withdrawn on 9 March 2023 with about $100bn queued for 10 March

Kiyotaki–Moore amplification: a two-period calibration with a collateral constraint at a loan-to-value of 0.8 and a 1% productivity shock, computing the fall in land prices and the round-by-round contraction in borrowing
The Gilchrist–Zakrajšek excess bond premium (the Federal Reserve's monthly series) at its October 2008 and March 2020 peaks, and its forecasting power for industrial production at twelve months

Schularick and Taylor's (2012) crisis predictor on the Jordà–Schularick–Taylor Macrohistory Database: five-year real credit growth as a predictor of banking crises across 17 countries, 1870–2008, with the estimated marginal effects
sources: Diamond and Dybvig (1983) JPE; Bernanke, Gertler and Gilchrist (1999) Handbook of Macroeconomics; Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) JPE
Minsky, Stabilizing an Unstable Economy (Yale, 1986); Minsky (1992) Levy Economics Institute WP 74, 'The Financial Instability Hypothesis'
Gorton and Metrick (2012) JFE; Adrian and Shin (2010) Journal of Financial Intermediation; Schularick and Taylor (2012) AER; Gilchrist and Zakrajšek (2012) AER
Federal Reserve Board, 'Review of the Federal Reserve's Supervision and Regulation of Silicon Valley Bank' (28 April 2023); SVB Financial Group Form 10-K for FY2022

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Inflation dynamics and expectations
days.headline_hint: Inflation Is What People Expect It to Be, Until the Day It Isn't
days.focus: The expectations-augmented Phillips curve from Friedman and Phelps, rational expectations and the Lucas critique, Sargent's regime-change endings of hyperinflations, sticky-information and noisy-information models with the Coibion–Gorodnichenko test on survey data, the measurement of expectations (surveys, breakevens), anchoring and the Fed's 2020 and 2025 frameworks, and the Bernanke–Blanchard decomposition of 2021–23. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can run the information-rigidity regression on SPF data, compute a forward breakeven, and decompose an inflation episode into its shocks.
parts: Friedman, Phelps and the natural rate: why the 1960s trade-off could not last
Rational expectations and the Lucas critique: the model's coefficients are not policy-invariant
Sargent's four endings: when a regime change stops an inflation without a recession
Sticky and noisy information: Mankiw–Reis, and the Coibion–Gorodnichenko test on the forecasters
Measuring expectations: Michigan, the SCE, the SPF and what a breakeven actually prices
Anchoring tested: 2021–23 by the Bernanke–Blanchard decomposition, and the framework the Fed rewrote in 2025
worked_examples: The Coibion–Gorodnichenko (2015) regression on Philadelphia Fed SPF inflation forecasts: ex-post forecast errors on forecast revisions, the coefficient of roughly 1.2 and the implied information rigidity λ ≈ 0.55 (an information update every six to seven months on average)

Computing the 5-year, 5-year-forward breakeven from FRED T5YIE and T10YIE and comparing with T5YIFR, then splitting a breakeven into expected inflation and an inflation risk premium with the Cleveland Fed model
Bernanke and Blanchard (2023): the contributions of energy, food, shortages and labour-market tightness (v/u) to quarterly core inflation 2020Q1–2023Q2, and why the labour-market share rises late

Ball's (1994) sacrifice ratio for the Volcker disinflation of 1980–83 against Sargent's near-zero-cost regime changes (Austria 1922, Germany 1923, Hungary 1924, Poland 1924), and the credibility difference that separates them
sources: Friedman (1968) AER; Phelps (1967) Economica; Lucas (1976) Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series; Sargent (1982) in Hall (ed.), Inflation: Causes and Effects
Mankiw and Reis (2002) QJE; Coibion and Gorodnichenko (2015) AER; Rudd (2021) FEDS 2021-062; Werning (2022) NBER WP 30260
Bernanke and Blanchard (2023) Brookings, 'What Caused the US Pandemic-Era Inflation?'; Ball (1994) in Mankiw (ed.), Monetary Policy
FOMC, Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy (August 2020; as revised 22 August 2025); Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, Survey of Professional Forecasters

days.subject: Economics
days.topic: Business-cycle measurement and nowcasting
days.headline_hint: The Recession Nobody Called, and the Rule That Called One Anyway
days.focus: How cycles are dated (the NBER committee), detrended (the HP filter versus Hamilton's regression filter) and summarised (dynamic factor models such as the CFNAI); the real-time data problem and ALFRED vintages; bridge-equation and factor-model nowcasts (GDPNow, the New York Fed Staff Nowcast); recession-probability models (the Estrella–Mishkin probit, the Sahm rule); Okun's law; GDP versus GDI. Practitioner depth on graduate tools. Afterwards the reader can reproduce a Sahm-rule reading, build a bridge-equation nowcast from the month's releases, and say what a nowcast's error bands mean before the advance estimate lands. The Kalman recursion beneath the factor models is stated and applied here, not derived: Mathematics (block 6) owns state-space theory and derives the filter as recursive Bayes.
parts: What a recession is: Burns–Mitchell, the NBER committee and the 2022 two-quarters argument
Trend and cycle: the HP filter's end-point problem and Hamilton's alternative
One factor for eighty-five series: Stock–Watson, the CFNAI and the state-space recursion that extracts it
Real-time data: vintages, revisions and why a backtest on today's FRED is leakage
Nowcasting GDP: bridge equations, GDPNow's thirteen subcomponents and the Staff Nowcast
Calling a turn: the yield-curve probit, the Sahm rule's 2024 false positive and Okun's law
worked_examples: The Sahm rule in real time: July 2024's three-month average unemployment rate of 4.13% against the prior twelve months' low of 3.6%, a reading of 0.53 on the 2 August 2024 jobs report, and what the following twelve months of UNRATE and the NBER's silence say about the rule's precision
HP filter (λ = 1,600) versus Hamilton's (2018) two-year-ahead regression filter on FRED GDPC1, showing how the HP trend for 2018–19 is revised as the 2020–21 observations arrive
An Estrella–Mishkin probit on FRED T10Y3M: the estimated coefficients and the twelve-month-ahead probability the spread assigned to the 2001, 2008 and 2020 recessions, and to 2023

A three-variable bridge-equation nowcast of a named quarter's real GDP from monthly retail sales (RSXFS), industrial production (INDPRO) and payrolls (PAYEMS), compared with the Atlanta Fed GDPNow print and the BEA advance estimate as archived in ALFRED
sources: Stock and Watson (1989) NBER Macroeconomics Annual and (2002) JBES; Giannone, Reichlin and Small (2008) JME; Bok, Caratelli, Giannone, Sbordone and Tambalotti (2018) Annual Review of Economics
Hamilton (2018) REStat, 'Why You Should Never Use the Hodrick-Prescott Filter'; Estrella and Mishkin (1998) REStat; Sahm (2019) in Recession Ready (The Hamilton Project)
NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee, 'Business Cycle Dating Procedure: Frequently Asked Questions'; Croushore and Stark (2001) Journal of Econometrics
Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, GDPNow methodology note; Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, CFNAI technical documentation; ALFRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Lagrangian mechanics, constraints and Noether's theorem
days.headline_hint: Every conservation law is a symmetry in disguise, and the proof fits on a page
days.focus: Day 101 of year one stated L = T − V and the Euler–Lagrange equations; today derives them from the calculus of variations, handles constraints with Lagrange multipliers so the constraint forces come back out, builds the velocity-dependent Lagrangian for a charge in a field, proves Noether's theorem for continuous symmetries, and sets up small oscillations as a generalised eigenvalue problem. Graduate level; afterwards the reader can write the Lagrangian of any holonomic system, extract its conserved quantities by inspection, and compute normal-mode frequencies.
parts: The path that makes the action stationary: the calculus of variations and the brachistochrone
Constraints are forces you have not been told about: Lagrange multipliers and the tension recovered
Every symmetry buys a conservation law: Noether's theorem proved, and Kepler's hidden vector
The charged particle: a velocity-dependent potential and the Lorentz force from L = ½mv² − qφ + qv·A
Small oscillations: the normal-mode eigenproblem and the three frequencies of carbon dioxide
worked_examples: The brachistochrone between two points 1 m apart and 1 m down: the cycloid's descent time against the straight line's, computed with g = 9.81 m/s²

Mercury's orbit as the Kepler Lagrangian's solution: a = 57.909 million km, e = 0.2056, period 87.969 d, the specific angular momentum and the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector whose conservation fixes the perihelion
The LHC dipole as the Lorentz-force Lagrangian: a 7 TeV proton in 8.33 T gives ρ = p/(qB) = 2,804 m, the machine's actual bending radius

Normal modes of the linear CO₂ molecule: the predicted ratio of asymmetric to symmetric stretch, √(1 + 2m_O/m_C) = 1.915, against the NIST-tabulated 2,349 cm⁻¹ and ≈1,333 cm⁻¹ (the latter split by Fermi resonance into 1,285 and 1,388 cm⁻¹)
sources: Goldstein, Poole & Safko, Classical Mechanics, 3rd ed. (2002), ch. 1–2, 6, 13
Landau & Lifshitz, Mechanics, 3rd ed. (1976), §§1–10, 23–24
Noether, 'Invariante Variationsprobleme', Nachr. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen (1918), pp. 235–257
NIST Chemistry WebBook, vibrational constants of CO₂

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Hamiltonian mechanics, canonical transformations and Hamilton–Jacobi
days.headline_hint: Change coordinates in phase space and Mercury's perihelion starts to drift before Einstein is even mentioned
days.focus: The Legendre transform to phase space, Poisson brackets as the algebra beneath the equations, canonical transformations and generating functions, Liouville's theorem, the Hamilton–Jacobi equation, action-angle variables and adiabatic invariants, and canonical perturbation theory applied to the Solar System. Graduate level; afterwards the reader can move between Lagrangian and Hamiltonian forms freely, recognise the Kepler problem's actions as orbital elements, and compute a secular perturbation by averaging over the fast angle.
parts: From velocity to momentum: the Legendre transform, Hamilton's equations and the pendulum's separatrix
Poisson brackets are the algebra beneath the equations
Changing coordinates without breaking the equations: generating functions, the symplectic condition and Liouville's theorem
Hamilton–Jacobi: mechanics as wave fronts, and the analogy Schrödinger followed
Action-angle variables and the adiabatic invariant: Kepler's actions are the Delaunay elements
Perturbation theory in phase space: why Mercury's perihelion drifts 532 arcseconds a century
worked_examples: The plane pendulum, 1 m long: the separatrix energy 2mgl, and the period at 90° amplitude from the complete elliptic integral, 1.18 times the small-angle period

Liouville's theorem at the LHC: normalised emittance is conserved so geometric emittance shrinks by βγ, a factor of 14.4 between injection at 450 GeV and 6.5 TeV, which is why the beam gets smaller as it gets faster
The harmonic oscillator taken to action-angle variables by the generating function F₁ = ½mωq² cot Q, then Kepler's Delaunay actions and the mean motion n = 2π/87.969 d for Mercury

Jupiter's secular effect on Mercury's perihelion in the ring approximation: (3/4) n (m_J/M_☉)(a/a_J)³ with m_J/M_☉ = 1/1047.35 and a/a_J = 0.07439 gives ≈159″/century against Clemence's 1947 tabulated ≈154″; Venus's larger α = 0.535 needs the Laplace-coefficient series, and the planetary total of 532″ leaves the 43″ residual for day 8
sources: Goldstein, Poole & Safko, Classical Mechanics, 3rd ed. (2002), ch. 8–10, 12
Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (1989), ch. 8–10
Murray & Dermott, Solar System Dynamics (1999), ch. 6–7
Clemence, 'The relativity effect in planetary motions', Rev. Mod. Phys. 19, 361 (1947)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Rigid-body dynamics: the inertia tensor, Euler's equations and the heavy top
days.headline_hint: The Earth wobbles on a 433-day cycle that Euler predicted at 305, and the gap is the planet confessing it is not rigid
days.focus: Angular velocity as a vector, the inertia tensor and its principal axes, Euler's equations in the body frame, torque-free motion of symmetric and asymmetric tops with the intermediate-axis theorem and Poinsot's construction, Euler angles and the heavy symmetric top, energy dissipation and the major-axis rule for spinning spacecraft, and the Earth treated as a top. Graduate level; afterwards the reader can compute an inertia tensor, predict free precession and nutation rates, and explain why a satellite spun about its long axis will flip.
parts: Angular velocity is a vector, and the inertia tensor is why you need one
Euler's equations: rotation seen from the body
Tumbling: the torque-free asymmetric top, the intermediate-axis theorem and the Dzhanibekov handle
The heavy top: precession, nutation and why it does not fall
Why spinning satellites flip: energy sinks and the major-axis rule, Explorer 1 in 1958
The Earth as a top: the Chandler wobble and the 26,000-year precession of the equinoxes
worked_examples: Earth's principal moments from IERS Conventions (2010): C = 8.0345 × 10³⁷ kg m², dynamical ellipticity H = (C − A)/C = 3.2737 × 10⁻³, giving Euler's free-precession period A/(C − A) ≈ 305 days against the observed 433-day Chandler wobble

Luni-solar precession from the heavy-top formula: the solar term (3/2)(n_☉²/ω) H cos ε with n_☉ = 1.991 × 10⁻⁷ rad/s, ω = 7.292 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s and ε = 23.44° gives ≈15.9″/yr; the Moon adds about 2.2 times that, and the total ≈50.3″/yr is the 25,800-year cycle

Explorer 1 (launched 31 January 1958): spun at roughly 750 rpm about its long, minimum-inertia axis, its four flexible whip antennas dissipated energy and within hours it was in a flat spin about the maximum-inertia axis — the case that wrote the major-axis rule into spacecraft design
The torque-free symmetric top: body-frame precession rate Ω = (I₃ − I₁)ω₃/I₁ for a spin-stabilised cylinder, worked with the moment ratio of a thin disc versus a long rod
sources: Goldstein, Poole & Safko, Classical Mechanics, 3rd ed. (2002), ch. 4–5
Landau & Lifshitz, Mechanics, 3rd ed. (1976), ch. VI
Hughes, Spacecraft Attitude Dynamics (1986; Dover 2004), ch. 4–5
IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, ch. 1 and 5

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Continuum mechanics: the stress tensor, Hooke's law and the Navier–Stokes equations
days.headline_hint: Two tensors, one equation of motion, and the reason a shear wave stops dead at the core of the Earth
days.focus: One derivation chain, carried from end to end: the strain tensor, Cauchy's proof that stress is a tensor and the equation of motion for any continuum; then Hooke's law in three dimensions with the Lamé constants, the elastic wave equation and its two speeds, and the pressurised cylinder as the one static elastic problem, solved thin-walled and thick-walled (Lamé) against the pipeline design rule in 49 CFR 192.105; then the Newtonian fluid's constitutive law, the Navier–Stokes equations derived from the same equation of motion, and Poiseuille flow as the one exact solution, checked against Poiseuille's own 1846 fourth-power law. Turbulence, plasticity and non-Newtonian fluids are explicitly out of scope; beams and buckling belong to the Rocketry block's structures lesson and compressible flow to its nozzle lesson. Graduate level; day 51 of year one gave Bernoulli and the Reynolds number, and this lesson gives the equations they come from. Afterwards the reader can compute wave speeds from moduli, the stress in a pressure vessel, and a laminar flow profile from first principles.
parts: Strain and stress: two tensors, and Cauchy's theorem that stress is one
The equation of motion for a continuum, and Hooke's law in three dimensions: the Lamé constants and the two speeds of sound in a solid
The pressurised cylinder: thin-wall hoop stress, Lamé's thick-wall solution and the pipeline rule
Navier–Stokes: Newton's second law for a fluid parcel, derived from the same stress tensor
Poiseuille flow: the one exact solution, and the fourth power Poiseuille measured in 1846
