worked_examples: Steel with E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.29, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³: λ = 107 GPa, μ = 77.5 GPa, v_P = √((λ + 2μ)/ρ) = 5.78 km/s, v_S = √(μ/ρ) = 3.14 km/s; then the Preliminary Reference Earth Model (Dziewonski & Anderson 1981) at the core–mantle boundary, 2,891 km down, where v_P falls from 13.72 to 8.06 km/s and v_S from 7.26 km/s to zero — μ = 0, the outer core is liquid, and the S-wave shadow zone from 103° to 142° is the observation

A 36-inch API 5L X70 gas pipeline with 0.75-inch wall in a Class 1 location: 49 CFR 192.105's P = (2St/D) × F × E × T with S = 70,000 psi, F = 0.72, E = T = 1 gives a design pressure of 2,100 psi (14.5 MPa); Lamé's thick-wall solution puts the peak hoop stress at p(r_o² + r_i²)/(r_o² − r_i²) = 23.5p against Barlow's thin-wall D/2t = 24p — the regulation's formula is the thin-wall limit, conservative by 2%

Water at 20 °C (η = 1.00 mPa s) through a 1 mm-bore, 1 m glass capillary under 1 kPa: Q = πr⁴Δp/(8ηL) = 24.5 μL/s, mean speed 3.1 cm/s, Re = 31 — laminar, as the formula requires; Poiseuille's 1846 memoir found the same Q ∝ D⁴ in tubes from 0.015 to 0.6 mm bore (Sutera & Skalak 1993), fourteen years before Hagenbach derived it from Navier–Stokes
sources: Landau & Lifshitz, Theory of Elasticity, 3rd ed. (1986), ch. I–III
Landau & Lifshitz, Fluid Mechanics, 2nd ed. (1987), ch. I–II
Dziewonski & Anderson, 'Preliminary reference Earth model', Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25, 297 (1981)
Sutera & Skalak, 'The History of Poiseuille's Law', Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech. 25, 1 (1993)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Hamiltonian chaos: the driven pendulum, KAM tori, the three-body problem and Hyperion's tumbling
days.headline_hint: A potato-shaped moon of Saturn cannot decide which way is up, and Poincaré's 1890 pictures of the three-body problem say it never will
days.focus: Where day 2's action-angle tori stop existing. Integrable motion as tori in phase space and Poincaré's surface of section as the instrument for seeing them; the periodically driven pendulum reduced to the standard map, with Chirikov's resonance-overlap estimate for when its stochastic layers merge; the KAM theorem stated (Kolmogorov, Arnold, Moser) with the golden-mean torus as the last to break and Greene's residue criterion that finds the breaking point to four digits; the three-body problem from Poincaré's homoclinic tangle to the Hénon–Heiles sections that fill with chaos as the energy rises; chaos in the real Solar System — Wisdom's 3:1 Kirkwood gap and the five-million-year Lyapunov horizon of the planets; and, built on day 3's rigid body, the spin–orbit problem that makes Hyperion tumble. The Mathematics block later owns the general theory of dynamical systems (existence and uniqueness, linearisation, Lyapunov functions, bifurcations); this lesson owns the Hamiltonian phenomenology and uses only the Lyapunov exponent as its measure. Graduate level (Lichtenberg & Lieberman; Ott ch. 7); afterwards the reader can draw a surface of section, estimate a chaos threshold by resonance overlap, and say what a Lyapunov time licenses and forbids for an ephemeris.
parts: Tori and sections: what integrable motion looks like in phase space, and Poincaré's way of looking
The driven pendulum and the standard map: resonance overlap and the stochastic layer around a separatrix
KAM: which tori survive a perturbation, the golden mean as the toughest, and Greene's 0.9716
The three-body problem: Poincaré's tangle, Hénon–Heiles and the sections that fill with chaos
Chaos in the Solar System: the 3:1 Kirkwood gap and the five-million-year horizon
Hyperion: a spin–orbit problem with no stable answer
worked_examples: The standard map p′ = p + K sin θ, θ′ = θ + p′: Chirikov's simple overlap of the two primary resonances predicts global chaos at K = π²/4 ≈ 2.47, the two-thirds rule with the next harmonics brings it to K ≈ 1, and Greene's residue method (1979) gives the last torus — golden-mean winding — breaking at K_c = 0.9716; the kicked rotor and a particle in a travelling wave are the same map

Hénon–Heiles (1964), H = ½(p_x² + p_y²) + ½(x² + y²) + x²y − y³/3: at E = 1/12 the surface of section is all closed curves, at E = 1/8 roughly half its area is chaotic, and at the escape energy E = 1/6 almost all of it is — one Hamiltonian at three energies

Wisdom (1983) at the 3:1 resonance with Jupiter, a = 2.50 AU: an asteroid sits at e < 0.1 for a hundred thousand years and then, in a burst of ten thousand, reaches e ≈ 0.35 and crosses the orbit of Mars; the chaotic zone's width matches the observed gap, and Laskar (1989) and Sussman & Wisdom (1992) give the Solar System a Lyapunov time of about 5 million years — an ephemeris 100 million years out is not a prediction

Hyperion: about 360 × 266 × 205 km, orbital period 21.28 d, e ≈ 0.10, asphericity ω₀ = √(3(B − A)/C) ≈ 0.89 (Wisdom, Peale & Mignard 1984): the synchronous state sits inside a chaotic zone with a Lyapunov time of a few tens of days, so the 13-day spin Voyager 2 reported (Thomas et al. 1984) was a snapshot rather than a period, and Klavetter's 1987 photometry (Astron. J. 97, 570; 98, 1855) found no period at all
sources: Lichtenberg & Lieberman, Regular and Chaotic Dynamics, 2nd ed. (1992), ch. 3–4
Ott, Chaos in Dynamical Systems, 2nd ed. (2002), ch. 7
Wisdom, Peale & Mignard, 'The chaotic rotation of Hyperion', Icarus 58, 137 (1984)
Wisdom, 'Urey Prize Lecture: Chaotic dynamics in the Solar System', Icarus 72, 241 (1987)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Electrodynamics in full: potentials, gauge, retarded fields and radiation
days.headline_hint: Bend an electron at LEP and it pays 3.4 GeV a lap in light; the bill is written in the Liénard–Wiechert potentials
days.focus: Day 85 of year one produced light from Maxwell's four equations; today solves them for any source: scalar and vector potentials and the freedom to choose a gauge (Coulomb and Lorenz), Poynting's theorem and the Maxwell stress tensor with radiation pressure, the retarded Green's function of the wave equation derived in the lesson — the Mathematics block's PDE and Fourier lessons come later, so the machinery is carried here — the retarded potentials and Jefimenko's equations, the Liénard–Wiechert potentials and the velocity and acceleration fields of a moving charge, Larmor's formula and dipole radiation with the half-wave antenna, and synchrotron radiation as the sustained worked example at LEP, the LHC and the Crab Nebula. Guided waves, waveguides and cavities are out of scope. Graduate level (Griffiths ch. 8, 10–11; Jackson ch. 6, 9, 14); afterwards the reader can compute the field of any prescribed source and the power an accelerating charge radiates, and read a synchrotron spectrum.
parts: Potentials and the freedom to choose a gauge: Coulomb, Lorenz and the two wave equations
Energy and momentum live in the field: Poynting's theorem, the stress tensor and the push of sunlight
Retarded time: the Green's function of the wave equation, carried here, and what the field knows about a charge that moved
The moving charge: Liénard–Wiechert, the velocity field and the acceleration field that falls off as 1/r
Radiation: Larmor, the dipole and the 73-ohm antenna
Synchrotron light: the cost of bending a fast charge at LEP and the LHC, and the electrons that light the Crab Nebula
worked_examples: IKAROS (JAXA, 2010): a 14 m × 14 m sail at 1 AU under 1,361 W/m² would feel 2I/c × 196 m² = 1.78 mN if perfectly reflecting; the team's reported measured thrust of about 1.1 mN (Tsuda et al. 2013) fixes the sail's effective reflectivity

Synchrotron loss per turn ΔE = (4π/3) r_e mc² β³γ⁴/ρ: LEP2 electrons at 104.5 GeV in ρ = 3,096 m lose 3.4 GeV per revolution; LHC protons at 7 TeV in ρ = 2,804 m lose 6.7 keV — the reason electron colliders went linear and proton colliders did not
The half-wave dipole: radiation resistance 73.1 Ω from the far-field pattern integrated over the sphere, and Hertz's 1887 apparatus as the first one

The Crab Nebula's X-ray electrons: in a field of ≈300 μG (the equipartition estimate; Hester 2008) a 10 keV synchrotron photon needs γ ≈ 4 × 10⁷, an electron of ≈22 TeV, whose radiative lifetime 6πm_ec/(σ_Tγ B²) is about six years against the nebula's roughly 970-year age since SN 1054 — so the electrons are being replenished now, and the pulsar's spin-down power 4π²IṖ/P³ ≈ 4.5 × 10³⁸ erg/s (P = 33.4 ms, Ṗ = 4.2 × 10⁻¹³, I = 10⁴⁵ g cm²) is what pays for it
sources: Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, 4th ed. (2017), ch. 8, 10–11
Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, 3rd ed. (1999), ch. 6, 9, 14
Rybicki & Lightman, Radiative Processes in Astrophysics (1979), ch. 3–4, 6
Hester, 'The Crab Nebula: An Astrophysical Chimera', Annu. Rev. Astron. Astrophys. 46, 127 (2008)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Special relativity in four-vector form and relativistic dynamics
days.headline_hint: A muon that should live 2.2 microseconds lived 64 in a CERN ring, and the four-vector says exactly why
days.focus: Day 96 of year one gave time dilation and E = mc²; today rebuilds the subject as geometry: the Minkowski metric, the Lorentz group as hyperbolic rotations with rapidity, four-velocity and four-momentum, invariant mass and the collider-versus-fixed-target arithmetic, decays in flight, the four-force and constant proper acceleration, the relativistic Lagrangian, and Maxwell's equations rewritten as one tensor equation with the field transformations that follow. Graduate level; afterwards the reader can solve any two-body relativistic kinematics problem by invariants and transform E and B between frames.
parts: Spacetime as geometry: the Minkowski metric and the Lorentz group
Four-vectors: velocity, momentum and the invariant mass
Collisions and thresholds: why colliders beat fixed targets
Decays in flight, and the muon that lived 29 times longer
Force, acceleration and the relativistic Lagrangian: the hyperbolic trajectory and the relativistic rocket
Electrodynamics was already relativistic: F^μν, the field transformations and the covariant Lorentz force
worked_examples: The Bevatron's design number: producing an antiproton in p + p → p + p + p + p̄ needs beam kinetic energy 6m_pc² = 5.63 GeV on a fixed target; the machine was built for 6.2 GeV and found the antiproton in 1955 (Chamberlain, Segrè, Wiegand & Ypsilantis)
The LHC at √s = 13.6 TeV: the fixed-target beam energy that would match it is s/2m_p ≈ 9.9 × 10⁷ GeV ≈ 10¹⁷ eV, the collider's whole argument in one line
The CERN muon storage ring (Bailey et al. 1977): γ = 29.33, so the 2.197 μs rest lifetime becomes 64.4 μs in the laboratory, confirmed to about 0.1%
A 7 TeV LHC proton (γ = 7,463) crossing a 1 T laboratory field sees, in its own frame, an electric field E′ = γvB ≈ 2.2 × 10¹² V/m — the field transformation with real numbers
sources: Taylor & Wheeler, Spacetime Physics, 2nd ed. (1992)
Rindler, Relativity: Special, General, and Cosmological, 2nd ed. (2006), ch. 1–7
Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, 3rd ed. (1999), ch. 11–12
Bailey et al., 'Measurements of relativistic time dilatation for positive and negative muons in a circular orbit', Nature 268, 301 (1977)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: General relativity I: tensor calculus carried here, geodesics, curvature, Einstein's equations and Schwarzschild
days.headline_hint: The 43 arcseconds nobody could account for fall out of one exact solution, and so does the 38 microseconds a day your phone's clock would drift
days.focus: Day 120 of year one described curved spacetime; today builds it, and because the Mathematics block has not yet run, builds the differential geometry too: the equivalence principle as a calculation; manifolds, the metric tensor, contravariant and covariant indices, the covariant derivative and the Christoffel symbols, constructed from year one's vectors and vector calculus (days 6, 65, 76) as a part of their own; the geodesic equation from an action and the Riemann tensor as the failure of parallel transport to return, with tidal forces as what curvature measures; Einstein's field equations with their Newtonian limit; the Schwarzschild solution derived and Birkhoff's theorem; and the classic tests worked from the metric — perihelion advance, light deflection, Shapiro delay, gravitational redshift and the GPS correction. Differential forms, Stokes' theorem in general and Gauss–Bonnet are left for the Mathematics block. Graduate level (Carroll ch. 2–5, Hartle ch. 6–10); afterwards the reader can compute Christoffel symbols and curvature from any metric, solve for its geodesics, and reproduce every Solar System test to the precision the data allow.
parts: The equivalence principle, done as a calculation: the falling laboratory and the Pound–Rebka tower
The mathematics, carried here: manifolds, the metric tensor, index gymnastics and the covariant derivative, built from year one's vector calculus
Geodesics from an action, and curvature as parallel transport's failure to return: Christoffel symbols, the Riemann tensor and tidal forces
Einstein's equations and their Newtonian limit: g₀₀ = 1 + 2Φ/c²
Schwarzschild: the one solution that carries the Solar System
Orbits and light in Schwarzschild: Mercury, the 1919 eclipse, Cassini and the GPS clock
worked_examples: The plane in polar coordinates has Γ^r_φφ = −r and Γ^φ_rφ = 1/r yet every component of Riemann vanishes; the 2-sphere of radius R, ds² = R²(dθ² + sin²θ dφ²), has Γ^θ_φφ = −sin θ cos θ, Γ^φ_θφ = cot θ, R_θφθφ = R² sin²θ and Gaussian curvature 1/R² — the by-hand calculation that shows curvature is what survives the choice of coordinates, done before it is done for spacetime
Mercury from the Schwarzschild effective potential: Δφ = 6πGM/(c²a(1 − e²)) per orbit with a = 0.3871 AU and e = 0.2056 gives 42.98″/century, the residual day 2 left after the planets' 532″
Light grazing the Sun: 4GM/(c²R_☉) = 1.75″, against Eddington's 1919 measurement and the 2.1 × 10⁻⁵ precision on the PPN parameter γ from Cassini's 2002 conjunction (Bertotti, Iess & Tortora 2003)

Two clocks in the Earth's field: Pound–Rebka (1960), a 22.5 m drop in the Harvard tower, Δν/ν = gh/c² = 2.46 × 10⁻¹⁵ resolved with the 14.4 keV Mössbauer line of ⁵⁷Fe; and GPS at 20,200 km, gravitational blueshift +45.7 μs/day against velocity dilation −7.1 μs/day, net +38.6 μs/day — a position error growing by about 10 km a day if uncorrected
sources: Carroll, Spacetime and Geometry: An Introduction to General Relativity (2004; Cambridge 2019), ch. 1–5
Hartle, Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein's General Relativity (2003), ch. 6–10, 20–22
Will, 'The Confrontation between General Relativity and Experiment', Living Rev. Relativ. 17, 4 (2014)
Bertotti, Iess & Tortora, 'A test of general relativity using radio links with the Cassini spacecraft', Nature 425, 374 (2003)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: General relativity II: black holes, gravitational waves and GW150914
days.headline_hint: Read the chirp mass straight off a waveform: two black holes, thirty suns each, and a mirror that moved a thousandth of a proton
days.focus: The Schwarzschild horizon in Kruskal coordinates and what it is not, the Kerr solution with its ergosphere and spin-dependent ISCO, black-hole thermodynamics with the Hawking temperature and Bekenstein entropy, linearised gravity and the wave equation for the metric, transverse-traceless gauge and the two polarisations, the quadrupole formula and its confirmation by the Hulse–Taylor pulsar, and the LIGO detection worked from the strain data. Graduate level (Carroll ch. 5–7, Maggiore vol. 1); afterwards the reader can compute a horizon, a Hawking temperature, the orbital decay of a binary and the chirp mass from a frequency sweep.
parts: Falling through r = 2GM/c²: what the horizon is and is not
Kerr and the shadow: spin, the innermost stable orbit and the M87* ring
Black holes have a temperature: Hawking, Bekenstein and the area law
Linearised gravity: a wave equation for the metric, and two ways a ring of dust can stretch
The quadrupole formula and the pulsar that proved it
GW150914: reading the chirp mass off the waveform, and what 4 km of laser did to see it
worked_examples: A one-solar-mass black hole: Schwarzschild radius 2.95 km, Hawking temperature ħc³/(8πGMk_B) = 6.2 × 10⁻⁸ K, entropy 1.0 × 10⁷⁷ k_B, evaporation time of order 10⁶⁷ years

PSR B1913+16 (Weisberg & Huang 2016): orbital period 7.75 h, eccentricity 0.617, the quadrupole-formula prediction Ṗ_b = −2.40 × 10⁻¹² against the observed value, agreeing to 0.2% after the Galactic acceleration correction

GW150914 (Abbott et al. 2016): from the sweep of frequency f and its rate ḟ in the last cycles, the chirp mass M_c = (c³/G)[(5/96)π⁻⁸ᐟ³ f⁻¹¹ᐟ³ ḟ]³ᐟ⁵ ≈ 30 M_☉, consistent with the 36 + 29 → 62 M_☉ fit and the 3 M_☉c² radiated; peak strain 10⁻²¹ over 4 km arms is ΔL ≈ 2 × 10⁻¹⁸ m
The Event Horizon Telescope's M87* ring (2019): diameter 42 ± 3 μas at 16.8 Mpc, shadow diameter ≈ 2√27 GM/c², so M ≈ 6.5 × 10⁹ M_☉
sources: Carroll, Spacetime and Geometry (2004; Cambridge 2019), ch. 5–7
Maggiore, Gravitational Waves, Vol. 1: Theory and Experiments (2008), ch. 1–4
Abbott et al. (LIGO/Virgo), 'Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger', Phys. Rev. Lett. 116, 061102 (2016)
Weisberg & Huang, 'Relativistic measurements from timing the binary pulsar PSR B1913+16', Astrophys. J. 829, 55 (2016)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Quantum mechanics I: Hilbert space, operators, the postulates and the Bell test
days.headline_hint: The state is a vector, the observable is a matrix, and a 2015 experiment in Delft closed the last loophole on what that means
days.focus: Day 106 of year one gave wavefunctions and the Schrödinger equation; today rebuilds quantum mechanics as linear algebra in Hilbert space: Dirac notation, Hermitian operators and the spectral theorem — proved in the lesson for finite dimensions and stated with its continuum caveats, since year one's days 37 and 41 only asserted it and the Mathematics block has not yet run — the measurement postulates and the Born rule, the Robertson uncertainty relation, pure and mixed states and the density matrix, unitary time evolution in the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures with Ehrenfest's theorem, the harmonic oscillator by ladder operators and the coherent state, and composite systems with entanglement and the CHSH inequality. Graduate level (Sakurai ch. 1–2); afterwards the reader can set up any finite-dimensional quantum problem as matrices and compute what an experiment will see.
parts: Stern–Gerlach, and why the state must be a vector
The mathematics, carried here: Hermitian operators and the spectral theorem, proved — what is measurable and why the eigenvalues are real
The general uncertainty principle and the density matrix
Time evolution: the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures, and Ehrenfest's theorem
The harmonic oscillator by ladder operators, and the coherent state that is laser light
Two particles, one state: tensor products, entanglement and the Bell test
worked_examples: A free electron wavepacket of width 1 nm: Ehrenfest and the Heisenberg-picture position operator give the spreading time 2mσ²/ħ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁴ s, and the same packet for a 1 μg dust grain never spreads at all
A 1 mW helium–neon laser at 632.8 nm in 1 ns: mean photon number 3.2 × 10⁶ as a coherent state, Poisson standard deviation 1,790 — shot noise with real numbers
The trapped ⁹Be⁺ ion at NIST (Monroe et al. 1996) as a harmonic oscillator near 11 MHz, whose motional states were prepared in a superposition of two coherent states

CHSH: the quantum bound 2√2 = 2.828 against the classical 2; Aspect, Dalibard & Roger (1982) measured S = 2.697 ± 0.015, and Hensen et al. (2015) S = 2.42 ± 0.20 with both locality and detection loopholes closed
sources: Sakurai & Napolitano, Modern Quantum Mechanics, 3rd ed. (2021), ch. 1–2
Shankar, Principles of Quantum Mechanics, 2nd ed. (1994), ch. 1–4, 7
Aspect, Dalibard & Roger, 'Experimental Test of Bell's Inequalities Using Time-Varying Analyzers', Phys. Rev. Lett. 49, 1804 (1982)
Hensen et al., 'Loophole-free Bell inequality violation using electron spins separated by 1.3 kilometres', Nature 526, 682 (2015)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Quantum mechanics II: angular momentum, spin and the rotation group
days.headline_hint: Turn a neutron through 360 degrees and it comes back with the wrong sign; the algebra of rotations said it would
days.focus: Because the Mathematics block has not yet run, the lesson opens with the group theory it needs, built from year one's matrices: what a group is, the rotation group SO(3) and its generators, the Lie algebra as the commutator table, and representations as the matrices that realise it. Then rotations as unitary operators and the commutation relations they force, the ladder derivation of the j, m spectrum from the algebra alone, orbital angular momentum and the spherical harmonics, spin-½ with the Pauli matrices and the SU(2)-versus-SO(3) distinction, spin precession in a magnetic field with NMR and the g-factor, and addition of angular momenta with Clebsch–Gordan coefficients, singlet and triplet states, and the Wigner–Eckart theorem stated. Graduate level (Sakurai ch. 3); afterwards the reader can couple two angular momenta by hand, compute a Larmor frequency, and read a spin-resolved experiment.
parts: The mathematics, carried here: groups, SO(3), generators and the Lie algebra — the algebra before the wavefunction
The ladder: deriving j and m from the commutators alone
Orbital angular momentum and the spherical harmonics
Spin-½: Pauli matrices, SU(2), and the neutron that needs 720 degrees
Spin in a magnetic field: Larmor precession, the MRI magnet and the electron's g-factor
Adding angular momenta: Clebsch–Gordan, singlet and triplet, and the 21-centimetre line
worked_examples: A 3 T clinical MRI magnet: proton γ/2π = 42.577 MHz/T gives a Larmor frequency of 127.7 MHz, and at 310 K the Boltzmann polarisation hν/k_BT ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁵ is why the scanner needs 10²⁵ protons to see anything
Neutron interferometry: Rauch et al. (1975) and Werner et al. (1975) measured a spinor periodicity of about 716° ± 4°, the 4π that separates SU(2) from SO(3)
The electron's g-factor: g/2 = 1.001 159 652 180 59 (13) (Fan et al. 2023), against Dirac's exactly 2 — the anomaly day 18 will derive as α/2π
Hydrogen's ground-state hyperfine splitting via the singlet–triplet Clebsch–Gordan coefficients: 5.874 μeV, i.e. 1,420.405 751 768 MHz, the 21 cm line that maps the Galaxy's hydrogen
sources: Sakurai & Napolitano, Modern Quantum Mechanics, 3rd ed. (2021), ch. 3
Townsend, A Modern Approach to Quantum Mechanics, 2nd ed. (2012), ch. 1–5
Werner, Colella, Overhauser & Eagen, 'Observation of the Phase Shift of a Neutron Due to Precession in a Magnetic Field', Phys. Rev. Lett. 35, 1053 (1975)
Fan, Myers, Sukra & Gabrielse, 'Measurement of the Electron Magnetic Moment', Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 071801 (2023)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Quantum mechanics III: the hydrogen atom and stationary perturbation theory
days.headline_hint: One transition in hydrogen is known to fifteen digits, and every digit past the fourth is a correction the textbook Hamiltonian left out
days.focus: The exact hydrogen solution with its hidden SO(4) degeneracy, the Rydberg constant and the 1S–2S frequency, non-degenerate and degenerate perturbation theory to second order, the three fine-structure corrections combined into one formula, the Lamb shift as the signpost to QED, the Zeeman and Paschen–Back regimes with the Landé g-factor, the Stark effect, and the variational method applied to helium. Graduate level (Griffiths ch. 4, 7–8; Sakurai ch. 5); afterwards the reader can compute any hydrogen-like level to order α⁴ and a variational ground state for a two-electron atom.
parts: Solving hydrogen exactly, and why its degeneracy is a hidden symmetry
The Rydberg constant to fifteen digits: 1S–2S and what the spectrum is now used for
Perturbation theory: correcting an eigenvalue when the Hamiltonian is nearly solvable, and the Stark effect in n = 2
Fine structure: three corrections that add to one formula, and the shift Lamb found in 1947
Atoms in fields: Zeeman, Paschen–Back, the Landé g-factor and Hale's sunspot magnetism
When perturbation fails: the variational principle and the helium atom
worked_examples: R_∞ = 10 973 731.568 157 m⁻¹ (CODATA 2022) with the reduced-mass correction, against the measured 1S–2S interval 2 466 061 413 187 035 (10) Hz (Parthey et al. 2011)
Fine structure of n = 2: E_fs = −(E_n α²/n²)(n/(j + ½) − ¾) gives the 2P₃/₂–2P₁/₂ splitting of 10.97 GHz; the Lamb shift 2S₁/₂–2P₁/₂ = 1,057.8 MHz is what the formula cannot give
Linear Stark effect in n = 2 at 10⁵ V/m: ±3ea₀E = ±15.9 μeV from the 4 × 4 degenerate block, diagonalised explicitly

Helium by the variational method: the trial charge Z_eff = 27/16 gives E = −77.5 eV against the first-order −74.8 eV and the measured −79.0 eV; Hale's 1908 Zeeman splitting of the Fe I 6173 Å line in a 3 kG sunspot, ≈0.13 Å with g = 2.5
sources: Griffiths & Schroeter, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, 3rd ed. (2018), ch. 4, 7–8
Sakurai & Napolitano, Modern Quantum Mechanics, 3rd ed. (2021), ch. 5.1–5.4
Parthey et al., 'Improved Measurement of the Hydrogen 1S–2S Transition Frequency', Phys. Rev. Lett. 107, 203001 (2011)
CODATA 2022 recommended values of the fundamental physical constants (NIST)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Quantum mechanics IV: time-dependent perturbation theory and scattering
days.headline_hint: Rutherford's gold foil, a caesium clock and a pion resonance are the same calculation: an amplitude, squared, per unit flux
days.focus: The interaction picture and the Dyson series, first-order transition amplitudes and Fermi's golden rule, the exactly solvable two-level Rabi problem and the Ramsey method behind the caesium second, spontaneous emission and the Einstein A coefficient, then scattering theory: cross-sections, the Lippmann–Schwinger equation with its outgoing-wave Green's function derived by the contour integral in the lesson (the Mathematics block's complex analysis comes later), the Born approximation and Rutherford as its Coulomb limit, partial waves and phase shifts, the optical theorem, scattering length and the Breit–Wigner resonance. Graduate level (Sakurai ch. 5.5–5.8 and 6); afterwards the reader can compute a transition rate, a radiative lifetime and a differential cross-section from a potential.
parts: The interaction picture and the Dyson series: perturbation theory in time
Fermi's golden rule and the Rabi flop: how the second is defined
Why excited atoms decay: spontaneous emission, the Einstein A coefficient and the 1.6 ns of hydrogen's 2P
Scattering as a boundary-value problem: cross-sections, Lippmann–Schwinger and Born
Rutherford from Born: the 1913 counts and the size of the nucleus
Partial waves: phase shifts, the scattering length and the resonance at 1,232 MeV
worked_examples: Hydrogen 2P → 1S: the dipole matrix element at Lyman-α 121.6 nm gives A = 6.27 × 10⁸ s⁻¹, a lifetime of 1.6 ns, and a natural linewidth of 100 MHz
The caesium clock: the 9 192 631 770 Hz hyperfine transition driven by Rabi oscillation, and why Ramsey's separated fields narrow the line
Geiger & Marsden (1913): 7.7 MeV alphas on gold, distance of closest approach 2Ze²/(4πε₀E) = 29.5 fm, the 1/sin⁴(θ/2) law and the fraction turned through more than 90°

Low-energy neutron–proton scattering: σ = π(3a_t² + a_s²) with a_t = 5.42 fm and a_s = −23.7 fm gives 20.4 b, matching experiment; the Δ(1232) in π⁺p at its unitarity limit 8π/k² ≈ 190 mb against the observed ≈200 mb peak with Γ = 117 MeV
sources: Sakurai & Napolitano, Modern Quantum Mechanics, 3rd ed. (2021), ch. 5.5–5.8, 6
Griffiths & Schroeter, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, 3rd ed. (2018), ch. 10–11
Geiger & Marsden, 'The Laws of Deflexion of α Particles through Large Angles', Phil. Mag. 25, 604 (1913)
Foot, Atomic Physics (2005), ch. 7

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Statistical mechanics I: ensembles, partition functions and phase transitions
days.headline_hint: A magnet and a bottle of carbon dioxide share a critical exponent, and the reason is that details stop mattering at the edge of a phase
days.focus: Day 63 of year one made entropy a count; today builds the machinery: the microcanonical, canonical and grand canonical ensembles with Liouville behind them, the partition function and everything thermodynamic from it, fluctuations, the classical ideal gas with Sackur–Tetrode and the Gibbs paradox, equipartition and its quantum failure, the Ising model in mean field and Onsager's exact solution, Landau theory, critical exponents and the idea of universality and the renormalisation group. Graduate level (Pathria ch. 1–5, 12; Kardar); afterwards the reader can write a partition function for a new system and extract its thermodynamics, and can say what a phase transition is mathematically.
parts: Counting states: the microcanonical ensemble and the Boltzmann entropy
The canonical ensemble and the partition function, from which everything follows
The classical ideal gas and its two puzzles: Gibbs's paradox and the vibration that stays frozen
The grand canonical ensemble: when particle number floats
The Ising model: mean field, Onsager, and what a phase transition is
Critical exponents, Landau theory and universality: why CO₂ and a magnet share a number
worked_examples: Sackur–Tetrode for argon at 298.15 K and 1 bar: the computed molar entropy 154.8 J/(mol K) against the calorimetric table's 154.85 — the partition function checked to four figures
Nitrogen's heat capacity: C_p/R = 3.50 at 298 K because the vibrational temperature Θ_v = 3,390 K leaves that mode frozen, contributing 0.6%; rotational Θ_r = 2.9 K is fully excited
The 2D square-lattice Ising model: mean-field T_c = 4J/k_B against Onsager's exact 2J/(k_B ln(1 + √2)) = 2.269 J/k_B, and β = ⅛ against mean field's ½
Guggenheim's 1945 coexistence curve for eight fluids collapsing to β ≈ ⅓, the 3D Ising value 0.326, and CO₂'s critical point at 304.13 K and 7.38 MPa
sources: Pathria & Beale, Statistical Mechanics, 4th ed. (2021), ch. 1–5, 12–14
Kardar, Statistical Physics of Particles (2007), ch. 4–5, and Statistical Physics of Fields (2007), ch. 1–4
Onsager, 'Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition', Phys. Rev. 65, 117 (1944)
Guggenheim, 'The Principle of Corresponding States', J. Chem. Phys. 13, 253 (1945)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Statistical mechanics II: identical particles and the quantum gases
days.headline_hint: The Pauli principle holds up a dead star of 1.4 solar masses, and the same bookkeeping says when a cloud of rubidium becomes one wave
days.focus: The symmetrisation postulate and the exchange interaction, Slater determinants, second quantisation with creation and annihilation operators, the Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac distributions from the grand canonical ensemble, the degenerate Fermi gas in metals and white dwarfs through the Chandrasekhar limit, Bose–Einstein condensation from Einstein's 1925 prediction to the 1995 rubidium cloud, and photons and phonons as bosonic gases with Planck's law, the CMB and Debye's T³. Graduate level (Pathria ch. 6–8); afterwards the reader can compute a Fermi energy, a condensation temperature and a low-temperature heat capacity, and knows the operator language day 18 will use.
parts: Indistinguishable means something: the symmetrisation postulate and the exchange interaction in helium
Second quantisation: counting occupations instead of labelling particles
The two distributions, derived in one grand-canonical stroke
The degenerate Fermi gas: copper, Pauli's pressure and the white dwarf's mass limit
Bose–Einstein condensation: the 1925 prediction and the 1995 rubidium cloud
Photons and phonons: Planck's law from a bosonic gas, the 2.7255 K sky and Debye's T³
worked_examples: Copper with n = 8.47 × 10²⁸ m⁻³: E_F = 7.0 eV, T_F = 8.2 × 10⁴ K, and the electronic heat-capacity coefficient γ = 0.50 mJ/(mol K²) free-electron against 0.69 measured
Sirius B (Bond et al. 2017): 1.018 M_☉ and 0.0084 R_☉ on the non-relativistic degenerate mass–radius relation, and the Chandrasekhar limit 1.44 (2/μ_e)² M_☉ derived from relativistic degeneracy

Helium-4 with n = 2.18 × 10²⁸ m⁻³: the ideal-Bose T_c = 3.31 ħ²n²ᐟ³/(mk_B) = 3.1 K against the λ-point 2.17 K; the JILA ⁸⁷Rb condensate (Anderson et al. 1995) at a reported 170 nK and 2.5 × 10¹² cm⁻³, and why a harmonic trap changes the formula
The CMB as a Planck spectrum: T = 2.7255 ± 0.0006 K (FIRAS), peak at 160.2 GHz, 411 photons per cm³, 0.26 eV per cm³; Debye temperatures of copper (343 K) and diamond (2,230 K) in the T³ law
sources: Pathria & Beale, Statistical Mechanics, 4th ed. (2021), ch. 6–8
Pethick & Smith, Bose–Einstein Condensation in Dilute Gases, 2nd ed. (2008), ch. 1–2
Anderson et al., 'Observation of Bose-Einstein Condensation in a Dilute Atomic Vapor', Science 269, 198 (1995)
Chandrasekhar, 'The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs', Astrophys. J. 74, 81 (1931)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Band theory and the semiconductor: Bloch's theorem, the Kronig–Penney model, effective mass, doping and the p–n junction
days.headline_hint: Ten billion stray electrons per cubic centimetre, a row of square wells, and the 60 millivolts no transistor can beat
days.focus: Crystal and reciprocal lattices with Bragg's law and Brillouin zones, Bloch's theorem proved, the Kronig–Penney model solved exactly so that the reader watches a band gap open from a row of square wells, the nearly-free-electron and tight-binding pictures of a band, band filling and the metal–insulator distinction, effective mass and holes, semiconductor carrier statistics from day 15's Fermi–Dirac distribution through the intrinsic density and doping, and the p–n junction through the built-in voltage, the depletion width, the Shockley diode equation and the transistor it made possible. The lesson closes with a two-page sketch — not a part — of superconductivity: the Meissner effect, the London penetration depth and the BCS gap equation Δ(0) = 1.764 k_BT_c stated for niobium, as the signpost to a subject this block has no room to derive. Graduate level (Ashcroft & Mermin; Kittel ch. 7–8; Sze & Ng); afterwards the reader can compute a band structure for a model potential, a band gap's consequences for carrier density, and a junction's built-in voltage, depletion width and saturation current.
parts: Crystals in reciprocal space: Bragg, Brillouin zones and why waves in a lattice have gaps
Bloch's theorem, proved, and the Kronig–Penney model solved: a gap opens from a row of square wells
The two pictures of a band: nearly-free electrons and tight binding, and what fills them — metals, insulators, holes and the effective mass
Semiconductor statistics: the intrinsic density, donors and acceptors, and where the Fermi level sits
The p–n junction: built-in voltage, depletion width and the Shockley diode equation
The transistor: the junction as a switch, and the 60 millivolts per decade that thermodynamics charges
worked_examples: Kronig–Penney with barrier strength P = 3π/2 (Kittel's example): the allowed bands in units of E₁ = ħ²π²/(2ma²) run 0.51–1.00, 2.25–4.00 and 5.57–9.00, so the first gap opens at the zone boundary k = π/a from E₁ to 2.25E₁; scaled to silicon's lattice constant a = 5.43 Å, E₁ = 1.28 eV and that gap is 1.6 eV wide — a toy, but the mechanism is silicon's

Intrinsic silicon at 300 K: n_i = √(N_cN_v) exp(−E_g/2k_BT) with N_c = 2.8 × 10¹⁹, N_v = 1.04 × 10¹⁹ cm⁻³ and E_g = 1.12 eV gives ≈7 × 10⁹ cm⁻³ against the accepted ≈1 × 10¹⁰; the effective masses behind N_c — silicon's longitudinal 0.98 and transverse 0.19 m_e in six valleys, GaAs's single 0.067 m_e — are why GaAs electrons are faster

A junction doped 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ on both sides: V_bi = (k_BT/q) ln(N_aN_d/n_i²) = 0.71 V, W = 0.43 μm, and a saturation current density of order 10⁻¹⁰ A/cm² that the diode equation turns into ≈1 A/cm² at 0.6 V forward bias

The subthreshold floor: (k_BT/q) ln 10 = 59.5 mV per decade at 300 K, the reason no conventional MOSFET turns on faster than that, from the same Boltzmann tail that set n_i; Bardeen and Brattain's point-contact transistor of 16 December 1947 as the moment the junction became a switch
sources: Ashcroft & Mermin, Solid State Physics (1976), ch. 4–12, 28
Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, 8th ed. (2005), ch. 7–8
Sze & Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (2007), ch. 1–2, 5
Kronig & Penney, 'Quantum Mechanics of Electrons in Crystal Lattices', Proc. R. Soc. A 130, 499 (1931)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Nuclear and particle physics: decays, cross-sections and the Standard Model as a map
days.headline_hint: Twenty-four orders of magnitude in alpha-decay half-lives collapse onto one straight line, and a tunnelling integral is the ruler
days.focus: Day 111 of year one gave binding energy and the decay modes; today gives the theory: the semi-empirical mass formula and the binding-energy curve, the shell model and the spin–orbit origin of magic numbers, alpha decay as Gamow tunnelling with the Geiger–Nuttall law, beta decay in Fermi's theory with the neutron-lifetime discrepancy, cross-sections and thermonuclear rates through the Gamow peak and the solar p–p chain, and the Standard Model laid out as a map — particles, vertices, conservation laws, Feynman diagrams used as bookkeeping — pinned by the Z width, the Higgs mass and the muon anomaly. Graduate level (Krane; Griffiths, Elementary Particles); afterwards the reader can estimate a half-life, a reaction rate and a decay's allowed channels from quantum numbers.
parts: The nucleus as a liquid drop: the semi-empirical mass formula and the binding-energy curve
Magic numbers: the shell model and the spin–orbit force that makes them
Alpha decay as tunnelling: Gamow's formula and twenty-four orders of magnitude
Beta decay, Fermi's constant and the neutron that will not agree on its lifetime
Cross-sections and rates: the Gamow peak and how the Sun burns
The Standard Model as a map: particles, vertices, conservation laws and the numbers that pin it
worked_examples: The mass formula with a_V = 15.75, a_S = 17.8, a_C = 0.711, a_A = 23.7, a_P = 11.18 MeV: ⁵⁶Fe at 8.79 MeV per nucleon, and the ≈200 MeV released when ²³⁵U splits
Gamow's tunnelling integral from ²³⁸U (E_α = 4.27 MeV, t½ = 4.468 × 10⁹ yr) to ²¹²Po (8.78 MeV, 0.299 μs): the log half-life against 1/√E line
The neutron lifetime: bottle experiments (UCNτ 2021: 877.75 ± 0.28 s) against beam experiments (887.7 ± 2.2 s), a 4σ disagreement still open, with G_F = 1.166 × 10⁻⁵ GeV⁻² from the muon

The Sun: the p–p chain's Gamow peak at ≈6 keV for T_c = 1.57 × 10⁷ K, the pp-neutrino flux ≈6 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻² s⁻¹ measured by Borexino (2014); the LEP Z lineshape giving N_ν = 2.9963 ± 0.0074 light neutrinos, and the Higgs at 125.1 GeV (ATLAS/CMS)
sources: Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (1988), ch. 3–5, 8–9, 11
Griffiths, Introduction to Elementary Particles, 2nd ed. (2008), ch. 1–2, 6–9
Particle Data Group, 'Review of Particle Physics', Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)
Gamow, 'Zur Quantentheorie des Atomkernes', Z. Phys. 51, 204 (1928)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: A taste of quantum field theory: fields, propagators, Feynman rules and a real cross-section
days.headline_hint: Two metal plates a micron apart attract because the vacuum between them has fewer ways to vibrate, and the same sum predicts a cross-section at PETRA
days.focus: Why relativity plus quantum mechanics forces fields and antiparticles, canonical quantisation of the scalar field as oscillators at every wavelength with the Casimir force as the vacuum's signature, the Dirac equation and the emergence of spin and g = 2, the Dyson series turned into Feynman rules for QED, the tree-level e⁺e⁻ → μ⁺μ⁻ cross-section computed all the way to picobarns, and a first honest look at loops, renormalisation, running couplings and the Higgs mechanism. Graduate level (Peskin & Schroeder ch. 2–5); afterwards the reader can quantise a free field, read a Feynman diagram as an integral, and compute one tree-level QED process.
parts: Why a field: relativity, quantum mechanics and the necessity of antiparticles
Quantising the scalar field: oscillators at every wavelength, and the Casimir force they exert
The Dirac equation: spin and g = 2 fall out of the square root of a wave equation
Interactions and the Feynman rules: the Dyson series turned into pictures
One tree-level cross-section, all the way: e⁺e⁻ → μ⁺μ⁻ at PETRA
Loops, running couplings and the Higgs: what renormalisation means and what the vacuum weighs
worked_examples: The Casimir pressure π²ħc/(240d⁴): 1.3 mPa at d = 1 μm, measured to 5% by Lamoreaux (1997) between 0.6 and 6 μm
σ(e⁺e⁻ → μ⁺μ⁻) = 4πα²/3s = 86.8 nb/(s in GeV²): 72.9 pb at PETRA's √s = 34.5 GeV, and the Z-interference correction that spoils it at LEP energies
Schwinger's one-loop anomaly a_e = α/2π = 0.001 161 41 against the measured 0.001 159 652 18 (day 11), and the running of α from 1/137.036 to 1/128.95 at the Z mass

The Higgs vacuum value v = 246.22 GeV and weak coupling g ≈ 0.652 give the tree-level m_W = gv/2 ≈ 80.2 GeV against the world average 80.37 GeV; the 2022 CDF value 80.43 ± 0.01 and the 2023 ATLAS 80.36 ± 0.02 as the open question
sources: Peskin & Schroeder, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory (1995), ch. 2–5, 7
Schwartz, Quantum Field Theory and the Standard Model (2014), ch. 2–5, 13, 16
Lamoreaux, 'Demonstration of the Casimir Force in the 0.6 to 6 μm Range', Phys. Rev. Lett. 78, 5 (1997)
Schwinger, 'On Quantum-Electrodynamics and the Magnetic Moment of the Electron', Phys. Rev. 73, 416 (1948)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Plasma physics: from single-particle drifts to magnetohydrodynamics and fusion
days.headline_hint: On 5 December 2022 a capsule the size of a peppercorn gave back more energy than the lasers put in; the arithmetic is Lawson's from 1957
days.focus: Debye shielding, the plasma parameter and the plasma frequency, single-particle motion with gyration, the E×B, gradient and curvature drifts and the magnetic mirror with its adiabatic invariant, the Vlasov equation and Landau damping, the two-fluid and MHD equations with frozen-in flux and Alfvén waves, tokamak equilibrium with the safety factor and the instabilities that limit it, and fusion by the numbers through cross-sections, reactivity, the Lawson triple product, JET, ITER and the NIF ignition shot. Graduate level (Chen; Freidberg); afterwards the reader can compute a Debye length, a drift velocity, an Alfvén speed and a confinement requirement for a stated plasma.
parts: What makes a gas a plasma: Debye shielding, the plasma frequency and the ionosphere's radio mirror
One particle in a field: gyration, drifts and the magnetic mirror that traps the Van Allen belts
From particles to fluids: Vlasov, Landau damping and the two-fluid equations
Magnetohydrodynamics: frozen-in flux, Alfvén waves and the solar wind
Confinement: tokamak equilibrium, the safety factor and the instabilities that fight it
Fusion by the numbers: cross-sections, the Lawson criterion, JET, ITER and the night NIF ignited
worked_examples: The ionospheric F layer at n_e = 10¹² m⁻³: f_p = 8.98√n_e = 9 MHz, which is why shortwave bounces and FM does not; the solar wind at 1 AU (n ≈ 5 cm⁻³, T ≈ 10⁵ K) has λ_D ≈ 10 m
The solar wind's Alfvén speed: B = 5 nT and ρ = 5 × 10⁶ protons/m³ give v_A = B/√(μ₀ρ) ≈ 49 km/s against a flow of 400 km/s — super-Alfvénic, which is why the Earth has a bow shock

ITER's design point: R = 6.2 m, B = 5.3 T, I_p = 15 MA, q₉₅ ≈ 3, Q = 10 (500 MW from 50 MW of heating), set against the triple-product threshold nTτ_E ≳ 3 × 10²¹ keV s m⁻³ and D–T reactivity at 15 keV
JET's 2021 record of 59 MJ over 5 s and its 1997 peak of 16 MW (Q = 0.67); NIF's 5 December 2022 shot, 2.05 MJ of laser energy in and 3.15 MJ of fusion yield out (Abu-Shawareb et al. 2024)
sources: Chen, Introduction to Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion, 3rd ed. (2016), ch. 1–9
Freidberg, Plasma Physics and Fusion Energy (2007), ch. 1–4, 11–13
Lawson, 'Some Criteria for a Power Producing Thermonuclear Reactor', Proc. Phys. Soc. B 70, 6 (1957)
Abu-Shawareb et al. (Indirect Drive ICF Collaboration), 'Achievement of Target Gain Larger than Unity in an Inertial Fusion Experiment', Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 065102 (2024)

days.subject: Physics
days.topic: Cosmology: Friedmann models and the observed universe
days.headline_hint: Put six numbers into one integral and out comes 13.8 billion years — then two of the six refuse to agree, and that is where cosmology stands
days.focus: The FLRW metric and the Friedmann equations from day 8's field equations, redshift, the three distances and the age integral, the thermal history done with day 15's distributions through neutrino decoupling and nucleosynthesis, recombination and the CMB with the sound horizon and the acoustic peaks, standard candles and standard rulers from Type Ia supernovae to DESI's baryon acoustic oscillations, the Hubble tension, and the evidence for dark matter, dark energy and inflation. Graduate level (Ryden; Dodelson & Schmidt); afterwards the reader can compute the age, size and composition of the universe from the Planck parameters and state precisely what the current tensions do and do not show.
parts: The Friedmann equations: Einstein's equations for a universe that is the same everywhere
Redshift, distances and the age integral: how 13.8 billion years is computed
The first three minutes as statistical mechanics: neutrinos, nucleosynthesis and the helium fraction
Recombination and the CMB: the sound horizon and the peak near ℓ = 220 that measured the geometry
Standard candles, standard rulers and the Hubble tension: supernovae, BAO and DESI
What the 95 percent is: dark matter, dark energy, inflation and where cosmology stands
worked_examples: Flat ΛCDM age t₀ = (2/3H₀√Ω_Λ) arcsinh√(Ω_Λ/Ω_m) with Planck 2018's H₀ = 67.4 km/s/Mpc, Ω_m = 0.315: 1/H₀ = 14.51 Gyr and t₀ = 13.80 Gyr against Planck's 13.797 ± 0.023
Nucleosynthesis with η = 6.1 × 10⁻¹⁰: the predicted primordial helium fraction Y_p ≈ 0.247 and D/H ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ against the observed 0.245 ± 0.004 and 2.53 × 10⁻⁵
Planck's acoustic scale 100θ* = 1.0411 ± 0.0003 gives ℓ_A = π/θ* ≈ 302, with the first peak at ℓ ≈ 220 once the phase shift is included; the sound horizon r_s = 147 Mpc as the ruler DESI uses

The Hubble tension: SH0ES (Riess et al. 2022) 73.0 ± 1.0 against Planck 67.4 ± 0.5, about 5σ; DESI DR2 BAO (2025) preferring evolving dark energy over ΛCDM at 3.1σ with CMB and 2.8–4.2σ with supernova compilations; NGC 3198's flat 150 km/s rotation curve to 30 kpc implying 1.6 × 10¹¹ M_☉ enclosed
sources: Ryden, Introduction to Cosmology, 2nd ed. (2017)
Dodelson & Schmidt, Modern Cosmology, 2nd ed. (2020), ch. 1–9
Planck Collaboration, 'Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters', Astron. Astrophys. 641, A6 (2020)
DESI Collaboration, 'DESI DR2 Results II: Measurements of Baryon Acoustic Oscillations and Cosmological Constraints', arXiv:2503.14738 (2025)

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: First-order logic and its limits
days.headline_hint: The Sentence That Says of Itself It Cannot Be Proved
days.focus: First-order logic as the instrument every argument in the block will be checked with, built honestly in the time available: Aristotle's syllogistic as a one-part prologue and the inference it could not represent; first-order syntax and semantics (terms, formulas, structures, satisfaction, logical consequence); soundness and Gödel's completeness theorem stated, with compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem as stated corollaries and what they mean for arithmetic; then the road to the first incompleteness theorem taken properly — Gödel numbering, the representability of syntax in arithmetic, the diagonal lemma and the fixed-point sentence — with the theorem sketched to the point where the reader sees why it holds. The second incompleteness theorem and Tarski's undefinability theorem are stated, placed and used, not proved; Turing machines and the halting problem belong to the Mathematics block (block 6, day 18) and are only pointed to here. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can formalise a natural-language argument and check its validity, explain to a sceptic why 'true but unprovable' is always relative to a system, and say why the Lucas–Penrose argument that minds beat machines fails.
parts: Aristotle's syllogism was a machine for validity, and it could not say 'every horse's head is an animal's head'
Frege's quantifier: first-order syntax and semantics — terms, formulas, structures, satisfaction, and what 'follows from' means
Soundness and completeness stated: proof matches truth, and compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem are why first-order logic cannot pin down the natural numbers
Arithmetic talks about itself: Gödel numbering, representability, and why 'x codes a proof of y' is an arithmetical relation
The diagonal lemma and the first incompleteness theorem, sketched to the point where it is seen: the sentence that says it is unprovable
Stated, not proved: the second theorem, Tarski's undefinability, what is left of Hilbert's programme, why Lucas–Penrose fails — and the halting problem left for block 6
worked_examples: De Morgan's 1847 inference — all horses are animals, therefore every horse's head is an animal's head — shown to be unrepresentable in Aristotle's syllogistic and then derived in first-order natural deduction line by line, with the structure that makes it valid written out and a countermodel constructed for the invalid converse.

Gödel numbering done on a real formula: under the Nagel–Newman coding (0 = 6, = 5) the sentence '0 = 0' becomes 2^6 · 3^5 · 5^6 = 243,000,000, then decoded back by prime factorisation; the same coding applied to a two-line proof to show that 'x is the code of a proof of y' is a relation the language of arithmetic can express, which is what the whole theorem rests on.

The diagonal lemma carried out on ¬Prov(x): the substitution function diag(n), which takes the code of a formula ψ(x) to the code of ψ applied to its own numeral, is representable; put θ(x) := ¬Prov(diag(x)), let m be the code of θ(x), and G := θ(m) — then diag(m) is the code of G, so PA proves G ↔ ¬Prov(⌜G⌝). From there the first half of the theorem is argued in full (if PA proved G it would prove Prov(⌜G⌝) and hence ¬G), the ω-consistency the second half needs is named, and Rosser's 1936 replacement of it by plain consistency is stated.

The Lucas–Penrose argument formalised in numbered premises and checked: the step 'I can see that G is true' is shown to require that the mind know its own consistency, which the second theorem — stated today, proved nowhere in this lesson — denies to any consistent system that can prove its own arithmetic.
sources: Gödel, 'On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems I' (1931), in van Heijenoort ed., From Frege to Gödel (Harvard 1967)
Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic, 2nd ed. (Academic Press 2001), chs. 2–3
Smith, An Introduction to Gödel's Theorems, 2nd ed. (Cambridge 2013)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems', 'Classical Logic', 'First-order Model Theory'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Knowledge, justification and scepticism
days.headline_hint: The Demon, the Ten Coins and the Fake Barns: Why Being Right Is Not Enough
days.focus: What knowledge is and whether we have any: Plato's justified-true-belief target, Descartes's sceptical arguments and the cogito, Gettier's counterexamples and every repair since (causal, sensitivity, safety, virtue, knowledge-first), the regress problem and the foundationalism–coherentism–reliabilism contest, and the closure argument for scepticism against Moore's proof and contextualism. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can run any proposed analysis of knowledge against the standard counterexamples and say precisely which premise a sceptic and a Moorean disagree about.
parts: Plato's Theaetetus set the target — true belief with an account — and left the account blank
Descartes's dream, demon and cogito: the arguments in premises, and Arnauld's circle checked
Gettier's three pages: why justified true belief fails, and the causal, sensitivity, safety and virtue repairs each tested on Smith's coins and Henry's barns
The regress: foundations, coherence or reliability — Sellars's myth of the given, BonJour, Goldman and the new evil demon
Moore's hands and the sceptic's closure argument are one modus ponens run in opposite directions: DeRose's contextualist verdict
Kant's Refutation of Idealism and Wittgenstein's hinges: is the sceptic even coherent, and what does scepticism cost a Bayesian?
worked_examples: Descartes's dreaming argument (AT VII 19) and demon argument (AT VII 22) written as numbered premises, then the cogito (AT VII 25), then the Cartesian circle from Arnauld's Fourth Objections (AT VII 214) traced to the exact step where clear-and-distinct perception is both premise and conclusion.

Gettier's Case I (Smith, Jones and the ten coins, Analysis 1963) and Goldman's fake-barn county (1976) run through justified true belief, the causal theory, Nozick's sensitivity condition and Sosa's safety condition, recording which condition each case violates and why sensitivity and safety give different verdicts on the barns.

Moore's proof of an external world and the closure-based sceptical argument laid out on the same three propositions — I know I have hands; if I know I have hands I know I am not a handless brain in a vat; I do not know I am not a brain in a vat — showing that the two are the same valid argument with a different premise denied.

The new evil demon problem for reliabilism: the demon-world twin whose beliefs are produced by unreliable processes yet seem equally justified, run to its conclusion and against Goldman's normal-worlds reply.
sources: Plato, Theaetetus, in Cooper ed., Plato: Complete Works (Hackett 1997)
Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy, in Cottingham, Stoothoff & Murdoch trans., The Philosophical Writings of Descartes, vol. II (Cambridge 1984)
Gettier, 'Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?', Analysis 23 (1963): 121–123; Nozick, Philosophical Explanations (Harvard 1981), ch. 3
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'The Analysis of Knowledge', 'Skepticism', 'Epistemic Closure'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Induction, confirmation and Bayesian epistemology
days.headline_hint: The Sun Has Always Risen — So What? Betting on Tomorrow With Real Money
days.focus: Hume's problem of induction and the two twentieth-century paradoxes of confirmation, then the Bayesian answer built from the ground up: why credences must be probabilities (Dutch book and accuracy arguments), conditionalisation, the Principal Principle, the problem of the priors and old evidence, and what 'evidence' means when statisticians disagree — likelihoodism, Bayes factors, error statistics and Lindley's paradox. Graduate level, with the mathematics of day 44 and day 61 of year one assumed; the reader afterwards can construct a Dutch book against an incoherent agent, compute a Bayesian confirmation measure, and say what the replication crisis looks like from each side of the statistics debate.
parts: Hume's fork: the problem of induction stated as a dilemma, and why 'it has worked so far' is the circle
Goodman's grue and Hempel's ravens: confirmation cannot be a matter of syntax alone
Why degrees of belief must obey the probability calculus: the Dutch book run with prices, and Joyce's accuracy argument
Conditionalisation, the Principal Principle and the priors: the ravens resolved with numbers, old evidence, and Sleeping Beauty
Evidence in the statistician's sense: the likelihood principle, Bayes factors against p-values, Mayo's severity, and Lindley's paradox
Reichenbach's pragmatic vindication and the convergence theorems: what remains of Hume's problem after Bayes
worked_examples: A Dutch book built in dollars against an agent whose credences in heads and tails sum to 1.1: the two bets priced at the agent's own fair odds, the sure loss computed, and the converse theorem (coherent credences cannot be booked) stated.

Hempel's ravens resolved quantitatively: with a stipulated population of 10,000 ravens among 10^9 non-black objects, the likelihood ratio a white shoe supplies for 'all ravens are black' is computed and shown to be positive but negligible, while a black raven's is large.

Ioannidis's 2005 positive-predictive-value calculation reproduced: with prior odds 1:10, power 0.8 and α = 0.05, PPV = 0.615, then the Bayesian reanalysis of the 2015 Reproducibility Project: Psychology (Etz & Vandekerckhove 2016), which found most original studies had offered only weak evidence to begin with.

Elga's Sleeping Beauty problem (2000): the halfer and thirder credences derived side by side from conditionalisation and the Principal Principle, locating the exact assumption about self-locating evidence on which they differ.
sources: Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, ed. Millican (Oxford World's Classics 2007), §IV; A Treatise of Human Nature, ed. Norton & Norton (Oxford 2000), 1.3.6
Goodman, Fact, Fiction, and Forecast, 4th ed. (Harvard 1983); Ramsey, 'Truth and Probability' (1926), in Mellor ed., Philosophical Papers (Cambridge 1990)
Howson & Urbach, Scientific Reasoning: The Bayesian Approach, 3rd ed. (Open Court 2006)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'The Problem of Induction', 'Bayesian Epistemology', 'Dutch Book Arguments', 'Confirmation'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Philosophy of science: falsification, paradigms, explanation, realism
days.headline_hint: Neptune Saved Newton and Vulcan Could Not: What a Failed Prediction Proves
days.focus: How science changes its mind and whether its theories are true: Popper's falsificationism and the Duhem–Quine problem, Kuhn's paradigms and incommensurability, Lakatos's research programmes, the models of explanation from Hempel to Woodward, and the realism debate — no-miracles against the pessimistic meta-induction, constructive empiricism and structural realism — with values and inductive risk at the end. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can say why a single anomaly refuted nothing in 1846 and everything in 1915, formalise the no-miracles argument and see where it commits the base-rate fallacy, and defend a significance threshold as an ethical choice.
parts: Popper's asymmetry — one black swan refutes, no number of white ones proves — and why falsification alone cannot guide a science
Duhem and Quine: no hypothesis meets experiment alone — Uranus, Neptune, Mercury and the planet Vulcan that was never there
Kuhn's paradigms: normal science, anomaly, crisis, revolution — and incommensurability tested on Copernicus and on Lavoisier
Lakatos and Feyerabend: is there a rational reconstruction of theory change, or only a history?
Explanation: Hempel's deductive-nomological model, the flagpole that breaks it, and the causal and unificationist replacements
Realism: no-miracles against the pessimistic meta-induction as a base-rate problem, van Fraassen's constructive empiricism, structural realism, and inductive risk at five sigma
worked_examples: Neptune against Vulcan on the real numbers: Uranus's residuals of roughly two arcminutes by 1845 resolved by Le Verrier's and Adams's new planet, versus Mercury's anomalous perihelion advance of 43 arcseconds per century (Le Verrier 1859, Newcomb 1882) that no auxiliary planet could absorb and that general relativity predicted to within an arcsecond in 1915 — the Duhem–Quine problem shown to have a rational, not merely sociological, resolution.

The deductive-nomological schema run forwards and backwards on the flagpole: a 10-metre pole and a sun at 30° elevation entail a 17.32-metre shadow; the same law and the shadow entail the pole's height, and the symmetry shows why entailment is not explanation.

The no-miracles argument written as a Bayesian inference — P(success | true) ≈ 1, P(success | false) = q — with a base rate for true theories drawn from Laudan's 1981 list of successful dead theories (caloric, phlogiston, the ether), showing that the posterior depends entirely on a prior the argument never supplies (Magnus & Callender 2004).

The 4 July 2012 Higgs announcement as an inductive-risk decision: five sigma corresponds to a one-sided p of about 3 × 10^-7; Douglas's 2000 argument that the threshold encodes a judgement about the relative costs of a false discovery and a missed one, not a fact about the boson.
sources: Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (Routledge Classics 2002); Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, 4th ed. (Chicago 2012)
Lakatos, 'Falsification and the Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes', in Lakatos & Musgrave eds., Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge (Cambridge 1970)
van Fraassen, The Scientific Image (Oxford 1980); Laudan, 'A Confutation of Convergent Realism', Philosophy of Science 48 (1981)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Karl Popper', 'Thomas Kuhn', 'Scientific Explanation', 'Scientific Realism', 'Underdetermination of Scientific Theory'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Philosophy of language: meaning, reference and truth
days.headline_hint: The Morning Star Was the Evening Star All Along — So What Did the Astronomer Learn?
days.focus: What words mean and how they attach to the world: Frege's sense and reference, Russell's theory of descriptions and its critics, Kripke's rigid designators and the causal-historical picture, Putnam's externalism, Tarski's semantic conception of truth and Davidson's programme, Quine's indeterminacy, and Wittgenstein's rule-following paradox in Kripke's sceptical form, with Grice's distinction between what is said and what is meant. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can formalise a definite description with scope, run the modal argument against descriptivism, and state exactly what fact the rule-following sceptic is demanding and why it is hard to supply.
parts: Frege's puzzle: 'Hesperus is Phosphorus' is informative and 'Hesperus is Hesperus' is not, so meaning is not reference
Russell's theory of descriptions makes 'the present King of France is bald' true or false without a king — Strawson and Donnellan object
Kripke against descriptivism: rigid designators, the modal and epistemic arguments, and the Gödel–Schmidt case
Putnam's Twin Earth: meanings are not in the head — natural kinds and the division of linguistic labour
Tarski's definition of truth, Davidson's truth-conditional meaning, and Quine's gavagai — how much of meaning is fixed?
Meaning as use: Wittgenstein's rule-following paradox, Kripke's 'quus', and Grice on what is said versus what is implicated
worked_examples: Russell's analysis of 'The present King of France is not bald' written in first-order logic under both scopes of negation, with its truth value in 1905 and today computed for each; then Strawson's presupposition reading and Donnellan's referential–attributive distinction applied to 'Smith's murderer is insane'.

Kripke's modal argument formalised: if 'Aristotle' meant 'the teacher of Alexander', then 'Aristotle taught Alexander' would be necessary; evaluated in possible-world semantics — introduced informally here and made rigorous as S5 on day 6 — and shown false, since Aristotle might have died young; then the Gödel–Schmidt case run to its conclusion against the description theory of reference.

Kripke's quus — x quus y = x + y when both are below 57, otherwise 5 — with the sceptical challenge stated as a demand for a fact about the speaker's past use, and the three candidate facts (dispositions, simplicity, an introspectible state) each shown to fail on Kripke's own criteria before the 'sceptical solution' is assessed.

Twin Earth run with the real chemistry: in 1750, before Cavendish and Lavoisier, Oscar and Twin Oscar share every psychological state while 'water' refers to H₂O for one and to XYZ for the other, so extension is not fixed by what is in the head.
sources: Frege, 'On Sense and Reference' (1892), in Beaney ed., The Frege Reader (Blackwell 1997); Russell, 'On Denoting', Mind 14 (1905): 479–493
Kripke, Naming and Necessity (Harvard 1980); Putnam, 'The Meaning of "Meaning"' (1975), in Mind, Language and Reality (Cambridge 1975)
Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations, 4th ed., trans. Anscombe, Hacker & Schulte (Wiley-Blackwell 2009), §§138–242; Kripke, Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language (Harvard 1982)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Reference', 'Descriptions', 'Theories of Meaning', 'Rule-Following and Intentionality'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Metaphysics: identity, modality, causation and time
days.headline_hint: Water Had to Be H₂O, and Two Pedestrians Cannot Agree What Day It Is in Andromeda
days.focus: The four core problems of metaphysics argued with their primary texts: identity over time (Leibniz's law, the ship of Theseus, the statue and the clay, perdurance), necessity and possible worlds after Kripke and Lewis with the modal logic that carries them, causation from Hume's regularities through Lewis's counterfactuals to Woodward's and Pearl's interventions, and time — McTaggart, presentism against eternalism, the relativistic argument for the block universe, and the thermodynamic arrow. Graduate level, with day 96 of year one assumed; the reader afterwards can prove the necessity of identity in five lines, run an interventionist causal model, and compute the simultaneity shift that the Rietdijk–Putnam argument turns on.
parts: Leibniz's law and the ship of Theseus: what survives replacement, the statue and the lump, and Lewis's four-dimensional answer
Necessity after Kripke: necessary a posteriori identities, essentialism, and the S5 logic that carries them
What is a possible world? Lewis's modal realism against the ersatzists, and why the incredulous stare is not an argument
Causation: Hume's regularity, Lewis's counterfactuals and the pre-emption cases that broke them, and Pearl's intervention as the modern answer
Time: McTaggart's paradox, presentism against eternalism, and the Rietdijk–Putnam argument from special relativity — with the numbers
The arrow: entropy, the Past Hypothesis, and whether the future is already fixed
worked_examples: Kripke's proof of the necessity of identity carried out in full — from ∀x □(x = x) and Leibniz's law to x = y → □(x = y) — then applied to Hesperus/Phosphorus and to 'water is H₂O', and contrasted with 'the number of planets is eight', where the non-rigid description blocks the inference.

Penrose's Andromeda paradox computed: two people passing on a street at a walking pace of 1.4 m/s have hyperplanes of simultaneity that differ, at the Andromeda galaxy 2.5 million light-years away, by Δt = v·d/c² ≈ 3.7 × 10^5 s, about four days — so an invasion fleet already launched for one is undecided for the other, which is Putnam's 1967 argument for eternalism.

Pearl's do-calculus on the barometer, the air pressure and the storm: a three-variable structural model with stipulated conditional probabilities in which P(storm | barometer falls) is high but P(storm | do(barometer falls)) equals the base rate, showing why correlation-based and intervention-based accounts of causation part company.

Late pre-emption run through Lewis's 1973 analysis: Suzy's rock shatters the bottle a moment before Billy's would have; 'had Suzy not thrown, the bottle would not have shattered' is false, so counterfactual dependence fails, and Lewis's 2000 'influence' repair is tested on the same case.
sources: Lewis, On the Plurality of Worlds (Blackwell 1986); Kripke, 'Identity and Necessity' (1971), in Munitz ed., Identity and Individuation (NYU Press 1971)
Lewis, 'Causation', Journal of Philosophy 70 (1973): 556–567; Woodward, Making Things Happen (Oxford 2003); Pearl, Causality, 2nd ed. (Cambridge 2009)
Putnam, 'Time and Physical Geometry', Journal of Philosophy 64 (1967): 240–247; Sider, Four-Dimensionalism (Oxford 2001)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Identity Over Time', 'Possible Worlds', 'Counterfactual Theories of Causation', 'Time', 'Thermodynamic Asymmetry in Time'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Philosophy of mathematics
days.headline_hint: Are Numbers Discovered or Made? A Slave Boy, a Fatal Letter and a Programme That Died in 1931
days.focus: What mathematical objects are and how we could know about them: Plato's recollection argument and Benacerraf's epistemological dilemma, Kant's synthetic a priori, Frege's logicism and the paradox that broke it, Hilbert's formalism and what Gödel's second theorem left of it, Brouwer's intuitionism and mathematics without excluded middle, structuralism and what numbers could not be, and the indispensability argument against Field's nominalism. Graduate level, with day 1 assumed; the reader afterwards can derive Russell's paradox from Basic Law V, tell a constructive proof from a non-constructive one, and say why 'is 1 a member of 3?' has no answer.
parts: Plato's slave boy and Benacerraf's dilemma: if numbers are abstract, how could we know them; if not, what makes arithmetic true?
Kant's synthetic a priori and Frege's logicism: Hume's Principle, Basic Law V, and Russell's letter of 16 June 1902
Hilbert's programme and its end: what the second incompleteness theorem did to finitary consistency proofs, and what Gentzen salvaged
Brouwer's intuitionism: rejecting the excluded middle, and what analysis looks like when every function is continuous
What numbers could not be: Zermelo against von Neumann, and the structuralist answer
Indispensability and the unreasonable effectiveness: Quine and Putnam against Field's Science Without Numbers, and what the physicist actually needs
worked_examples: Meno 82b–85b reconstructed step by step: the slave boy's 2-by-2 square of area 4, the demand for area 8, the failed guesses of side 4 (area 16) and side 3 (area 9), and the diagonal answer (side √8) — read first as Plato's argument for recollection and then as Benacerraf's problem about how a causally isolated fact could be learned.

Russell's paradox derived in five lines from Frege's Basic Law V (the extension of F equals the extension of G iff the same things fall under F and G), then Hume's Principle stated and Boolos's 1987 result explained: it is consistent and, with second-order logic, yields the Peano axioms (Frege's theorem).

The Zermelo and von Neumann constructions of 0, 1, 2, 3 written out — Zermelo's 3 = {{{∅}}}, von Neumann's 3 = {∅, {∅}, {∅, {∅}}} — so that '1 ∈ 3' is true on one and false on the other, which is Benacerraf's 1965 argument that neither is the number three.

A non-constructive proof and its constructive replacement: either √2^√2 is rational or (√2^√2)^√2 = 2 is, which proves an irrational power can be rational without saying which; then the Gelfond–Schneider theorem (1934) supplies the witness a = √2^√2, b = √2, and the intuitionist's complaint is made precise.
sources: Benacerraf & Putnam eds., Philosophy of Mathematics: Selected Readings, 2nd ed. (Cambridge 1983) — Benacerraf 'Mathematical Truth', Hilbert, Brouwer, Gödel, Quine
Frege, The Foundations of Arithmetic, trans. Austin, 2nd rev. ed. (Northwestern 1980); Plato, Meno, in Cooper ed., Plato: Complete Works (Hackett 1997)
Shapiro, Thinking About Mathematics: The Philosophy of Mathematics (Oxford 2000); Field, Science Without Numbers, 2nd ed. (Oxford 2016)

Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Philosophy of Mathematics', 'Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics', 'Intuitionism in the Philosophy of Mathematics', 'Indispensability Arguments in the Philosophy of Mathematics'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Philosophy of mind: consciousness, functionalism, the hard problem, machine minds
days.headline_hint: The Room That Speaks Chinese and the Bat No One Can Imagine Being
days.focus: The mind–body problem argued from Descartes to the present: substance dualism and the interaction problem, behaviourism, identity theory and functionalism with multiple realisability, Searle's Chinese Room in premises, the anti-physicalist arguments (Nagel, Jackson, Kripke, Chalmers's zombies) checked with the modal logic of day 6, the physicalist replies and the measurable theories (global workspace, integrated information) including the 2025 adversarial test, and whether a machine — specifically a large language model — could be a candidate for understanding or consciousness. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can state the hard problem so that both sides accept the statement, and locate the exact premise on which the zombie argument stands or falls.
parts: Descartes's real distinction from Meditation VI, and Princess Elisabeth's question he never answered: how does an unextended thing move an arm?
From behaviourism to functionalism: Ryle's category mistake, Smart's brain processes, Putnam's multiple realisability, and the Turing machine as a theory of mind
Searle's Chinese Room in numbered premises: the systems reply, the robot reply, and where the disagreement actually sits
Nagel's bat, Jackson's Mary and Chalmers's zombies: the knowledge and conceivability arguments checked in S5 — this is the hard problem
The physicalist replies and the theories that measure: phenomenal concepts, Dennett's illusionism, global workspace, integrated information, and the 2025 Cogitate result
Machine minds: Turing's test, Block's blockhead, and whether a large language model satisfies any indicator of consciousness (Butlin, Long et al. 2023)
worked_examples: Searle's own 1990 axiomatisation of the Chinese Room — programs are syntactic; minds have semantic contents; syntax is neither constitutive of nor sufficient for semantics; therefore programs are not minds — checked for validity, then the systems reply and the robot reply run against the third premise to its conclusion, and Searle's 'internalise the whole system' rejoinder assessed.

The zombie argument in the modal logic of day 6: P (the complete physical truth) and Q (a phenomenal truth); conceivability of P ∧ ¬Q; conceivability entails possibility; possibility of P ∧ ¬Q refutes □(P → Q) — then Kripke's a-posteriori-necessity escape (as with water and H₂O) and Chalmers's two-dimensional reply that the escape is unavailable here because phenomenal concepts have no contingent mode of presentation.

Jackson's Mary (1982) formalised as an argument from new knowledge to new facts, then the ability hypothesis (Lewis, Nemirow) and the old-fact-new-guise reply each tested for whether it explains why Mary's surprise on leaving the room is rational.

Butlin, Long et al.'s 2023 indicator list (recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order representation, agency and embodiment) applied to a transformer language model of the kind day 116 of year one described, indicator by indicator, with the Cogitate Consortium's Nature 2025 finding — that neither global workspace theory nor integrated information theory passed all its preregistered predictions in 256 participants — as the reason the list cannot yet settle the question.
sources: Chalmers ed., Philosophy of Mind: Classical and Contemporary Readings, 2nd ed. (Oxford 2021) — Descartes, Ryle, Smart, Putnam, Nagel, Jackson, Block
Searle, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3 (1980): 417–457
Chalmers, The Conscious Mind (Oxford 1996); Butlin, Long et al., 'Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness' (2023), arXiv:2308.08708
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Consciousness', 'Functionalism', 'The Chinese Room Argument', 'Zombies', 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Personal identity and free will
days.headline_hint: If the Teletransporter Makes Two of You, Which One Owes the Mortgage?
days.focus: What makes a person at one time the same person as one at another, and whether anything we do is up to us: Locke's memory criterion and Reid's objection, Parfit's psychological continuity, fission and the argument that identity is not what matters, animalism and the narrative self; then the Consequence Argument formalised with its inference rule and the counterexample to it, Frankfurt cases, compatibilism and the manipulation argument, and what the Libet experiments actually measured. Graduate level, with day 6 and day 8 assumed; the reader afterwards can run Parfit's fission case to each of its four possible answers, write van Inwagen's argument with rule β and break it, and say what a readiness potential is evidence for.
parts: Locke's prince and cobbler, Reid's brave officer, and the ancestral relation that repairs the memory criterion
The teletransporter, fission and the combined spectrum: Parfit's argument that identity is not what matters, run to its conclusion
Animalism, the narrative self, and what Hume found when he looked inward: too many thinkers or too few?
Free will: van Inwagen's Consequence Argument formalised, rule β, and the coin that was never tossed
Frankfurt cases and compatibilism: does responsibility need alternate possibilities? Strawson's reactive attitudes and Pereboom's four cases
Libet's 550 milliseconds: what the readiness potential shows and does not, Schurger's reanalysis, and Kant's third antinomy
worked_examples: Reid's brave officer (1785): the boy flogged for robbing an orchard, the officer who remembers the flogging, the general who remembers the officer's capture of the standard but not the flogging — Locke's criterion makes the general identical to the officer and the officer to the boy but the general not identical to the boy, a transitivity failure written out formally; Parfit's ancestral 'Relation R' shown to restore transitivity at the cost of allowing branching.

Parfit's 'My Division' (Reasons and Persons §89): each hemisphere transplanted into a different body; the four answers — I survive as neither, as one, as both, or the question is empty — each carried to contradiction or acceptance, and the conclusion that what matters (Relation R) can hold without identity.

The Consequence Argument in van Inwagen's third formulation: N-operator, rule α (if □p then Np) and rule β (if Np and N(p → q) then Nq); then McKay and Johnson's 1996 counterexample — a coin that was not tossed, with Np for 'no heads' and Np for 'no tails' agglomerating to N(no heads and no tails), which is false — and van Inwagen's revised β-2.

Libet's 1983 timings — readiness-potential onset about 550 ms before movement, reported conscious intention about 200 ms before, muscle activity at zero — and Schurger, Sitt and Dehaene's 2012 stochastic-accumulator model showing the same averaged curve arises from noise crossing a threshold, so that the RP is not evidence of an unconscious decision.
sources: Parfit, Reasons and Persons (Oxford 1984), Part III; Williams, 'The Self and the Future', Philosophical Review 79 (1970)
Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, ed. Nidditch (Oxford 1975), II.xxvii; Reid, Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man (1785), III.6
van Inwagen, An Essay on Free Will (Oxford 1983); Frankfurt, 'Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility', Journal of Philosophy 66 (1969); Pereboom, Living Without Free Will (Cambridge 2001)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Personal Identity', 'Free Will', 'Compatibilism', 'Arguments for Incompatibilism'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Decision theory and rationality
days.headline_hint: One Box or Two? The Argument Where Each Side Is Certain the Other Has Lost Its Mind
