days.focus: What it is to choose rationally, treated as a normative question: the von Neumann–Morgenstern and Savage representation theorems and what each axiom claims, the Allais and Ellsberg paradoxes with their original numbers read as challenges to the axioms rather than as findings about people, St Petersburg and Pascal's wager under unbounded utility, Newcomb's problem as the fault line between evidential and causal decision theory, the bounded-rationality debate over whether a bias is a failure of rationality at all, and Parfit's challenge to the rational authority of self-interest across time. This is the year's normative decision theory: the descriptive theory — prospect theory with its estimated parameters, β–δ discounting and the field evidence — belongs to the Economics block's behavioural lesson (block 3, day 18) and to year one's day 140 and is assumed here, not re-taught; the Wealth Management blocks take both as given. Graduate level, closing the first half and handing to the second; the reader afterwards can elicit a utility function from stated preferences, show which axiom a paradox violates and say whether that axiom was ever a requirement of rationality, and compute both sides of Newcomb's problem before saying which he takes.
parts: From Pascal to von Neumann: expected utility as a representation theorem, and what completeness, transitivity, continuity and independence actually assert
Allais and Ellsberg with the original payoffs: which axiom each breaks, Savage's recantation, and whether independence and the sure-thing principle were ever requirements of rationality
St Petersburg and Pascal's wager: unbounded utility, Bernoulli's logarithm, and the mugging that follows
Newcomb's problem: evidential against causal decision theory with the numbers, 'why ain'cha rich?', and the smoking lesion

Bounded rationality as a normative question: Simon's satisficing, Gigerenzer against Kahneman, and whether the biases of day 140 and the Economics block are failures of rationality or ecologically rational
Rationality across time: Parfit on self-interest, present aims and discounting the future self — the hand-off to ethics
worked_examples: Allais's 1953 choices with the original 100-million-franc payoffs: the modal pattern (the sure 100 million over the gamble; the 10% chance of 500 million over the 11% chance of 100 million) written as two expected-utility inequalities that cannot both hold, then the same pair rewritten in Savage's sure-thing form to expose the common consequence being ignored — with Savage's own report (Foundations of Statistics §5.6) that he chose the Allais pattern and, on seeing the violation, reversed his preferences, which is the paradox read normatively; the descriptive reproduction by a prospect-theory weighting function is left to the Economics block's behavioural lesson.

Ellsberg's urn — 30 red balls, 60 black or yellow in unknown proportion — with the two bet pairs, showing that the usual preferences imply P(black) < 1/3 in one pair and P(black) > 1/3 in the other, so no single credence rationalises them; ambiguity aversion as a violation of Savage's sure-thing principle.

St Petersburg valued with Bernoulli's logarithmic utility at his own wealth levels: the certainty equivalent is about 2 ducats for a pauper, about 3 for a player with 10 ducats, about 4 with 100 and about 6 with 1,000 — reproduced from the 1738 paper — and then Pascal's mugging, where the same move fails.

Newcomb with a predictor that is right 90% of the time: evidential expected value of one-boxing 0.9 × $1,000,000 = $900,000 against two-boxing 0.9 × $1,000 + 0.1 × $1,001,000 = $101,000; causal decision theory's dominance argument for two-boxing; then the smoking-lesion case, where the same two theories swap the intuitive verdict.
sources: von Neumann & Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, 60th anniversary ed. (Princeton 2004); Savage, The Foundations of Statistics, 2nd ed. (Dover 1972)
Nozick, 'Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice' (1969), in Rescher ed., Essays in Honor of Carl G. Hempel (Reidel 1969); Lewis, 'Why Ain'cha Rich?', Noûs 15 (1981)

Allais, 'Le comportement de l'homme rationnel devant le risque', Econometrica 21 (1953); Ellsberg, 'Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms', Quarterly Journal of Economics 75 (1961); Bernoulli (1738), trans. Econometrica 22 (1954)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Decision Theory', 'Causal Decision Theory', 'The St. Petersburg Paradox', 'Pascal's Wager', 'Bounded Rationality'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Metaethics: is there anything to know?
days.headline_hint: Is 'Wrong' a Fact About the World or a Boo Dressed as a Fact?
days.focus: Whether moral claims can be true and what would make them so: Hume's is–ought gap and Moore's open question as constraints every theory must meet, Mackie's error theory, expressivism from Ayer to Gibbard and the Frege–Geach problem, naturalist realism and the Moral Twin Earth objection, Kantian constructivism, non-naturalism after Parfit, the evolutionary debunking argument in Bayesian form, and moral epistemology through reflective equilibrium and disagreement. Graduate level, using the language and epistemology of the first half; the reader afterwards can classify any metaethical position by its answers to three questions and run the Frege–Geach test on a real inference.
parts: Hume's is–ought and Moore's open question: the two arguments every metaethics must survive, formalised
Mackie's error theory: queerness, relativity, and the companions-in-guilt reply from epistemic reasons
Expressivism from Ayer to Blackburn and Gibbard: the Frege–Geach problem run on a real modus ponens, and what quasi-realism answers
Naturalism and constructivism: Cornell realism, Moral Twin Earth, Railton's reforming definitions, Korsgaard's sources of normativity
Non-naturalism after Parfit and Street's Darwinian dilemma: the debunking argument in Bayesian shape, and the third-factor reply
Moral epistemology: reflective equilibrium, intuitions as evidence, and what the peer-disagreement problem of day 2 does to moral confidence
worked_examples: Moore's open-question argument (Principia Ethica §13) applied to Mill's Utilitarianism chapter 4: Mill's inference from 'the only proof that a thing is visible is that people see it' to 'the only proof that a thing is desirable is that people desire it' written as an analogy and checked, showing the equivocation between 'able to be desired' and 'worthy of desire' that Moore charged and that Mill's defenders (Crisp) contest.

The Frege–Geach problem on 'If lying is wrong, then getting your little brother to lie is wrong; lying is wrong; so getting your little brother to lie is wrong': valid on a descriptivist reading; on Ayer's reading the antecedent expresses no attitude, so the inference has no logical form — then Blackburn's higher-order-attitude semantics and Schroeder's 2008 objection that it cannot deliver the right logic for negation.

Mackie's argument from queerness in numbered premises, and Cuneo's 2007 parity argument: epistemic reasons (you ought to believe what your evidence supports) are exactly as queer, so the error theorist must reject them too, which is self-undermining — assessed with Streumer's reply that the position may be true but unbelievable.

Street's 2006 Darwinian dilemma as a tracking argument: the probability that natural selection produced evaluative attitudes that coincide with mind-independent moral truths, computed on each horn (no relation between selection and truth; a tracking relation), and Enoch's third-factor reply that survival and goodness are correlated through a common cause.

connect_back.subject: Economics
connect_back.topic: What economics is trying to answer

sources: Moore, Principia Ethica, rev. ed., ed. Baldwin (Cambridge 1993); Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, ed. Norton & Norton (Oxford 2000), 3.1.1
Mackie, Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong (Penguin 1977); Blackburn, Ruling Passions (Oxford 1998); Gibbard, Thinking How to Live (Harvard 2003)
Street, 'A Darwinian Dilemma for Realist Theories of Value', Philosophical Studies 127 (2006): 109–166; Parfit, On What Matters, vol. 2 (Oxford 2011)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Metaethics', 'Moral Realism', 'Moral Anti-Realism', 'Moral Cognitivism vs. Non-Cognitivism'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Consequentialism
days.headline_hint: The Greatest Good for the Greatest Number, Priced in Bed Nets
days.focus: The theory that the right act is the one with the best outcome, argued from its founders and against its best critics: Bentham's calculus and Mill's proof, Sidgwick's dualism of practical reason, the act, rule, expected and scalar forms in the decision-theoretic language of day 10, the objections that bite (separateness of persons, integrity, demandingness with the real cost of saving a life), the limits of aggregation, and population ethics through the Repugnant Conclusion and the impossibility theorems. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can state consequentialism as an optimisation problem, show exactly what Mill's proof proves, and run the Mere Addition Paradox with numbers to the point where he must give up one of three intuitions.
parts: Bentham's seven circumstances and Mill's proof: what chapter 4 of Utilitarianism actually argues
Sidgwick's dualism and the forms of the theory: act, rule, expected, satisficing and scalar consequentialism as optimisation problems
The objections that bite: the separateness of persons, Williams's Jim and George, and the demandingness objection with the real cost of a life
Aggregation and its limits: Taurek's numbers, the transmitter room, and whether five deaths are worse than one
Population: the Repugnant Conclusion, the Mere Addition Paradox with numbers, and Arrhenius's impossibility theorems
What survives: two-level utilitarianism, Sidgwick's esoteric morality, and effective altruism as the theory in practice
worked_examples: Mill's proof (Utilitarianism ch. 4) in numbered steps — each person's happiness is a good to that person; therefore the general happiness is a good to the aggregate of persons — with the fallacy-of-composition charge tested against Mill's 1868 letter to Henry Jones, where he disclaims the aggregate reading.

Singer's principle (1972) with current numbers: GiveWell's 2023 cost-per-life-saved estimates for its top malaria charities (roughly $3,000–5,500) against the 2023 US median household income of $80,610 (Census P60-282), computing what the strong and moderate versions of the principle would each require of a median household and what the demandingness objection therefore amounts to in dollars.

Parfit's Mere Addition Paradox with figures: A (10 billion people at welfare 100), A+ (A plus 10 billion at welfare 50), B (20 billion at welfare 80) — total welfare 10^12, 1.5 × 10^12, 1.6 × 10^12 — iterated to Z (10^15 people at welfare 1), then the Average view's Sadistic Conclusion and the Critical-Level view's cost, so that Arrhenius's theorem is seen rather than stated.

Taurek's 'Should the Numbers Count?' (1977): one person needs the whole dose, five need a fifth each; Taurek's coin-flip argument in premises, Scanlon's tie-breaker reply, and Otsuka's objection that the tie-breaker smuggles aggregation back in.
sources: Mill, Utilitarianism, ed. Crisp (Oxford 1998); Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), ed. Burns & Hart (Oxford 1996), ch. 4
Sidgwick, The Methods of Ethics, 7th ed. (Macmillan 1907; Hackett reprint 1981); Smart & Williams, Utilitarianism: For and Against (Cambridge 1973)

Singer, 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality', Philosophy & Public Affairs 1 (1972); Parfit, Reasons and Persons (Oxford 1984), Part IV; Arrhenius, 'An Impossibility Theorem for Welfarist Axiologies', Economics and Philosophy 16 (2000)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Consequentialism', 'Rule Consequentialism', 'The Repugnant Conclusion'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Deontology and contractualism: Kant, Ross, Scanlon
days.headline_hint: The Lie You Cannot Universalise and the Broadcast You May Not Interrupt
days.focus: The theories that put persons before outcomes: Kant's categorical imperative in its formulas, run on his own four examples and on the murderer at the door; rights as side-constraints and the doctrine of double effect across the trolley variants with the 2020 cross-cultural data; Ross's prima facie duties and particularism; Scanlon's contractualism with the Rescue Principle and the transmitter room; and Parfit's argument that Kantians, contractualists and rule consequentialists are climbing the same mountain. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can universalise a maxim and say which kind of contradiction results, apply double effect's four conditions to a case, and derive a principle by reasonable rejection.
parts: The good will and the Formula of Universal Law: the four examples of the Groundwork run, and contradiction in conception told from contradiction in will
Humanity as an end and the kingdom of ends: what 'merely as a means' forbids, and the murderer at the door against Constant and Korsgaard
Rights as side-constraints and the doctrine of double effect: Switch, Loop and Footbridge with 70,000 participants' verdicts
Ross's prima facie duties and moral particularism: is there a decision procedure, or only judgement?
Scanlon's contractualism: principles no one could reasonably reject, the Rescue Principle, and why the numbers do not count in the transmitter room
Parfit's Triple Theory: do Kant, Scanlon and rule consequentialism converge, and what would show they do not?
worked_examples: The lying promise (Groundwork 4:422) universalised: the maxim stated, the universalised world described, the contradiction in conception derived (promising becomes impossible), then Korsgaard's practical-contradiction reading tested against the logical and teleological readings, and the false-positive problem — 'play tennis at 10 on Sunday when the court is free' — that any reading must handle.

Switch, Loop and Footbridge run through the four conditions of double effect in a table, showing that Loop fails the means condition while most people (72% in Awad et al.'s 2020 study of 70,000 participants in 42 countries, against 81% for Switch and 51% for Footbridge) still permit it — the data as a problem for the doctrine, and Kamm's principle of permissible harm as the repair.

Scanlon's transmitter room (What We Owe to Each Other, ch. 5): Jones's severe pain for an hour against a World Cup broadcast to a million viewers; each viewer's complaint compared pairwise with Jones's and found weaker, so no aggregate of them can reasonably reject the principle 'rescue Jones' — then Parfit's objection that this also forbids rescuing many from a lesser harm, and Scanlon's later concessions.

Kant's 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' (1797, 8:425–430) reconstructed as an argument about responsibility for consequences, and Korsgaard's 1986 two-level reply (ideal theory under the Formula of Humanity, non-ideal theory under the Formula of Universal Law) shown to license the lie without abandoning Kant.
sources: Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, trans. Gregor, rev. ed. Timmermann (Cambridge Texts 2012); Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' (1797), in Practical Philosophy, trans. Gregor (Cambridge 1996)
Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other (Harvard 1998); Parfit, On What Matters, vol. 1 (Oxford 2011), chs. 16–17
Thomson, 'The Trolley Problem', Yale Law Journal 94 (1985): 1395–1415; Ross, The Right and the Good (1930), ed. Stratton-Lake (Oxford 2002); Awad et al., PNAS 117 (2020): 2332–2337
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Kant's Moral Philosophy', 'Deontological Ethics', 'Contractualism', 'The Doctrine of Double Effect'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Virtue, character and the meaning of a life: Aristotle or Nietzsche?
days.headline_hint: A Seminarian in a Hurry Walks Past a Man in Distress: What Character Is, and Whether Anyone Has One
days.focus: The ethics of the whole life rather than the single act: Aristotle's function argument and the doctrine of the mean, the twentieth-century revival through Anscombe, Hursthouse and MacIntyre, the situationist challenge from social psychology with its actual numbers, Nietzsche's genealogy as a debunking of morality, and the existentialist inheritance — Kierkegaard, Sartre, Camus, Heidegger — ending on whether a life can mean anything without a transcendent guarantee (Tolstoy, Nagel, Williams, Wolf, Scheffler). Graduate level; the reader afterwards can state what virtue ethics tells an agent to do, weigh the Darley–Batson data as evidence against global traits, and run Williams's argument that immortality would be unbearable.
parts: Aristotle's function argument: eudaimonia as activity of soul in accordance with virtue — Nicomachean Ethics I.7 formalised and attacked
Anscombe's 'Modern Moral Philosophy' and the revival: Hursthouse's v-rules, MacIntyre's practices, and whether virtue ethics can say what to do
The situationist challenge: Milgram, the Good Samaritan study, the dime in the phone booth — Doris and Harman against character, and the reply
Nietzsche's Genealogy: master and slave morality, ressentiment, and the genealogical argument as debunking — MacIntyre's 'Nietzsche or Aristotle?'
Existence precedes essence: Kierkegaard's knight of faith, Sartre's student, Camus's Sisyphus, and Heidegger's being-toward-death
Meaning without the transcendent? Tolstoy's Confession, Nagel's Absurd, Williams's Makropulos case, Wolf's fitting fulfilment, and Scheffler's afterlife
worked_examples: Nicomachean Ethics I.7 (1097b22–1098a20) in numbered premises — every kind of thing with a function has its good in performing it well; the function of a human being is activity of the rational soul; therefore the human good is rational activity performed well, that is, in accordance with virtue — with Glassen's 1957 and Nagel's 1972 objections placed at the exact step where 'function' becomes 'good'.

Darley and Batson's 1973 Princeton seminarians: 40 subjects, 63% helped the slumped man when unhurried, 45% when moderately hurried, 10% when late — and being primed with the parable of the Good Samaritan made no difference; alongside Isen and Levin's 1972 phone-booth study (14 of 16 dime-finders helped, 1 of 25 others) and Milgram's 65% to 450 volts — run as Doris's argument that robust global traits do not exist, then Kamtekar's reply that Aristotelian virtue was never a statistical trait.

Sartre's student (Existentialism Is a Humanism, 1946), torn between joining the Free French and staying with his mother, run through the Formula of Universal Law, the utilitarian sum and Hursthouse's v-rules, showing why Sartre claims no doctrine decides and what that claim presupposes about reasons.

Williams's Makropulos case (1973): Elina Makropulos at 342, and the two conditions on a desirable immortality — that it be the same person who lives on and that she retain categorical desires — argued to be jointly unsatisfiable, then Fischer's 1994 reply that repeatable pleasures need not exhaust themselves.

connect_back.subject: Finance
connect_back.topic: Wealth management and the long horizon

sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, trans. Irwin, 2nd ed. (Hackett 1999); Anscombe, 'Modern Moral Philosophy', Philosophy 33 (1958): 1–19; MacIntyre, After Virtue, 3rd ed. (Notre Dame 2007)
Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality, trans. Clark & Swensen (Hackett 1998); Doris, Lack of Character (Cambridge 2002); Darley & Batson, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 27 (1973)

Sartre, Existentialism Is a Humanism, trans. Macomber (Yale 2007); Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, trans. O'Brien (Vintage 1991); Williams, 'The Makropulos Case', in Problems of the Self (Cambridge 1973); Wolf, Meaning in Life and Why It Matters (Princeton 2010)

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Philosophy of religion
days.headline_hint: The Argument That Proves God in Five Lines — and Its Mirror Image That Proves the Opposite
days.focus: Whether there is a God and whether it would be rational to believe so: the ontological argument in Anselm's and Plantinga's modal forms checked line by line, the cosmological arguments and their regress, fine-tuning as a Bayesian inference with the cosmological constant's numbers and the anthropic objection, the logical and evidential problems of evil with the free-will defence and sceptical theism, Hume on miracles as a testimony calculation, Pascal's wager with day 10's decision theory, and Reformed epistemology's claim that belief can be properly basic. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can show that Plantinga's argument is valid and why that settles nothing, compute the posterior odds of a miracle from witness reliability, and state the problem of evil in a form a theist accepts as the problem.
parts: Anselm's ontological argument and its modal descendant: Plantinga's S5 version is valid — and the reverse argument is equally valid
Cosmological arguments: Aquinas's Second Way, Leibniz's sufficient reason, the Kalam, and the replies of Hume and Russell
Fine-tuning as Bayes: the cosmological constant's 10^-120, the multiverse, the inverse gambler's fallacy and the anthropic selection effect
The problem of evil: Mackie's logical argument in premises, Plantinga's free-will defence, Rowe's fawn, and sceptical theism
Hume on miracles with numbers, Pascal's wager with infinite utilities and the many-gods matrix, and James's will to believe
Euthyphro, religious experience and Reformed epistemology: can belief in God be properly basic, and what does that cost the epistemology of day 2?
worked_examples: Plantinga's modal ontological argument (The Nature of Necessity, ch. 10) formalised in S5: possibly a maximally great being exists; maximal greatness entails existence in every world; ◇□p → □p; therefore necessarily a maximally great being exists — checked valid, then the parody premise 'possibly no maximally great being exists' run through the same logic to the opposite conclusion (Oppy), showing that the entire weight rests on which possibility premise one grants.

Fine-tuning computed: the observed cosmological constant is roughly 10^-120 of the value quantum field theory naively predicts (day 120 of year one), so P(life-permitting | chance) is taken as ~10^-120 against P(life-permitting | design) near 1; the likelihood ratio is enormous, but the posterior depends on the prior for design and on the multiverse-plus-selection alternative — Hacking's 1987 inverse gambler's fallacy and White's 2000 reply run on a dice example.

Hume's Enquiry §X as Bayes: with a prior probability of 10^-9 for a resurrection and a single witness whose testimony is reliable 999 times in 1,000, posterior odds are 10^-9 × 999 ≈ 10^-6; with three independent witnesses of the same reliability the factor is 999^3 and the posterior odds are about even — Earman's 2000 point that Hume's maxim ignores the multiplication of independent testimony.

Pascal's wager as a decision matrix with infinite utility, then Hájek's 2003 objection that any mixed strategy with positive probability of belief has the same infinite expected value, and the many-gods objection as a matrix with rival deities in the columns.
sources: Anselm, Proslogion, in Basic Writings, trans. Williams (Hackett 2007); Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity (Oxford 1974), ch. 10; Oppy, Ontological Arguments and Belief in God (Cambridge 1995)
Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion and Other Writings, ed. Coleman (Cambridge Texts 2007); Hume, Enquiry §X; Earman, Hume's Abject Failure (Oxford 2000)
Mackie, The Miracle of Theism (Oxford 1982); Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', Mind 64 (1955); Rowe, 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism', American Philosophical Quarterly 16 (1979)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Ontological Arguments', 'Cosmological Argument', 'Fine-Tuning', 'The Problem of Evil', 'Miracles', 'Pascal's Wager'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Political philosophy: the social contract and its critics
days.headline_hint: Wilt Chamberlain's Quarter Million and the Veil of Ignorance: Who Gets to Keep What
days.focus: What could justify a state and a distribution: Hobbes's state of nature as a game with its matrix identified, Locke's labour theory of property with its provisos and the consent problem, Rousseau's general will and Mill's harm principle as two ideas of liberty, Rawls's original position deriving the two principles against Harsanyi's expected-utility objection with the difference principle applied to real income shares, Nozick's entitlement theory and the Wilt Chamberlain argument with Cohen's reply, and the critics — Marx, Okin, Mills, Sen, Hayek and the democratic-legitimacy problem. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can write the state of nature as a payoff matrix, run the original-position choice as a decision under uncertainty, and say whether liberty upsets patterns.
parts: Hobbes's state of nature as a game: the Foole's argument, prisoner's dilemma or assurance game, and why the sovereign changes the payoffs
Locke's property and consent: mixing labour, 'enough and as good', the spoilage proviso, and Hume's ship against tacit consent
Rousseau's general will and Mill's harm principle: freedom as self-legislation against freedom as non-interference — Berlin's two concepts and Pettit's third
Rawls: the original position derives the two principles — maximin against Harsanyi's expected utility, and the difference principle on real income quintiles
Nozick's entitlement theory and Wilt Chamberlain: liberty upsets patterns, and Cohen's reply that self-ownership does not entail world-ownership
The critics: Marx on the rights of man, Okin on the family, Mills's racial contract, Sen's capabilities against primary goods, Hayek's knowledge problem, and Estlund on democratic authority
worked_examples: Hobbes's state of nature as a 2×2 matrix with numerical payoffs: with T > R > P > S it is a prisoner's dilemma and the Foole is right that defection dominates; with R > T > P > S (Kavka 1986, Hampton 1986) it is an assurance game and the sovereign's role is to make mutual compliance the equilibrium — the text of Leviathan chapters 13–15 read for which ordering Hobbes actually asserts.

The original-position choice as decision under uncertainty: Principle A guarantees the worst-off 20 with an average of 50; Principle B gives the worst-off 5 with an average of 60; Harsanyi's 1975 argument that a rational chooser with 1/n probability of each position picks B, against Rawls's three conditions (deep uncertainty, a satisfactory minimum, unacceptable downside) under which maximin is the rational rule — then the difference principle read against the Census Bureau's 2023 shares of aggregate income by quintile (about 3 percent to the lowest fifth, about half to the top fifth).

Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, ch. 7): start from the patterned distribution D1, one million fans each drop 25 cents in the box, Chamberlain ends the season $250,000 richer in D2; the argument that any patterned principle must forbid such transfers written in premises, then Cohen's 1995 reply that the fans' consent does not settle the claims of third parties and that self-ownership is compatible with joint ownership of the world.

Locke's provisos tested on Nozick's tomato-juice case (pouring one's can into the sea) and on the Homestead Act of 1862's 160-acre grants: whether 'enough and as good' was left for others, and what Waldron's reading of the spoilage limit implies once money is introduced (Second Treatise §§46–50).
sources: Hobbes, Leviathan, ed. Curley (Hackett 1994); Locke, Two Treatises of Government, ed. Laslett (Cambridge 1988); Rousseau, The Social Contract and Other Later Political Writings, ed. Gourevitch (Cambridge 1997); Mill, On Liberty and Other Essays, ed. Gray (Oxford World's Classics 1991)
Rawls, A Theory of Justice, rev. ed. (Harvard 1999); Harsanyi, 'Can the Maximin Principle Serve as a Basis for Morality?', American Political Science Review 69 (1975)

Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (Basic Books 1974); Cohen, Self-Ownership, Freedom, and Equality (Cambridge 1995); Mills, The Racial Contract (Cornell 1997); Okin, Justice, Gender, and the Family (Basic Books 1989)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Contemporary Approaches to the Social Contract', 'Hobbes's Moral and Political Philosophy', 'Original Position', 'Libertarianism', 'Distributive Justice'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Philosophy of law
days.headline_hint: Elmer Palmer Poisoned His Grandfather to Inherit — and the Statute Said Nothing About It
days.focus: What law is and what makes it binding: Austin's command theory and Hart's rule of recognition, the Hart–Fuller debate over Nazi law and the inner morality of law, Dworkin's principles and law as integrity through Riggs v. Palmer, Raz's service conception and the exclusive–inclusive positivism dispute, legal realism, constitutional interpretation through Heller and Waldron's case against judicial review, and the justification of punishment with the 2022 American numbers. Graduate level with a practitioner's eye on real cases; the reader afterwards can say what a positivist and a natural lawyer each claim about a wicked statute, reconstruct a judicial opinion as an argument about the sources of law, and state what a retributivist and a deterrence theorist each need to be true.
parts: Austin's gunman writ large and Hart's demolition: primary and secondary rules, the rule of recognition, and what makes the Constitution law
The Hart–Fuller debate: the grudge informer, the eight ways to fail to make law, and what Pappe found in the German court records
Dworkin against Hart: Riggs v. Palmer, principles that are not rules, the semantic sting, and Hercules deciding Brown
Raz's authority, Kelsen's Grundnorm and the realists: the service conception, exclusive against inclusive positivism, and Holmes's bad man
Interpretation: originalism against living constitutionalism on District of Columbia v. Heller, and Waldron's case against judicial review
Punishment: Kant's island, Bentham's calculus, Feinberg's expressive theory — and 1,230,100 people in American prisons
worked_examples: Riggs v. Palmer, 115 N.Y. 506 (1889): the statute of wills contains no exception for a legatee who murders the testator; Judge Earl's majority applies the principle that no one may profit from his own wrong, Judge Gray's dissent applies the statute — reconstructed as Dworkin's 1967 argument that principles are legally binding without a pedigree, then Hart's Postscript reply that the rule of recognition can incorporate principles (inclusive positivism), and Raz's argument that it cannot.

The grudge informer: a 1944 denunciation under Nazi statutes and the 1949 Bamberg Oberlandesgericht decision, run through Hart's positivist resolution (a retroactive statute, openly) and Fuller's natural-law resolution (the statutes were not law), with Fuller's eight desiderata applied as a checklist to the Nazi decrees — and Pappe's 1960 correction that the court did not in fact hold the statutes void.

District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008): the Second Amendment's prefatory and operative clauses read under Scalia's original-public-meaning method and under Stevens's purposive dissent, laid out as two arguments sharing the same text and diverging on the theory of interpretation, without adjudicating the politics.

Kant's island (Metaphysics of Morals 6:333) — the last murderer must be executed before the society disbands — formalised as the retributivist claim that desert is sufficient for punishment, against Bentham's claim that only deterrence justifies the cost, tested on the Bureau of Justice Statistics' yearend 2022 figures: 1,230,100 people in state and federal prisons, 355 sentenced prisoners per 100,000 residents.

connect_back.subject: Accounting
connect_back.topic: Audit, controls and GAAP vs IFRS

sources: Hart, The Concept of Law, 3rd ed., with Postscript (Oxford 2012); Hart, 'Positivism and the Separation of Law and Morals', Harvard Law Review 71 (1958); Fuller, 'Positivism and Fidelity to Law', Harvard Law Review 71 (1958)
Dworkin, Law's Empire (Harvard 1986); Dworkin, 'The Model of Rules', University of Chicago Law Review 35 (1967); Riggs v. Palmer, 115 N.Y. 506 (1889)

Fuller, The Morality of Law, rev. ed. (Yale 1969); Raz, The Authority of Law, 2nd ed. (Oxford 2009); Scalia, A Matter of Interpretation (Princeton 1997); Waldron, 'The Core of the Case Against Judicial Review', Yale Law Journal 115 (2006)

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Philosophy of economics and markets: value, fairness, efficiency
days.headline_hint: Nine Thousand Dollars a Megawatt-Hour: When Is a Price Unjust, and Who Decides?
days.focus: The moral and conceptual foundations under the paper's own subject: what economic value is (Aristotle, the labour theory and the marginalist revolution with the transformation problem worked), what efficiency means and does not (Pareto, Kaldor–Hicks, the welfare theorems, Scitovsky), Arrow's theorem and Sen's liberal paradox with actual preference profiles, fairness in exchange (exploitation, price gouging in Winter Storm Uri, noxious markets), whether homo economicus is a normative claim, and the equality–efficiency trade-off from Okun's bucket to luck egalitarianism and relational equality. Graduate level; the reader afterwards can run a Kaldor–Hicks test on a real policy and say what it leaves out, construct a Condorcet cycle, and give the strongest case on each side of a price-gouging law.
parts: What is value? Aristotle's use and exchange, Smith and Marx's labour, the marginalists — and the transformation problem worked in two sectors
Pareto, Kaldor–Hicks and the welfare theorems: what 'efficient' asserts, what it does not, and the Scitovsky reversal
Arrow's theorem and Sen's Paretian liberal: no social welfare function, and why efficiency and liberty collide over Lady Chatterley
Fairness in exchange: exploitation, price gouging in the Texas freeze, and noxious markets in kidneys, surrogacy and votes
Homo economicus as a normative claim: revealed preference, Sen's rational fools, Friedman's 'as if', and the positive–normative line of day 11
Efficiency against equality: Okun's leaky bucket with a number, equality of what, luck egalitarianism against relational equality
worked_examples: Marx's transformation problem in a two-department model with different organic compositions of capital: labour values computed, then prices of production with an equalised profit rate, showing that total value equals total price only under conditions Bortkiewicz (1907) identified — and Samuelson's 1971 verdict on what the 'transformation' therefore amounts to.

Arrow's theorem on a three-voter profile (A > B > C; B > C > A; C > A > B) producing a Condorcet cycle, then the Borda count shown to violate independence of irrelevant alternatives when a fourth candidate is added; Sen's 1970 Lady Chatterley case (Prude and Lewd, one copy of the novel, two rights and one Pareto step) laid out as a table that cycles.

Winter Storm Uri, 15–19 February 2021: ERCOT's wholesale price held at the $9,000-per-megawatt-hour cap for days and Griddy's wholesale-indexed customers were billed thousands of dollars — run through Zwolinski's 2008 defence of price gouging (allocation, incentives, consent) and Snyder's and Satz's objections (vulnerability, the conditions of fair bargaining), with the numbers on both sides of the ledger.

A Kaldor–Hicks compensation test on the 2018 Section 232 steel tariffs using the Peterson Institute's estimate of roughly $650,000 in user costs per steel job protected: the potential-Pareto verdict, the Scitovsky reversal check, and what the test cannot say about who was actually compensated.
sources: Hausman, McPherson & Satz, Economic Analysis, Moral Philosophy, and Public Policy, 3rd ed. (Cambridge 2017)

Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values, 3rd ed. (Yale 2012); Sen, 'The Impossibility of a Paretian Liberal', Journal of Political Economy 78 (1970): 152–157; Sen, 'Rational Fools', Philosophy & Public Affairs 6 (1977)

Satz, Why Some Things Should Not Be for Sale (Oxford 2010); Sandel, What Money Can't Buy (Farrar, Straus and Giroux 2012); Zwolinski, 'The Ethics of Price Gouging', Business Ethics Quarterly 18 (2008); Marx, Capital, vol. I, trans. Fowkes (Penguin 1976), ch. 1
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Philosophy of Economics', 'Social Choice Theory', 'Exploitation', 'Markets', 'Egalitarianism'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: Ethics of technology and artificial intelligence
days.headline_hint: The Risk Score Was Fair Two Ways and Unfair the Third — and the Arithmetic Says It Had to Be
days.focus: Applied ethics where the paper's AI coverage meets the second half's theories: the impossibility of satisfying all fairness criteria at once with the COMPAS numbers, privacy as contextual integrity and differential privacy's epsilon as a moral parameter, autonomy and manipulation by recommender systems, responsibility gaps in autonomous vehicles and weapons with the NTSB's Tempe timeline, the moral status of machines and what 'value alignment' could mean, and the governance structure of the EU AI Act. Practitioner depth: the reader could audit a classifier on Monday, state which fairness criterion he chose and why, and explain to a colleague what the alignment problem is a problem about.
parts: Fairness cannot be had all at once: COMPAS, and the Chouldechova–Kleinberg impossibility proved with the ProPublica numbers
Privacy: Warren and Brandeis, Nissenbaum's contextual integrity, and differential privacy's ε as a moral quantity — the 2020 Census's 19.61
Autonomy and manipulation: nudges against manipulation, recommender systems, and the Frankfurtian will of day 9
Responsibility gaps: Matthias, the Tempe crash timeline, autonomous weapons, and why the trolley problem is the wrong frame for a car
The moral status of machines and the alignment problem as philosophy: Gabriel's five targets, the orthogonality thesis, and what day 8 and day 11 say the problem is
Governance: the EU AI Act's risk tiers, dual use, open weights, and Collingridge's dilemma
worked_examples: The COMPAS impossibility with the Broward County numbers: two-year recidivism base rates of about 51% for Black and 39% for white defendants, the score calibrated at roughly 0.61 positive predictive value for both; Chouldechova's identity FPR = [p/(1−p)]·[(1−PPV)/PPV]·(1−FNR) then forces false-positive rates near 45% and 23% (ProPublica's 45% and 23%) unless the false-negative rates are made unequal instead — the theorem seen in the arithmetic, and the choice among criteria shown to be a moral choice.

Differential privacy made concrete: the Laplace mechanism on a population count with noise scale 1/ε, compared at ε = 1 and at the ε = 19.61 the Census Bureau chose for the 2020 redistricting file, and the privacy-loss budget interpreted as a bound on how much any one person's presence can change what an adversary learns — a moral parameter with a number.

NTSB report HWY18MH010 on the 18 March 2018 Tempe crash that killed Elaine Herzberg: the system first detected her 5.6 seconds before impact, never classified her as a pedestrian, and emergency braking was suppressed by design — the responsibility distributed across developer, safety driver (who pleaded guilty to endangerment in 2023), regulator and victim, run through Matthias's 2004 responsibility gap.

Gabriel's 2020 five alignment targets — instructions, expressed intentions, revealed preferences, informed preferences or interests, values — applied to a single concrete request ('find me the most profitable trade') to show that they come apart, and which metaethical position from day 11 each target presupposes.
sources: Chouldechova, 'Fair Prediction with Disparate Impact', Big Data 5 (2017); Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan, 'Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores' (2016), arXiv:1609.05807
Nissenbaum, Privacy in Context (Stanford 2010); Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (Now 2014); NTSB, Highway Accident Report HWY18MH010 (2019)

Gabriel, 'Artificial Intelligence, Values, and Alignment', Minds and Machines 30 (2020): 411–437; Matthias, 'The Responsibility Gap', Ethics and Information Technology 6 (2004); Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics', 'Privacy and Information Technology', 'The Ethics of Manipulation'

days.subject: Philosophy
days.topic: The ethics of risk and future generations
days.headline_hint: How Much Is a Life in the Year 2200 Worth This Morning? Stern, Nordhaus and the Number That Decides
days.focus: The capstone: decisions that impose risk on people who cannot consent and on people who do not yet exist — risk-weighted expected utility and the precautionary principle made precise, the Ramsey discount rule with Stern's and Nordhaus's parameters and what a pure time preference of zero costs, Parfit's non-identity problem, longtermism and the fanaticism objection with Ord's existential-risk estimates, Weitzman's dismal theorem under fat-tailed climate sensitivity, the paradoxes of deterrence, and what an intergenerational theory of justice finally requires. Graduate level, drawing on the whole block; the reader afterwards can carry a real policy through the discount rate, the person-affecting principle and the fanaticism test, naming the premise that carries each step.
parts: Risk to whom? Expected utility against Buchak's risk-weighted utility, the precautionary principle made precise, and the one-in-a-million standard
Discounting the future: the Ramsey rule with Stern's and Nordhaus's numbers, why Parfit and Broome say pure time preference is indefensible, and Weitzman's declining rate
The non-identity problem: depletion, the fourteen-year-old mother, and why 'harming future people' needs a principle we do not have
Longtermism and fanaticism: the expected value of the far future, Ord's one in six, Pascal's mugging returned, and the epistemic case against
Catastrophe: Weitzman's dismal theorem with the IPCC's fat tail, the paradoxes of deterrence, and when cost-benefit analysis stops working
What we owe the future, decided: Rawls's just savings, Jonas's imperative of responsibility, Scheffler's afterlife conjecture, and the reader's own ledger
worked_examples: The Ramsey rule r = δ + ηg with Stern's parameters (δ = 0.1%, η = 1) and Nordhaus's (δ = 1.5%, η = 2) at a growth rate of 1.3%: discount rates of 1.4% and 4.1%, so that $1 trillion of damage in the year 2200 is worth about $61 billion today on Stern's numbers and about $0.27 billion on Nordhaus's — a factor of roughly 220 that rests entirely on δ and η, which are ethical parameters; then Parfit's Appendix F and Broome's argument that δ > 0 is discrimination by date of birth.

Parfit's Depletion case (Reasons and Persons §123) and the fourteen-year-old girl (§120): the policy that lowers the quality of life two centuries hence also changes who is conceived, so no one who lives is worse off than they would otherwise have been — the narrow and wide person-affecting principles each applied, and the conclusion that either the intuition or the principle must go.

Ord's 2020 estimates — total existential risk this century one in six, of which unaligned AI one in ten, engineered pandemics one in thirty, nuclear war and climate one in a thousand each, asteroid one in a million — used with Greaves and MacAskill's 10^16 potential future lives to compute the expected value of a 0.1-percentage-point risk reduction, showing why fanaticism results, then Tarsney's 2023 epistemic challenge and Thorstad's objection that the value of risk reduction depends on background risk.

Weitzman's dismal theorem run on the IPCC AR6 climate-sensitivity range (likely 2.5–4 °C, very likely 2–5 °C, best estimate 3 °C): with a fat-tailed posterior and constant relative risk aversion η = 2, the expected marginal utility of consumption diverges, and the willingness to pay to remove the tail is unbounded — what that says about the discounting exercise above and about what the precautionary principle was trying to express.
sources: Parfit, Reasons and Persons (Oxford 1984), chs. 16–19 and Appendix F; Broome, Climate Matters: Ethics in a Warming World (Norton 2012)

Nordhaus, 'A Review of the Stern Review on the Economics of Climate Change', Journal of Economic Literature 45 (2007): 686–702; Weitzman, 'On Modeling and Interpreting the Economics of Catastrophic Climate Change', Review of Economics and Statistics 91 (2009)
Ord, The Precipice (Bloomsbury 2020); Greaves & MacAskill, 'The Case for Strong Longtermism', GPI Working Paper 5-2021; Buchak, Risk and Rationality (Oxford 2013)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: 'Intergenerational Justice', 'The Nonidentity Problem', 'Risk', 'Climate Justice'

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Real analysis: metric spaces, completeness, uniform convergence
days.headline_hint: The Number Line Has No Holes, and That Is Why Anything Converges
days.focus: Rebuilds the limits of year-one day 9 on a foundation that can bear weight: metric spaces, Cauchy sequences and the construction of the reals as the completion of the rationals, compactness (Bolzano–Weierstrass, Heine–Borel), and the difference between pointwise and uniform convergence that decides when a limit may pass through an integral or a derivative. Ends with the Banach contraction-mapping theorem, proved in full and immediately put to work on Kepler's equation. Afterwards the reader can state exactly which property of the reals a convergence argument is using, recognise when an interchange of limits is illegal, and turn a fixed-point iteration into a convergence guarantee with an explicit error bound.
parts: Distance Is All You Need: Metric Spaces and What 'Close' Means Without Coordinates
Cauchy Sequences and the Holes in the Rationals: Completeness Constructed, Not Assumed
Compactness: Why Every Bounded Sequence in R^n Surrenders a Convergent Subsequence
Pointwise Is Not Enough: Uniform Convergence and When Limits Commute with Integrals
The Contraction Mapping Theorem: One Proof That Solves Kepler's Equation and Guarantees Every ODE
worked_examples: Kepler's equation E = M + e sin E for Mars (e = 0.0934) at mean anomaly M = 30°, iterated as a contraction with constant e: the fixed point 0.574341 rad reached to 1e-7 in six iterations, against the bound e^n |E_1 − E_0|; then a Molniya-class orbit (e = 0.74), where the same bound predicts thirty iterations for four decimals and the geometric slowdown is visible

√2 has no rational Cauchy limit (the classical proof), then Newton's iteration x ← (x + 2/x)/2 from 1.5: 1.41667, 1.414216, 1.41421356237…, with the number of correct digits doubling each step exactly as the quadratic-convergence theorem promises

f_n(x) = x^n on [0,1]: pointwise limit discontinuous, sup-norm distance to the limit equal to 1 forever, and what that costs; then the Weierstrass M-test on the series for e^x on [−R, R], which is what makes term-by-term differentiation of the exponential legal (year-one day 24 used it without asking)

Continuity without uniform continuity: 1/x on (0,1] with the explicit ε–δ failure, and why Heine–Borel rescues it on [δ,1] — the compactness that makes every continuous function on a closed interval Riemann-integrable
sources: Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed. (McGraw-Hill, 1976), ch. 2–3, 7 and Theorem 9.23
Abbott, Understanding Analysis, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2015)
Tao, Analysis II, 4th ed. (Hindustan Book Agency/Springer, 2022)
Colwell, Solving Kepler's Equation over Three Centuries (Willmann-Bell, 1993)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Linear algebra at depth: the spectral theorem and numerical linear algebra
days.headline_hint: Every Symmetric Matrix Is Secretly a List of Stretches
days.focus: Year-one days 37 and 41 stated that symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors; today proves it, then builds the factorisations (LU, QR, Cholesky, Schur, SVD) that working software actually uses, the Perron–Frobenius theorem that governs Markov chains and PageRank, and the conditioning theory that says how many digits of a computed answer are real. Ends with how eigenvalues are really found: power iteration, Householder reflections and the shifted QR algorithm. Afterwards the reader can prove the spectral theorem, choose the right factorisation for a problem, factor a covariance matrix for simulation, and diagnose an ill-conditioned system before trusting its solution.
parts: The Spectral Theorem: Why a Symmetric Matrix Has Real Eigenvalues and Orthogonal Eigenvectors, Proved
Four Factorisations and What Each Is For: LU, QR, Cholesky, Schur — and the SVD Revisited Through Symmetry
Perron–Frobenius: Positive Matrices Have a Dominant Eigenvalue, and Markov Chains Have a Stationary State
Condition Numbers: How Much of Your Answer Is Real
How Eigenvalues Are Actually Computed: Power Iteration, Householder Reflections and the QR Algorithm
worked_examples: The one-year letter-rating transition matrix from Moody's Annual Default Study (the published table for the most recent year): Perron–Frobenius gives the stationary distribution by power iteration, the second eigenvalue gives the mixing time, and the row for Baa says how long an investment-grade credit takes to forget where it started

Cholesky factor of the 3×3 covariance matrix of monthly returns of the S&P 500, the 10-year Treasury (via TLT) and gold (via GLD), from Yahoo Finance closes 2016–2025: the triangular matrix L with LLᵀ = Σ, computed by hand, that turns independent normals into correlated ones for the Monte Carlo of day 12
The Hilbert matrix H_5 (condition number ≈ 4.8×10^5) and H_10 (≈ 1.6×10^13): solving Hx = b in double precision and counting the digits lost against the bound ‖δx‖/‖x‖ ≤ κ(H)·ε_machine
Three steps of the unshifted QR algorithm on a 3×3 symmetric matrix by hand, the off-diagonal decay at the rate |λ_2/λ_1|, and the Wilkinson shift that turns linear convergence cubic
sources: Trefethen & Bau, Numerical Linear Algebra (SIAM, 1997)
Golub & Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 4th ed. (Johns Hopkins, 2013)
Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed. (Springer, 2024)
Horn & Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed. (Cambridge, 2013), ch. 8 (Perron–Frobenius)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Measure, Lebesgue integration and the foundations of probability
days.headline_hint: How to Measure a Set So Badly Behaved It Has No Length — and Why Probability Needed It
days.focus: Why length cannot be assigned to every subset of the line (Vitali), how Lebesgue measure is built (outer measure, Carathéodory), and how integrating by slicing the range instead of the domain yields the three convergence theorems the Riemann integral of day 18 could never give. Then Kolmogorov's move: probability is measure with total mass one, random variables are measurable functions, independence is a product structure, and Borel–Cantelli and the strong law of large numbers follow as theorems — the strong law proved in full. Closes with Radon–Nikodym, the theorem that lets one measure be written as a density against another, which is the likelihood ratio of day 13 and the risk-neutral density of day 10. Afterwards the reader can say precisely what 'almost surely' means and prove it.
parts: Why Length Cannot Be Assigned to Every Set: Vitali's Construction and the Need for σ-Algebras
Building Lebesgue Measure: Outer Measure, Carathéodory's Criterion and the Sets That Pass
The Lebesgue Integral: Integrating by Slicing the Range, and the Three Convergence Theorems
Probability Is Measure with Total Mass One: Random Variables, Independence and Borel–Cantelli
The Strong Law of Large Numbers, Proved: Almost Sure Convergence and What 'Almost' Means
Radon–Nikodym: One Measure Written as a Density Against Another — the Likelihood Ratio, the Risk-Neutral Density
worked_examples: The Cantor set: total removed length Σ (1/3)(2/3)^k = 1, so measure zero — yet uncountable by the ternary-expansion bijection, and the Cantor function that climbs from 0 to 1 with derivative zero almost everywhere
Dirichlet's indicator of the rationals on [0,1]: Riemann integral undefined (every upper sum 1, every lower sum 0), Lebesgue integral 0 in one line because the rationals are a null set

The Radon–Nikodym derivative dQ/dP for one-year S&P 500 log-returns modelled as normal with drift 10% and volatility 16% under P versus drift r = 4.25% under Q: the density exp(−λZ − λ²/2) with market price of risk λ = 0.36, and the factor (about 2.2) by which it up-weights a −20% year

Borel–Cantelli both ways: independent daily 1-in-1,000 events occur infinitely often with probability one; events with p_n = 1/n² occur only finitely often — and why a 'once-in-a-century' flood that recurs is not a paradox
sources: Folland, Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications, 2nd ed. (Wiley, 1999)
Williams, Probability with Martingales (Cambridge, 1991), ch. 1–7
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed. (Cambridge, 2019), ch. 1–2
Tao, An Introduction to Measure Theory (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 126, 2011)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Martingales
days.headline_hint: A Fair Game Cannot Be Beaten, and the Proof Is a Stopping Time
days.focus: Conditional expectation defined properly (as a Radon–Nikodym derivative and as an orthogonal projection in L²), then filtrations, martingales, stopping times and Doob's optional stopping theorem, Doob's maximal inequality, the martingale convergence theorem, and Azuma–Hoeffding concentration. Every result is proved and then spent on something real: gambler's ruin at true casino odds, the waiting time for a pattern, the one-period binomial option and Samuelson's theorem that properly anticipated prices are martingales. Afterwards the reader can recognise a martingale, prove a betting system cannot work, and see why 'the discounted price is a martingale under Q' is a theorem rather than a slogan.
parts: Conditional Expectation Is a Projection: Defining E[X | G] via Radon–Nikodym and via Least Squares in L²
Filtrations, Martingales and Fair Games: Doob's Definition and the Examples That Are Not Random Walks
Stopping Times and the Optional Stopping Theorem: When You May Quit and Expect Nothing
Doob's Inequalities and the Martingale Convergence Theorem: Bounded Martingales Settle Down
Azuma–Hoeffding: Concentration for Bounded Increments, and What the Bound Is Worth on a Real Portfolio
Prices as Martingales: Samuelson's Theorem, the Binomial Model and the Fundamental Theorem in One Period
worked_examples: Gambler's ruin at American roulette (p = 18/38 on red): the probability of turning $1,000 into $2,000 in $10 bets is 2.66×10^−5, from the martingale (q/p)^{S_n} and optional stopping — and the same calculation for a single $1,000 bet (0.474), which is why the mathematics says bet big and rarely if you must bet at all
Waiting for ABRACADABRA: a monkey typing uniformly at random takes 26^11 + 26^4 + 26 keystrokes on average, proved with Williams' martingale of fair gamblers arriving one per keystroke

A one-month binomial call on SPY calibrated to 16% annual volatility (u = e^{0.16√(1/12)}, d = 1/u) with r = 4.25%: the risk-neutral probability q = (e^{rΔt} − d)/(u − d) is the unique one making the discounted price a martingale, and the hedge ratio that replicates the call

Azuma's bound on a 60/40 portfolio's 21-day drawdown given daily moves bounded by ±3%: P(loss > 15%) ≤ exp(−15²/(2·21·9)) ≈ 0.55 — an honest demonstration that a worst-case bound on bounded increments is nearly vacuous, and why the CLT and the GARCH model fitted in block 1 (Finance & Markets) day 3 are used instead
sources: Williams, Probability with Martingales (Cambridge, 1991), ch. 9–14
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed. (Cambridge, 2019), ch. 4
Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance I: The Binomial Asset Pricing Model (Springer, 2004)
Samuelson, 'Proof That Properly Anticipated Prices Fluctuate Randomly', Industrial Management Review 6 (1965); Azuma, Tôhoku Math. J. 19 (1967)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: ODEs and dynamical systems: existence and uniqueness, linearisation and Hartman–Grobman, Lyapunov functions, bifurcation theory and Poincaré–Bendixson
days.headline_hint: Where the Flow Goes: The Theorems Behind Every Phase Portrait, From Picard's Contraction to Hopf's Cycle
days.focus: The theory underneath the phenomena block 4 (Physics) day 5 showed. Existence and uniqueness of solutions proved by Picard iteration (the contraction of day 1) with Grönwall's inequality and the non-Lipschitz equation whose solutions are not unique; linear systems solved by the matrix exponential, so that the eigenvalues of day 2 draw the phase portrait; the qualitative theory near equilibrium — linearisation, the Hartman–Grobman theorem stated with its proof idea, stable and unstable manifolds, and Lyapunov's direct method with LaSalle's invariance principle proved; the theory of limit cycles in the plane — Poincaré–Bendixson proved from the Jordan curve theorem, Bendixson–Dulac ruling cycles out, Liénard's theorem ruling one in; and bifurcation theory done properly — saddle-node, transcritical, pitchfork and Hopf as normal forms, with the centre-manifold reduction that justifies them. Chaos enters only as a definition: the Lyapunov exponent as a number, computed exactly for the doubling map, so that the Lorenz, Feigenbaum and KAM phenomenology the Physics block has already shown has its theorem-shaped meaning. Afterwards the reader can prove a solution exists and is unique, classify an equilibrium from a Jacobian and say when linearisation is trustworthy, build a Lyapunov function, prove a limit cycle exists or cannot, and compute the normal form of a bifurcation.
parts: Existence and Uniqueness, Proved: Picard Iteration as a Contraction, Grönwall's Inequality, and the Equation x' = √|x| Whose Solutions Are Not Unique
Linear Systems and the Matrix Exponential: Eigenvalues Draw the Phase Portrait, and Lanchester's Square Law Is a Saddle
Near an Equilibrium: Linearisation, Hartman–Grobman, Stable and Unstable Manifolds, and the Centre That Linearisation Cannot Decide
Lyapunov's Direct Method: Energy Functions Without Energy, LaSalle's Invariance Principle, and Global Stability Proved
Cycles in the Plane: Poincaré–Bendixson Proved, Bendixson–Dulac Rules Cycles Out, Liénard Rules One In
Bifurcations as Normal Forms: Saddle-Node, Transcritical, Pitchfork and Hopf via the Centre Manifold — and Chaos Defined by the Lyapunov Exponent (ln 2 for the Doubling Map)
worked_examples: The damped pendulum θ'' + 0.5 θ' + sin θ = 0: Jacobians at (0,0) and (π,0), eigenvalues −0.25 ± 0.968i (spiral sink) and +0.781 / −1.281 (saddle), Hartman–Grobman licensing both local pictures, the energy E = θ'²/2 + 1 − cos θ as a Lyapunov function with Ė = −0.5 θ'² ≤ 0 and LaSalle's principle closing the gap where Ė = 0, and the saddle's stable manifold as the separatrix between swinging and rotating

Lanchester's 1916 square law x' = −a y, y' = −b x as a linear system: the matrix exponential in cosh(√(ab) t) and sinh(√(ab) t), eigenvalues ±√(ab), the saddle at the origin and the invariant hyperbolas b x² − a y² = constant that give the law its name; then Engel's 1954 fit to the Iwo Jima record (19 February – 26 March 1945; about 21,000 defenders against roughly 73,000 US troops landed in stages), the two attrition coefficients estimated from the daily returns, and the predicted US strength curve set against the actual one

The SIR model with births and deaths, S' = μN − βSI/N − μS, I' = βSI/N − (γ + μ)I: the disease-free equilibrium loses stability at R₀ = β/(γ + μ) = 1 in a transcritical bifurcation, the endemic equilibrium S* = N/R₀ is born at the same moment, and the Lyapunov function V = S − S* ln S + I − I* ln I (Korobeinikov & Wake 2002) proves it globally stable for R₀ > 1; then measles at R₀ = 12–18: a herd-immunity threshold 1 − 1/R₀ of 92–94%, an endemic mean age at infection L/(R₀ − 1) ≈ 4.6–7.2 years for a 79-year life expectancy (which is what pre-vaccine records show), and the CDC's most recent kindergarten MMR coverage figure (about 92.5% for the 2024–25 school year) read against the threshold

The Hopf bifurcation computed: the Van der Pol oscillator ẍ − μ(1 − x²)ẋ + x = 0 has a unique limit cycle for every μ > 0 by Liénard's theorem, of amplitude 2 + O(μ²) and period 2π + O(μ²) near the bifurcation (the normal-form coefficient worked out) and of period (3 − 2 ln 2)μ ≈ 1.614μ in the relaxation limit; then the same normal-form computation on the Hodgkin–Huxley 1952 squid-axon equations, where the resting state loses stability in a subcritical Hopf near an injected current of about 9.8 μA/cm², which is why a neuron's repetitive firing switches on at finite amplitude rather than growing from zero
sources: Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, 2nd ed. (Westview, 2015), ch. 5–8
Hirsch, Smale & Devaney, Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos, 3rd ed. (Academic Press, 2013)

Perko, Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, 3rd ed. (Springer, 2001); Guckenheimer & Holmes, Nonlinear Oscillations, Dynamical Systems, and Bifurcations of Vector Fields (Springer, 1983), ch. 3

Lanchester, Aircraft in Warfare (Constable, 1916) and Engel, 'A Verification of Lanchester's Law', Operations Research 2 (1954); Kermack & McKendrick, Proc. Roy. Soc. A 115 (1927) and Korobeinikov & Wake, Applied Mathematics Letters 15 (2002); van der Pol, Phil. Mag. 2 (1926); Hodgkin & Huxley, J. Physiol. 117 (1952)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Partial differential equations: heat, wave, Laplace
days.headline_hint: Kelvin's Wrong Answer: How the Heat Equation Dated the Earth and What It Missed
days.focus: The three model equations of mathematical physics and why they behave so differently: classification by characteristics, the heat equation's Gaussian kernel and maximum principle (and why it cannot run backwards), d'Alembert's solution and energy conservation for the wave equation, harmonic functions and the mean-value property for Laplace. Separation of variables is derived rather than recited, with the Sturm–Liouville theory that explains why the eigenfunctions are orthogonal and a series solution is inevitable. The lesson closes on Kelvin's 1862 half-space cooling calculation, reproduced to his 96-million-year answer, and on the physics (convection, radioactivity) that made it wrong. Afterwards the reader can solve each of the three equations on a real domain and say what uniqueness theorem guarantees the answer.
parts: Three Equations, Three Worlds: Why Heat, Wave and Laplace Behave So Differently (Classification and Characteristics)
The Heat Equation: The Gaussian Kernel, the Maximum Principle, and Why Time Cannot Run Backwards
The Wave Equation: D'Alembert's Formula, Energy Conservation and the Plucked String
Laplace's Equation: Harmonic Functions, the Mean-Value Property and Uniqueness for Steady States
Separation of Variables and Sturm–Liouville: Why Eigenfunctions Are Orthogonal and Series Solutions Are Inevitable
Kelvin Dates the Earth: The Half-Space Cooling Problem, Its 96-Million-Year Answer, and Perry's Objection
worked_examples: Kelvin's 1862 calculation reproduced: a half-space initially at 3,900 °C cooling by conduction with diffusivity κ = 1.2×10^−6 m²/s until the surface gradient falls to 1 °F per 50 ft (36.5 K/km) gives t = T₀²/(πκG²) ≈ 96 million years; then Perry's 1895 objection (a convecting interior) and radioactive heating, which turn the same equation into a 4.5-billion-year-consistent one

The low E string of a 25.5-inch-scale guitar (82.41 Hz, L = 0.648 m): wave speed c = 2Lf = 106.8 m/s, the tension from a real string's published linear density, and the harmonic amplitudes d'Alembert's formula predicts for a pluck at one-fifth of the length (the fifth harmonic absent)

The annual temperature wave into the ground at Bridgeville with soil diffusivity ≈ 5×10^−7 m²/s: e-folding depth √(2κ/ω) ≈ 2.2 m and a phase lag that puts the coldest soil at that depth in late spring — the frost-line and cellar arithmetic

Steady temperature in a square plate with three sides at 0 °C and one at 100 °C: the sine-series solution with coefficients 400/π, 0, 400/(3π), …, the value at the centre 25 °C confirmed by the superposition symmetry, and the mean-value property checked numerically
sources: Evans, Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed. (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 19, 2010)
Strauss, Partial Differential Equations: An Introduction, 2nd ed. (Wiley, 2008)
Carslaw & Jaeger, Conduction of Heat in Solids, 2nd ed. (Oxford, 1959)

W. Thomson (Kelvin), 'On the Secular Cooling of the Earth', Trans. Roy. Soc. Edinburgh 23 (1862); England, Molnar & Richter, 'John Perry's neglected critique of Kelvin's age for the Earth', GSA Today 17(1) (2007)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Complex analysis: Cauchy, residues, conformal maps
days.headline_hint: One Derivative Buys Infinitely Many: The Strange Rigidity of Complex Functions
days.focus: The Cauchy–Riemann equations and what complex differentiability really demands; Cauchy's theorem and integral formula proved, and the consequences that make the subject feel like magic — infinitely many derivatives from one, Liouville, Taylor and Laurent series, the classification of singularities and the residue theorem. Residues are then used to evaluate real integrals and Fourier and Laplace transforms; the argument principle is turned into the Nyquist stability criterion of control engineering; and conformal maps carry Laplace's equation from a circle to an airfoil (Joukowski) with the lift computed. Afterwards the reader can evaluate integrals by contour, count zeros of a polynomial in a region, and see why a closed-loop system's stability is a winding number.
parts: Holomorphic Means Rigid: Cauchy–Riemann, and Why a Complex Derivative Is a Rotation-and-Scale
Cauchy's Theorem and Integral Formula: The Boundary Knows the Interior, So One Derivative Buys Them All
Liouville, Taylor, Laurent: Entire Functions Are Boring, Singularities Are Classified, and the Residue Is Born
The Residue Theorem at Work: Real Integrals, Fourier Transforms and Laplace Inversion Done by Contour
The Argument Principle Counts Zeros: Rouché, and Nyquist's Stability Criterion for a Control Loop
Conformal Maps: Angles Preserved, Laplace's Equation Transported, and Joukowski's Circle Becomes a Wing
worked_examples: ∫ dx/(1 + x²) = π and ∫ cos(kx)/(1 + x²) dx = π e^{−|k|} by the residue at i: the characteristic function of the Cauchy distribution, its non-differentiability at 0, and the proof that this distribution has no mean — the CLT that day 8 will prove fails for it, on purpose

Nyquist's criterion for the loop G(s) = K/(s(s+1)(s+2)): the Nyquist plot's crossing of the real axis at −K/6, the encirclement count of −1 changing as K passes 6, agreement with Routh–Hurwitz on s³ + 3s² + 2s + K, and the gain margin a pitch autopilot lives on

The Joukowski transform ζ = z + a²/z applied to a circle offset by (−0.1a, 0.1a): the cambered airfoil it draws, the Kutta condition fixing the circulation Γ = 4πaV sin(α + β), and the lift per unit span L' = ρVΓ at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) for V = 50 m/s and α = 4°
Bromwich inversion of the Laplace transform 1/√s: the keyhole contour around the branch cut and the recovery of 1/√(πt), the signature of the half-space heat problem from day 6
sources: Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, 3rd ed. (McGraw-Hill, 1979)
Stein & Shakarchi, Complex Analysis (Princeton, 2003)
Needham, Visual Complex Analysis (Oxford, 1997)
Anderson, Fundamentals of Aerodynamics, 6th ed. (McGraw-Hill, 2017), ch. 4; Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, 5th ed. (Pearson, 2010), ch. 7 (the Nyquist criterion)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Fourier and harmonic analysis
days.headline_hint: Any Signal Is a Sum of Tones — and the Central Limit Theorem Falls Out of the Transform
days.focus: Fourier's claim that any periodic function is a sum of sines, and its rescue: Dirichlet's and Fejér's convergence theorems, the Gibbs overshoot computed exactly, and Carleson's theorem stated. Then the transform on the line — inversion, Plancherel's isometry, convolution, with the residue calculus of day 7 doing the evaluations — used three ways: to solve the heat equation of day 6 by the kernel, to prove the central limit theorem of year-one day 57 through characteristic functions and Lévy's continuity theorem, and to state the uncertainty principle as a theorem about functions that quantum mechanics inherits. Ends with sampling (Shannon–Nyquist), aliasing, the discrete transform and the FFT. Afterwards the reader can prove the CLT, bound its error, and read a spectrum.
parts: Fourier's Claim and Its Rescue: Convergence of Fourier Series — Dirichlet, Fejér, Gibbs's 8.95% and Carleson
The Fourier Transform on the Line: Inversion, Plancherel's Isometry, and Convolution Turned into Multiplication
The Heat Kernel by Transform, and the Characteristic Function: The Central Limit Theorem Proved via Lévy Continuity
The Uncertainty Principle Is a Theorem About Functions: Gaussians Saturate It, and Quantum Mechanics Inherits It
Sampling and the Discrete Transform: Shannon's Theorem, Aliasing, and the FFT That Made It All Computable
worked_examples: The square wave's partial sums: the overshoot converging to (1/π)Si(π) − 1/2 = 8.949% of the jump, computed from the Dirichlet kernel, and why no number of terms removes it while Fejér averaging does

The CLT for daily S&P 500 returns proved via characteristic functions, then the Berry–Esseen bound with C ≤ 0.4748 (Shevtsova 2011) evaluated using the realised third absolute moment of 2000–2025 daily returns: how many trading days the normal approximation needs to be within 1% in the tail, and why fat tails push that number up

The Mauna Loa monthly CO₂ record (NOAA GML, 1958–present) through the FFT: the quadratic trend removed, the annual line and its harmonics, the seasonal amplitude (about 3 ppm) read off the spectrum and the sampling theorem applied to monthly data

CD audio at 44.1 kHz: the Nyquist limit at 22.05 kHz, a 30 kHz tone aliasing to 14.1 kHz, and the operation count of Cooley–Tukey on 2^16 samples (≈ 5×10^5 complex multiplications against ≈ 4×10^9 for the naive DFT)
sources: Stein & Shakarchi, Fourier Analysis: An Introduction (Princeton, 2003)
Körner, Fourier Analysis (Cambridge, 1988)
Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed. (Cambridge, 2019), ch. 3; Shevtsova, 'On the absolute constants in the Berry–Esseen type inequalities', arXiv:1111.6554 (2011)
Cooley & Tukey, 'An Algorithm for the Machine Calculation of Complex Fourier Series', Math. Comp. 19 (1965); Shannon, 'Communication in the Presence of Noise', Proc. IRE 37 (1949)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Brownian motion and Itô calculus
days.headline_hint: The Path That Wiggles at Every Scale: Building Brownian Motion and Learning to Integrate Against It
days.focus: What a continuous random path must be (Bachelier 1900, Einstein 1905, Wiener 1923), Kolmogorov's extension theorem guaranteeing it exists, and Lévy's explicit construction on the Haar basis with the uniform convergence of day 1 doing the work. Then the two facts everything else rests on — nowhere differentiable, yet finite and deterministic quadratic variation — and the Itô integral built from them: why Riemann–Stieltjes fails, why the left endpoint matters, and the isometry that defines the integral on L². Itô's lemma is proved, applied to geometric Brownian motion, and read backwards: realised variance from intraday prices is quadratic variation. Afterwards the reader can construct Brownian motion, compute an Itô integral from the definition, and apply Itô's lemma correctly with the second-order term.
parts: From Bachelier to Wiener: What a Continuous Random Path Must Be, and Kolmogorov's Guarantee That It Exists
Constructing Brownian Motion: Lévy's Interpolation, the Haar Basis and Uniform Convergence Doing the Work
Nowhere Differentiable, Yet Finite Quadratic Variation: The Property Everything Else Follows From
The Itô Integral: Why Riemann Fails, Why the Left Endpoint Matters, and the Isometry That Defines It
Itô's Lemma, Proved: The Second-Order Term, and the Geometric Brownian Motion It Solves
Realised Variance Is Quadratic Variation: Reading Volatility Off Intraday Prices
worked_examples: Realised variance of SPY from its 78 five-minute returns on a named trading day versus the squared close-to-close return, annualised and compared with that day's VIX close: quadratic variation estimated, with the Andersen–Bollerslev–Diebold–Labys trade-off between sampling frequency and microstructure noise made explicit

The Lévy–Ciesielski construction carried to level 4 on [0,1] with actual Gaussian draws: the path at the 16 dyadic points, the Schauder-function increments, and the sup-norm bound on the remainder that proves uniform convergence

Itô on ln S for dS = μS dt + σS dW with the S&P 500's long-run nominal estimates μ ≈ 10%, σ ≈ 16%: the −σ²/2 = −1.28% per year drag on the median path, and $10,000 for 30 years growing to a mean of $200,900 but a median of $136,800 — the volatility drag year-one day 40 could only name

∫₀^T W dW = (W_T² − T)/2 computed from the Itô definition on a partition (the −T is the quadratic variation appearing), contrasted with the Stratonovich answer W_T²/2, and what the difference means for a hedger who cannot see the future
sources: Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance II: Continuous-Time Models (Springer, 2004), ch. 3–4
Karatzas & Shreve, Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus, 2nd ed. (Springer, 1991)
Mörters & Peres, Brownian Motion (Cambridge, 2010)
Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold & Labys, 'Modeling and Forecasting Realized Volatility', Econometrica 71 (2003); Itô, 'Stochastic Integral', Proc. Imp. Acad. Tokyo 20 (1944)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: SDEs, Girsanov, Feynman–Kac and Black–Scholes as a PDE
days.headline_hint: Change the Measure, Not the Price: Girsanov, Feynman–Kac and Black–Scholes Rewritten as Heat
days.focus: Stochastic differential equations with existence and uniqueness, and the three models every desk uses (geometric Brownian motion, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck/Vasicek, Cox–Ingersoll–Ross with its Feller condition). Feynman–Kac, proved, ties every parabolic PDE to an expectation; Girsanov's theorem makes the Radon–Nikodym derivative of day 3 dynamic and changes a drift by changing a measure; and the Black–Scholes equation of year-one day 99 is derived by delta-hedging, transformed by an explicit change of variables into the heat equation of day 6, and solved by the heat kernel to recover the formula. Ends with the fundamental theorem of asset pricing and a term structure from the Vasicek bond price. Afterwards the reader can derive, transform and solve the pricing PDE, and say which measure a given expectation is taken under and why.
parts: Stochastic Differential Equations: Existence, Uniqueness, and the Three Models Everyone Uses (GBM, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck/Vasicek, CIR)
Feynman–Kac: Every Parabolic PDE Is an Expectation, and Every Expectation Solves a PDE
Girsanov's Theorem: Changing the Drift by Changing the Measure — the Radon–Nikodym Derivative of Day 3 Made Dynamic
Black–Scholes as a PDE: Delta-Hedging Derives It, a Change of Variables Turns It Into the Heat Equation, and the Heat Kernel Prices the Call
The Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing: No Arbitrage ⇔ an Equivalent Martingale Measure, and What Goes Wrong Without Completeness
Bond Prices from a Short-Rate SDE: Vasicek's Closed Form and the Term Structure It Implies
worked_examples: Vasicek with the Chan–Karolyi–Longstaff–Sanders (1992) estimates on the 1964–1989 one-month T-bill (κ ≈ 0.18, θ ≈ 8.7%, σ ≈ 2%): mean-reversion half-life ln 2/κ ≈ 3.9 years, the zero-coupon price P(t,T) = A(τ) e^{−B(τ) r} for a 10-year bond from r = 4.25%, and the yield curve it draws against the actual Treasury curve on the run date

The Black–Scholes PDE to the heat equation: the substitution S = Ke^x, t = T − 2τ/σ², V = K e^{αx + βτ} u(x, τ) with α and β computed explicitly (α = −(k−1)/2, β = −(k+1)²/4, k = 2r/σ²), and the day-99 call price recovered for a listed SPX call on the run date (strike, expiry and Cboe implied volatility named)

Girsanov for the S&P 500 with μ = 10%, r = 4.25%, σ = 16%: market price of risk λ = 0.36, the density process exp(−λW_t − λ²t/2), and the one-year probability of a fall of more than 20% under P (about 2.6%) versus under Q (about 5.7%) — the same event, two measures, and why put prices look 'expensive' to a P-thinker

The Feller condition 2κθ ≥ σ² for CIR checked on the CKLS CIR estimates, and what a violation means for the short rate reaching zero — with the 2009–2015 and 2020–2021 zero-bound episodes as the empirical test

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Convex optimisation and duality
days.headline_hint: Every Convex Problem Carries a Shadow Problem, and the Shadow Tells the Price
days.focus: Convex sets and functions, the separating hyperplane theorem, and why for convex problems a local minimum is global; Lagrange duality with weak duality always and strong duality under Slater's condition, proved; the KKT conditions and the economic meaning of a multiplier as a shadow price. Linear programming through Stigler's diet problem and Dantzig's simplex, quadratic programming through the Markowitz frontier of year-one day 62 solved exactly, then L1 sparsity (LASSO), the Kelly criterion as concave growth maximisation, and a sketch of interior-point methods. Afterwards the reader can recognise a convex problem, write its dual, read a multiplier as a price, and solve a mean–variance portfolio by hand.

Lagrange Duality: The Dual Function, Weak Duality Always, Strong Duality Under Slater — Proved

Linear Programming and the Diet Problem: Simplex, the Dual Diet, and Stigler's $39.69
Quadratic Programs and the Markowitz Frontier: Solving Mean–Variance Exactly, With and Without Short Sales
Beyond the Textbook: L1 and Sparsity (LASSO), the Kelly Criterion as Concave Growth, and Interior-Point Methods

Markowitz with three assets — the S&P 500, the 10-year Treasury and gold — using the 2016–2025 monthly means and the covariance factored on day 2: the KKT system solved by hand, the minimum-variance weights, the tangency portfolio at r = 4.25%, and the multiplier on the return constraint equal to the slope of the frontier

Kelly at American-roulette odds (edge negative, f* < 0, so do not play) versus a 55/45 even-money edge: f* = 2p − 1 = 10%, growth 0.50% per bet, the half-Kelly compromise, and the drawdown distribution that explains why practitioners take less

LASSO on a five-factor regression of a fund's returns on the Fama–French factors: the subgradient KKT condition that sets a coefficient to exactly zero, and the value of λ at which momentum drops out of the fit
