days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Numerical methods and error control
days.headline_hint: The Missile That Missed by 0.34 Seconds: Error, Its Control, and the Art of Computing Honestly
days.focus: Floating point as a finite set with rounding rules (IEEE 754), the cancellation and accumulation errors that follow, and two real disasters they caused; root finding with convergence orders proved (bisection, Newton, secant); quadrature with derived error terms (trapezoid, Simpson, Romberg, Gauss–Legendre); ODE integrators from Euler to adaptive Runge–Kutta and the symplectic methods orbits require; Monte Carlo with its 1/√N law, variance reduction and Euler–Maruyama for the SDEs of day 10. Closes with backward error and conditioning as the discipline for reporting a computed number. Afterwards the reader can choose a method, bound its error, and say how many digits of a result to believe.

Root Finding: Bisection's Guarantee, Newton's Speed, and Convergence Orders Proved

Propagating the ISS (NORAD 25544, a real two-line element on the run date) for one day at 10-second steps with forward Euler, RK4 and Störmer–Verlet: the energy drift of each, the position error against the next day's TLE, and why the symplectic method's energy error stays bounded

Gauss–Legendre with five nodes on the Black–Scholes integral ∫ (Ke^x − K)⁺ φ(x) dx against the closed form of day 10, then Simpson at the same cost; the degree-9 exactness demonstrated on a polynomial and the kink at the strike explaining why the error is worse than the theorem promises

Monte Carlo pricing of an arithmetic-average Asian call on the S&P 500 (σ = 16%, r = 4.25%, one year, monthly fixings): the plain estimator's standard error at N = 100,000, then antithetic variates and a geometric-Asian control variate, with the variance-reduction factor measured rather than assumed

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Likelihood, Fisher information and the theory of testing
days.headline_hint: The Likelihood Knows the Answer's Precision Before You Do — Fisher's Bound and the Drift You Cannot Estimate
days.focus: Year-one day 61 said what a p-value is; today builds the theory underneath: sufficiency and the factorisation theorem, Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound proved by Cauchy–Schwarz, the asymptotic theory of maximum likelihood (consistency, normality, efficiency), and the trinity of tests (likelihood ratio, Wald, score) with the Neyman–Pearson lemma proved. The second half is about how testing goes wrong in practice — multiple comparisons, the garden of forking paths, boundary problems, and the t = 3 hurdle now applied to published factors — and about power and severity. Afterwards the reader can compute a standard error from the information matrix, derive a test, and judge a published t-statistic for what it is worth.

Fisher Information and the Cramér–Rao Bound: The Precision Limit, Proved via Cauchy–Schwarz
Maximum Likelihood Asymptotics: Consistency, Normality, Efficiency — and the Drift You Cannot Estimate
The Trinity of Tests — Likelihood Ratio, Wald, Score — and Neyman–Pearson's Lemma, Proved
Multiple Testing and the Garden of Forking Paths: Bonferroni, Benjamini–Hochberg, and the t = 3 Hurdle for Factors
Power, Effect Size and Severity: What a Non-Rejection Means and When a Rejection Means Nothing
worked_examples: Estimating GBM's drift from 1957–2025 daily S&P 500 closes: the MLE μ̂ has standard error σ/√T = 16%/√68 ≈ 1.9 percentage points regardless of sampling frequency (Merton 1980), while σ̂'s standard error σ/√(2n) shrinks with every extra observation — the 2×2 Fisher information matrix computed explicitly and the equity premium shown to be a parameter the data barely constrain

The Cramér–Rao bound for a Bernoulli p from n trials, p(1 − p)/n, attained by the sample proportion; then the Cauchy location model of day 7, where the sample mean has no variance at all and the MLE achieves the bound 2/n

Harvey, Liu and Zhu's 316 published factors: with Bonferroni at 5% the per-test p-value is 1.58×10^−4 (t ≈ 3.78), with Benjamini–Hochberg the hurdle lands near t ≈ 3.0, and the momentum and value t-statistics from the Fama–French data library judged against each

The likelihood-ratio test of GARCH(1,1) against constant variance on daily S&P 500 returns: Wilks' theorem gives χ² with 2 degrees of freedom, the statistic is in the hundreds, and the boundary at α = β = 0 where Wilks' theorem does not apply and the null distribution is a mixture

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Bayesian inference and MCMC
days.headline_hint: Belief as a Distribution You Cannot Write Down — So You Walk Through It Instead
days.focus: Bayes at full strength: conjugate updating, Laplace's rule of succession, where priors come from (Jeffreys' invariance, reference and hierarchical priors) and why 'flat' is a choice. Then the machinery that made Bayesian computation possible: Markov chains and their stationary laws with the ergodic theorem MCMC rests on (Perron–Frobenius from day 2, martingale tools from day 4), Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs sampling derived from detailed balance, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo borrowed from mechanics, and the diagnostics (R̂, effective sample size) that say whether a chain has converged. Ends with Black–Litterman as Bayes on a real portfolio. Afterwards the reader can write a posterior, sample it, diagnose the sampler, and read a Black–Litterman allocation as a prior-times-likelihood.

Where Priors Come From: Jeffreys' Invariance, Reference Priors, Hierarchies, and Why 'Flat' Is a Choice

Metropolis–Hastings and Gibbs: Sampling a Posterior You Can Only Evaluate Up to a Constant
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo: Borrowing Physics to Explore High Dimensions, and Diagnosing When a Chain Has Not Converged
Black–Litterman as Bayes: Equilibrium as Prior, Views as Data, and the Portfolio That Results

Black–Litterman with three assets (US equities, EAFE equities, US aggregate bonds) at their current market-cap weights, risk aversion δ = 2.5, τ = 0.05 and one view (EAFE outperforms US by 2% with stated uncertainty): the implied equilibrium returns Π = δΣw, the posterior mean by the Black–Litterman formula, and the resulting weights, each step with numbers

Metropolis–Hastings on the Vasicek posterior using the CKLS T-bill parameters of day 10 as a synthetic truth: a Gaussian random-walk proposal, acceptance rate tuned toward 25–40%, trace plots, R̂ across four chains and the effective sample size against the nominal 40,000 draws

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on a 100-dimensional correlated Gaussian: leapfrog steps, the Hamiltonian error that sets the acceptance rate, and the comparison with a random-walk proposal that needs thousands of steps to cross the distribution once

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Information theory
days.headline_hint: Surprise, Measured in Bits: Shannon's Theorems and the Gambler Who Rediscovered Them
days.focus: Entropy from Shannon's axioms with the uniqueness proof, the source-coding theorem with Kraft's inequality and Huffman's optimality proved, relative entropy and mutual information (with Fisher information of day 13 as the curvature of KL), and the noisy-channel theorem with Shannon–Hartley applied to a real deep-space link. Then Kelly's 1956 discovery that a gambler's optimal growth rate is a channel capacity — closing the loop with day 11 — and cross-entropy as the quantity language models are trained on and measured by. Afterwards the reader can compute an entropy, build an optimal code, size a communication link, and read a bits-per-token figure as a statement about a model's knowledge.
parts: Entropy Is Expected Surprise: Shannon's Axioms, the Uniqueness Proof, and the Entropy of English
Source Coding: Kraft's Inequality, Huffman's Optimality Proof, and Why You Cannot Compress Below H
Relative Entropy and Mutual Information: KL as the Cost of the Wrong Model, Fisher Information as Its Curvature
Channel Capacity: The Noisy-Channel Theorem, Shannon–Hartley, and Voyager's 160 Bits per Second from 25 Billion Kilometres
Kelly's Discovery: The Growth Rate of a Gambler's Wealth Is a Channel Capacity
Cross-Entropy in Practice: Language Models Measured in Bits per Token, and the Maximum-Entropy Origin of the Exponential Family

Voyager 1's downlink: 22.4 W at X-band through a 3.7 m high-gain antenna to a 70 m Deep Space Network dish at about 24.7 billion km — free-space loss ≈ 319 dB, the received power in watts, the noise floor at the receiver's system temperature, and Shannon–Hartley's capacity set beside the actual 160 bits per second (JPL DESCANSO)

KL(P‖Q) between the physical and risk-neutral one-year S&P 500 return distributions of day 10: λ²/2 = 0.065 nats, and by Stein's lemma the number of years of returns needed to tell the two measures apart at a stated error rate

Kelly on the 55/45 even-money bet of day 11: growth rate = 1 − H(0.55) = 0.0072 bits per bet, identical to the 0.50% per-bet log growth found there; then GPT-2 (Radford et al. 2019) at 0.93 bits per byte on enwik8 against the 4.18 bits of letter-frequency coding — what a language model has learned, in bits

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: State-space models and the Kalman filter as Bayesian recursion, with the spectral view
days.headline_hint: The Filter That Flew to the Moon Is Bayes' Rule Run Forward: State Space, Kalman, and the Spectrum of a Series
days.focus: Block 1 (Finance & Markets) day 3 fitted AR, unit-root, cointegration and GARCH models to real series and stated GARCH without derivation; today supplies the theory those models sit inside and then goes where they cannot. A review part restates stationarity, Wold's theorem and ARMA/GARCH in one pass and shows that every one of them is a special case of the linear Gaussian state-space model. The state-space form is then built properly — local level, local linear trend, seasonal, dynamic regression, ARMA in companion form, stochastic volatility — and the Kalman filter is derived as recursive Bayes (Gaussian prior times Gaussian likelihood; the conditional-expectation projection of day 4), with the Riccati recursion, its steady state and the prediction-error decomposition that makes the likelihood computable, so hyperparameters are estimated by maximum likelihood (day 13) or sampled (day 14). Smoothing (Rauch–Tung–Striebel), missing observations and the disturbance smoother follow. The spectral view completes it: the spectral density as the Fourier transform (day 8) of the autocovariance, the periodogram, Whittle's likelihood, and the Wiener–Kolmogorov filter of which Kalman's is the finite-sample, time-domain form. Non-linear and non-Gaussian extensions (extended, unscented and particle filters) are defined and left to the Rocketry block's navigation lesson for the engineering. Afterwards the reader can write any classical series model in state-space form, run and smooth a Kalman filter by hand, estimate its hyperparameters, read a spectrum, and say what the filter is assuming when it is trusted.
parts: What Finance Day 3 Fitted, Restated as Theory: Stationarity, Wold's Theorem, and ARMA and GARCH as Special Cases of One State-Space Form
The Linear Gaussian State-Space Model: Local Level, Local Linear Trend, Seasonal, Dynamic Regression, Companion-Form ARMA and Stochastic Volatility
The Kalman Filter as Recursive Bayes: Predict, Update, the Riccati Recursion and Its Steady State — Derived, Then Run by Hand
Smoothing, Missing Data and the Likelihood: Rauch–Tung–Striebel, the Prediction-Error Decomposition, and Hyperparameters by Maximum Likelihood or MCMC
The Spectral View: Spectral Density as the Fourier Transform of Autocovariance, the Periodogram, Whittle's Likelihood, and the Wiener–Kolmogorov Filter Kalman Made Recursive
Beyond Linear and Gaussian: Extended, Unscented and Particle Filters Defined — and the Apollo Structure Handed to the Rocketry Block for the Engineering
worked_examples: The local-level model on the Nile annual flow at Aswan (Durbin & Koopman's 1871–1970 series): the Kalman recursion for the first three years by hand from a diffuse prior, the maximum-likelihood variances σ²_ε ≈ 15,099 and σ²_η ≈ 1,469 with signal-to-noise ratio q ≈ 0.097, the steady-state gain from the Riccati equation, the Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoothed level, and the 1899 drop (the year the Aswan dam works began) that the smoothed state reveals and the filtered state only suspects

Trend inflation as an unobserved component: the Stock–Watson (2007) model π_t = τ_t + ε_t, τ_t = τ_{t−1} + η_t run on quarterly core PCE inflation (FRED PCEPILFE, 1960–2025) — the constant-variance version by exact maximum likelihood through the prediction-error decomposition, the filtered trend through 2021–22, how much of the 2022 spike the filter assigned to the permanent component in real time versus in smoothed hindsight, and why the stochastic-volatility version needs the sampler of day 14

The spectrum of a series: the spectral density of an AR(1) with φ = 0.9, f(ω) ∝ 1/(1 − 2φ cos ω + φ²), whose ratio f(0)/f(π) = ((1 + φ)/(1 − φ))² = 361 says where the variance lives; then the periodogram of quarterly US real GDP growth (FRED GDPC1, 1947–2025) with the 6–32-quarter business-cycle band of Baxter and King (1999) read off it, the band-pass filter as a window in the frequency domain, and the Whittle likelihood compared with the exact Kalman likelihood on the same series

A one-dimensional tracking filter for a rocket's altitude: radar with 50 m noise, an accelerometer with 0.1 m/s² noise, the two-state model, the gains from the Riccati recursion run to steady state, the innovation sequence checked for whiteness — the same structure the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory used for Apollo's onboard navigation (McGee & Schmidt 1985), with the full strapdown error-state engineering left to the Rocketry block

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Abstract algebra: groups, rings, fields, symmetry
days.headline_hint: Symmetry Is a Group, and Groups Decide What Equations Can Be Solved
days.focus: Groups as symmetry made precise, with Lagrange's theorem proved through cosets, homomorphisms and quotients with the first isomorphism theorem, group actions and Burnside's counting; rings and fields with polynomial rings, ideals and the finite field GF(2^8) that AES computes in; Galois's idea that solvability of an equation is a property of a group, with the unsolvability of the quintic sketched honestly; and continuous symmetry — Lie groups, SO(3), quaternions and gimbal lock, and Noether's theorem tying symmetry to conservation. Afterwards the reader can prove Lagrange's theorem, multiply in a finite field, compose rotations without singularities, and explain why there is no quintic formula.
parts: Groups Are Symmetry Made Precise: Axioms, Examples, and Lagrange's Theorem Proved Through Cosets
Homomorphisms, Normal Subgroups and Quotients: The First Isomorphism Theorem and What It Lets You Ignore
Group Actions and Counting: Orbits, Stabilisers, Burnside's Lemma and the Rubik's Cube's 4.3×10^19
Rings and Fields: Polynomials, Ideals, Finite Fields, and the GF(2^8) Arithmetic Inside AES
Galois's Idea: Why the Quintic Has No Formula — Solvability as a Property of a Group
Continuous Symmetry: Lie Groups, SO(3), Quaternions, Gimbal Lock, and Noether's Theorem
worked_examples: The Rubik's cube group: the order 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 from the orbit–stabiliser count (8!·3^8·12!·2^12)/12, the three parity constraints that supply the divisor 12, and Lagrange's theorem applied to the subgroup generated by one face turn
Multiplying in GF(2^8) with AES's polynomial x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1: the FIPS 197 example {57}·{83} = {c1} by hand, and the MixColumns step of FIPS 197 §5.1.3 applied to one real state column

Apollo's three-gimbal inertial platform and Collins' July 1969 'fourth gimbal for Christmas' remark: Euler angles as a chart of SO(3) that fails at 90° pitch, and the unit quaternion (a point on S³ double-covering SO(3)) that composes two named spacecraft rotations with no singularity

Burnside's lemma counting the distinct two-colourings of a cube's faces (10 = (2^6 + 6·2^3 + 3·2^4 + 8·2^2 + 6·2^3)/24), and the crystallographic restriction that allows only 17 wallpaper groups and forbids five-fold symmetry — until Shechtman's 1982 quasicrystals

Artin, Algebra, 2nd ed. (Pearson, 2011)
