days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Computability, complexity and cryptography
days.headline_hint: What Cannot Be Computed, What Cannot Be Computed Quickly, and the Arithmetic Fact That Holds Up the Internet
days.focus: Three questions in one lesson, each with its theorem. What can be computed at all: Turing machines, the Church–Turing thesis, the universal machine, and the halting problem proved by diagonalisation — the theorem block 5 (Philosophy) day 1 only pointed to — with Rice's theorem and the busy-beaver function as its concrete face. What can be computed quickly: time classes, P and NP, polynomial-time reductions, Cook–Levin sketched and NP-completeness carried through one reduction by hand, coNP, and what P = NP would and would not mean. And what that hardness can be turned into: one-way functions and pseudorandomness, then the number theory RSA actually needs — Euclid and Bézout, the Chinese remainder theorem, Euler's theorem, exponentiation by squaring, Miller–Rabin — trimmed to that and no more. RSA and Diffie–Hellman with correctness proved and hardness assumptions named, semantic security and padding, the TLS 1.3 handshake as Diffie–Hellman on Curve25519, elliptic curves with the group law and secp256k1's ECDSA, and Shor's algorithm as the reason BQP is not believed to sit inside P, with the resource estimates and the post-quantum standard (FIPS 203) the migration rests on. Afterwards the reader can prove a problem undecidable by reduction, place a problem in P or show it NP-complete, run RSA and a Diffie–Hellman exchange by hand, double a point on an elliptic curve, and say what a quantum computer would and would not break.
parts: What a Computer Is: Turing's Machine, the Church–Turing Thesis, the Universal Machine, and the Halting Problem Proved by Diagonalisation
The Uncomputable Made Concrete: Rice's Theorem, the Busy Beaver, and Why BB(5) = 47,176,870 Was Only Settled in 2024
P, NP and Reductions: Cook–Levin, One NP-Completeness Proof Carried Through by Hand, coNP, and What P = NP Would Actually Mean
Hardness You Can Use: One-Way Functions, Pseudorandomness, and the Number Theory RSA Needs (Euclid, Bézout, CRT, Euler, Miller–Rabin) — No More
RSA, Diffie–Hellman and TLS 1.3: Correctness Proved, Hardness Assumptions Named, Padding and Semantic Security, and the Handshake Run on Curve25519
Elliptic Curves and the Quantum Threat: The Group Law, secp256k1 and ECDSA, Shor's Order-Finding via the Quantum Fourier Transform of Day 8, and the ML-KEM (FIPS 203) Migration
worked_examples: The halting problem proved by diagonalisation in full, then made concrete: Radó's busy-beaver function BB(n) grows faster than any computable function, BB(5) = 47,176,870 steps was settled only in 2024 by the bbchallenge collaboration with a Coq-verified proof, and BB(6) already exceeds 10↑↑15 — the arithmetic reason no program will ever decide halting in general — alongside the reduction that shows Rice's theorem makes every non-trivial semantic property of programs undecidable

NP-completeness carried through by hand: 3-SAT reduced to CLIQUE on the formula (x ∨ y ∨ ¬z) ∧ (¬x ∨ y ∨ z) ∧ (x ∨ ¬y ∨ z) — nine vertices, edges between compatible literals in different clauses, a 3-clique found and read back as a satisfying assignment; then the scale hardness reaches in practice: the Boolean Pythagorean triples problem (Heule, Kullmann & Marek 2016), where 7,824 is the largest n admitting a two-colouring, settled by a SAT solver in two days on 800 cores with a 200-terabyte proof — NP-hard in theory, solved in fact, and what that does and does not say about P versus NP

RSA by hand and at scale: p = 61, q = 53, e = 17 give n = 3233, φ(n) = 3120, d = 2753 by the extended Euclidean algorithm, m = 65 encrypted to c = 2790 and decrypted back; then RSA-2048 key generation with real arithmetic — the prime number theorem makes a random odd 1024-bit integer prime about one time in 355, Miller–Rabin with 64 rounds leaves a composite a chance below 4^−64 ≈ 3×10^−39 of passing, e = 65537 as the fast public exponent — set against RSA-250 (829 bits) factored in February 2020 with about 2,700 core-years by the number field sieve, whose L(1/3) running time is why 2048 bits is still out of reach classically

The Diffie–Hellman exchange inside TLS 1.3, traced on RFC 8448's published handshake: Curve25519 with p = 2^255 − 19 and base point u = 9, the client's and server's 32-byte X25519 key shares as printed in RFC 8448 §3, the Montgomery ladder that computes the shared secret, and HKDF-Extract/Expand (RFC 8446 §7.1) turning it into the handshake traffic keys; the group law itself worked by hand on the small model y² = x³ + 7 over F₁₇ — secp256k1's curve with a toy prime — with point doubling by the tangent formula and the order of the group counted
sources: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed. (Cengage, 2013), ch. 3–5 and 7
Arora & Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach (Cambridge, 2009); Katz & Lindell, Introduction to Modern Cryptography, 3rd ed. (CRC, 2021)

Turing, 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem', Proc. London Math. Soc. 42 (1936); Cook, 'The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures', STOC (1971); Rivest, Shamir & Adleman, CACM 21 (1978); Diffie & Hellman, IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 22 (1976); Heule, Kullmann & Marek, 'Solving and Verifying the Boolean Pythagorean Triples Problem via Cube-and-Conquer', SAT 2016 (LNCS 9710)

RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3, 2018), RFC 8448 (Example Handshake Traces for TLS 1.3, 2019) and RFC 7748 (Curve25519/X25519, 2016); SEC 2: Recommended Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters v2.0 (Certicom, 2010); NIST FIPS 203 (2024); Shor, SIAM J. Computing 26 (1997); Gidney & Ekerå, Quantum 5, 433 (2021)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Graph theory and networks
days.headline_hint: The Shape of Who Connects to Whom: From Königsberg's Bridges to the Banks That Fail Together
days.focus: Graphs from Euler's bridges onward — degrees, trees, Cayley's formula — then flows and cuts with max-flow min-cut proved as the LP duality of day 11, spectral graph theory (the Laplacian, Fiedler's vector, Cheeger's inequality) with the linear algebra of day 2, random walks and PageRank as a Markov chain with the damping factor explained, random-graph theory (the Erdős–Rényi giant component, small worlds, heavy tails), and contagion on a financial network through Eisenberg–Noe's clearing vector on real interbank topology. Afterwards the reader can compute a max-flow and its dual cut, a Fiedler partition, a PageRank vector and a clearing vector, and read a network statistic for what it implies about fragility.
parts: Euler's Bridges and the Birth of the Subject: Degrees, Paths, Trees and Cayley's n^{n−2}
Flows and Cuts: Max-Flow Min-Cut as LP Duality, Menger's Theorem, and Dijkstra's Shortest Paths
Spectral Graph Theory: The Laplacian, Fiedler's Vector, Cheeger's Inequality and What Eigenvalues Say About Cutting a Graph
Random Walks and PageRank: A Markov Chain on the Web, Perron–Frobenius Again, and the Damping Factor 0.85
Random Graphs and Real Networks: Erdős–Rényi's Giant Component, Small Worlds, Heavy Tails
Contagion on a Network: Eisenberg–Noe's Clearing Vector and the Topology of Interbank Payments
worked_examples: PageRank on a seven-page web by power iteration with d = 0.85: the Google matrix, the dangling-node fix, the stationary vector to four decimals after 20 iterations, and the convergence rate set by the damping factor (Brin & Page 1998)

The Fedwire interbank payment network (Soramäki et al. 2007): roughly 6,600 banks and 70,000 daily links, a 25-bank core that is almost completely connected, a degree distribution with a power-law tail, and what the Cheeger constant of such a core–periphery graph says about how a shock spreads

Eisenberg–Noe on a four-bank system with stated interbank liabilities and outside assets: the clearing vector found by the fictitious-default algorithm, the bank whose shortfall cascades, and the fixed-point theorem (the lattice version of day 1's idea) that guarantees it exists
Erdős–Rényi with n = 10,000 and mean degree c = 1.5: the giant-component fraction from S = 1 − e^{−cS} (≈ 0.583), and the Fiedler vector of a two-community stochastic block model recovering the split
sources: Diestel, Graph Theory, 5th ed. (Springer GTM 173, 2017)
Newman, Networks, 2nd ed. (Oxford, 2018)
Chung, Spectral Graph Theory (AMS CBMS 92, 1997)

Eisenberg & Noe, 'Systemic Risk in Financial Systems', Management Science 47 (2001); Soramäki, Bech, Arnold, Glass & Beyeler, 'The Topology of Interbank Payment Flows', Physica A 379 (2007); Brin & Page, Computer Networks and ISDN Systems 30 (1998)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Manifolds, differential forms, Stokes' theorem in full generality, connections and Gauss–Bonnet
days.headline_hint: Sixty Corners, Twelve Degrees Each: Why Every Closed Surface Adds Up to 720°, and What a Bug on It Can Measure
days.focus: The geometry the Physics block used and did not build. Block 4 (Physics) days 8–9 wrote Christoffel symbols and the Riemann tensor to do relativity; today constructs the mathematics beneath them and goes where relativity never needed to: manifolds and charts (coordinates are local and optional), tangent vectors as derivations, differential forms with the exterior derivative and d² = 0, integration on oriented manifolds and Stokes' theorem proved in full generality — with Green, Gauss and the classical Stokes of year-one day 76 falling out as the cases k = 1 and 2 — and de Rham's idea that a closed form which is not exact detects a hole. Then Riemannian structure: the metric, the Levi-Civita connection characterised and computed, parallel transport and holonomy, the Riemann tensor as the failure of transport to return, Gauss's Theorema Egregium proved, and Gauss–Bonnet in its local form (a geodesic triangle's angle excess is its integrated curvature) and its global form (total curvature equals 2πχ, so a topological number constrains geometry everywhere). The capstone is a count, not a metric: Descartes' angle-defect theorem on a real polyhedral surface, which is Gauss–Bonnet with the curvature concentrated at the corners. Afterwards the reader can integrate a form over a manifold, apply Stokes' theorem in any dimension, compute Christoffel symbols and Gauss curvature from a metric, transport a vector around a loop and predict its rotation, and verify Gauss–Bonnet on a surface he can hold.
parts: Manifolds and Charts: Coordinates Are Local and Optional — the Sphere Has No Global Map, and Tangent Vectors Are Derivations
Differential Forms and the Exterior Derivative: d² = 0, Wedge Products, and Why Every Vector-Calculus Identity Is One Identity
Integration on Manifolds and Stokes' Theorem in Full Generality, Proved: Green, Gauss and the Classical Stokes as the Cases k = 1 and 2
Closed but Not Exact: The Angle Form on the Punctured Plane, Winding Numbers, and de Rham's Idea That Forms Detect Holes
Connections and Curvature: The Levi-Civita Connection, Christoffel Symbols, Parallel Transport and Holonomy, the Riemann Tensor, and the Theorema Egregium Proved
Gauss–Bonnet, Local and Global: A Geodesic Triangle's Excess Is Its Curvature, a Closed Surface's Total Curvature Is 2πχ, and Descartes Counted It at the Corners
worked_examples: Descartes' angle-defect count on the truncated icosahedron — the C₆₀ molecule of Kroto et al. (1985) and the football: 60 vertices, 90 edges, 32 faces (12 pentagons, 20 hexagons), V − E + F = 2, a defect of 360° − (108° + 120° + 120°) = 12° at every vertex and 60 × 12° = 720° = 4π in total, which is Gauss–Bonnet with the curvature concentrated at the corners; then Császár's polyhedral torus (7 vertices, 21 edges, 14 triangles, χ = 0), whose defects — positive on the outer rim, negative inside — sum to exactly zero

Stokes' theorem checked in two dimensions and then used in one: for F = (−y, x, 0), the flux of curl F = (0, 0, 2) through the upper unit hemisphere and the circulation around the equator are both 2π; then the angle form ω = (x dy − y dx)/(x² + y²) on the punctured plane — dω = 0 everywhere, yet ∮ω = 2π around the unit circle, so ω is closed but not exact and its integral counts windings; the argument principle of day 7, (1/2πi)∮ f′/f dz, is exactly this form pulled back through f

The Theorema Egregium on the WGS 84 ellipsoid (a = 6,378,137 m, 1/f = 298.257223563) at Bridgeville's latitude 40.36° N: the metric in (φ, λ), its Christoffel symbols, the meridional and prime-vertical radii M = 6,362,213 m and N = 6,387,109 m, and the Gauss curvature 1/(MN) = 2.46×10^−14 m^−2 computed from the metric alone; then the geodesic equations integrated from Pittsburgh International (40.4915° N, 80.2329° W) to Heathrow (51.4700° N, 0.4543° W): 5,971 km on the mean sphere, initial heading 049.5°, and the ellipsoidal correction

Holonomy and excess as integrated curvature: a vector parallel-transported once around the 40.36° N latitude circle returns rotated by 2π(1 − sin φ) = 126.9°, which is the curvature 1/R² times the polar cap's area — so a Foucault pendulum at Bridgeville precesses 360° × sin 40.36° = 233.1° per sidereal day (a full turn in 36.96 h, against 271.1° and 31.8 h at Foucault's Panthéon at 48.85° N); then the geodesic triangle Pittsburgh–Heathrow–São Paulo Guarulhos (sides Pittsburgh–Heathrow 5,971 km, Pittsburgh–Guarulhos 7,920 km, Heathrow–Guarulhos 9,460 km) with angles 97.89°, 70.27° and 53.25° summing to 221.41°, whose excess of 41.41° = 0.7227 rad times R² = 6,371² km² gives an area of 2.93×10^7 km², 5.75% of the Earth's surface — Gauss–Bonnet's local form on a triangle you could fly
sources: Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds (Benjamin, 1965); Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed. (Springer GTM 218, 2012), ch. 14–17
do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces, revised 2nd ed. (Dover, 2016), ch. 4; Lee, Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, 2nd ed. (Springer GTM 176, 2018)

Richeson, Euler's Gem: The Polyhedron Formula and the Birth of Topology (Princeton, 2008); Kroto, Heath, O'Brien, Curl & Smalley, 'C60: Buckminsterfullerene', Nature 318 (1985); Császár, 'A polyhedron without diagonals', Acta Sci. Math. Szeged 13 (1949)
NIMA TR8350.2, Department of Defense World Geodetic System 1984, 3rd ed. (2000); Foucault, 'Démonstration physique du mouvement de rotation de la Terre au moyen du pendule', Comptes Rendus 32 (1851)

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: The state and its origins: Weber, Tilly, Olson
days.headline_hint: The Protection Racket That Learned to Keep Books
days.focus: Weber's definition of the state as the monopoly of legitimate violence over a territory; Tilly's bellicist account (war made the state and the state made war) with the coercion–capital typology and the consolidation count; Olson's stationary bandit and the McGuire–Olson derivation of the autocrat's tax rate under an encompassing interest; North, Wallis and Weingast's limited-access order; state capacity as fiscal, legal and administrative capacity in Besley and Persson. Graduate comparative politics. Afterwards the reader can distinguish the Weberian, contractarian and predatory accounts, derive the bandit's revenue-maximizing rate, and read a tax-to-GDP ratio as a measure of what a state can do.
parts: What a State Is: Weber's Definition and What It Leaves Out
War Made the State: Tilly's Bellicist Account and Its Numbers
The Stationary Bandit: Olson's Model and the Autocrat's Optimal Tax Rate
Limited-Access Orders: North, Wallis and Weingast on Violence and Rents
State Capacity as a Ladder: Fiscal, Legal and Administrative, Measured
worked_examples: Tilly's consolidation count — roughly 500 independent political units in Europe around 1500 to about 25 by 1900 (Tilly 1975; Coercion, Capital, and European States 1992) — read as a survival process, with the size-and-revenue threshold that killed the small units.

The McGuire–Olson stationary bandit: with a deadweight-loss function calibrated to a standard Laffer-curve elasticity, derive the revenue-maximizing tax rate for a bandit who consumes everything against one with an encompassing interest, then set both beside the OECD Revenue Statistics range (2023: OECD average 33.9% of GDP, United States 25.2%, Mexico 17.7%, France 43.8%; Denmark 45.2% in 2024).

Britain's fiscal-military state after 1688: the tax-revenue and debt series in Brewer's The Sinews of Power and O'Brien's fiscal data, 1688–1815, showing how excise plus a parliamentary credit commitment built a taxable capacity several times France's.

Besley and Persson's fiscal-capacity panel (Pillars of Prosperity, 2011): the share of GDP taxed and the income-tax share of revenue regressed on past external war and executive constraints — the sign and size of the war coefficient reconstructed.
sources: Max Weber, 'Politics as a Vocation' (1919), in From Max Weber: Essays in Sociology, ed. Gerth and Mills (Oxford, 1946); Weber, Economy and Society (1922; Roth and Wittich ed., California, 1978)

Charles Tilly, Coercion, Capital, and European States, AD 990–1992 (rev. ed., Blackwell, 1992); Tilly, 'War Making and State Making as Organized Crime', in Evans, Rueschemeyer and Skocpol (eds.), Bringing the State Back In (Cambridge, 1985)

Mancur Olson, 'Dictatorship, Democracy, and Development', American Political Science Review 87(3), 1993; McGuire and Olson, 'The Economics of Autocracy and Majority Rule', Journal of Economic Literature 34(1), 1996
North, Wallis and Weingast, Violence and Social Orders (Cambridge, 2009); Besley and Persson, Pillars of Prosperity (Princeton, 2011); OECD, Revenue Statistics 2025

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Theories of democracy: Schumpeter, Dahl, Przeworski and the deliberative turn
days.headline_hint: Democracy, Defined Down to Something You Can Count
days.focus: Schumpeter's competitive-elite definition; Dahl's polyarchy on the contestation–inclusion plane with its seven institutions; Przeworski's minimalist account of why losers comply; deliberative democracy from Habermas to Fishkin's deliberative poll and its measured effects; the measurement problem (Polity, Freedom House, V-Dem) and why the indices disagree; the modernization debate — Lipset, Przeworski–Limongi's exogenous-versus-endogenous result, Boix–Stokes, Acemoglu–Robinson. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can say which definition a dataset encodes, decompose a V-Dem index into its components, and state precisely what the income–democracy evidence does and does not show.
parts: The Competitive Struggle for the Vote: Schumpeter's Minimal Definition
Contestation and Inclusion: Dahl's Polyarchy and Its Seven Institutions
Why Losers Comply: Przeworski's Minimalist Democracy as an Equilibrium
Talking It Through: Deliberative Democracy from Habermas to the Deliberative Poll
Does Money Make Democrats? Lipset, Przeworski–Limongi and the Modernization Evidence
Counting Democracies: Polity, Freedom House and V-Dem, and Why They Disagree
worked_examples: Przeworski and Limongi's survival result (135 countries, 1950–1990): no democracy has fallen in a country richer than Argentina in 1975 ($6,055 per head in 1985 PPP dollars); the expected life of democracy by income band rebuilt from their transition probabilities.

V-Dem v15 (2025): the Liberal Democracy Index for the United States and Hungary, 2009–2024, decomposed into the electoral and liberal-component sub-indices and the expert-coding aggregation step (the Bayesian item-response model), to see which components moved and when.

Fishkin's 'America in One Room' (September 2019, 523 participants): the pre/post shifts on the 26 policy proposals and the measured fall in partisan polarization reported in Fishkin, Siu, Diamond and Bradburn (APSR 2021).

Dahl's two dimensions on three real cases: the United Kingdom before and after the 1918 and 1928 Representation of the People Acts, and South Africa in 1994, placed on the contestation–inclusion plane with the franchise numbers.
sources: Joseph Schumpeter, Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942; Harper Perennial, 2008), ch. 22; Robert Dahl, Polyarchy (Yale, 1971) and Democracy and Its Critics (Yale, 1989)

Przeworski, Alvarez, Cheibub and Limongi, Democracy and Development (Cambridge, 2000); Przeworski and Limongi, 'Modernization: Theories and Facts', World Politics 49(2), 1997; Lipset, 'Some Social Requisites of Democracy', APSR 53(1), 1959
Fishkin, Democracy When the People Are Thinking (Oxford, 2018); Fishkin, Siu, Diamond and Bradburn, 'Is Deliberation an Antidote to Extreme Partisan Polarization?', APSR 115(4), 2021
Coppedge et al., V-Dem Codebook v15 (2025); Boix and Stokes, 'Endogenous Democratization', World Politics 55(4), 2003

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Presidential, parliamentary and semi-presidential government; coalition formation and survival
days.headline_hint: Who Can Fire Whom: The One Question That Sorts the World's Democracies
days.focus: The Linz thesis on the perils of presidentialism and Cheibub's rebuttal that the military legacy explains the gap; Shugart and Carey's typology, including premier-presidential and president-parliamentary hybrids; confidence, dissolution and the vote that falls a government; coalition theory from Riker's minimal winning coalition to Laver–Shepsle portfolio allocation; Gamson's law and the formateur's bonus; cabinet duration as a hazard process. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can classify any constitution by the origin and survival of its executive, predict a portfolio split from seat shares, and read a hazard model of government termination.
parts: Two Questions Sort Every Constitution: Origin and Survival of the Executive
The Perils of Presidentialism — and Cheibub's Answer That It Was the Army All Along
Confidence, Dissolution and the Vote That Falls a Government
Who Gets Which Ministry: From Minimal Winning Coalitions to Gamson's Law
How Long Cabinets Live: Duration, Hazard and the Events That End Them
The Hybrids: Semi-Presidentialism, Cohabitation and the Fifth Republic
worked_examples: Cheibub's regime-survival data, 1946–2002: presidential democracies lived on average 24 years and parliamentary ones 58, and the military-legacy variable that absorbs the difference once it is in the hazard model.
The Callaghan government's fall on 28 March 1979: the no-confidence motion carried 311–310 — how the whips counted, what one absent member was worth, and the dissolution and election that followed.

Gamson's law on the 2021 German 'traffic-light' coalition: SPD 206, Greens 118 and FDP 92 Bundestag seats against the Scholz cabinet's ministry split, with the formateur's bonus measured as Warwick and Druckman measure it.

Israel's five elections from April 2019 to November 2022 as a case of failed formation: the 61-seat threshold, the 28-day mandate rule and the caretaker periods, read through Laver and Shepsle's portfolio-allocation model.
sources: Juan Linz, 'The Perils of Presidentialism', Journal of Democracy 1(1), 1990; José Antonio Cheibub, Presidentialism, Parliamentarism, and Democracy (Cambridge, 2007)
Shugart and Carey, Presidents and Assemblies (Cambridge, 1992); Laver and Schofield, Multiparty Government (Michigan, 1998 pb)
Strøm, Müller and Bergman (eds.), Cabinets and Coalition Bargaining (Oxford, 2008); Laver and Shepsle, Making and Breaking Governments (Cambridge, 1996)
Gamson, 'A Theory of Coalition Formation', American Sociological Review 26(3), 1961; Warwick and Druckman, 'The Portfolio Allocation Paradox', European Journal of Political Research 45(4), 2006

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Electoral systems, Duverger's law and the shape of party systems
days.headline_hint: The Formula That Turns 34% of the Votes into 63% of the Seats
days.focus: Majoritarian and proportional families and their formulas (plurality, runoff, ranked choice, list PR under D'Hondt and Sainte-Laguë, STV, MMP), with the divisor methods set up as a quotient matrix — each party's vote divided by the divisor sequence — whose largest entries pick the seats; district magnitude and thresholds as the master variables; Cox's M+1 rule and Duverger's mechanical and psychological effects, read as seat maximisation by parties deciding whether to enter and by voters deciding whether to desert; disproportionality (Gallagher) and fragmentation (Laakso–Taagepera); apportionment by Huntington–Hill; Lipset–Rokkan cleavages and the freezing hypothesis; Sartori's party-system typology and polarization. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can compute any allocation by hand from the quotient matrix, measure a system's disproportionality and effective number of parties, and predict how a rule change would reshape a party system.
parts: Votes into Seats: The Allocation Formulas as a Quotient Matrix, Worked by Hand
District Magnitude Is the Master Variable: Cox's M+1 Rule, Duverger's Two Effects and Entry as Seat Maximisation
Measuring the Damage: The Gallagher Index and the Effective Number of Parties
Apportionment Before Allocation: Huntington–Hill and the Seat Decided by 89 People
Where Parties Come From: Lipset–Rokkan Cleavages, Freezing and Realignment
Counting Party Systems: Sartori's Typology and the Measurement of Polarization
worked_examples: The 2024 UK general election: Labour's 33.7% of the vote and 411 of 650 seats; the Gallagher index of about 24 (the Electoral Reform Society's 24.4, the highest on record against 1983's 20.6), and the effective number of parties by votes and by seats.

D'Hondt and Sainte-Laguë on the 2023 Dutch general election (Kiesraad official return; 150 seats in one national district, PVV first with 37): the quotient matrix — each party's vote over 1, 2, 3, … and again over 1, 3, 5, … — with the 150 largest entries picking the seats, recomputed under both divisors and again with a hypothetical 5% threshold; then the same matrix on the 2025 Bundestag second votes (630 seats; CDU/CSU 28.5%, AfD 20.8%, SPD 16.4%, Greens 11.6%, Left 8.8%, with BSW at 4.97% and FDP at 4.3% below the threshold) beside the 735-seat chamber of 2021, swollen by overhang and levelling seats, that the 2023 reform was written to end.
Huntington–Hill on the 2020 census apportionment: the priority values that gave the 435th seat to Minnesota and left New York 89 residents short.

Duverger at the district level: Canada and India as the standing counterexamples, with Chhibber and Kollman's national-versus-district effective-number series, and the entry decision written as an optimisation — a third party enters where M+1 leaves it a seat to win and withdraws where it does not.
sources: Maurice Duverger, Political Parties (Wiley, 1954); Gary Cox, Making Votes Count (Cambridge, 1997); Taagepera and Shugart, Seats and Votes (Yale, 1989)
Gallagher, 'Proportionality, Disproportionality and Electoral Systems', Electoral Studies 10(1), 1991; Laakso and Taagepera, 'Effective Number of Parties', Comparative Political Studies 12(1), 1979

Lipset and Rokkan (eds.), Party Systems and Voter Alignments (Free Press, 1967); Sartori, Parties and Party Systems (Cambridge, 1976); Chhibber and Kollman, The Formation of National Party Systems (Princeton, 2004)

Balinski and Young, Fair Representation (2nd ed., Brookings, 2001); UK Electoral Commission and Kiesraad official results, 2024 and 2023; Bundeswahlleiterin, official results of the 2021 and 2025 Bundestag elections

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: The US constitutional order: separation of powers, federalism, the Senate, the filibuster and the Electoral College
days.headline_hint: Madison's Machine: How Many Hands Must Agree Before Anything Moves
days.focus: Federalist 10 and 51 as a theory of faction and ambition; Tsebelis's veto-player count for the United States; federalism as Riker's bargain and as fiscal federalism (Tiebout, Oates, Weingast), including the grant formulas that carry it; Senate malapportionment and the filibuster's rules and history (Rule XXII in 1917, the 1975 change to three-fifths, the 2013 and 2017 nuclear options, reconciliation and the Byrd rule); the Electoral College's mechanics, faithless electors and inversion probability; Article V rigidity. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can count the veto players on any bill, compute a state's FMAP, estimate an inversion probability, and say exactly what changed in 2013 and 2017.
parts: Ambition Counteracting Ambition: Federalist 10, 51 and the Veto-Player Count
The Federal Bargain: Riker, Tiebout, Oates and the Money That Holds It Together
The Senate: Malapportionment by Design and What It Buys
Rule XXII: The Filibuster's Arithmetic, Its History and the Two Nuclear Options
The Electoral College: Mechanics, Faithless Electors and the Probability of Inversion
Article V: Why the Constitution Almost Never Changes
worked_examples: Senate malapportionment from the 2020 census: Wyoming (576,851) against California (39,538,223), a 68-to-1 ratio, and the share of the national population that can elect a Senate majority, computed from the fifty state counts.

The FMAP formula in 42 U.S.C. §1396d(b) — FMAP = 1 − 0.45 × (state per-capita income ÷ US per-capita income)², floored at 50% and capped at 83% — applied to Pennsylvania's FY2026 percentage as published in the Federal Register, and what a one-point move is worth in federal dollars.

The 2016 result: 304 electoral votes to 227 on 46.1% to 48.2% of the popular vote (62,984,828 to 65,853,514); Chiafalo v. Washington (2020, 9–0) on the faithless electors; and Geruso, Spears and Talesara's (2022) inversion-probability estimates for a close election.

Cloture as a time series from the Senate's own table: 328 motions filed in the 116th Congress, 336 in the 117th, 266 in the 118th; the 52–48 votes of 21 November 2013 and 6 April 2017 that ended the 60-vote threshold for nominations.

connect_back.subject: Mathematics
connect_back.topic: Law of large numbers and the CLT

sources: Hamilton, Madison and Jay, The Federalist Papers (1787–88; Rossiter ed., Signet, 2003), Nos. 10, 47, 51, 62, 68, 78; George Tsebelis, Veto Players (Princeton, 2002); Dahl, How Democratic Is the American Constitution? (2nd ed., Yale, 2003)
Koger, Filibustering (Chicago, 2010); Wawro and Schickler, Filibuster (Princeton, 2006); Senate Rule XXII and the Senate's cloture-motion tables; 2 U.S.C. §644 (the Byrd rule)

Riker, Federalism: Origin, Operation, Significance (Little, Brown, 1964); Tiebout, 'A Pure Theory of Local Expenditures', JPE 64(5), 1956; Oates, Fiscal Federalism (1972); Weingast, 'The Economic Role of Political Institutions', JLEO 11(1), 1995; 42 U.S.C. §1396d(b)

Geruso, Spears and Talesara, 'Inversions in US Presidential Elections: 1836–2016', AEJ: Applied Economics 14(1), 2022; Lutz, 'Toward a Theory of Constitutional Amendment', APSR 88(2), 1994; Chiafalo v. Washington, 591 U.S. 578 (2020)

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Congress and the spatial model of legislating
days.headline_hint: The Line That Runs Through the Senate, and the Sixtieth Person Standing on It
days.focus: Black's median voter theorem under single-peaked preferences; Arrow's theorem and McKelvey's chaos in more than one dimension; Shepsle's structure-induced equilibrium and the committee system; Krehbiel's pivotal politics with the filibuster and veto pivots and the gridlock interval; Cox and McCubbins's cartel agenda control and the majority roll rate; Mayhew's electoral connection and the unified-versus-divided evidence; Poole–Rosenthal NOMINATE as measurement. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can derive the median-voter result, locate the pivots on real DW-NOMINATE scores, compute a gridlock interval, and read a roll-call scaling for what it is.
parts: Black's Theorem: Why the Median Wins When There Is One Dimension
Arrow and McKelvey: Why Anything Can Win When There Are Two
Structure-Induced Equilibrium: Committees, Rules and the Agenda as the Cure for Chaos
Pivotal Politics: The Filibuster Pivot, the Veto Pivot and the Gridlock Interval
The Cartel: Cox, McCubbins and Why the Majority Is Almost Never Rolled
The Electoral Connection, and What NOMINATE Actually Measures
worked_examples: Pivotal politics on real scores: the 118th Senate's DW-NOMINATE first-dimension positions (Voteview), the 41st and 60th senators, the 34th (veto) senator and the resulting gridlock interval, with the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (51–48 under reconciliation) and the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (51–50 with the Vice President) placed against it.
The 29 September 2008 House vote on the first TARP bill, 205–228: a leadership defeat read through the cartel model's roll rate, and the 263–171 passage on 3 October after the Senate's amended bill.

Mayhew's Divided We Govern count — 267 significant enactments 1946–1990 with no unified-versus-divided difference — against Binder's measure of gridlock as the share of the salient agenda left unenacted.
McKelvey in two dimensions with three legislators at real coordinates: an agenda that carries the outcome from any point to any other by a sequence of majority votes, built step by step.
sources: Duncan Black, 'On the Rationale of Group Decision-making', JPE 56(1), 1948; Arrow, Social Choice and Individual Values (2nd ed., Yale, 1963); McKelvey, 'Intransitivities in Multidimensional Voting Models', Journal of Economic Theory 12(3), 1976; Shepsle, AJPS 23(1), 1979
Keith Krehbiel, Pivotal Politics (Chicago, 1998); Cox and McCubbins, Setting the Agenda (Cambridge, 2005)
Mayhew, Congress: The Electoral Connection (2nd ed., Yale, 2004) and Divided We Govern (2nd ed., Yale, 2005); Binder, Stalemate (Brookings, 2003)
Poole and Rosenthal, Ideology and Congress (Transaction, 2007); Lewis et al., Voteview: Congressional Roll-Call Votes Database (voteview.com)

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: The presidency and executive power
days.headline_hint: The Power to Persuade, and the Pen That Doesn't Need To
days.focus: Neustadt's power as bargaining, reputation and prestige; Moe's politicized presidency; Howell's unilateral-action model set inside the gridlock interval; Kernell's going public and Edwards's evidence that it rarely moves opinion; Skowronek's political time; the legal architecture — Jackson's three zones in Youngstown, the War Powers Resolution, emergency powers under the National Emergencies Act and IEEPA, the removal power from Humphrey's Executor to Seila Law and the 2025–26 cases, with the Federal Reserve's carve-out (the Wilcox stay order's 'uniquely structured, quasi-private entity' and Trump v. Cook) as the live boundary of the unitary-executive claim, and Trump v. United States on immunity. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can place any executive act in Jackson's framework, model when a president acts alone, say where central-bank independence now rests in removal doctrine, and read the executive-order and veto record as data.
parts: Presidential Power Is the Power to Persuade: Neustadt's Bargaining President
Power Without Persuasion: Howell's Model of Unilateral Action Inside the Gridlock Interval
Going Public, and the Evidence That the Bully Pulpit Is Mostly a Pulpit
Jackson's Three Zones: Youngstown, the War Powers Resolution and Emergency Powers
Who Can the President Fire? Removal, the Unitary Executive, the Federal Reserve Carve-Out and the 2025–26 Cases
Political Time: Skowronek's Cycle of Reconstruction, Articulation and Disjunction
worked_examples: Executive orders as data from the Federal Register's disposition tables (Roosevelt 3,721; Truman 907; Obama 276; Trump 220 in the first term; Biden 162; the second Trump term's count through the day the lesson runs), normalized per year in office and read against unified and divided government.

The War Powers Resolution override of 7 November 1973: House 284–135 and Senate 75–18 over Nixon's veto, checked against the two-thirds requirement, and the sixty-day clock as presidents of both parties have actually treated it since.

Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer (1952, 6–3) and Trump v. United States (2024, 6–3): the steel seizure and the official-acts immunity holding each placed in Jackson's zones, with the IEEPA tariff cases (argued November 2025), Trump v. Slaughter on the FTC's removal protection (argued December 2025) and Trump v. Cook on a Federal Reserve governor's (argued January 2026) as the live cases — status and holdings checked the morning the lesson runs.
The second impeachment trial vote of 13 February 2021, 57–43 to convict against the 67 required: the supermajority as a design choice, set beside the 1868 (35–19) and 1999 (45–55 and 50–50) counts.
sources: Richard Neustadt, Presidential Power and the Modern Presidents (Free Press, 1990); Terry Moe, 'The Politicized Presidency', in Chubb and Peterson (eds.), The New Direction in American Politics (Brookings, 1985)

William Howell, Power without Persuasion (Princeton, 2003); Kernell, Going Public (4th ed., CQ Press, 2007); Edwards, On Deaf Ears (Yale, 2003); Skowronek, The Politics Presidents Make (Harvard, 1993)

Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952); Trump v. United States, 603 U.S. 593 (2024); Humphrey's Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935); Seila Law v. CFPB, 591 U.S. 197 (2020); Trump v. Wilcox, 605 U.S. ___ (2025) (stay order); War Powers Resolution, 50 U.S.C. §§1541–1548; IEEPA, 50 U.S.C. §§1701–1708
Federal Register, Executive Orders Disposition Tables; Senate Journal, impeachment trial roll calls (1868, 1999, 2020, 2021)

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Courts, judicial review and constitutional interpretation
days.headline_hint: Nine Votes, Three Theories of Why They Fall the Way They Do
days.focus: Marbury and the counter-majoritarian difficulty (Bickel) with Dahl's 1957 answer; the legal, attitudinal and strategic models of judicial behaviour and their tests (Segal–Cover scores, Epstein–Knight); Martin–Quinn dynamic ideal points and the median justice; the interpretive schools — originalism, textualism, purposivism, Dworkin's law as integrity, Balkin's living originalism — each stated at full strength with its best case; stare decisis and overrulings; Rosenberg on whether courts change anything; constitutional courts elsewhere (Kelsen, Karlsruhe, the UK Miller cases). Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can read a term's Martin–Quinn scores, predict a vote from a Segal–Cover score, and state each interpretive theory in the form its holders would accept.
parts: Marbury's Move and Bickel's Difficulty: Where Judicial Review Comes From and Why It Worries People
Three Models of the Judicial Mind: Legal, Attitudinal, Strategic — and How Each Is Tested
Measuring the Bench: Segal–Cover Scores, Martin–Quinn Ideal Points and the Median Justice
How to Read a Constitution: Originalism, Textualism, Purposivism and Law as Integrity, Each at Full Strength
Precedent as Capital: Stare Decisis, Overrulings and Dobbs
The Hollow Hope? What Courts Change, and Constitutional Courts Elsewhere
worked_examples: Martin–Quinn scores for the October 2023 and 2024 terms: the median justice located, the spread computed, and both set against the SCOTUSblog Stat Pack's unanimity rate and count of 6–3 ideological splits.

Segal–Cover scores against votes: the newspaper-editorial coding of nominees and its correlation with civil-liberties votes in Segal and Spaeth, extended to Barrett (confirmed 52–48, 2020) and Jackson (53–47, 2022), with Bork's 42–58 rejection in 1987 as the confirmation-politics benchmark.

Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization (2022): the 6–3 judgment and the 5–4 overruling of Roe read through the stare decisis factors the opinions themselves list, with Loper Bright's 6–3 overruling of Chevron in 2024 as the second data point.

Rosenberg's test on Brown v. Board: Southern Black students in integrated schools near zero in 1954–55 and still about 1% in 1964, before the 1964 Civil Rights Act and 1965 ESEA funding moved the number — the table, and the reply from Brown's defenders.
sources: Alexander Bickel, The Least Dangerous Branch (Bobbs-Merrill, 1962); Dahl, 'Decision-Making in a Democracy', Journal of Public Law 6, 1957; Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. 137 (1803)

Segal and Spaeth, The Supreme Court and the Attitudinal Model Revisited (Cambridge, 2002); Epstein and Knight, The Choices Justices Make (CQ Press, 1998); Martin and Quinn, 'Dynamic Ideal Point Estimation via Markov Chain Monte Carlo', Political Analysis 10(2), 2002
Scalia, A Matter of Interpretation (Princeton, 1997); Dworkin, Law's Empire (Harvard, 1986); Balkin, Living Originalism (Harvard, 2011); Rosenberg, The Hollow Hope (2nd ed., Chicago, 2008)
Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, 597 U.S. 215 (2022); Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024); SCOTUSblog Stat Packs OT2023 and OT2024

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Bureaucracy, the administrative state and regulation
days.headline_hint: The Fourth Branch: Who Controls the People Who Write the Rules
days.focus: Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy and Wilson's typology of agencies; Niskanen's budget-maximizer and Dunleavy's bureau-shaping reply; the principal–agent frame — McCubbins–Schwartz fire alarms, McNollgast's administrative procedures as control, Epstein–O'Halloran on when Congress delegates; capture (Stigler, Peltzman) and autonomy (Carpenter); the legal machinery — the APA's notice-and-comment and arbitrary-and-capricious review, Executive Order 12866, OMB Circular A-4 cost-benefit analysis and the value of a statistical life; Chevron to Loper Bright, the major-questions doctrine and nondelegation. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can read a regulatory impact analysis, judge a delegation under the current doctrines, and place an agency on Wilson's grid.
parts: Weber's Iron Cage and Wilson's Grid: What Agencies Are and How They Differ
Budget Maximizers and Their Critics: Niskanen, Dunleavy and the Evidence
Police Patrols, Fire Alarms and Procedure: How Congress Controls What It Cannot Watch
Capture and Autonomy: Stigler's Theory, Peltzman's Extension and Carpenter's Rebuttal
The Rulebook: The APA, Executive Order 12866 and the Cost-Benefit Analysis of a Real Rule
From Chevron to Loper Bright: Deference, Major Questions and Nondelegation
worked_examples: EPA's 2024 fine-particulate (PM2.5) standard, 12 to 9 micrograms per cubic metre: the regulatory impact analysis's up to $46 billion in net health benefits against $590 million in compliance costs in 2032 and up to 4,500 premature deaths avoided — rebuilt from the value of a statistical life (DOT's 2024 guidance of $13.7 million; EPA's own figure) and the concentration–response function, at the discount rates Circular A-4 requires.

Epstein and O'Halloran's discretion index applied to the 1934 Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act, Section 232 of the 1962 Trade Expansion Act and Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act — the delegated authority and constraints behind the 2025 tariff actions.
Stigler's trucking case: ICC route and entry regulation from 1935 to the Motor Carrier Act of 1980, with the change in freight rates and in the value of operating certificates as the capture test.
Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024, 6–3) and West Virginia v. EPA (2022, 6–3): the holdings stated exactly, and what each changes for a notice-and-comment rule an agency proposes tomorrow.
sources: James Q. Wilson, Bureaucracy (Basic Books, 1989); Niskanen, Bureaucracy and Representative Government (Aldine-Atherton, 1971); Carpenter, The Forging of Bureaucratic Autonomy (Princeton, 2001)

McCubbins and Schwartz, 'Congressional Oversight Overlooked', AJPS 28(1), 1984; McCubbins, Noll and Weingast, 'Administrative Procedures as Instruments of Political Control', JLEO 3(2), 1987; Epstein and O'Halloran, Delegating Powers (Cambridge, 1999); Stigler, 'The Theory of Economic Regulation', Bell Journal of Economics 2(1), 1971

Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. §§551–559, 701–706; Executive Order 12866 (1993); OMB Circular A-4 (2003, with the 2023 revision and its 2025 status); Loper Bright, 603 U.S. 369 (2024); West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697 (2022)
EPA, Regulatory Impact Analysis for the Final Revisions to the PM NAAQS (EPA-452/R-24-006, February 2024); US DOT, Departmental Guidance on Valuation of a Statistical Life (2024)

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Public opinion and voting behaviour
days.headline_hint: The Voter Who Isn't There: What Sixty Years of Surveys Say People Actually Do
days.focus: Converse's belief-systems finding on constraint and stability; the Michigan model's party identification as unmoved mover and the perceptual screen; Zaller's Receive-Accept-Sample model with its exposure–acceptance curves; retrospective and economic voting (Fiorina, Kinder–Kiewiet's sociotropic result, Lewis-Beck); Achen and Bartels's realist account and the rebuttals; the macro polity, policy mood and Wlezien's thermostat; the calculus of voting, turnout and the mobilization experiments; the fundamentals models. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can run a Zaller simulation, read the ANES panel evidence, and forecast a presidential vote share from fundamentals with its error band.
parts: Converse's Bombshell: Non-Attitudes, Constraint and the 1956–60 Panel
The Unmoved Mover: Party Identification and the Perceptual Screen
Receive, Accept, Sample: Zaller's Model of How Elites Move Opinion
Throwing the Rascals Out: Retrospective Voting, the Economy and What Voters Punish
Democracy for Realists and Its Critics: Shark Attacks, Blind Retrospection and the Rebuttals
Why Anyone Votes: Riker–Ordeshook, the Mobilization Experiments and the Fundamentals Models
worked_examples: Bartels's perceptual screen (2002): inflation fell from 13.5% in 1980 to 4.1% in 1988, yet in the 1988 ANES a majority of strong Democrats said it had got worse — the partisan gap tabulated by strength of identification.
Zaller's two-message model fitted to the Vietnam series: support for the war by political awareness among liberals and conservatives, 1964–1970, and why the most aware liberals turned first.

Gerber and Green's 1998 New Haven field experiment (29,380 registered voters): door-to-door canvassing raised turnout by roughly eight to nine points, direct mail by under one, phone calls not at all — the intent-to-treat and treatment-on-treated arithmetic.

Fundamentals for 2024: Abramowitz's time-for-change model and Fair's equation with the actual second-quarter growth, net approval and incumbency inputs, against the certified national result of 49.8% to 48.3%.
sources: Converse, 'The Nature of Belief Systems in Mass Publics', in Apter (ed.), Ideology and Discontent (Free Press, 1964); Campbell, Converse, Miller and Stokes, The American Voter (Wiley, 1960); Bartels, 'Beyond the Running Tally', Political Behavior 24(2), 2002

John Zaller, The Nature and Origins of Mass Opinion (Cambridge, 1992); Fiorina, Retrospective Voting in American National Elections (Yale, 1981); Erikson, MacKuen and Stimson, The Macro Polity (Cambridge, 2002)
Achen and Bartels, Democracy for Realists (Princeton, 2016); Fowler and Hall, 'Do Shark Attacks Influence Presidential Elections?', Journal of Politics 80(4), 2018

Riker and Ordeshook, 'A Theory of the Calculus of Voting', APSR 62(1), 1968; Gerber and Green, 'The Effects of Canvassing, Telephone Calls, and Direct Mail on Voter Turnout', APSR 94(3), 2000; ANES Cumulative Data File

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Polling methodology at depth, and a real election result decomposed
days.headline_hint: Plus or Minus Three Points, and Everything That Phrase Hides
days.focus: Sampling theory (simple-random-sample variance, the finite-population correction, the ±3.1 points for n = 1,000); design effects and effective sample size (Kish); weighting and raking; likely-voter screens; nonresponse and its partisan skew, with response rates fallen from 36% in 1997 to 6% in 2018; MRP; herding and aggregation; the AAPOR post-mortems for 2016 and 2020 and the 2024 miss measured; then the certified 2024 Pennsylvania result decomposed by county and by group with shift-share arithmetic into turnout and persuasion, using the validated-voter studies. Practitioner level. Afterwards the reader can compute a poll's true margin of error from its weights, judge a likely-voter screen, and decompose a swing into its parts.
parts: What a Margin of Error Is: Sampling Variance, the Finite-Population Correction and n = 1,000
Weights, Raking and the Design Effect: Why the Real Error Is Larger
Who Answers the Phone: Nonresponse, Partisan Skew and the 2016 and 2020 Post-Mortems
Likely Voters, MRP and Herding: The Modelling Choices Under the Number
The Certified Count: Pennsylvania 2024, County by County
Turnout or Persuasion? Shift-Share Decomposition of the Swing and the Polls' Error
worked_examples: A poll of n = 1,000 with p = 0.5: the ±3.1-point half-width; the same poll with raked weights whose coefficient of variation is 0.6, giving a Kish design effect of 1.36 and an effective n of about 735; then the margin on the Trump–Harris difference, roughly twice the margin on either share.

AAPOR's 2020 task-force numbers: national polls in the final two weeks overstated the Biden margin by 3.9 points and state polls by 4.3, the largest error since 1980; the 2016 state-poll error traced to unweighted education; and the 2024 national polling average set against the certified 49.8% to 48.3%.

Pennsylvania 2024, certified 4 December 2024: Trump 3,543,308, Harris 3,423,042 — a 120,266-vote, 1.7-point margin — decomposed against 2020 by county (Allegheny, Philadelphia, Lackawanna, Luzerne, Erie) into turnout change and margin change with the shift-share identity.

Wang, Rothschild, Goel and Gelman's Xbox poll (2015): about 750,000 responses from a sample 93% male and 65% under 30, corrected by multilevel regression and poststratification to a forecast within the error of the professional polls — the cells, and the shrinkage step.
sources: Leslie Kish, Survey Sampling (Wiley, 1965); Groves, Fowler, Couper, Lepkowski, Singer and Tourangeau, Survey Methodology (2nd ed., Wiley, 2009)

AAPOR Task Force on 2020 Pre-Election Polling (Clinton et al., 2021); Kennedy et al., 'An Evaluation of the 2016 Election Polls in the United States', Public Opinion Quarterly 82(1), 2018; Pew Research Center, 'Response Rates in Telephone Surveys Have Resumed Their Decline' (2019)

Wang, Rothschild, Goel and Gelman, 'Forecasting Elections with Non-Representative Polls', International Journal of Forecasting 31(3), 2015; Gelman, Goel, Rivers and Rothschild, 'The Mythical Swing Voter', Quarterly Journal of Political Science 11(1), 2016

Pennsylvania Department of State, certified 2024 general election returns (county-level); FEC, Federal Elections 2024; Catalist, 'What Happened 2024'; Pew Research Center, 2024 validated-voter study (2025)

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Political economy: Downs, the median voter, rent seeking and political business cycles
days.headline_hint: Why Politicians Converge, Why Lobbies Win and Why the Economy Warms Up Before a Vote
days.focus: Downs's model of party competition and rational ignorance; the Meltzer–Richard model of redistribution as a function of the mean-to-median income ratio; rent seeking — Tullock's rectangle against Harberger's triangle and Krueger's estimates; opportunistic and partisan political business cycles (Nordhaus, Hibbs, Alesina's rational partisan model) and the evidence; time inconsistency and central-bank independence (Kydland–Prescott, Rogoff) as the institutional response, tied to year one's monetary lesson; Persson and Tabellini on how constitutions shape fiscal outcomes. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can derive the Meltzer–Richard tax rate from real income data, size a rent-seeking loss, and test a political business cycle against FRED series.
parts: Downs: Parties as Firms, Voters as Customers and the Convergence to the Median
Rational Ignorance: Why the Median Voter Doesn't Know and Doesn't Need To
Meltzer and Richard: Redistribution as the Distance Between the Mean and the Median
Tullock's Rectangle: Rent Seeking, Krueger's Numbers and the Real Cost of a Licence
Political Business Cycles: Nordhaus, Hibbs, Alesina and the Data That Tests Them
Tying Ulysses: Time Inconsistency, Rogoff's Conservative Central Banker and Independence
worked_examples: Meltzer–Richard on Census P60-286 (income year 2024): median household income $83,730 against the mean from the same report — the mean-to-median ratio, the model's implied tax rate under a stated deadweight-loss parameter, and why the observed federal take is nowhere near it.

Krueger's rent-seeking estimates: import-licence rents at 7.3% of Indian national income in 1964 and about 15% of Turkish GNP in 1968, reconstructed from the premium-times-quantity method, with Tullock's argument that the whole rectangle is dissipated.

Nordhaus tested on FRED: US unemployment and real disposable income growth in the eight quarters before each presidential election since 1960, the Nixon–Burns 1971–72 episode from the tapes (Abrams 2006), and the 2024 easing cycle as the neutral contemporary comparison.
Downs with real positions: DW-NOMINATE-based estimates of candidate and voter positions in a 2024 Senate race, and the divergence from the median that Calvert–Wittman policy motivation predicts.
sources: Anthony Downs, An Economic Theory of Democracy (Harper, 1957); Meltzer and Richard, 'A Rational Theory of the Size of Government', JPE 89(5), 1981; Persson and Tabellini, Political Economics (MIT, 2000)
Tullock, 'The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft', Western Economic Journal 5(3), 1967; Krueger, 'The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society', AER 64(3), 1974

Nordhaus, 'The Political Business Cycle', Review of Economic Studies 42(2), 1975; Hibbs, 'Political Parties and Macroeconomic Policy', APSR 71(4), 1977; Alesina, Roubini and Cohen, Political Cycles and the Macroeconomy (MIT, 1997); Abrams, 'How Richard Nixon Pressured Arthur Burns', JEP 20(4), 2006

Kydland and Prescott, 'Rules Rather than Discretion', JPE 85(3), 1977; Rogoff, 'The Optimal Degree of Commitment to an Intermediate Monetary Target', QJE 100(4), 1985; US Census Bureau, Income in the United States: 2024 (P60-286)

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Collective action, interest groups and the money in politics
days.headline_hint: Why Four Thousand Sugar Growers Beat Three Hundred Million Consumers
days.focus: Olson's logic with the formal group-size result and selective incentives; Ostrom's commons and design principles as the empirical counter; Grossman–Helpman's protection-for-sale model and the Goldberg–Maggi estimate; the Tullock paradox and Ansolabehere, de Figueiredo and Snyder on why there is so little money in politics; lobbying as legislative subsidy (Hall–Deardorff) and the status-quo advantage in Baumgartner et al.; Schattschneider's upper-class accent and Gilens–Page; campaign finance law from Buckley to Citizens United with the 2024 cycle's numbers. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can derive the under-provision result, set up the Grossman–Helpman first-order condition, and read the lobbying-disclosure and FEC data for what they show.
parts: The Logic of Collective Action: Olson's Model and the Group That Cannot Organize
Governing the Commons: Ostrom's Cases and Design Principles as the Empirical Reply
Protection for Sale: Grossman–Helpman's Model and Goldberg–Maggi's Estimate
The Tullock Paradox: Why So Little Money Buys So Much — or Doesn't
Lobbying as Subsidy and the Status Quo's Advantage: What the Disclosure Data Show
Whose Chorus: Schattschneider, Gilens–Page and the Campaign Finance Regime After Citizens United
worked_examples: Olson's under-provision with numbers: a public good with linear benefit and quadratic cost across N members — equilibrium provision as a function of N, and the exploitation of the great by the small when one large member carries the burden.

The US sugar program: loan rates, tariff-rate quotas and marketing allotments; the USDA and GAO estimates of the consumer cost (roughly $2–4 billion a year across studies) against about 4,000 beet and cane farms, and the growers' reported lobbying and PAC totals — concentrated benefits and diffuse costs, per head.

Goldberg and Maggi (1999) on 1983 US tariff and non-tariff data: the estimated weight on welfare 50 to 88 times the weight on contributions, and what that implies for an organized sector's tariff in the Grossman–Helpman formula.

OpenSecrets 2024: $4.4 billion in federal lobbying (the National Association of Realtors first at $86.3 million; health the largest sector at $743.9 million) beside the roughly $15.9 billion 2024 election cycle — read against Ansolabehere et al.'s 'so little money' calculation.
sources: Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (2nd ed., Harvard, 1971); Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons (Cambridge, 1990); Schattschneider, The Semisovereign People (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1960)
Grossman and Helpman, 'Protection for Sale', AER 84(4), 1994; Goldberg and Maggi, 'Protection for Sale: An Empirical Investigation', AER 89(5), 1999

Ansolabehere, de Figueiredo and Snyder, 'Why Is There So Little Money in U.S. Politics?', JEP 17(1), 2003; Hall and Deardorff, 'Lobbying as Legislative Subsidy', APSR 100(1), 2006; Baumgartner, Berry, Hojnacki, Kimball and Leech, Lobbying and Policy Change (Chicago, 2009); Gilens and Page, Perspectives on Politics 12(3), 2014

Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1 (1976); Citizens United v. FEC, 558 U.S. 310 (2010); OpenSecrets federal lobbying and 2024 cycle totals; GAO, Sugar Program (GAO/RCED-00-126, 2000); USDA ERS sugar briefing

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Game-theoretic models of politics: bargaining, commitment, signalling and cascades
days.headline_hint: The Proposer's Two-Thirds: What Politics Looks Like When You Write Down the Game
days.focus: Legislative bargaining (Baron–Ferejohn under a closed rule; Romer–Rosenthal agenda setting); credible commitment (North and Weingast's 1688, Weingast's sovereign-transgression game, Acemoglu and Robinson's democratization as a commitment device); signalling (Fearon's audience costs, cheap talk against costly signals); threshold and cascade models (Granovetter, Kuran, Lohmann) applied to protest; selectorate theory; probabilistic voting and valence. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can solve the Baron–Ferejohn game, set up a commitment game and find its equilibrium, and build a cascade from a threshold distribution.
parts: Divide the Dollar: Baron–Ferejohn Bargaining and the Proposer's Advantage
The Agenda Setter's Threat: Romer–Rosenthal and Take-It-or-Leave-It Politics
Credible Commitment: 1688, the Sovereign Transgression Game and Democratization as a Promise
Costly Signals: Audience Costs, Cheap Talk and What a Threat Is Worth
Thresholds and Cascades: Granovetter, Kuran and the Leipzig Mondays
Selectorate Theory: Winning Coalitions, Loyalty Norms and Why Some Leaders Build Roads
worked_examples: Baron–Ferejohn with n = 3 under a closed rule and discount factor δ: the proposer keeps 1 − δ(n − 1)/(2n) — two-thirds when δ = 1 — buying one vote at δ/n; then the 435-member House with δ = 0.9, and the comparison with the actual distribution of a real earmark bill.

North and Weingast's 1688: the interest rate on English government debt from the 1690s to the 1730s and the growth of borrowing after the Glorious Revolution as evidence of credible commitment, with the later critiques (Sussman and Yafeh; Stasavage) on what the series actually shows.

Lohmann's Leipzig series: the Monday demonstrations of autumn 1989 (about 70,000 on 9 October, rising into the hundreds of thousands over the following weeks, from Lohmann's Table 1) fitted to a Granovetter threshold distribution to locate the tipping point.

Fearon's audience-cost game with numbers: the escalation ladder, the leader's back-down cost and the separating equilibrium, then Tomz's (2007) survey-experimental estimates of how much backing down costs in approval.
sources: Baron and Ferejohn, 'Bargaining in Legislatures', APSR 83(4), 1989; Romer and Rosenthal, 'Political Resource Allocation, Controlled Agendas, and the Status Quo', Public Choice 33(4), 1978; McCarty and Meirowitz, Political Game Theory (Cambridge, 2007)

North and Weingast, 'Constitutions and Commitment', Journal of Economic History 49(4), 1989; Weingast, 'The Political Foundations of Democracy and the Rule of Law', APSR 91(2), 1997; Acemoglu and Robinson, Economic Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (Cambridge, 2006)

Fearon, 'Domestic Political Audiences and the Escalation of International Disputes', APSR 88(3), 1994; Tomz, 'Domestic Audience Costs in International Relations', International Organization 61(4), 2007; Kuran, 'Now Out of Never', World Politics 44(1), 1991; Lohmann, 'The Dynamics of Informational Cascades', World Politics 47(1), 1994
Bueno de Mesquita, Smith, Siverson and Morrow, The Logic of Political Survival (MIT, 2003); Granovetter, 'Threshold Models of Collective Behavior', American Journal of Sociology 83(6), 1978

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: International relations theory and institutions: realism, liberalism, constructivism
days.headline_hint: Anarchy Is What States Make of It — or Is It What Makes States?
days.focus: Structural realism (Waltz's balance of power, Mearsheimer's offensive realism, Walt's balance of threat); the liberal tradition (Keohane's institutions under anarchy, complex interdependence, Moravcsik's preference-based liberalism, the democratic peace and its dyadic evidence); constructivism (Wendt's anarchy, norms, identity); institutions as equilibria (Axelrod's cooperation, Koremenos–Lipson–Snidal's rational design); alliances — NATO's Article 5 and burden-sharing — and the polarity debate about China. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can state each paradigm's core claim and its falsifier, read a dyad-year democratic-peace regression, and apply the rational-design variables to a real treaty.
parts: Structure Over Statesmen: Waltz's Balance of Power and Mearsheimer's Offensive Turn
Cooperation Under Anarchy: Axelrod, Keohane and Why Institutions Survive the Hegemon
The Democratic Peace: Kant's Claim, Oneal and Russett's Dyads and the Objections
Anarchy Is What States Make of It: Wendt, Norms and the Constructivist Research Program
Rational Design: Why Treaties Look the Way They Do
Alliances and Burden-Sharing: Article 5, the 2% Rule and the Hague Pledge
worked_examples: NATO's numbers: Article 5 invoked once (12 September 2001); the allies at or above 2% of GDP in 2024 by NATO's own estimates, with Poland highest above 4%; the Hague Summit pledge of June 2025 — 3.5% of GDP for core defence plus up to 1.5% for related spending by 2035, Spain excepted — read through Olson and Zeckhauser's 1966 model of alliance public goods.

Oneal and Russett's dyad-year logit (Triangulating Peace, 2001): the democracy, trade-dependence and IGO-membership coefficients on militarized-dispute onset converted to changes in predicted probability, and Gartzke's 'capitalist peace' re-specification.

The UN Security Council veto record from the Dag Hammarskjöld Library: counts by permanent member since 1946 and the post-2022 pattern, as a test of realist against institutionalist expectations about great-power behaviour inside institutions.

Koremenos, Lipson and Snidal's design variables applied to the 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty: membership, scope, centralization, control and flexibility (the Article X withdrawal clause; the 1995 indefinite extension).
sources: Kenneth Waltz, Theory of International Politics (Addison-Wesley, 1979); Mearsheimer, The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (updated ed., Norton, 2014); Walt, The Origins of Alliances (Cornell, 1987)
Keohane, After Hegemony (Princeton, 1984); Axelrod, The Evolution of Cooperation (Basic Books, 1984); Moravcsik, 'Taking Preferences Seriously', International Organization 51(4), 1997

Wendt, 'Anarchy Is What States Make of It', International Organization 46(2), 1992; Russett and Oneal, Triangulating Peace (Norton, 2001); Koremenos, Lipson and Snidal, 'The Rational Design of International Institutions', IO 55(4), 2001

Olson and Zeckhauser, 'An Economic Theory of Alliances', Review of Economics and Statistics 48(3), 1966; NATO, Defence Expenditure of NATO Countries (2025) and The Hague Summit Declaration (25 June 2025)

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: The causes of war and deterrence theory, including nuclear strategy
days.headline_hint: War Is a Bargaining Failure: Fearon's Three Reasons, and the Bomb That Changed the Terms
days.focus: Fearon's rationalist explanations (private information with incentives to misrepresent, commitment problems, indivisibility) and Powell's elaboration of the commitment problem; Blainey on disagreement about relative power; Jervis's security dilemma and the offense–defense balance; Schelling on deterrence, compellence and the threat that leaves something to chance; the nuclear revolution and its critics (Brodie, Wohlstetter, Jervis, Lieber and Press); the stability–instability paradox; counterforce arithmetic; arms control from SALT to New START's lapse on 5 February 2026 and the current force numbers. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can draw a war as a bargaining failure with the bargaining range on a line, compute a single-shot kill probability, and read the SIPRI and Nuclear Notebook tables.
parts: The Puzzle: If War Is Costly, Why Does a Bargain Not Always Exist?
Fearon's Three Mechanisms and Powell's Commitment Problem, Drawn on a Line
The Security Dilemma and the Offense–Defense Balance: Jervis's Four Worlds
Schelling's Arms and Influence: Deterrence, Compellence and Leaving Something to Chance
The Nuclear Revolution and Its Critics: From Wohlstetter's Delicate Balance to the New Era of Counterforce
The Arithmetic of the Arsenal: Kill Probability, Survivability and the End of New START
worked_examples: The bargaining model with numbers: two states dividing a good worth 1, war costs c_A and c_B, win probability p — the bargaining range [p − c_A, p + c_B] drawn, then collapsed by private information about p or by a shift in p over time (Powell), with 1914 and 2022 as the illustrations, each attributed to the scholars who read them that way.

Single-shot kill probability against a hardened silo: the lethal-radius/CEP formula as set out in Lieber and Press (2017), with the public figures for a Minuteman III-class warhead and a 2,000-psi silo, and the two-on-one shot that follows.

SIPRI Yearbook 2025 (January 2025): 12,241 warheads worldwide, Russia 5,459, the United States 5,177, China at least 600 and growing by about 100 a year — set against New START's 1,550 deployed warheads, 700 deployed launchers and 800 total launchers, limits that lapsed on 5 February 2026 with no successor in force.

The Cuban Missile Crisis as brinkmanship: the 1962 strategic balance from the Nuclear Notebook series, the quarantine as a threat that left something to chance, and the Jupiter trade as the side payment that closed the bargaining range.
sources: Fearon, 'Rationalist Explanations for War', International Organization 49(3), 1995; Powell, 'War as a Commitment Problem', IO 60(1), 2006; Blainey, The Causes of War (3rd ed., Free Press, 1988)

Jervis, 'Cooperation under the Security Dilemma', World Politics 30(2), 1978; Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict (Harvard, 1960) and Arms and Influence (Yale, 1966); Sagan and Waltz, The Spread of Nuclear Weapons: An Enduring Debate (3rd ed., Norton, 2013)

Lieber and Press, 'The New Era of Counterforce', International Security 41(4), 2017; Wohlstetter, 'The Delicate Balance of Terror', Foreign Affairs 37(2), 1959; Allison and Zelikow, Essence of Decision (2nd ed., Longman, 1999)

SIPRI Yearbook 2025, ch. 6 'World Nuclear Forces'; Kristensen and Korda, 'Nuclear Notebook' (US and Russian nuclear forces, 2025), Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists; New START Treaty text (2010) and the US State Department's expiry notice (February 2026)

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: International political economy: trade politics, sanctions and the dollar system
days.headline_hint: The Weapon in the Plumbing: How Trade, Sanctions and the Dollar Became Statecraft
days.focus: The domestic politics of trade — Stolper–Samuelson coalitions (Rogowski), specific factors (Frieden), the China-shock evidence (Autor, Dorn and Hanson) and the institutional story from the 1934 RTAA to Sections 232 and 301; hegemonic stability (Kindleberger, Krasner, Gilpin) and open-economy politics; sanctions theory and evidence (Hufbauer et al.'s roughly one-third success rate, Pape's five, Drezner's sanctions paradox) with two episodes in numbers; weaponized interdependence (Farrell–Newman) and the dollar system — reserves, invoicing, SWIFT, the exorbitant privilege and Triffin's dilemma. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can predict a trade cleavage from factor endowments, code a sanctions episode as the datasets do, and read the COFER and BIS tables as measures of dollar centrality.
parts: Who Wants Free Trade: Stolper–Samuelson, Rogowski's Coalitions and the Specific-Factors Reply
The China Shock and the Institutions of Trade Policy: From the RTAA to Sections 232 and 301
Hegemonic Stability: Kindleberger's Lender of Last Resort and the Politics of an Open System
Do Sanctions Work? Hufbauer's Third, Pape's Five and Drezner's Paradox
Two Episodes in Numbers: Iran 2012 and Russia 2022
Weaponized Interdependence and the Dollar: Reserves, Invoicing, SWIFT and Triffin's Dilemma
worked_examples: Russia 2022: roughly $300 billion of the central bank's reserves immobilized out of about $630 billion, seven banks removed from SWIFT in March 2022, the $60 oil price cap from 5 December 2022 — against a 2022 GDP outcome of about −1.2% (IMF) to −2.1% (Rosstat) versus the IMF's April 2022 forecast of −8.5%, and what the gap says about adaptation, enforcement and third-country trade.

Iran 2012–13: oil exports falling from about 2.5 million barrels a day to about 1.1, the rial's collapse and the IMF's estimate of the 2012 contraction, coded as Hufbauer et al. would code the episode, with the 2015 JCPOA as the outcome variable.

The dollar's shares: IMF COFER (about 57% of allocated reserves in 2025, the euro about 21%), the BIS Triennial Survey's share of foreign-exchange turnover and SWIFT's payment-currency share, arranged as Farrell and Newman's chokepoints.

Rogowski's 2×2 on the 2025 tariffs: the United States as capital- and land-abundant and labour-scarce, the predicted against the observed coalitions, with Autor, Dorn and Hanson's commuting-zone estimates of the China shock as the evidence on who lost.

connect_back.topic: Exchange rates and the balance of payments

sources: Ronald Rogowski, Commerce and Coalitions (Princeton, 1989); Frieden, 'Invested Interests', International Organization 45(4), 1991; Autor, Dorn and Hanson, 'The China Syndrome', AER 103(6), 2013; Bailey, Goldstein and Weingast, 'The Institutional Roots of American Trade Policy', World Politics 49(3), 1997

Hufbauer, Schott, Elliott and Oegg, Economic Sanctions Reconsidered (3rd ed., Peterson Institute, 2007); Pape, 'Why Economic Sanctions Do Not Work', International Security 22(2), 1997; Drezner, 'The Hidden Hand of Economic Coercion', IO 57(3), 2003
