IMF, Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves (COFER); BIS Triennial Central Bank Survey (2025); CRS, 'Russia's War on Ukraine: Financial and Trade Sanctions' (IF12062); IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2022

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Authoritarianism and democratic backsliding
days.headline_hint: How Democracies Die Now: Slowly, Legally and by the Votes of the People Inside Them
days.focus: Linz's regime typology and the Geddes–Wright–Frantz personalist, party and military categories; Svolik's two problems of authoritarian rule — control and power-sharing — with the leader-exit data; Levitsky and Way's competitive authoritarianism; Bermeo's forms of backsliding (executive aggrandizement, strategic manipulation); Scheppele's autocratic legalism; Guriev and Treisman's spin dictators; polarization and the public's willingness to punish (Graham–Svolik); measurement and the V-Dem 2025 picture; the cases — Weimar 1933, Hungary since 2010, Poland 2015–2023, Venezuela, Turkey — and the neutral rules for reporting claims about the United States. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can classify a regime by the standard datasets, describe the mechanisms of erosion with their indicators, and read an expert-survey index for exactly what it is.
parts: Kinds of Non-Democracy: Linz, Geddes–Wright–Frantz and the Personalist Turn
The Two Problems of the Dictator: Svolik on Control, Power-Sharing and Who Actually Removes Autocrats
Competitive Authoritarianism and Spin Dictators: Winning Unfair Elections Without Tanks
Backsliding's Mechanisms: Aggrandizement, Manipulation and Autocratic Legalism, Case by Case
Will Voters Stop It? Polarization, Graham–Svolik and the Price of a Democratic Principle
Reading the Indices: V-Dem 2025, Freedom House and the Neutral Way to Talk About Home
worked_examples: Svolik's leader-exit table for dictators 1946–2008: the shares removed by regime insiders (a clear majority), by popular uprising, by foreign intervention and by assassination, taken from his Chapter 1 table, and what the split implies for coup-proofing and power-sharing institutions.

The Enabling Act of 23 March 1933: 444–94 in the Reichstag, the two-thirds requirement met with the 81 KPD deputies absent and the SPD's 94 votes against — a constitutional amendment used to end a constitution.

Hungary 2010–2024 in V-Dem v15: the Liberal Democracy Index's path and the sub-indices that fell first (judicial constraints, media), against Scheppele's account of the 2011 Fundamental Law and the cardinal-law technique; Poland's 2015–2023 sequence and the 2023 election (turnout 74.4%) as the reversal case.

V-Dem Democracy Report 2025: 74% of the world's population living in autocracies by V-Dem's classification and 44 countries autocratizing; the report's listing of the United States among its 2025 autocratizers reported as V-Dem's claim with its coding basis, alongside Bright Line Watch's expert-survey series — what each measures and what neither settles.
sources: Milan Svolik, The Politics of Authoritarian Rule (Cambridge, 2012); Geddes, Wright and Frantz, How Dictatorships Work (Cambridge, 2018); Linz, Totalitarian and Authoritarian Regimes (Lynne Rienner, 2000)
Levitsky and Way, Competitive Authoritarianism (Cambridge, 2010); Guriev and Treisman, Spin Dictators (Princeton, 2022); Levitsky and Ziblatt, How Democracies Die (Crown, 2018)

Bermeo, 'On Democratic Backsliding', Journal of Democracy 27(1), 2016; Scheppele, 'Autocratic Legalism', University of Chicago Law Review 85(2), 2018; Graham and Svolik, 'Democracy in America?', APSR 114(2), 2020
V-Dem Institute, Democracy Report 2025: 25 Years of Autocratization; Bright Line Watch expert surveys; Reichstag protocols, 23 March 1933

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: Nationalism and identity, revolutions and state failure
days.headline_hint: Imagined Communities, Real Wars: When Identity Builds States and When It Breaks Them
days.focus: Theories of nationalism (Gellner's industrial functionalism, Anderson's print capitalism, Smith's ethno-symbolism, Brubaker's nationhood as event); ethnicity as constructed and politically chosen (Posner's Chewa–Tumbuka natural experiment, Chandra's head counts, Wimmer's waves of war); revolutions — Skocpol's structural account, Goldstone's demographic-structural model, Kuran's preference falsification for 1979 and 1989, Chenoweth and Stephan on nonviolent campaigns; civil-war onset — Fearon–Laitin's insurgency model against Collier–Hoeffler's greed and grievance and Cederman's horizontal inequality; state failure as the loss of Weber's monopoly (Somalia, Libya, Haiti; Herbst on African states; the Fragile States Index). Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can state each theory of nationalism with its best case, read a civil-war onset logit, and describe the mechanism by which a state loses its monopoly of force.
parts: Nations Before Nationalism? Gellner, Anderson and Smith on Where the Idea Came From
Ethnicity as a Political Choice: Posner's Border, Chandra's Head Counts and Wimmer's Waves of War
States and Social Revolutions: Skocpol's Structures, Goldstone's Demography, Kuran's Surprise
Why Civil Resistance Works: Chenoweth and Stephan's Data and the 3.5% Claim Examined
Civil War Onset: Insurgency, Greed, Grievance and Horizontal Inequality in the Regressions
State Failure: Losing the Monopoly, and How Somalia, Libya and Haiti Fit Weber's Definition
worked_examples: Fearon and Laitin's onset logit (127 civil wars, 1945–1999): $1,000 less in per-capita income associated with 41% greater annual odds of onset, with the mountainous-terrain and population effects, and why ethnic and religious fractionalization drop out once income is in.

Chenoweth and Stephan's NAVCO data: 323 maximalist campaigns 1900–2006, nonviolent campaigns succeeding about 53% of the time against about 26% for violent ones — the coding rules, the selection problem, and Chenoweth's later revisions to the 3.5%-participation claim.

Posner's natural experiment: Chewas and Tumbukas on either side of the Zambia–Malawi border, the survey evidence that the same cleavage is politically salient in one country and not the other, and what the border does that a regression cannot.

Goldstone's demographic-structural model against the series for 1640s England and 1780s France (population, prices, elite recruitment), and Kuran's threshold reading of Iran 1978–79 and East Germany 1989.
sources: Ernest Gellner, Nations and Nationalism (2nd ed., Cornell, 2008); Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (rev. ed., Verso, 2006); Anthony Smith, The Ethnic Origins of Nations (Blackwell, 1986); Wimmer, Waves of War (Cambridge, 2013)

Theda Skocpol, States and Social Revolutions (Cambridge, 1979); Goldstone, Revolution and Rebellion in the Early Modern World (California, 1991); Chenoweth and Stephan, Why Civil Resistance Works (Columbia, 2011)

Fearon and Laitin, 'Ethnicity, Insurgency, and Civil War', APSR 97(1), 2003; Collier and Hoeffler, 'Greed and Grievance in Civil War', Oxford Economic Papers 56(4), 2004; Cederman, Gleditsch and Buhaug, Inequality, Grievances, and Civil War (Cambridge, 2013)

Posner, 'The Political Salience of Cultural Difference', APSR 98(4), 2004; Chandra, Why Ethnic Parties Succeed (Cambridge, 2004); Herbst, States and Power in Africa (Princeton, 2000); UCDP/PRIO Armed Conflict Dataset

days.subject: Political Science
days.topic: How to read political science research: close elections, lotteries, survey experiments and the replication record
days.headline_hint: Barely Won, Barely Lost: Where Political Scientists Found Their Experiments, and How They Learned to Check Them
days.focus: Takes the causal toolkit as taught in the Economics block (day 6, 'Econometrics for causal inference: IV, diff-in-diff, RDD' — potential outcomes, instruments, difference-in-differences, discontinuities, synthetic control) as read, and asks what political science added to it and what it got wrong. Close-election regression discontinuity: Lee's incumbency estimate, Caughey and Sekhon's sorting challenge, Eggers et al.'s audit of more than 40,000 close races and de la Cuesta and Imai's catalogue of misreadings; redistricting as a natural experiment (Ansolabehere, Snyder and Stewart's old-voters/new-voters design for the personal vote) and Sekhon and Titiunik's demonstration that it is neither natural nor an experiment; lotteries in politics — the 1969 draft lottery on political attitudes (Erikson–Stoker), India's reserved village-council seats (Chattopadhyay–Duflo; Dunning–Nilekani), state-senate term lengths drawn from a jar (Titiunik) — placed on Dunning's continuum of plausibility; survey experiments — list experiments, vignettes and conjoint analysis with the average marginal component effect (Hainmueller, Hopkins and Yamamoto); the generalisation problem of field experiments and the Metaketa answer; the pre-registration turn (Monogan's case, the EGAP registry, the 2014 DA-RT statement, results-blind review) and the replication record — the caliper test for publication bias (Gerber–Malhotra), Franco, Malhotra and Simonovits's file drawer, the LaCour retraction and Broockman and Kalla's rerun, Camerer et al.'s 21 Nature/Science experiments and Coppock's Mechanical Turk replications; and a protocol for reading any paper. Graduate level. Afterwards the reader can identify the design in any empirical paper, state its identifying assumption in one sentence, say what would break it, check a result against its pre-registration, and read the replication record for what it shows.
parts: What Political Science Borrowed and What It Added: The Toolkit Taken as Read
Barely Won, Barely Lost: Close Elections as Experiments, from Lee to the 40,000-Race Audit
Redrawn Lines and Numbered Balls: Redistricting, the Draft Lottery and Dunning's Continuum of Plausibility
Asking the Question as an Experiment: List Experiments, Vignettes and the Conjoint's Average Marginal Component Effect
Say It Before You See It: Pre-Registration, Results-Blind Review and the Metaketa Trials
The Replication Record: LaCour's Data, Broockman and Kalla's Rerun, and a Protocol for Reading Any Paper
worked_examples: Lee (2008) on US House elections 1946–1998: party incumbency raises the probability of holding the seat by about 0.40–0.45 and the vote share by about 0.08 at the discontinuity — then Caughey and Sekhon's (2011) finding that in the closest postwar House races the winners were disproportionately the incumbent party's and the better-financed candidates, a failure of as-if randomness in the running variable, and Eggers, Fowler, Hainmueller, Hall and Snyder's (2015) audit of more than 40,000 close races in other US and foreign elections where no such imbalance appears, so the postwar House is the exception rather than the rule.

Two lotteries: Erikson and Stoker (2011) on the 1969 draft lottery in the Jennings–Niemi class-of-1965 panel — men whose birthdays drew draft-vulnerable numbers turned more anti-war and more Democratic, with the partisan shift still detectable in later waves — and Titiunik's (2016) Arkansas, Illinois and Texas state-senate term lengths assigned by lot after redistricting, with the two-year senators' higher abstention and lower bill counts; each placed on Dunning's continuum, against Sekhon and Titiunik's (2012) redistricting case at the other end.

Hainmueller and Hopkins's (2015) immigration conjoint: 1,407 respondents choosing between pairs of immigrant profiles randomised on nine attributes, roughly 14,000 rated profiles in all; the average marginal component effects for education, professional occupation, English fluency and plans to work set against a country-of-origin effect near zero except for the Iraq penalty — the AMCE computed as a difference in choice probability, the Hainmueller–Hopkins–Yamamoto identification assumptions, and the standard error that the profile count, not the respondent count, determines.

LaCour and Green (2014) against Broockman and Kalla (2016): the irregularities — a survey firm with no record of the study, a panel retention rate no firm had achieved, thermometer distributions that matched the public 2012 CCAP survey too closely — the retraction of 28 May 2015, then the pre-registered Miami rerun (56 canvassers, 501 voters, a ten-minute conversation) with an effect on transgender tolerance still present three months later; set beside Franco, Malhotra and Simonovits's 221 TESS studies (strong results 40 points more likely to be published and 60 points more likely to be written up than nulls) and Metaketa I's seven coordinated, pre-registered trials in six countries with a pooled effect of voter information on incumbent support indistinguishable from zero.
sources: Dunning, Natural Experiments in the Social Sciences: A Design-Based Approach (Cambridge, 2012); Gerber and Green, Field Experiments (Norton, 2012); Mutz, Population-Based Survey Experiments (Princeton, 2011)

Lee, 'Randomized Experiments from Non-random Selection in U.S. House Elections', Journal of Econometrics 142(2), 2008; Caughey and Sekhon, 'Elections and the Regression Discontinuity Design', Political Analysis 19(4), 2011; Eggers, Fowler, Hainmueller, Hall and Snyder, 'On the Validity of the Regression Discontinuity Design for Estimating Electoral Effects', AJPS 59(1), 2015; de la Cuesta and Imai, Annual Review of Political Science 19, 2016; Sekhon and Titiunik, 'When Natural Experiments Are Neither Natural nor Experiments', APSR 106(1), 2012; Ansolabehere, Snyder and Stewart, AJPS 44(1), 2000

Erikson and Stoker, 'Caught in the Draft', APSR 105(2), 2011; Titiunik, 'Drawing Your Senator from a Jar', Political Science Research and Methods 4(2), 2016; Chattopadhyay and Duflo, Econometrica 72(5), 2004; Dunning and Nilekani, APSR 107(1), 2013; Hainmueller, Hopkins and Yamamoto, 'Causal Inference in Conjoint Analysis', Political Analysis 22(1), 2014; Hainmueller and Hopkins, 'The Hidden American Immigration Consensus', AJPS 59(3), 2015; Kuklinski, Cobb and Gilens, Journal of Politics 59(2), 1997

Broockman, Kalla and Aronow, 'Irregularities in LaCour (2014)' (May 2015); Broockman and Kalla, 'Durably Reducing Transphobia', Science 352(6282), 2016; Dunning et al., 'Voter Information Campaigns and Political Accountability', Science Advances 5(7), 2019; Franco, Malhotra and Simonovits, 'Publication Bias in the Social Sciences', Science 345(6203), 2014; Gerber and Malhotra, QJPS 3(3), 2008; Camerer et al., Nature Human Behaviour 2, 2018; Coppock, PSRM 7(3), 2019; Monogan, Political Analysis 21(1), 2013; DA-RT Joint Statement of Political Science Journal Editors (2014)

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Compressible flow and nozzle design
days.headline_hint: The Throat Is a Speed Trap: Why Every Rocket Chokes on Purpose
days.focus: The isentropic relations derived from the one-dimensional conservation laws, the area–Mach relation and choking, the thrust coefficient as the nozzle's own figure of merit, over- and under-expansion with flow separation and side loads, and the contour problem (conical, Rao bell, method of characteristics, dual-bell, aerospike). Graduate gas-dynamics level, with the thermodynamics of year one's day 58 assumed. Afterwards the reader can size a throat and exit for a given chamber pressure, gamma and ambient, and compute the sea-level and vacuum thrust of a real engine to within a few percent of its published figures. Compressible flow is this lesson's own: the Physics block's continuum-mechanics lesson (block 4, lesson 4) stops at the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations, so the one-dimensional compressible conservation laws are built here from year one's day 51 (Bernoulli, the Reynolds number) and day 58 (the laws of thermodynamics), not assumed from anywhere else.
parts: Bernoulli breaks at Mach 0.3, and the fix is the energy equation: stagnation properties and the isentropic relations
Why the throat chokes: the area–Mach relation and a design that can only work one way
The thrust coefficient: separating the chamber's job from the nozzle's
Over-expanded, under-expanded, separated: what happens when the nozzle is wrong for the altitude
Drawing the contour: conical, Rao bell and the method of characteristics
Altitude compensation: dual-bell, aerospike, and why most engines don't bother
worked_examples: Merlin 1D versus Merlin Vacuum: thrust coefficient and thrust at sea level and in vacuum from Pc ≈ 9.7 MPa, expansion ratios 16 and 165 and γ ≈ 1.22, compared with SpaceX's published 845 kN (SL), 914 kN (vac) and 981 kN (MVac) figures

RS-25 at sea level: exit pressure at ε = 69 and Pc ≈ 20.6 MPa against the Summerfield separation limit, explaining the 366 s sea-level / 452 s vacuum Isp split and the nozzle's near-separated start-up
Raptor 2 and Raptor 3 (Pc 300–350 bar, ~230–280 tf sea-level thrust): throat and exit diameters implied by the published thrust and a sea-level expansion ratio in the mid-30s, and the RVac extension
Ariane 5 flight V157 (11 December 2002): the Vulcain 2 nozzle-extension failure from thermal loads and start-up side loads on an over-expanded nozzle, as reconstructed by the inquiry board
sources: Anderson, Modern Compressible Flow: With Historical Perspective, 3rd ed. (McGraw-Hill, 2003), ch. 3–5
Sutton & Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed. (Wiley, 2017), ch. 3
Rao, G.V.R., "Exhaust Nozzle Contour for Optimum Thrust", Jet Propulsion 28(6), 1958
Hagemann, Immich, Nguyen & Dumnov, "Advanced Rocket Nozzles", Journal of Propulsion and Power 14(5), 1998

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Combustion thermochemistry and performance prediction
days.headline_hint: Three Thousand Five Hundred Kelvin, From a Table of Enthalpies
days.focus: Adiabatic flame temperature with dissociation by Gibbs-energy minimisation (the NASA CEA method), the ideal characteristic velocity c*, thrust coefficient and specific impulse built from first principles, frozen versus shifting equilibrium in the nozzle, and why the optimum mixture ratio is fuel-rich. Graduate combustion level. Afterwards the reader can predict c* and vacuum Isp for a real propellant pair at a real chamber pressure to within a few percent of the delivered number and account for the gap line by line.
parts: Enthalpy of formation, and why the flame temperature is an energy balance before it is a chemistry problem
Dissociation caps the temperature: equilibrium constants and Gibbs minimisation the way CEA does it
c*, the number that belongs to the chamber alone
Frozen or shifting: recombination in the nozzle and the two Isp answers
Why the optimum mixture ratio is fuel-rich, and what RP-1, methane and hydrogen each buy
From ideal to delivered: the efficiency ledger (c* efficiency, CF efficiency, divergence, boundary layer)
worked_examples: LOX/RP-1 at O/F 2.27 and 70 bar: a hand flame temperature with a dissociation correction against the CEA output near 3,670 K, ideal c* ≈ 1,780 m/s, and Merlin 1D's implied c* efficiency from its published chamber pressure, throat area and mass flow
LOX/LH2 at O/F 6.0 and 20.6 MPa (RS-25): ideal c* ≈ 2,430 m/s and ideal vacuum Isp against the delivered 452 s
LOX/CH4 at O/F ≈ 3.6 and 300 bar (Raptor): why the flame temperature exceeds hydrogen's while the Isp is lower, and the RVac's published vacuum Isp near 380 s
RL10C-1-1 (LOX/LH2, expander cycle, 453.8 s published): the delivered-versus-ideal gap as the best-case efficiency ledger
sources: Gordon & McBride, "Computer Program for Calculation of Complex Chemical Equilibrium Compositions and Applications", NASA RP-1311, Parts I (1994) and II (1996)
Sutton & Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed. (2017), ch. 5
Turns, An Introduction to Combustion: Concepts and Applications, 3rd ed. (McGraw-Hill, 2012), ch. 2
Huzel & Huang, Modern Engineering for Design of Liquid-Propellant Rocket Engines (AIAA, 1992), ch. 1

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Engine cycles and the pressure budget
days.headline_hint: Every Bar Has to Come From Somewhere: The Ledger Inside a Staged-Combustion Engine
days.focus: The pump-fed cycles — gas generator, expander, fuel-rich and oxidiser-rich staged combustion, full-flow staged combustion — plus pressure-fed and electric-pump, treated as pressure and power balances: what the turbine must deliver, what every drop costs, what closing the cycle forces on the pumps. The expander's square–cube limit, the gas generator's Isp penalty, and why full-flow is what lets Raptor run past 300 bar. Afterwards the reader can draw the pressure schedule of a real engine from pump inlet to injector face and compute its turbine power.
parts: The power balance: pump work equals turbine work, and turbine work is bought with propellant
Gas generator: throw away three percent to keep the turbine cool (Merlin, Vulcain 2.1, F-1)
Expander: the engine that runs on its own cooling jacket, and the square–cube law that caps it (RL10, Vinci)
Staged combustion, fuel-rich and oxidiser-rich: the preburner as a pressure amplifier (RS-25, RD-180, BE-4)
Full-flow: two preburners, gas–gas injection, and why it is the cycle with the most margin (Raptor)
Pressure-fed and electric-pump: the cycles that skip the turbine (Kestrel, SuperDraco, Rutherford)
worked_examples: RS-25 pressure schedule: chamber 20.6 MPa, fuel-rich preburner and high-pressure fuel turbopump discharge from the published figures; HPFTP power from the LH2 flow, density and head, against the published tens-of-megawatts figure
Merlin 1D's gas-generator penalty: the gas-generator flow fraction, the turbine-exhaust Isp, and the delivered 311 s vacuum Isp against what the main chamber alone would deliver
RL10C-1-1: hydrogen enthalpy pickup in the jacket at its published chamber pressure, the turbine power that pickup can buy, and why scaling the same cycle to Vulcain 2.1's 1,370 kN breaks it

Rutherford: 37 kW-class brushless motors on each pump, battery mass for Electron's first-stage burn at ~224 kN of liftoff thrust, and the thrust level at which the electric cycle's mass penalty crosses a gas generator's
sources: Huzel & Huang, Modern Engineering for Design of Liquid-Propellant Rocket Engines (AIAA, 1992), ch. 2–3
Sutton & Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed. (2017), ch. 6 and 10
Manski, Goertz, Saßnick, Hulka, Goracke & Levack, "Cycles for Earth-to-Orbit Propulsion", Journal of Propulsion and Power 14(5), 1998
NASA SP-8107, "Turbopump Systems for Liquid Rocket Engines" (1974)

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Turbomachinery: pumps, turbines, inducers, cavitation and pogo
days.headline_hint: Ten Thousand Horsepower in a Machine You Can Lift: The Turbopump
days.focus: Euler's turbomachine equation, specific speed and the choice of pump geometry, impeller and volute sizing, NPSH and the Thoma number, inducers and the suction specific speeds rocket pumps reach, cavitation and its dynamic compliance, impulse and reaction turbines with partial admission, bearings and seals, and the feed-system/structure coupling called pogo. Graduate turbomachinery level. Afterwards the reader can size a pump stage (speed, diameter, head, power) for a real engine and estimate its cavitation margin from the tank pressure.
parts: Euler's equation: head is angular momentum, so shaft speed is everything
Specific speed chooses the geometry: a single centrifugal stage for oxygen, three stages for hydrogen
Cavitation: vapour pressure, NPSH, the Thoma number, and why tank pressure is a pump problem
The inducer: buying suction margin with a screw, and the suction specific speeds rocket pumps reach
Turbines: impulse versus reaction, partial admission, and the blade that sees 900 K at 35,000 rpm
Pogo: when the feed line, the pump's cavitation compliance and the vehicle's first longitudinal mode agree on a frequency
worked_examples: RS-25 high-pressure fuel turbopump (three-stage, ~35,000 rpm) and oxidiser turbopump (~28,000 rpm): head, power and specific speed from the published discharge pressures and flows, and why hydrogen needs three stages where oxygen needs one

Merlin 1D's single-shaft turbopump (~36,000 rpm, ~7.5 MW reported): NPSH available from Falcon 9's tank pressure and hydrostatic head against NPSH required with an inducer at a suction specific speed near 30,000 (US units)

Apollo 13 (11 April 1970): the S-II centre J-2's early cutoff from pogo, and the Saturn V LOX prevalve accumulator fix, with the frequency coincidence computed from published feed-line and structural data
BE-4's LOX pump: cavitation-number sweep for normal-boiling-point versus subcooled oxygen at Vulcan's and New Glenn's tank pressures
sources: Brennen, Hydrodynamics of Pumps (Cambridge University Press, 2011)
NASA SP-8052, "Liquid Rocket Engine Turbopump Inducers" (1971)
NASA SP-8055, "Prevention of Coupled Structure-Propulsion Instability (Pogo)" (1970)
Sutton & Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed. (2017), ch. 10

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Injectors and combustion instability
days.headline_hint: The F-1 Was Bombed Two Thousand Times Before It Flew: The Physics of Screech
days.focus: Injector element families (impinging doublets and triplets, shear and swirl coaxial, pintle) with atomisation, mixing and the pressure-drop rule; the Rayleigh criterion; low-frequency chugging as a feed-system loop, intermediate-frequency buzz, and high-frequency acoustic instability computed from the chamber's Bessel-function eigenmodes; baffles, acoustic cavities and injector redesign; bomb rating. Afterwards the reader can compute the acoustic mode frequencies of a real chamber and say which stabilising device addresses which mode and why.
parts: Atomise, mix, vaporise: what an injector element does in the first ten centimetres
Five families of element, and what each engine chose: F-1 impinging jets, RS-25 shear coaxial, RD-170 swirl coaxial, Merlin's pintle
Rayleigh's criterion: heat released in phase with pressure is an amplifier
Chugging: the injector pressure drop is a decoupling capacitor, and the 15–25 percent rule
Screech: tangential and radial modes from the roots of J′ₘ, and the F-1's first tangential mode
Baffles, cavities and bombs: how Project First rated the F-1 stable, and how Raptor's gas–gas injection changes the problem
worked_examples: F-1 chamber: first and second tangential and first radial mode frequencies from the chamber diameter and the hot-gas sound speed of LOX/RP-1 combustion products, against the instability frequency documented by Oefelein & Yang, and the 1965 baffle configuration that fixed it
Merlin 1D's pintle: injector pressure drop as a fraction of a 9.7 MPa chamber and the chugging margin it buys, with the TRW lunar-module descent engine lineage and its 10–60 percent throttling
RS-25 shear-coaxial element: LOX-post recess, hydrogen-to-oxygen velocity ratio and the momentum-flux ratio that governs atomisation
A chug-loop stability calculation for a pressure-fed engine (Kestrel on Falcon 1's second stage) from feed-line inertance, tank pressure and injector drop
sources: Harrje & Reardon (eds), "Liquid Propellant Rocket Combustion Instability", NASA SP-194 (1972)
Yang & Anderson (eds), Liquid Rocket Engine Combustion Instability, AIAA Progress in Astronautics and Aeronautics vol. 169 (1995)
Oefelein & Yang, "Comprehensive Review of Liquid-Propellant Combustion Instabilities in F-1 Engines", Journal of Propulsion and Power 9(5), 1993
Sutton & Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed. (2017), ch. 8–9

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Thrust chamber cooling: regenerative, film, ablative, radiative
days.headline_hint: A Hundred Megawatts Per Square Metre, and the Wall Is Copper
days.focus: Gas-side convection by the Bartz correlation with the radiative contribution, conduction through copper-alloy liners, coolant-side convection in channels with the near-critical corrections, the jacket pressure drop that feeds Lesson 3's budget, thermal stress and low-cycle fatigue of the liner, film and dump cooling, and ablative and radiatively cooled hardware. Graduate heat-transfer level. Afterwards the reader can compute the throat heat flux and wall temperatures of a real engine and size its coolant channels.
parts: Where the heat comes from: Bartz's equation and why the throat is the worst place
Through the wall: conduction, the copper alloys (NARloy-Z, GRCop-42, CuCrZr) and the temperature a liner can take
Into the coolant: channel geometry, velocity, Nusselt correlations and the near-critical trap
Film, dump and transpiration: buying margin with propellant, from the F-1's turbine exhaust to Merlin's film
Ablative and radiative: when you don't cool at all (the lunar-module descent engine, Kestrel, MVac's niobium extension)
Thermal cycling and the dog-house: how liners fail after N flights
worked_examples: RS-25 throat: Bartz heat flux at Pc 20.6 MPa (published order 100 MW/m²), NARloy-Z hot-wall temperature with hydrogen coolant entering near 40 K, and the published jacket pressure drop
Merlin 1D throat with RP-1 as coolant: heat flux, the coking limit on the coolant-side wall temperature, and the film-cooling fraction that closes the gap
Raptor at 300 bar: throat flux scaling with Pc^0.8 and what the step from Raptor 1 to Raptor 3's 350 bar did to the cooling design
Merlin Vacuum's radiatively cooled niobium-alloy nozzle extension: equilibrium wall temperature from the radiation balance at ε ≈ 165
sources: Bartz, D.R., "A Simple Equation for Rapid Estimation of Rocket Nozzle Convective Heat Transfer Coefficients", Jet Propulsion 27(1), 1957
Huzel & Huang, Modern Engineering for Design of Liquid-Propellant Rocket Engines (AIAA, 1992), ch. 4
NASA SP-8087, "Liquid Rocket Engine Fluid-Cooled Combustion Chambers" (1972)
Sutton & Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed. (2017), ch. 8

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Solid and hybrid motors: internal ballistics
days.headline_hint: A Motor With No Valves: How a Solid Rocket Decides Its Own Chamber Pressure
days.focus: The burn-rate law, the Kn equilibrium and its stability condition, grain geometry as the throttle and the thrust–time curve, erosive burning and temperature sensitivity, propellant families (PBAN, HTPB/AP/Al, double-base), case and nozzle design with carbon-carbon throats and phenolic insulators, two-phase-flow losses, and hybrid regression-rate physics with its mixture-ratio shift. Afterwards the reader can predict the pressure–time curve of a real motor from its grain geometry and burn-rate constants, and explain what a nozzle-insulator defect does to it.
parts: Vieille's law and the equilibrium the motor finds by itself: Pc = (ρ·a·Kn·c*)^(1/(1−n))
Why n must be less than one, and what temperature sensitivity does to a January launch
Grain geometry is the throttle: star, finocyl, BATES, and the Shuttle booster's eleven-point star
The nozzle problem: throat erosion, insulator defects, and what the Vulcan GEM-63XL anomalies and Vega-C VV22 had in common
Hybrids: the flame is a boundary layer, regression goes as G_ox^0.8, and the O/F drifts through the burn
Sizing a booster: P120C from propellant mass to burn time, and what strap-ons buy Ariane 64 and Vulcan
worked_examples: P120C (Ariane 6 booster and Vega-C first stage): ~142 t of HTPB/AP/Al in a monolithic carbon-fibre case, ~130 s burn, peak thrust near 4,650 kN — average Kn and burn rate consistent with the published thrust curve
Space Shuttle RSRM: PBAN propellant, eleven-point star transitioning to double-truncated cone, ~500 t of propellant, and the thrust bucket near 50 s designed for max Q

GEM-63XL: the nozzle-insulator manufacturing defect on Vulcan Cert-2 (4 October 2024, nozzle lost at T+37 s) and the second booster anomaly on USSF-87 (12 February 2026) — thrust asymmetry and the BE-4 gimbal compensation, quantified; and Vega-C VV22 (20 December 2022), the Zefiro-40 carbon-carbon throat-insert erosion as throat-area growth against pressure decay
A nitrous-oxide/HTPB hybrid on the SpaceShipTwo pattern: port-diameter growth, regression rate by Marxman's law and the O/F shift over a 60 s burn
sources: Sutton & Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed. (2017), ch. 12–15
NASA SP-8076, "Solid Propellant Grain Design and Internal Ballistics" (1972)
Chiaverini & Kuo (eds), Fundamentals of Hybrid Rocket Combustion and Propulsion, AIAA Progress in Astronautics and Aeronautics vol. 218 (2007)
Davenas (ed.), Solid Rocket Propulsion Technology (Pergamon, 1993)

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Cryogenic propellants, tanks, pressurisation and slosh
days.headline_hint: Sixty-Six Kelvin: What Densified Oxygen Buys, and What It Costs at the Pad
days.focus: Properties of LOX, LH2, LCH4 and RP-1 from the NIST data, densification and its mass benefit, boil-off from heat leak through insulation and structure with the vent-mass arithmetic, pressurisation by helium and autogenous gas with ullage collapse and the COPV, tank sizing as a pressure vessel (hoop stress, minimum gauge, common bulkheads, balloon tanks), and slosh as Abramson's pendulum model with baffle damping. Afterwards the reader can size a stage's tanks, pressurant and baffles, and compute its boil-off on the pad and in orbit.
parts: Densities, vapour pressures, latent heats: the NIST numbers that set every stage's shape
Densification: 66 K oxygen and −7 °C RP-1 on Falcon 9, the mass it buys, and the T−35-minute load it forces
Boil-off: heat leak through multilayer insulation and struts, the vent-mass arithmetic, and the depot problem for Starship
Pressurisation: helium bottles, autogenous gas, ullage collapse, and what CRS-7 and AMOS-6 taught about composite overwrapped pressure vessels
The tank as a pressure vessel: hoop stress, minimum gauge, Al-Li 2195, 304L stainless and Centaur's balloon
Slosh: Abramson's pendulum, the first-mode frequency, baffle damping, and Falcon 1 flight 2
worked_examples: Falcon 9 first stage: ~411 t of propellant at a kerolox mixture ratio near 2.3 with LOX at ~66 K and RP-1 at ~266 K — tank volumes against normal-boiling-point loading, and the payload sensitivity of the extra mass through the rocket equation
A Starship depot: ~1,200 t of methalox in a 9 m stainless tank, daily boil-off for an assumed insulation heat leak in W/m², and the extra tanker flights it adds to an Artemis HLS refuelling campaign
Centaur V's pressure-stabilised stainless tank: hoop stress at sub-millimetre gauge and a few bar of ullage pressure, and why it cannot stand unpressurised
Falcon 1 flight 2 (21 March 2007): second-stage LOX slosh coupling with the control loop — the first-mode slosh frequency from tank radius and fill height against the control bandwidth
sources: Abramson (ed.), "The Dynamic Behavior of Liquids in Moving Containers", NASA SP-106 (1966)
Barron & Nellis, Cryogenic Heat Transfer, 2nd ed. (CRC Press, 2016)
NASA SP-8112, "Pressurization Systems for Liquid Rockets" (1975)
NIST Chemistry WebBook / REFPROP thermophysical property data for oxygen, hydrogen, methane and n-dodecane surrogates

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Structures and loads: buckling, stiffened shells and mass fractions
days.headline_hint: The Rocket Is a Beer Can Under Six g: Buckling, Stiffeners and the Knockdown Factor
days.focus: The load set (axial thrust times load factor, bending from q·α and wind, internal pressure as a stabiliser, acoustic and random vibration, separation shock), the classical buckling of thin cylinders and the empirical knockdown factor of NASA SP-8007 and its 2020 revision, stiffening architectures (monocoque, isogrid, orthogrid, skin-stringer, composite sandwich), factors of safety per NASA-STD-5001B, and how all of it lands in the structural coefficient the rocket equation cares about. Afterwards the reader can size a tank wall and its stiffening for a real stage and compute its mass fraction.
parts: The load set: what a Falcon 9 core sees at liftoff, max Q and MECO, in newtons and newton-metres
Euler to Donnell: why the classical buckling stress of a thin shell is never reached, and the knockdown factor
Pressure stabilisation: the tank pressure that turns a beer can into a beam
Stiffening architectures: isogrid, orthogrid, stringers and rings, and the mass each buys per unit of buckling load
Factors of safety and test: NASA-STD-5001B, proof, qualification, and the mass-growth allowance
The structural coefficient: from wall gauge to ε, and why Falcon 9's first stage is about five percent structure
worked_examples: Falcon 9 first stage: axial load at max Q and near MECO on a 3.7 m Al-Li 2195 shell, and the wall gauge for buckling with an SP-8007 knockdown, with and without tank pressure
Starship: a 9 m 304L stainless shell of millimetre-class gauge — buckling of the unpressurised ship during the belly-flop and why the pressure schedule matters
Electron: a 1.2 m carbon-composite tank — the laminate stiffness needed for the same buckling load and the mass comparison with aluminium
Structural-coefficient audit from published masses: Falcon 9 stage one (~22.2 t dry, ~433 t wet), Centaur V, the Starship ship and Electron, with recovery hardware separated out
sources: NASA/SP-8007-2020, "Buckling of Thin-Walled Circular Cylinders" (revised 2020)
NASA-STD-5001B, "Structural Design and Test Factors of Safety for Spaceflight Hardware"
Bruhn, Analysis and Design of Flight Vehicle Structures (Jacobs, 1973)
AIAA S-120A-2015, "Mass Properties Control for Space Systems"

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Ascent trajectory optimisation: gravity turn, optimal control and losses
days.headline_hint: Falling Sideways on Purpose: The Calculus of Variations Flies Every Rocket
days.focus: The point-mass ascent equations over a rotating Earth, the gravity turn and its pitch-over kick, Pontryagin's minimum principle applied to vacuum ascent (the linear- and bilinear-tangent steering laws), the Saturn V Iterative Guidance Mode and Shuttle Powered Explicit Guidance as closed-loop implementations, direct transcription and convex methods, and the loss budget reconstructed by integration rather than by rule of thumb. Afterwards the reader can integrate a real vehicle's ascent and read its gravity, drag and steering losses off the result.
parts: The equations of ascent: thrust, gravity, drag and the rotating Earth in one state vector
The gravity turn: one kick, then let gravity steer — and why the kick angle is the whole design
Pontryagin's principle in a vacuum: the costate, the Hamiltonian, and the bilinear tangent law
Closed-loop guidance: the Iterative Guidance Mode on Saturn V, Powered Explicit Guidance on the Shuttle, and what 'explicit' means
Direct methods: collocation, convexification, and why the 2010s changed the tools
The loss budget by integration: gravity, drag, steering and back-pressure losses on Falcon 9 to low Earth orbit
worked_examples: Falcon 9 to a 200 km, 28.5° orbit from Cape Canaveral: numerical integration with published masses (~549 t at liftoff, ~7.6 MN sea-level thrust, Merlin 282/311 s, MVac 348 s), reconstructing the gravity, drag and steering losses and comparing MECO with a webcast profile near 2.3 km/s at ~70 km
Saturn V (Apollo 11): the IGM's target set and the historical loss budget from the NASA post-flight trajectory reconstruction
A bilinear-tangent steering solution for the MVac from MECO to insertion, solved as a two-point boundary-value problem
Electron's nine-Rutherford first stage: a high thrust-to-weight, low and fast trajectory — the drag-loss penalty of a 1.2 m vehicle against a 3.7 m one
sources: Bryson & Ho, Applied Optimal Control (Hemisphere, 1975), ch. 2–3
Chandler & Smith, "Development of the Iterative Guidance Mode with Its Application to Various Vehicles and Missions", Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets 4(7), 1967
McHenry, Brand, Long, Cockrell & Thibodeau, "Space Shuttle Ascent Guidance, Navigation, and Control", Journal of the Astronautical Sciences 27(1), 1979
Betts, Practical Methods for Optimal Control and Estimation Using Nonlinear Programming, 2nd ed. (SIAM, 2010)

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Staging optimisation and the reusability penalty
days.headline_hint: Where to Cut the Rocket: Lagrange Multipliers and the Price of Bringing the Booster Home
days.focus: The multi-stage rocket equation with unequal Isp and structural coefficients, the Lagrange-multiplier solution for the optimal Δv split, sensitivities to ε and Isp, parallel staging and strap-ons, hot staging and kick stages, and the reusable booster's landing reserve treated as a staging problem. Afterwards the reader can find the optimal staging of a real two- or three-stage vehicle and put a number on the payload cost of recovering the first stage.
parts: Two stages, one number: Δv as a sum of logarithms, and the structural coefficient that ruins it
The Lagrangian: the optimal split with unequal Isp and ε, solved to the end
Sensitivities: a second of Isp on the upper stage against a kilogram on the lower
Parallel staging: strap-on solids, crossfeed, and what Falcon Heavy's core throttle-down is for
Hot staging and kick stages: Starship's interstage and Electron's Curie
The reusability tax: the landing reserve, MECO velocity, and the third of the payload it can cost
worked_examples: Falcon 9 Block 5 from published stage masses (stage one ~22.2 t dry / ~433 t wet; stage two ~4 t dry with ~100–107 t of propellant) and Isps: the expendable LEO payload against the 22.8 t SpaceX quotes, then with a landing reserve for drone-ship and return-to-launch-site recovery against the quoted reusable figures
Saturn V's three-stage split with the historical Isp and structural ratios against the flown S-IC cutoff near 2.7 km/s
Ariane 62 versus Ariane 64: what two more P120C boosters do to GTO payload (4.5 t to 11.5 t) as a parallel-staging calculation
Starship/Super Heavy: hot staging and the booster's landing reserve, and their effect on the ship's insertion mass
sources: Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, 4th ed. (Butterworth-Heinemann, 2020), ch. 11
Wiesel, Spaceflight Dynamics, 3rd ed. (Aphelion Press, 2010), ch. 7
Sutton & Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed. (2017), ch. 4
SpaceX, Falcon User's Guide (September 2021) and the published Falcon 9 / Falcon Heavy performance figures

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Navigation in flight: strapdown inertial mechanisation and the error-state Kalman filter
days.headline_hint: Knowing Where You Are at Two Kilometres a Second: The Error-State Filter, Flown Rather Than Derived
days.focus: The engineering of launch-vehicle navigation, with the filter itself cited rather than re-derived: the Mathematics block's state-space lesson (block 6, lesson 16) derived the Kalman filter as recursive Bayes, ran it by hand and defined the extended filter, and today wires that recursion to hardware. Strapdown inertial mechanisation (quaternion attitude integration with coning and sculling corrections, specific force resolved into the navigation frame, the Earth-rate and transport-rate terms, a gravity model with J2 in it), the sensor error budget (bias, scale factor, angle and velocity random walk, misalignment, g-sensitivity) and how each term grows over a nine-minute ascent, the fifteen-state error-state formulation (position, velocity, attitude, accelerometer and gyro bias) with its linearised dynamics, state transition matrix and covariance propagation, GNSS aiding in loose and tight coupling with the innovation test, redundancy and voting in triple-string flight computers, and the failure case of Ariane 501. Graduate navigation level. Afterwards the reader can propagate a real IMU's error budget through a Falcon 9 ascent, write the error-state model a GNSS-aided navigator runs, and read its covariance at insertion against the vehicle's published injection accuracy.
parts: The strapdown loop: gyros integrate a quaternion, accelerometers give specific force, and gravity is a model with J2 in it
How errors grow: bias, scale factor, random walk and misalignment, and the ½·b·t² that makes navigation-grade cost what it does
The filter, cited: the fifteen-state error model, its transition matrix and covariance propagation — the Mathematics block's recursion with an IMU inside it
GNSS aiding: loose and tight coupling, the innovation test, and what jamming and a rocket's dynamics do to the loop
Apollo to Falcon: the AGC's state vector and landing-radar update, and how a triple-redundant modern flight computer votes
Ariane 501: an unprotected 64-bit-to-16-bit conversion in the inertial reference system, and what redundancy cannot fix
worked_examples: A 540 s ascent with a tactical-grade IMU (1 mg accelerometer bias, 1°/h gyro bias, 0.1°/√h angle random walk) against navigation-grade (30 µg, 0.01°/h, 0.002°/√h): position and velocity error at insertion by propagating the error-state model along the trajectory, term by term, and which of the two meets a low-Earth-orbit insertion requirement unaided

The Falcon 9 telemetry budget on Crew Dragon Demo-2 (30 May 2020): the webcast's one-hertz speed and altitude trace differentiated into a specific-force profile, the fifteen-state covariance propagated through max Q (T+0:58), MECO (T+2:33) and SECO-1 (T+8:47) for the tactical-grade unit with and without a 1 Hz GNSS position update, and the resulting 3σ insertion ellipse set against the low-Earth-orbit injection accuracies the Falcon User's Guide quotes (perigee ±10 km, apogee ±15 km, inclination ±0.1°, 3σ)

Apollo 11's lunar module landing (20 July 1969): the landing-radar altitude and velocity updates into the guidance computer's state vector, with the altitude-dependent weighting function from Klumpp's 1974 account of the descent guidance and the Guidance System Operations Plan

Ariane 5 flight 501 (4 June 1996): the horizontal-bias overflow at H0+36.7 s in the inertial reference system, reconstructed from the Inquiry Board report — the backup unit failing first and the active unit 72 ms later, for the same reason
sources: Savage, P.G., "Strapdown Inertial Navigation Integration Algorithm Design", Parts 1 (Attitude Algorithms) and 2 (Velocity and Position Algorithms), Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics 21(1) and 21(2), 1998
Titterton & Weston, Strapdown Inertial Navigation Technology, 2nd ed. (IET, 2004)
Groves, Principles of GNSS, Inertial, and Multisensor Integrated Navigation Systems, 2nd ed. (Artech House, 2013)
Lions et al., "Ariane 501 Inquiry Board Report" (ESA/CNES, 19 July 1996)

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Flight control and thrust vector control
days.headline_hint: Balancing a Broomstick at Max Q: Control Laws for a Rocket That Wants to Flip
days.focus: Rigid-body pitch and yaw dynamics of a launch vehicle with the centre of pressure ahead of the centre of mass, control authority from gimbal angle, the classical attitude loop and its gain schedule with dynamic pressure, drift-minimum and load-relief control, the flexible-body problem (bending modes, notch and phase stabilisation), slosh in the loop, thrust-vector-control actuator sizing, and aerodynamic surfaces (grid fins, Starship's flaps) with control allocation. Afterwards the reader can design and analyse a stabilising attitude loop for a real vehicle and show its margins against bending and slosh.
parts: The plant: aerodynamic instability, time-to-double, and how much gimbal a Falcon 9 needs at max Q
The rigid-body loop: proportional-derivative attitude control, gain scheduling with q, and the drift-minimum principle
Bending modes: the Saturn V's first mode near one hertz, sensor placement, and notch versus phase stabilisation
Slosh as a control problem: the pendulum in the loop, and the phase that undid Falcon 1 flight 2
Thrust vector control: hydraulic and electric actuators, gimbal rates, and the F-1's outboard-only gimballing
Aerodynamic control: grid fins on Falcon 9 and Super Heavy, four flaps on Starship, and control allocation
worked_examples: Falcon 9 near max Q (~T+70 s, dynamic pressure of order 30 kPa): aerodynamic moment for a 2° angle of attack from a CP–CG offset, the gimbal angle required of nine Merlins within their published range, and the time-to-double
Saturn V S-IC flight control: the published first bending mode and the filter design that phase-stabilised it, from NASA TN D-5869
Falcon 1 flight 2 (21 March 2007): the second-stage slosh mode against the loop's phase margin, showing why the oscillation grew only late in the burn
Thrust-vector actuator sizing for an RS-25-class engine (±10.5° pitch, ±8.5° yaw, published slew rates): hydraulic force and power from engine inertia and gimbal geometry
sources: Greensite, "Analysis and Design of Space Vehicle Flight Control Systems", NASA CR-820 (1967)
Haeussermann, "Description and Performance of the Saturn Launch Vehicle's Navigation, Guidance, and Control System", NASA TN D-5869 (1970)
Wie, Space Vehicle Dynamics and Control, 2nd ed. (AIAA, 2008)
Blakelock, Automatic Control of Aircraft and Missiles, 2nd ed. (Wiley, 1991)

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Orbital perturbations: J2, drag, third bodies and station keeping
days.headline_hint: The Earth Is Not a Point: What Oblateness, Air and the Moon Do to an Orbit Every Day
days.focus: The geopotential expansion and J2, Gauss's planetary equations and the secular rates of node and perigee, sun-synchronous and Molniya orbits as exploitations of them, atmospheric drag and lifetime with a density model, luni-solar and solar-radiation-pressure perturbations, GEO station-keeping budgets, LEO constellation maintenance and the ISS reboost. Afterwards the reader can compute a real satellite's nodal drift, drag lifetime and annual station-keeping Δv.
parts: The geopotential: spherical harmonics, J2 = 1.08263 × 10⁻³, and the disturbing function
Gauss's planetary equations: how a small force becomes a secular drift in Ω and ω
Sun-synchronous by design: Landsat's 98.2° at 705 km, and the Molniya trick at 63.4°
Drag: density models, the ballistic coefficient, lifetime, and the February 2022 Starlink loss
Third bodies and sunlight: GEO inclination drift, triaxiality, and the fifty metres per second a year that sets a satellite's life
Station keeping in practice: ISS reboosts, Starlink's Hall thrusters, and the GEO box
worked_examples: Landsat 8 and 9: the nodal regression rate from a, e, i and J2 shown to equal 0.9856°/day, and the altitude–inclination pair that holds the ~10:00 descending-node crossing
Starlink at a ~210 km insertion versus 550 km operational: drag lifetime under the 3–4 February 2022 geomagnetic-storm density enhancement, and why up to 40 of 49 satellites were lost
The ISS near 420 km: monthly altitude decay from the published ballistic coefficient and a density model, and the reboost propellant per year
A GEO satellite's annual north–south and east–west station-keeping Δv from the luni-solar inclination drift (0.75–0.95°/yr) and the triaxiality longitude drift at its slot
sources: Vallado, Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications, 4th ed. (Microcosm Press, 2013), ch. 8–9
Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, 4th ed. (2020), ch. 10
Montenbruck & Gill, Satellite Orbits: Models, Methods and Applications (Springer, 2000)
Soop, Handbook of Geostationary Orbits (Kluwer, 1994)

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Lambert's problem and rendezvous
days.headline_hint: Two Points, One Time of Flight: Lambert's Problem and the Art of Catching a Space Station
days.focus: Lambert's problem in the universal-variable formulation with Stumpff functions, its multi-revolution solutions and modern solvers, then relative motion: the Clohessy–Wiltshire equations derived and solved in closed form, two-impulse targeting, the phasing and co-elliptic sequence used for the ISS, R-bar and V-bar approaches, the two-orbit Soyuz profile, and docking dynamics. Afterwards the reader can solve a real Lambert transfer and design a CW approach to a target.
parts: Lambert's problem stated, and why the answer is a transcendental equation in one variable
Universal variables and Stumpff functions: one algorithm for ellipse, parabola and hyperbola
Multiple revolutions and modern solvers: Izzo's method and what a trajectory tool actually runs
Hill's frame: deriving the Clohessy–Wiltshire equations and their closed-form state transition matrix
Targeting: the two-impulse CW intercept, the football orbit, and the R-bar and V-bar approaches
The ISS profile end to end: phasing, co-elliptic, terminal — from Gemini 6A and 7 to Crew Dragon and the three-hour Soyuz
worked_examples: Lambert between two ISS-altitude positions 90° apart with a 2,000 s time of flight, solved by universal variables, and the two-impulse Δv compared with the CW solution
A CW intercept of the ISS (n ≈ 1.13 × 10⁻³ rad/s) from 10 km behind on V-bar in one half-period: the impulses and the relative trajectory they produce
Crew Dragon's ~28-hour phasing profile against Soyuz MS-17's 3 h 3 min two-orbit rendezvous (14 October 2020): the phasing-orbit altitude difference that buys the time
Gemini 6A and 7 (15 December 1965): the first rendezvous, reconstructed with its catch-up orbit
sources: Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, 4th ed. (2020), ch. 5 and 7
Izzo, D., "Revisiting Lambert's Problem", Celestial Mechanics and Dynamical Astronomy 121(1), 2015
Clohessy & Wiltshire, "Terminal Guidance System for Satellite Rendezvous", Journal of the Aerospace Sciences 27(9), 1960
Fehse, Automated Rendezvous and Docking of Spacecraft (Cambridge University Press, 2003)

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Interplanetary transfer: patched conics, gravity assists and porkchop plots
days.headline_hint: The Porkchop Plot: Why Mars Has a Door That Opens Every Twenty-Six Months
days.focus: Patched conics with spheres of influence, C3 and hyperbolic excess velocity, the departure hyperbola and the Oberth effect, ephemerides and Lambert-driven porkchop plots (departure-by-arrival contours of C3 and arrival v∞), gravity assists as a rotation of v∞ in the planet's frame with the Tisserand constraint, launch-vehicle C3 curves, and what launching off-window costs. Afterwards the reader can build a Mars porkchop plot from ephemerides and read a mission's launch window off a real vehicle's C3 curve.
parts: Spheres of influence and the patched conic: three two-body problems glued at the edges
Leaving: C3, v∞, the departure hyperbola, and why a bigger rocket buys a shorter trip
The porkchop plot: Lambert across a grid of dates, and the shape of the late-2026 Mars window
Gravity assists: rotating v∞ for free, the Tisserand criterion, and Europa Clipper's Mars–Earth route
Arriving: the hyperbolic approach, B-plane targeting, orbit insertion and aerocapture
Off-window: ESCAPADE's loiter near Sun–Earth L2 and what a launch outside the porkchop costs
worked_examples: Mars 2020 Perseverance (departure 30 July 2020, arrival 18 February 2021): C3 and arrival v∞ recomputed by Lambert from JPL Horizons ephemerides, against the published values

Europa Clipper on a fully expendable Falcon Heavy (14 October 2024): the C3 it needed against a direct Jupiter transfer, with the Mars flyby (1 March 2025) and Earth flyby (December 2026) as v∞ rotations toward an April 2030 arrival
A porkchop plot for the late-2026 Mars window built from Horizons, showing the Type I and Type II lobes and the minimum-C3 date
ESCAPADE on New Glenn NG-2 (13 November 2025): the loiter orbit and late-2026 Mars departure as a Δv budget compared with a direct in-window launch

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Reentry aerothermodynamics, thermal protection and propulsive landing
days.headline_hint: Most of the Energy Never Touches the Ship: Entry Heating, Ablators and the Hoverslam
days.focus: The entry equations and the Allen–Eggers ballistic solution, lifting entry and the corridor, stagnation-point heating by Sutton–Graves with the radiative term at lunar-return speed, the TPS families (reusable ceramics, reinforced carbon-carbon, the ablators Avcoat and PICA) with the char-layer energy balance, then powered descent: the boostback, entry and landing Δv budget, the gravity loss of hovering, minimum-throttle constraints and the hoverslam, and convex powered-descent guidance. Afterwards the reader can compute the peak heating and heat load of a real entry, size an ablator, and build a booster's recovery Δv budget.
parts: Where the energy goes: the entry equations and Allen–Eggers's closed-form ballistic solution
Stagnation heating: Sutton–Graves, nose radius, and the radiative term that appears at eleven kilometres a second
Lifting entry and skips: Apollo's L/D of 0.3, the Shuttle's 1.1, Orion's skip, and the corridor
Thermal protection: tiles, carbon-carbon, ablators, the char-layer energy balance, and what Artemis I's Avcoat did
Powered descent: the Δv budget for boostback, entry and landing, and the gravity loss of hovering
The hoverslam and the divert: minimum throttle, convex guidance, and how Falcon 9 and New Glenn land
worked_examples: Orion at ~11 km/s (Artemis I, splashdown 11 December 2022): Sutton–Graves convective flux for the published nose radius plus the Tauber–Sutton radiative term, integrated heat load against Avcoat thickness, and the skip-entry char loss explained by the permeability finding NASA announced in December 2024

The Starship ship entering from ~7.5 km/s: peak flux on the hexagonal tiles by Sutton–Graves for its ballistic coefficient, and the deliberate tile-removal experiment and splashdown on Flight 10 (26 August 2025)

Falcon 9 booster recovery: boostback (return-to-launch-site), entry-burn and landing-burn Δv reconstructed from a named mission's webcast telemetry, and the single-Merlin landing thrust-to-weight at the published throttle floor that forces the hoverslam
New Glenn NG-2 (13 November 2025): the three-engine-to-one BE-4 landing burn onto Jacklyn at T+9:15, and the hover margin a ~2,400 kN engine leaves a 7 m booster

Sutton & Graves, "A General Stagnation-Point Convective-Heating Equation for Arbitrary Gas Mixtures", NASA TR R-376 (1971)
Anderson, Hypersonic and High-Temperature Gas Dynamics, 3rd ed. (AIAA, 2019)
Açıkmeşe & Ploen, "Convex Programming Approach to Powered Descent Guidance for Mars Landing", Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics 30(5), 2007

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Reusability engineering and economics
days.headline_hint: Thirty-Seven Flights on One Booster: The Fatigue Curve Meets the Balance Sheet
days.focus: What limits a booster's life (thermal low-cycle fatigue of the chamber liner, turbine creep and cracking, base heating on entry, landing-leg and structure fatigue, pressure-vessel cycles), inspection and refurbishment practice, turnaround time, and then the economics: fixed versus marginal cost, amortisation over N flights, the payload penalty from Lesson 11 priced in, the Shuttle as counter-example, and launch pricing. Practitioner level. Afterwards the reader can build a per-flight cost model for a reusable vehicle and find the flight count at which it beats an expendable one.
parts: What wears out: the liner's thermal cycles, the turbine's creep, the base's entry heating
Inspection and refurbishment: what is examined between flights, and why the engine swap is the unit of maintenance
The Shuttle as counter-example: 135 flights, the SSME teardown, and why refurbishment ate the savings
The cost model: fixed, marginal, amortisation over N, and the reusability payload tax priced in
Turnaround and cadence: from nine days between flights to a hundred Falcon 9 launches in under eight months
Electron, New Glenn and Starship: three different bets on the same equation
worked_examples: Falcon 9 booster B1067: 37 flights by 25 August 2026 against SpaceX's stated 40-flight qualification goal; a booster amortised at an assumed build cost over 10, 20 and 40 flights, against the published ~$70 million list price and independent marginal-cost estimates
The Space Shuttle: the 2011 Nature lifetime-cost estimate (about $1.5 billion per flight in 2010 dollars) decomposed into fixed and marginal cost, and the SSME post-flight inspection regime
Break-even flight count as a two-variable table over refurbishment fraction and payload penalty (from Lesson 11) for a Falcon 9-like vehicle
Electron booster recovery: the first reflown Rutherford engine (2024) and the marine-recovery economics of a 300 kg-class vehicle

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Range safety and launch operations
days.headline_hint: The Line the Rocket May Not Cross: Expected Casualty, the Flight Termination System and the Countdown
days.focus: The public-safety framework (14 CFR Part 450, the RCC 321 risk criteria and the 1 × 10⁻⁴ expected-casualty limit), the instantaneous impact point and debris footprints, destruct lines and the autonomous flight safety system under RCC 319, launch commit criteria including the lightning rules, the countdown and propellant-load timeline, wet dress rehearsal and static fire, collision avoidance and airspace closure, and three historical cases. Practitioner level. Afterwards the reader can compute an expected-casualty estimate for a simple trajectory and read a countdown timeline as an engineer.
parts: Ec ≤ 1 × 10⁻⁴: how a failure probability, a debris model and a population grid become a go/no-go
The instantaneous impact point: where the rocket would land if it died now, and the lines it may not cross
Flight termination: ordnance and thrust termination, RCC 319, and the autonomous system Falcon 9 introduced in 2017
Three cases: Challenger's range-safety destruct at T+110 s, Starship Flight 1's forty-second termination delay, Astra LV0006's sideways launch
Launch commit criteria: winds aloft, the lightning rules, upper-level shear, and the ISS's instantaneous window
The countdown as a procedure: densified-propellant load from T−35 minutes, holds, abort modes and scrub turnaround
worked_examples: An expected-casualty calculation for a hypothetical failure at T+60 s on a Cape Canaveral azimuth: failure probability, debris dispersion, census population density, and the sum over the grid against the 1 × 10⁻⁴ limit of 14 CFR §450.101
Challenger (28 January 1986): the Rogers Commission timeline — breakup at T+73 s, solid-booster destruct at T+110 s — and the impact point the range safety officer was watching
Starship Flight 1 (20 April 2023): flight-termination activation and the roughly forty seconds to breakup that the FAA-overseen mishap investigation addressed
A Falcon 9 countdown for an ISS cargo mission: the RP-1 and LOX load timeline, the instantaneous window from the station's plane crossing (Lesson 14), and the lightning-rule violation that scrubs
sources: 14 CFR Part 450, "Launch and Reentry Licensing Requirements" (FAA, 2020), and FAA Advisory Circular 450.101-1
Range Commanders Council, RCC 319-19 "Flight Termination Systems Commonality Standard" and RCC 321-20 "Common Risk Criteria Standards for National Test Ranges"
Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (Rogers Commission, 6 June 1986)
NASA-STD-4010, "Standard for Lightning Launch Commit Criteria for Space Flight"

days.subject: Rocketry
days.topic: Electric and nuclear thermal propulsion
days.headline_hint: Three Thousand Seconds of Isp at a Tenth of a Newton: The Slow Engines That Win
days.focus: The physics of gridded-ion and Hall thrusters (ionisation, the space-charge limit, E×B drift, the Hall parameter, erosion and magnetic shielding), the power–thrust–Isp triangle and the mission-optimal Isp, low-thrust trajectories by Edelbaum's spiral and the flown examples, the propellant shift from xenon to krypton and argon, and nuclear thermal propulsion from the Rover/NERVA data to the 2025 cancellation of DRACO. Afterwards the reader can size an electric propulsion system for a real orbit-raising or interplanetary mission and set it, honestly, beside the chemical stages of the previous nineteen lessons.
parts: Thrust from power: T = 2ηP/(g₀·Isp), and why the optimal Isp is a mission number, not an engine number
Gridded ion: Child–Langmuir, the space-charge limit, and NSTAR's 92 mN at 2.3 kW
Hall thrusters: E×B, the Hall parameter, magnetic shielding, and the argon economics of Starlink
Low-thrust trajectories: Edelbaum's spiral, GEO orbit-raising in months, and Psyche's Mars flyby
Nuclear thermal: NERVA's Isp near 850 s, the reactor–nozzle energy balance, and the hydrogen tank that eats the advantage
The honest comparison: a Mars cargo mission by Starship, by a 100 kW solar-electric tug and by a nuclear-thermal stage, side by side
worked_examples: Dawn's NSTAR thrusters (Isp ~3,100 s, ~92 mN at 2.3 kW): more than 11 km/s of Δv from 425 kg of xenon, checked against the rocket equation and the power budget
Starlink V2 mini's argon Hall thruster (published ~170 mN, Isp ~2,500 s, kilowatt-class): orbit raising from ~350 km to 550 km by Edelbaum's formula — time, propellant and power
Psyche's SPT-140 Hall thrusters (launched 13 October 2023): cruise Δv and the May 2026 Mars gravity assist as a low-thrust mission design

NERVA XE-Prime and Phoebus 2A: Isp from a ~2,500 K hydrogen exhaust with dissociation, a Mars-transfer stage mass comparison against a Raptor-class chemical stage near 380 s, and DRACO's 2025 cancellation on launch-cost grounds

Edelbaum, T.N., "Propulsion Requirements for Controllable Satellites", ARS Journal 31(8), 1961
Koenig, D.R., "Experience Gained from the Space Nuclear Rocket Program (Rover)", Los Alamos National Laboratory LA-10062-H (1986)
Brophy, J.R., "NASA's Deep Space 1 Ion Engine (Plenary)", Review of Scientific Instruments 73(2), 2002

days.subject: AI, Technology & Coding
days.topic: Inside the block: attention variants and positional schemes
days.headline_hint: One write-head is all you need: how the memory bill for attention was cut twenty-fold without losing the plot
days.focus: Takes the multi-head attention of year-one day 116 and follows the engineering that came after it: multi-query and grouped-query attention, DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention as a low-rank factorisation of the KV cache, FlashAttention's IO-aware tiling and why exact attention became memory-bound rather than compute-bound; then the positional problem — sinusoidal, learned, rotary (RoPE), ALiBi, no positions at all — and how context is extended after training (position interpolation, YaRN), plus the block's other design choices (pre-norm versus post-norm, RMSNorm, SwiGLU). Afterwards the reader can compute the KV-cache bytes per token of any published architecture and say what each variant gives up. refresh: check the attention variant of record in current frontier open-weight models (MLA successors, sliding-window and hybrid linear-attention blocks such as Gated DeltaNet/Mamba hybrids) and the current context-extension method before writing.
parts: Where the bytes go: the KV cache as the real cost of attention
Sharing keys: multi-query, grouped-query and the accuracy they keep
Compress, don't share: multi-head latent attention as a low-rank factorisation
Exact attention without the quadratic memory: FlashAttention and the IO model
Where am I? Sinusoids, rotations, biases and the case for no positions at all
Stretching the window: position interpolation, YaRN and what extension actually costs
worked_examples: KV-cache bytes per token for Llama 2 70B (80 layers, 8 KV heads of dimension 128 in bf16: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 ≈ 328 KB) versus the same model with 64 KV heads (≈ 2.6 MB), and the maximum concurrent batch each allows on an 80 GB H100 at 4,096 tokens of context once the 140 GB of weights are sharded across two cards

DeepSeek-V2/V3's MLA: the per-token cache with a 512-dimensional compressed latent plus a 64-dimensional decoupled RoPE key, computed from the technical reports, set against GQA at the same layer count

FlashAttention arithmetic on the paper's own A100 (40 GB HBM at 1.5 TB/s; 20 MB on-chip SRAM at 19 TB/s): the tile size that lets the online softmax fit, and the HBM traffic saved for a 4,096-token sequence at head dimension 128

RoPE by hand: rotating a two-dimensional query/key pair at positions 3 and 7 and showing the dot product depends only on the offset 4; then the YaRN scaling factor for extending Llama 3's 8K base window to 128K

days.subject: AI, Technology & Coding
days.topic: Mixture of experts
days.headline_hint: A trillion parameters, thirty billion at a time: the routing trick behind every frontier model
days.focus: Sparse mixture-of-experts from the routing gate outward: top-k gating and its gradients, the total-versus-active parameter distinction and why it decouples capacity from FLOPs, load balancing (auxiliary losses, capacity factors, the auxiliary-loss-free bias method), shared experts and fine-grained expert segmentation, expert parallelism and the all-to-all communication that dominates MoE training and serving, and the failure modes — routing collapse, token dropping, memory that does not shrink with the FLOPs. Afterwards the reader can read an MoE model card and derive its training FLOPs, its serving memory and its per-token active compute. refresh: check the expert counts, routing rules and load-balancing methods of the current open-weight frontier MoEs (DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, Llama and Mixtral successors) before writing.
parts: Capacity without compute: why the parameter count and the FLOP count came apart
The gate: top-k routing, its non-differentiable core and the gradient that gets through
Keeping the experts busy: balancing losses, capacity factors and the loss-free alternative
Shared experts, fine-grained experts and what one token actually visits
The all-to-all: expert parallelism and the network bill that MoE never escapes

A load-balancing calculation: the Switch Transformer auxiliary loss for a batch of 1,024 tokens over 8 experts with observed routing fractions (0.40, 0.20, 0.10, 0.10, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05), and the capacity factor at which tokens begin to drop

days.subject: AI, Technology & Coding
days.topic: Training at scale I: data pipelines, tokenisation and scaling laws
days.headline_hint: Twenty tokens per parameter: the arithmetic that decides how big to build and how long to train
days.focus: Year-one day 121 stated tokenisation and scaling laws; this lesson does them properly. The web-scale data pipeline (Common Crawl, extraction, language identification, quality filters, exact and MinHash deduplication, mixture weights, contamination checks, the synthetic-data turn); byte-pair encoding down to the merge table, SentencePiece and byte fallback, vocabulary size as a cost lever and why the same paragraph costs different languages different money; then the scaling-law fits — Kaplan versus Chinchilla, the 6ND FLOP rule, compute-optimal versus inference-optimal overtraining, data-constrained scaling and repeated epochs. Afterwards the reader can size a training run from a compute budget and price a tokeniser's choices. refresh: check the current public data-pipeline papers (FineWeb and Dolma successors), current tokeniser conventions, and the state of the synthetic-data and data-wall debate before writing.

The tokeniser is a compression scheme: BPE to the merge table
The price of a language: tokens per word, vocabulary size and the fertility tax
Fitting the loss curve: Kaplan, Chinchilla and the 6ND rule
Past the optimum on purpose: overtraining for inference and the data-constrained regime
worked_examples: Chinchilla's own numbers: 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens against Gopher's 280B on 300B, the FLOPs of each at 6ND, and the loss-per-FLOP fit that gives roughly 20 tokens per parameter
Llama 3 405B at 15.6T tokens — about 38 tokens per parameter, deliberately past compute-optimal — with the paper's own scaling fit and the inference saving that justifies it

A BPE walkthrough on a 40-word English paragraph and its French translation under the Llama 3 128K-vocabulary tokeniser: token counts, the fertility ratio and the cost difference at a published per-million-token price
FineWeb's deduplication and filter ablations: the reported token counts at each pipeline stage and the benchmark deltas that justified each filter

Grattafiori/Dubey et al., 'The Llama 3 Herd of Models' (2024), §3 on pre-training data and scaling laws

days.subject: AI, Technology & Coding
days.topic: Compute and hardware: GPUs, TPUs, interconnect and the economics of a cluster
days.headline_hint: Six years or four: the depreciation assumption that decides whether an AI data centre makes money
days.focus: The machine and its accounts. GPU anatomy (SMs, tensor cores, HBM, the memory hierarchy), the TPU's systolic array and pod topology, precision formats and their throughput, interconnect (NVLink and NVSwitch inside the node, InfiniBand and Ethernet across it, the NVL72 rack-scale domain, TPU optical circuit switching), the roofline model stated here for the first time (day 6 runs the serving stack on it), power and cooling as the binding constraints (kW per rack, PUE, grid interconnection), and the economics — cost per GPU-hour built from capex, depreciation, power, networking and utilisation; the useful-life assumption; and how these appear in real 10-Ks and S-1s. Afterwards the reader can build a cost-per-GPU-hour model and read a hyperscaler's capex line critically. refresh: check the current accelerator generation and its specifications, current cluster sizes and rental prices, and the latest 10-K/S-1 disclosures on useful life and capex before writing.

The other architecture: systolic arrays, TPU pods and optical switching
Wiring ten thousand of them: NVLink domains, InfiniBand fabrics and where the bandwidth cliffs are
Watts and water: power density, cooling and the grid as the real bottleneck
Cost per GPU-hour: capex, depreciation, power and utilisation in one model
In the filings: capex, useful lives and the numbers to watch in a 10-K

Llama 3's 16,384-GPU cluster as power: 16,384 × 700 W GPU-only, node overhead, PUE, and the megawatts a substation must deliver

days.subject: AI, Technology & Coding
days.topic: Training at scale II: parallelism, optimisers and the run itself
days.headline_hint: Sixteen thousand GPUs and 466 interruptions: what a fifty-four-day training run is actually made of
days.focus: The mechanics of the run. The four parallelisms (data, tensor, pipeline, expert) plus sequence/context parallelism and ZeRO/FSDP sharding, with the communication volume of each derived rather than asserted and set against the interconnect bandwidths of day 4; the per-GPU memory budget (weights, gradients, optimiser states, activations, checkpointing); mixed precision (bf16, FP8) and loss scaling; AdamW to the update rule and its bytes per parameter, Muon and the second-order turn, learning-rate schedules (cosine, warmup-stable-decay), batch-size ramps, gradient clipping, loss spikes and their diagnostics; and the operational reality — checkpoint cadence, MFU, straggler and hardware-failure rates. Afterwards the reader can lay a training job out on a given cluster and estimate its wall-clock and MFU. refresh: check the optimiser of record (Muon and successors), FP8/FP4 training practice and the latest published cluster-reliability statistics before writing.
parts: The memory budget: why a 70B model does not fit on one 80 GB GPU even to hold still
Four ways to cut a model: data, tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism, with their bytes on the wire
Sharding the optimiser: ZeRO stages, FSDP and the trade of memory for bandwidth
The update rule: AdamW derived, Muon's orthogonalised step, and the schedules around them
When it goes wrong: loss spikes, divergence, stragglers and the arithmetic of a checkpoint
Model FLOPs utilisation: what 40% means and where the other 60% went

Tensor-parallel communication for one transformer layer of hidden size 8,192 at TP = 8 with a 4M-token global batch: the all-reduce bytes per step against NVLink (900 GB/s) and InfiniBand (400 Gb/s), and why tensor parallelism stays inside the node

days.subject: AI, Technology & Coding
days.topic: Inference and serving: KV caches, batching, quantisation, speculative decoding and the cost of a token
days.headline_hint: Prefill is a matrix multiply, decode is a memory read: why one token costs what it costs
days.focus: The serving stack built up from the roofline of day 4. Prefill versus decode and their opposite bottlenecks; arithmetic intensity and the H100's ridge point; the KV cache as the scarce resource, continuous batching, PagedAttention and prefix caching; quantisation formats (int8, int4, FP8, FP4; GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant; KV-cache quantisation) and the accuracy they cost; speculative decoding with its expected acceptance derived, Medusa and EAGLE heads; disaggregated prefill/decode; and the unit economics — cost per million tokens from GPU-hour price, batch size and utilisation, reconciled to a public price list. Afterwards the reader can price a token for any published model on any published GPU. refresh: check current GPU rental prices, the speculative-decoding methods of record, FP4 inference practice and the labs' current per-token price lists before writing.

The roofline: arithmetic intensity, the ridge point, and why batch size is everything
Managing the cache: continuous batching, paged memory and prefix reuse
Smaller numbers: quantisation formats, calibration methods and the accuracy they cost
Guess and verify: speculative decoding and its expected tokens per step
