days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Life insurance product mechanics and taxation
days.headline_hint: Every permanent policy is term insurance plus a savings account with peculiar rules: the reserve arithmetic, §7702, the seven-pay test and the illustrations that sell them
days.focus: Product mechanics from the mortality table up: annual renewable and level term priced from the 2017 CSO table, the net level premium and prospective reserve of whole life, non-forfeiture options and participating dividends, universal life's cost-of-insurance and crediting mechanics with the §7702 corridor and the guideline-premium versus cash-value-accumulation tests at the 2% insurance interest rate set in 2021, indexed universal life's caps and floors under Actuarial Guideline 49-A, variable life, and no-lapse guarantees. Then the tax: §101(a), §72(e) inside build-up, the seven-pay test of §7702A and LIFO treatment of MECs, policy loans, the transfer-for-value rule, §1035 exchanges, the Goodman triangle and §101(j). The reader can afterwards read an illustration and say what is guaranteed, what is assumed, and what the IRS calls it.

Whole life is a level premium for a rising risk: net premiums, reserves and where the cash value comes from
Universal life: unbundling the policy, the corridor, and what the 2021 change to §7702 did to premiums
Indexed and variable life: caps, participation rates, AG 49-A and the S&P 500's actual distribution
The seven-pay test and the MEC: when a policy stops being insurance for tax purposes
Taxation of the whole life cycle: death benefits, withdrawals, loans, exchanges and the transfer-for-value trap

An indexed universal life crediting formula (9% cap, 0% floor, 100% participation, annual point-to-point) applied to every calendar-year S&P 500 price return from 1957 through 2025: the fraction of years capped, the fraction floored, and the resulting average credited rate against the illustrated 6%

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Disability income insurance

The reader can afterwards compute Dana's replacement gap after tax, price the elimination period against the day-4 reserve, and read a group certificate for the clauses that will bite.

SSDI: the five-step test, the waiting period, substantial gainful activity and the approval odds

The reader can afterwards choose between the Hartwells' two employer plans on expected cost and value the HSA over 30 years.

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Tax-loss harvesting and direct indexing
days.headline_hint: A loss is worth its tax rate today minus its tax rate later: the wash-sale rule, a real 2022 harvest, and what the academic estimates of harvesting alpha really say
days.focus: Harvesting taken to the bottom: §1091's wash-sale rule (thirty days either side, substantially identical, IRAs and spouses per Rev. Rul. 2008-5), the netting rules of §1(h) and the $3,000 ordinary offset with indefinite carryforward, specific-identification lot selection under Reg. §1.1012-1(c), the true economics (deferral value, the rate arbitrage between short-term and long-term, the step-up or charitable exit that makes deferral permanent) and the literature (Arnott, Berkin and Ye 2001; Chaudhuri, Burnham and Lo 2020) with its assumptions exposed. Then direct indexing: separately managed accounts harvesting single names, tracking error, loss decay as basis rises, fees, and when it does not pay. Also the mirror image, gain harvesting into the 0% bracket. The reader can afterwards execute and value a harvest for the Hartwells and decide whether direct indexing is worth its fee.
parts: §1091 and 'substantially identical': what the statute says, what the rulings added, and what nobody has ruled
Netting, carryforwards and lot selection: the mechanics on Form 8949 and Schedule D
What a harvested loss is actually worth: deferral, rate arbitrage and the permanent exits
The alpha literature: 0.5% a year, 1.08% a year, and the assumptions behind each
Direct indexing: single-name harvesting, tracking error, loss decay and the fee
Harvesting gains: the 0% bracket and the low-income year
worked_examples: 500 shares of Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI) bought at the close on January 3, 2022 and harvested at the close on June 16, 2022 into iShares Core S&P Total U.S. Stock Market ETF (ITOT), using the two funds' actual closes: a short-term loss near $29,500, worth $7,080 against short-term gains at 24% today versus $4,425 of extra long-term tax in ten years, or $2,717 in present value at 5%, a net gain of about $4,360

Arnott, Berkin and Ye (2001) and Chaudhuri, Burnham and Lo (2020): reconstructing the 1926-2018 harvesting alpha of 1.08 percentage points a year, and what happens to it under the Hartwells' actual gain realisations and a 2.5% turnover

A direct-indexing account tracking the S&P 500 with 0.35% fee: the harvested-loss yield in years one through five from a published provider disclosure, the point at which loss decay leaves the fee uncovered, and the tracking error budget

Gain harvesting in a low-income year: a married couple with $70,000 of ordinary taxable income realising $28,900 of long-term gains to fill the 2026 0% bracket to $98,900, resetting basis at zero federal cost and 3.07% Pennsylvania cost
sources: IRC §1091, §1211, §1212, §1(h); Rev. Rul. 2008-5; Treas. Reg. §1.1012-1(c); IRS Publication 550 and the Form 8949 and Schedule D instructions
Arnott, R., Berkin, A. and Ye, J., 'Loss Harvesting: What's It Worth to the Taxable Investor?', Journal of Wealth Management 3(4), 2001
Chaudhuri, S., Burnham, T. and Lo, A., 'An Empirical Evaluation of Tax-Loss-Harvesting Alpha', Financial Analysts Journal 76(3), 2020
Vanguard Research, 'Personalized indexing: A portfolio construction plan' and the Parametric Portfolio Associates published tax-management methodology

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Concentrated positions
days.headline_hint: Four percent of stocks created all of the market's net wealth: the case against the single stock, and eight ways out that are not simply selling
days.focus: The concentrated position as the commonest wealth-destroying exposure in employee households: Bessembinder's evidence on single-stock outcomes, the volatility and drawdown arithmetic versus the index, and then the exits at statute depth: staged sales and the capital-gains stacking that prices them (with NIIT and the 20% bracket), gifting appreciated shares and the 30%-of-AGI limit, donor-advised funds, charitable remainder trusts under §664 and the §7520 rate, exchange funds under §721 and the qualifying-asset requirement, collars and the constructive-sale rule of §1259, prepaid variable forwards, Rule 10b5-1 plans as amended in 2022, net unrealised appreciation under §402(e)(4), §1042 for ESOP sales and §1202 for qualified small-business stock as expanded in 2025. The reader can afterwards lay out a multi-year exit for a real position and price each route after tax.
parts: Bessembinder's tables: why the median stock loses to a Treasury bill over its life
Selling is a tax problem: stacking, NIIT, the 20% bracket and the multi-year schedule
Give it away well: appreciated shares, donor-advised funds and the charitable remainder trust priced at the §7520 rate
Pool it: exchange funds, the seven-year lockup and the 20% qualifying-asset rule
Hedge it: collars, constructive sales, variable prepaid forwards and what the IRS has said
Special doors: 10b5-1 plans, NUA, §1042 and §1202 after the 2025 expansion
worked_examples: An employee holding 4,000 shares of NVIDIA vested between 2019 and 2021 with an aggregate basis of $60,000, marked at the close on the run date: the tax on selling everything in one year (15% then 20% above $613,700 MFJ taxable income in 2026, plus 3.8% NIIT and 3.07% Pennsylvania) against a four-year staged sale that keeps each year in the 15% band

Bessembinder (2018): 4% of listed U.S. common stocks account for the entire net gain over Treasury bills from 1926 to 2016, and the median stock's lifetime buy-and-hold return is below the bill; the drawdown history of a single mega-cap name against the S&P 500 over the same holding period

A charitable remainder unitrust funded with $500,000 of the NVIDIA shares paying 5% to the Hartwells for their joint lives: the remainder factor from IRS Publication 1458 at the §7520 rate for the run month, the 10% remainder test, the income-tax deduction and the four-tier ordering of the payouts

A six-month zero-cost collar on NVIDIA at the run date's CBOE quotes (put at 90% of spot, call struck where its premium pays for the put), checked against year one's Black-Scholes at the quoted implied volatility, and whether the band is wide enough to escape §1259
sources: Bessembinder, H., 'Do stocks outperform Treasury bills?', Journal of Financial Economics 129(3), 2018

IRC §664 and Treas. Reg. §1.664-3; IRS Publication 1458 (actuarial factors) and the monthly §7520 rate; IRC §721(b) and Treas. Reg. §1.351-1(c) (investment company and qualifying assets); IRC §1259; Rev. Rul. 2003-7 (prepaid forwards)
SEC Rule 10b5-1 as amended (Release No. 33-11138, December 2022); IRC §402(e)(4) (net unrealised appreciation); §1042; §1202 as amended by P.L. 119-21
Welch, S., 'Diversifying Concentrated Holdings', in Evensky, H. et al. (eds.), The New Wealth Management (CFA Institute/Wiley, 2011)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Monte Carlo and the safe-withdrawal research
days.headline_hint: The 4% rule is a 1966 artifact with a 95% confidence interval: what Bengen, Trinity and Morningstar actually measured, and how to simulate a retirement honestly
days.focus: The withdrawal-rate literature read as primary research, not as a rule of thumb: Bengen's 1994 method and data, the Trinity study's success tables, Pfau's international evidence, Blanchett-Finke-Pfau on low yields, Bengen's own later revisions and Morningstar's 2025 base case of 3.9% with 5.2% under guardrails and 4.5% from a TIPS ladder. Then the machinery: parametric lognormal simulation, block bootstrap of Shiller's data, regime and valuation conditioning through CAPE, the sensitivity of success probability to the expected-return input, the magnitude of failure as a better objective than its probability, and Milevsky and Robinson's closed-form ruin probability from the reciprocal gamma distribution, derived and computed. The reader can afterwards build a defensible simulation, criticise anyone else's, and state the Hartwells' sustainable rate with its uncertainty.
parts: Bengen 1994 and Trinity 1998: the data, the method and the worst start year they found
The historical SAFEMAX by start year, 1926 to 1995, from Shiller's data
Parametric, bootstrapped and regime-based Monte Carlo: three ways to get three different answers
The expected return is the whole answer: sensitivity, CAPE and the case for conditioning
Ruin in closed form: the Milevsky-Robinson derivation and the number it gives
Morningstar's 3.9%, the TIPS ladder's 4.5% and what the Hartwells should take from all of it
worked_examples: Bengen's 1994 table reconstructed with Ibbotson-style data: the 30-year maximum safe rate for a 50/50 portfolio for each start year 1926-1976, with 1966's 4.15% as the binding case; the Trinity 1998 success rates for 4% and 5% at 30 years and 75/25

The distribution of 30-year SAFEMAX across start years from Shiller's monthly S&P and 10-year Treasury series with CPI, 1926-1995: median, minimum, and the 15-year real return that explains most of the variance

Milevsky and Robinson (2005): with a 3% real expected return, 12% volatility, 4% spending and an exponential remaining lifetime with median 21 years, the reciprocal-gamma parameters (alpha about 3.05, beta about 0.024) give a lifetime ruin probability near 23%; the same at 3% spending and at 8% volatility

A 10,000-path Monte Carlo for a $1.5 million portfolio spending $60,000 real: success probability at expected real returns of 2%, 3% and 4% (the last two roughly 1/CAPE at the run date), showing the probability swinging by more than 30 points on one input
sources: Bengen, W., 'Determining Withdrawal Rates Using Historical Data', Journal of Financial Planning 7(4), October 1994; Cooley, P., Hubbard, C. and Walz, D., 'Retirement Savings: Choosing a Withdrawal Rate That Is Sustainable', AAII Journal, February 1998
Milevsky, M. and Robinson, C., 'A Sustainable Spending Rate without Simulation', Financial Analysts Journal 61(6), 2005
Morningstar, The State of Retirement Income 2025; Blanchett, D., Finke, M. and Pfau, W., 'Low Bond Yields and Safe Portfolio Withdrawal Rates', Journal of Wealth Management 16(2), 2013
Shiller, R., online U.S. stock market data (monthly, 1871-present) accompanying Irrational Exuberance, 3rd ed. (Princeton, 2015)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Sequence-of-returns risk and dynamic withdrawal policies
days.headline_hint: Two retirees with identical average returns and half a million dollars between them: the path-dependence of withdrawals, and the spending rules that trade certainty for survival
days.focus: Sequence risk formalised: the terminal-wealth recursion under withdrawals, why the order of returns matters only when cash flows are present, the first-decade real return as the dominant variable, the retirement red zone, and the accumulation-phase mirror. Then the dynamic policies with their rules stated exactly and tested on real data: constant-percentage, Guyton-Klinger guardrails, Vanguard's ceiling-and-floor, RMD-based spending from the Uniform Lifetime Table, Bengen's floor-and-ceiling, the rising equity glidepath of Pfau and Kitces, bucket strategies and Estrada's critique, and the non-portfolio hedges (delaying Social Security, paying off the mortgage, partial annuitisation, previewed for block 2). The reader can afterwards run the 2000 retiree through each rule with actual returns and explain the trade each rule makes.
parts: The recursion: why order matters once money is moving, and the accumulation mirror
The 2000 retiree and the 2009 retiree: identical decades on average, opposite outcomes
The first ten years decide: Kitces's correlation and the retirement red zone
Guardrails, ceilings and floors: Guyton-Klinger and Vanguard's rules applied to real history
RMD-based, floor-and-ceiling and the rising equity glidepath
What the Hartwells' plan should say about sequence, thirty years before they retire
worked_examples: A $1 million 60/40 portfolio withdrawing $40,000 real from January 2000 versus from March 2009, using annual S&P 500 total returns, 10-year Treasury returns and CPI from Damodaran's historical series: the 2000 retiree's real balance after 25 years against the 2009 retiree's, with the average annual return of each 25-year window shown to be within a point

The same 2000 retiree under Guyton-Klinger: the capital-preservation cut triggered in 2003 and 2009 (withdrawal rate 20% above initial), the prosperity-rule raises, the inflation-rule skips, and the terminal wealth against the constant-real-dollar rule

Kitces (2008): the correlation of the 30-year safe withdrawal rate with the first 15 years' real return (about 0.91) reproduced from Shiller's data, and the corresponding weakness of the 30-year average return as a predictor

The Pfau-Kitces rising glidepath (30% equity at retirement rising to 60% over 30 years) versus a static 60/40 for the 1966 and 2000 start years, and the RMD-based rule's first-year spending at age 72 from the Uniform Lifetime Table (1/27.4, 3.65%)
sources: Guyton, J. and Klinger, W., 'Decision Rules and Maximum Initial Withdrawal Rates', Journal of Financial Planning 19(3), 2006

Pfau, W. and Kitces, M., 'Reducing Retirement Risk with a Rising Equity Glide Path', Journal of Financial Planning 27(1), 2014; Kitces, M., 'Understanding Sequence of Return Risk and Safe Withdrawal Rates', The Kitces Report, 2008

Estrada, J., 'The Bucket Approach for Retirement: A Suboptimal Behavioral Trick?', Journal of Wealth Management 21(4), 2019; Vanguard Research, 'From assets to income: A goals-based approach to retirement spending'
Damodaran, A., 'Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills: 1928-present' (NYU Stern data page); Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-9 (Uniform Lifetime Table)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: The individual income tax at depth: brackets, capital gains, NIIT and the AMT
days.headline_hint: One household, three tax systems: the Form 1040 walked from gross income to the check, then the capital-gains stack and the alternative minimum tax computed by hand
days.focus: The federal individual income tax as a machine, at the run year's figures: gross income, above-the-line adjustments, AGI, the standard deduction versus itemized after the 2025 law (the $40,400 SALT cap with its phase-down, the permanent $750,000 mortgage limit, the 0.5% charitable floor, the 2/37 limitation for the top bracket), §199A for Marcus's S-corporation, the ordinary brackets, the capital-gains stack at 0/15/20 with the worksheet done by hand, §1250 and collectibles, the child tax credit and its phase-out, the net investment income tax and additional Medicare tax, and the AMT with its 2026 exemption, 50% phase-out, 26/28 rates and preference items. The lesson maps the household's effective marginal rate across income, including cliffs, and finishes with withholding and the §6654 safe harbours. The reader can afterwards compute the Hartwells' federal and Pennsylvania liability from the primary tables and identify every threshold they are near.
parts: The architecture of Form 1040: what is income, what comes off above the line, and why AGI is the number everything keys on
Deductions after 2025: standard versus itemized, the SALT cap and phase-down, the charitable floor and the 2/37 haircut
§199A for a pass-through owner: the 20% deduction, the thresholds and the specified-service question
The ordinary brackets and the capital-gains stack: the worksheet by hand
NIIT, additional Medicare tax, the credit phase-outs and Pennsylvania's flat 3.07%: the true marginal rate curve
The alternative minimum tax: exemption, phase-out, preferences and the credit that comes back
worked_examples: The Hartwells' 2026 return computed line by line: W-2 wages $244,000, S-corporation K-1 $40,000, interest and dividends $6,000, long-term gains $12,000, Dana's $20,000 401(k) deferral and the $8,750 HSA: AGI $273,250, taxable income $241,050 after the $32,200 standard deduction, ordinary tax about $41,600 from the 2026 brackets with $16,000 of preferential income stacked at 15%, child tax credits $4,400, NIIT about $684 on the excess over $250,000, net federal about $37,900; Pennsylvania at 3.07% on about $293,000 (no deduction for the 401(k) deferral) about $9,000

The capital-gains worksheet by hand for a couple with $80,000 of ordinary taxable income and $40,000 of long-term gains: $18,900 taxed at 0% up to the 2026 $98,900 threshold and $21,100 at 15%, and the marginal rate on the next dollar of wages (12% plus the 15% it pushes off the 0% shelf, 27%)

A $600,000 MFJ itemizer in 2026 with $40,400 of SALT (phase-down begins at $505,000 MAGI), $30,000 of mortgage interest and $20,000 of charity: regular tax versus tentative minimum tax with the $140,200 exemption intact below the $1,000,000 phase-out, the 28% rate above $244,500 of AMTI, and whether AMT applies

The Hartwells' effective marginal rate curve from $200,000 to $450,000 of AGI: the 24% bracket, the NIIT switching on at $250,000, the Roth phase-out at $242,000-$252,000, the child credit phase-out at $400,000, and the §6654 110%-of-prior-year safe harbour for their estimated payments
sources: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026 inflation adjustments: brackets, standard deduction, AMT, capital-gains thresholds) and IRS Publication 17, Your Federal Income Tax
Form 1040 instructions (Qualified Dividends and Capital Gain Tax Worksheet) and Form 6251 and Form 8960 instructions for the run year
Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, PA-40 instructions and Personal Income Tax Guide (compensation; retirement contributions); Pennsylvania Act 32 local earned income tax

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Employee benefits and equity compensation
days.headline_hint: Paid in paper: RSUs, options, purchase plans and deferred compensation taxed event by event, with the withholding trap, the AMT trap and the option-value trap
days.focus: Equity compensation at statute depth: restricted stock and RSUs under §83 with the supplemental-withholding shortfall, the §83(b) election and its 30-day rule, incentive stock options under §422 (the $100,000 rule, qualifying and disqualifying dispositions, the AMT preference and the AMT credit), non-qualified options and the early-exercise decision as an option-value question using year one's Black-Scholes, §423 employee stock purchase plans with the lookback and the $25,000 limit, and non-qualified deferred compensation under §409A and §3121(v)(2). Then the rest of the benefits package: §125 cafeteria plans, health and dependent-care FSAs at the run year's limits, group term, employer student-loan assistance under §127, Roth matching and the mandatory Roth catch-up for higher earners from 2026, and after-tax contributions to the §415(c) limit. The reader can afterwards tax any grant on any date, decide when to exercise, and read Dana's total compensation statement as a planner.
parts: §83 and the RSU: taxed at vest, withheld at 22%, and the April surprise for a 32% earner
Restricted stock and the §83(b) election: thirty days, no extensions, and the bet you are making
Incentive stock options: qualifying dispositions, the AMT preference and the credit that returns
Non-qualified options and the question of when: time value, the Greeks and the taxes
The §423 purchase plan: lookback, the $25,000 limit and the two holding periods
Deferred compensation and the rest of the package: §409A, FSAs, §127 and the Roth catch-up rule
worked_examples: Dana's grant of 400 RSUs in PPG Industries (NYSE: PPG) vesting 25 a quarter: the 100 shares that vest on a stated date in the run year at PPG's close that day, withheld at the 22% supplemental rate though her marginal rate is 24% federal plus 3.07% Pennsylvania, the sell-to-cover share count, the basis and holding period established at vest, and the underwithholding to fix on Form W-4

Apple's employee stock purchase plan as disclosed in its Form 10-K (purchase at 85% of the lower of the fair market value at the start or end of a six-month offering period): a $12,000 contribution over one real offering period using Apple's closes on the offering dates, the purchase price, the immediate gain, the annualised return on the average money in the plan, and the ordinary-versus-capital split in a qualifying and a disqualifying disposition

Dana's brother at a Pittsburgh start-up with 10,000 ISOs at a $2.00 strike and a $9.00 §409A valuation: exercising all in one year adds $70,000 of AMT preference; his tentative minimum tax as a single filer with $140,000 of wages against the 2026 $90,100 exemption and 26% rate, the crossover exercise quantity that avoids AMT, and the §83(b) alternative had he exercised at grant

A 10-year non-qualified option on a $50 stock at a $50 strike with 30% implied volatility: the Black-Scholes value at grant, the time value forfeited by exercising at $75 in year four, and the after-tax comparison of exercising now versus holding two more years at the Hartwells' rates
sources: IRS Publication 525, Taxable and Nontaxable Income; Forms 3921 and 3922 instructions; Treas. Reg. §31.3402(g)-1 (supplemental wage withholding)
Treasury and IRS final regulations on catch-up contributions under SECURE 2.0 §603 (T.D. 10037, September 2025); IRS Notice 2025-67
Apple Inc., Form 10-K, Note on share-based compensation (Employee Stock Purchase Plan terms); PPG Industries, Form 10-K, stock-based compensation note
days.exam_map: CFP Principal Knowledge Domain F, Retirement Savings and Income Planning (non-qualified plan rules and options; qualified plan rules) and Domain E, Tax Planning (tax implications of special circumstances: equity compensation)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Roth versus traditional, charitable strategies and bunching: the integrated year
days.headline_hint: The whole household in one tax year: every dollar of savings ordered, the Roth question settled by arithmetic, the gifts bunched under the new floor, and the liability stated before and after
days.focus: The capstone integrates the block into one plan. Roth versus traditional is done as the commutative-property argument with its real exceptions (the limit asymmetry, tax diversification, the marginal rate on withdrawals once Social Security and Medicare premiums are in the picture, and Pennsylvania's refusal to deduct deferrals while exempting retirement distributions), the backdoor Roth with the pro-rata rule and Form 8606, conversions filled to the top of a target bracket, and the 2026 Roth-catch-up and Roth-match rules. Charitable planning is done under the 2025 law: the 0.5%-of-AGI floor, the 35% value cap, the non-itemizer deduction, appreciated-stock gifts and the 30% limit, donor-advised-fund bunching, and qualified charitable distributions at the 2026 $111,000 limit for the Hartwells' parents. The lesson closes by ordering the Hartwells' $70,000 of savings capacity across every account in the block and stating the household's liability before and after, with the limits cited to the revenue procedure for the run year.
parts: The commutative property and its exceptions: when Roth wins, when traditional wins, and why the answer is usually both
Pennsylvania changes the answer: a state that taxes the contribution and exempts the withdrawal
The backdoor, the pro-rata rule and the conversion filled to the bracket top
Charity after 2025: the floor, the cap, the non-itemizer deduction and gifts of appreciated stock
Bunching through a donor-advised fund, and the qualified charitable distribution for the older generation
The Hartwells' integrated year: seventy thousand dollars ordered across every account in the block
worked_examples: Dana's $20,000 deferral as traditional at a 24% federal rate versus Roth, withdrawn at 22% and at 24% in 25 years at 6%, with Pennsylvania's 3.07% applied to the contribution in both cases and to neither withdrawal; then the limit asymmetry: a full $24,500 Roth deferral against a $24,500 traditional deferral plus the $5,880 of tax saved invested in a taxable account

The backdoor Roth for both spouses at the 2026 $7,500 limit, blocked by Marcus's $95,000 SEP-IRA under the §408(d)(2) pro-rata rule: the taxable fraction of a $7,500 conversion with the SEP in place (about 92.7%) versus after rolling the SEP into a solo 401(k), on Form 8606

The Hartwells' $8,000 of annual giving under the 2026 rules: the 0.5%-of-AGI floor ($1,366 on $273,250) reduces the deductible gift to $6,634; three years bunched into a donor-advised fund funded with $24,000 of PPG shares carrying a $9,000 basis, deducting fair value, avoiding $15,000 of gain, and itemizing $46,000 against the $32,200 standard deduction; Dana's parents' $20,000 qualified charitable distribution against the $111,000 2026 limit

The integrated plan: $70,000 of capacity ordered as the 401(k) to the match, the family HSA ($8,750), the PA 529 ($19,000 per beneficiary per spouse deductible at 3.07%), the 401(k) to the $24,500 limit, two backdoor Roths, the donor-advised fund and the taxable account; federal, NIIT and Pennsylvania liability before and after, the effective marginal rate at the end, and whether AGI lands below the $250,000 NIIT threshold
sources: IRC §408A, §408(d)(2), §402A, §414(v)(7) (Roth catch-up), §170(b), §170(p) (non-itemizer deduction) and §68 as amended by P.L. 119-21; §408(d)(8) (qualified charitable distributions); IRS Publications 590-A, 590-B and 526; Form 8606 instructions
Rev. Proc. 2025-32 and IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 limits: standard deduction $32,200 MFJ, IRA $7,500, 401(k) $24,500, QCD $111,000, gift exclusion $19,000)

Reichenstein, W., 'Tax-Efficient Sequencing of Accounts to Tap in Retirement', Journal of Financial Planning, 2006; Kitces, M., 'The Taxation of Roth Conversions and the Commutative Property' (Nerd's Eye View)
Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, Personal Income Tax Guide, Chapter 7 (Gross Compensation: retirement plan contributions and distributions)
days.exam_map: CFP Principal Knowledge Domain E, Tax Planning (tax reduction and management techniques; charitable and philanthropic contributions and deductions) and Domain F (Roth versus traditional retirement savings)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Qualified plans: the rulebook
days.headline_hint: Why the government pays for your 401(k) — and what it demands in return
days.focus: The statutory architecture of employer plans — ERISA and §401(a) — read as a bargain: tax deferral in exchange for coverage, nondiscrimination, vesting and funding. Defined contribution and defined benefit plans, cash balance hybrids, the run-year §402(g)/§415/§401(a)(17) limits and the SECURE 2.0 catch-ups, ADP/ACP and top-heavy testing, safe harbors, PBGC insurance, and the owner-only and small-business family (SEP, SIMPLE, solo 401(k)) with the self-employed contribution arithmetic. Every limit is printed for the year the lesson runs and checked against that year's IRS notice. Afterwards the reader can read a summary plan description and a Form 5500 and say what the plan may and may not do.
parts: The bargain: what §401(a) buys and what ERISA demands
Defined contribution plans and the three ceilings: §402(g), §415(c) and §401(a)(17)
Defined benefit and cash balance plans: the accrual formula, §415(b) and the PBGC backstop
Nondiscrimination in numbers: coverage, ADP/ACP, top-heavy and the safe harbors
The owner's plans: SEP, SIMPLE, solo 401(k) and the self-employed arithmetic
Loans, hardship, in-service withdrawals and the plan document as the final word
worked_examples: A 52-year-old earning $210,000 in 2026: the $24,500 elective deferral plus the $8,000 catch-up, a 6% match, and after-tax contributions up to the $72,000 §415(c) ceiling (IRS Notice 2025-67) — the full stack, and how the age 60–63 super catch-up of $11,250 changes it.

IBM's 2024 replacement of its 401(k) match with a 5% cash-balance credit in its Personal Pension Plan (IBM 2023 Form 10-K pension note): what a cash balance plan is, the hypothetical account, and the interest credit.
An ADP test on a 60-employee plan: HCE average deferral 7.1% against NHCE 4.0% fails the two-percentage-point test — the refund, the QNEC, and the price of a 3% non-elective safe harbor instead.

A sole proprietor with $180,000 of Schedule C profit: net earnings × 0.9235, the half-SE-tax deduction, the 20%-of-net SEP contribution against a solo 401(k) with deferral plus 20% — the exact dollars, and why the solo-k wins until both reach the §415(c) ceiling.
sources: IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living limits) and the notice for the run year; PBGC Maximum Monthly Guarantee Tables (2026: $7,789.77 at 65)
Tripodi, The ERISA Outline Book (current annual edition)
IRS Publication 560, Retirement Plans for Small Business (run year)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Rollovers, IRAs and the Roth conversion arithmetic
days.headline_hint: Money in motion: the sixty days, the once-a-year trap, and when paying tax early is the winning move
days.focus: Distribution and rollover law first — direct versus indirect rollovers, the 20% withholding, the 60-day and once-per-year rules after Bobrow, net unrealized appreciation, and the §72(t) exceptions including the substantially-equal-payment methods of Notice 2022-6 — then the IRA rules with the run-year deductibility and Roth phase-outs, the backdoor and mega-backdoor routes and the §408(d)(2) pro-rata rule, and finally the conversion decision done as arithmetic: marginal rate now against marginal rate later, tax paid from outside funds, partial conversions to the top of a bracket, and the two five-year clocks. The reader leaves able to design a conversion schedule and defend it in numbers.
parts: Leaving a plan: direct rollovers, the 20% withholding trap and the 60-day clock
Net unrealized appreciation and §72(t): the exceptions that reward reading the statute
Traditional and Roth IRAs: the run-year limits, phase-outs and the backdoor
The pro-rata rule and the mega-backdoor: aggregation, Form 8606 and the plan-side route
The conversion equation: when (1 − t now) beats (1 − t later), and what outside money changes
The two five-year clocks, the end of recharacterisation, and a conversion schedule for a gap-years couple
worked_examples: A $900,000 401(k) holding $220,000 of employer stock with $40,000 of basis: NUA under §402(e)(4) — ordinary tax on the basis now, long-term gain on $180,000 later — against a full rollover, at 2026 brackets.
Bobrow v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2014-21: the two 60-day rollovers the Tax Court ruled were one too many, and the once-per-12-months rule the IRS adopted in Announcement 2014-15.

A 58-year-old with a $1,400,000 IRA and $60,000 of other income converting $100,000 a year for five years to fill the 22% bracket (top of bracket $211,400 MFJ in 2026), tax paid from a taxable account, against leaving it for RMDs at 24%.

The pro-rata trap: a $7,500 non-deductible contribution converted while $150,000 of pre-tax IRA money sits elsewhere — 95.2% of the conversion taxable — and the reverse rollover into a 401(k) that clears the denominator.
sources: IRS Notice 2022-6 (substantially equal periodic payments); IRS Publications 590-A and 590-B (run year)
Bobrow v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2014-21; IRS Announcement 2014-15
Slott, The New Retirement Savings Time Bomb (2021 ed.)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Required minimum distributions and inherited accounts
days.headline_hint: The table that empties your account on a schedule — and the ten-year clock the heirs inherit
days.focus: The RMD regime after SECURE, SECURE 2.0 and the July 2024 final regulations (T.D. 10001): required beginning dates by birth year, the Uniform Lifetime and Joint tables, the still-working exception, aggregation, the §4974 excise and its correction window, and Roth accounts' exemption. Then the beneficiary side to the bottom: eligible designated beneficiaries, the ten-year rule with annual distributions in years one through nine when death follows the required beginning date, spousal options including the SECURE 2.0 election, see-through trusts (conduit and accumulation), and the Single Life Table's recalculation rules. The reader can compute any RMD and lay out a ten-year drawdown that minimises the family's tax.
parts: Required beginning dates and the Uniform Lifetime Table: where the divisor comes from
Aggregation, the still-working exception, annuitised balances and the §4974 excise
Who is a designated beneficiary: the five eligible classes and everyone else
The ten-year rule as finally written: T.D. 10001 and the years one-to-nine distributions
Spouses, trusts and the see-through rules: conduit versus accumulation after SECURE
Planning the drawdown: even-spread, bracket-fill and the QCD offset
worked_examples: A $2,000,000 IRA owner turning 73 in 2026 (born 1953): divisor 26.5 gives a $75,472 first RMD; the same balance at 80 (20.2) and 90 (12.2), and what that does to the owner's bracket — from the Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-9 tables.

A 50-year-old daughter inherits $1,000,000 in 2026 from a father who died at 78 after his RBD: Single Life divisor at 51 (35.3) gives a $28,329 year-one RMD, reducing by one each year, and the year-ten balloon against an even ten-year spread at 2026 brackets.
A 60-year-old widow inheriting her husband's $800,000 IRA: treat-as-own against remaining a beneficiary with the SECURE 2.0 spousal election, and when each is right.
An accumulation trust for a disabled child as IRA beneficiary: 2026 trust brackets (37% above $16,000) against the child's own rate, and why the applicable multi-beneficiary trust matters.
sources: IRS Publication 590-B (run year), Appendix B life-expectancy tables
Choate, Life and Death Planning for Retirement Benefits (8th ed., 2019, with online updates)
days.exam_map: Retirement Savings and Income Planning — Distribution rules and taxation; Estate Planning — Property titling and beneficiary designations

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Social Security: the benefit formula and the claiming decision
days.headline_hint: Ninety, thirty-two, fifteen: the three numbers behind every Social Security check
days.focus: The Old-Age and Survivors program computed from its statute: indexing an earnings record with the average wage index, the 35-year AIME, the bend-point formula with the run-year bend points ($1,286 and $7,749 for 2026), full retirement age by birth year, the early-reduction and delayed-credit fractions, spousal, survivor and divorced-spouse benefits and how each reduces, the earnings test, the taxation of benefits and the provisional-income 'torpedo', COLA mechanics, and the Social Security Fairness Act's repeal of WEP and GPO. Then claiming as a decision under longevity uncertainty — Shoven-Slavov, break-even, the couple's asymmetry — and the Trustees' solvency arithmetic. The reader can compute a PIA by hand and defend a claiming strategy.
parts: From earnings record to AIME: indexing, the thirty-five years and the zeros
The PIA formula and its bend points, and how the COLA rides on top
Retirement-age arithmetic: 5/9 of 1% and 2/3 of 1%, spouses, survivors and divorced spouses
The earnings test and the taxation of benefits: the provisional-income torpedo
Claiming under uncertainty: break-even, Shoven-Slavov and the couple's asymmetry
The trust funds: the Trustees' depletion date and what 'payable' means
worked_examples: A hypothetical Bridgeville engineer born in 1964 with a 38-year earnings record: index each year by the SSA average wage index series, take the top 35, compute the AIME, apply the 2026 bend points — PIA to the dollar, then the age-62 (70%) and age-70 (124%) amounts.

A couple with PIAs of $3,400 and $1,600: the higher earner delays to 70 while the lower earner claims at 62 or files at FRA for the spousal top-up — present values at a 2% real rate over joint lifetimes from the SSA period life table.
A widow at 60 taking the survivor benefit at 71.5% against waiting to 67, alongside her own retirement benefit at 70: the switching strategy in dollars.
A 64-year-old earning $60,000 while claiming: $1 withheld per $2 over the 2026 limit of $24,480 — the months withheld and the recomputation at full retirement age.
sources: Social Security Act §§202, 203, 215; 20 C.F.R. Part 404; SSA POMS RS 00605 (PIA computations)
SSA, 2026 Cost-of-Living Adjustment Fact Sheet; SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Annual Trustees Report (run-year edition; 2025: OASI depletion 2033)
Shoven and Slavov, 'Does It Pay to Delay Social Security?', Journal of Pension Economics and Finance 13(2), 2014
Kotlikoff, Moeller and Solman, Get What's Yours: The Revised Secrets to Maxing Out Your Social Security (2016)
days.exam_map: Retirement Savings and Income Planning — Social Security and Medicare planning

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Medicare, IRMAA and the cost of health care in retirement
days.headline_hint: The two-year lookback that turns a Roth conversion into a Medicare surcharge
days.focus: Medicare as an enrollment-and-pricing machine: Parts A, B, C and D, the Medigap letters and the Plan F closure, the seven-month initial window and the special and general periods, the lifetime Part B and Part D penalties, the run-year premiums and deductibles, and IRMAA — the tiers, the two-year MAGI lookback and the SSA-44 life-changing-event appeal. Then the cost of the whole retirement: the pre-65 bridge through COBRA or the marketplace with the premium-tax-credit table in force that year, the health savings account as a retirement account and the six-month Medicare look-back on contributions, Medicare Advantage against Medigap economics, and the retiree-cost estimates of Fidelity and EBRI. The reader can price a household's health care from 60 to 90 and manage MAGI around the cliffs.
parts: The four parts, the ten letters and the windows that close: Medicare's enrollment law
Premiums, deductibles and the Part D cap for the run year
IRMAA: the tiers, the two-year lookback and the cliffs measured in dollars
The pre-65 bridge: COBRA, the marketplace and the premium-tax-credit arithmetic in force
The HSA in retirement and the Medicare six-month rule
Pricing sixty to ninety: Fidelity, EBRI and a household's own health-cost line
worked_examples: A single 67-year-old with $105,000 of MAGI who converted $30,000 of IRA to Roth in 2024: the 2026 tier-one threshold of $109,000 crossed by $4,000 — the Part B standard $202.90 replaced by the tier-one amount plus the Part D adjustment for twelve months, as a percentage of the excess income.

A 62-year-old Allegheny County couple with $58,000 of MAGI buying a silver marketplace plan: the applicable-percentage table in force for the run year (the enhanced credits of 2021–2025 having lapsed unless Congress extended them) against the poverty guideline for two, the credit, and the subsidy lost per dollar of conversion income.
A worker who enrolled in Part B 26 months late without creditable coverage: two full 12-month periods, a 20% lifetime surcharge on $202.90, capitalised over 25 years.

An HSA holder retiring at 66 who files for Social Security: Part A backdated six months, the excess-contribution arithmetic, and the 2026 limits ($4,400 self-only, $8,750 family, $1,000 catch-up) for the last clean year.
sources: Social Security Act Title XVIII; 42 C.F.R. Parts 406–408 and 423; 42 U.S.C. §1395r(i) (IRMAA); SSA Form SSA-44
CMS, 2026 Medicare Parts A & B Premiums and Deductibles fact sheet (Part B $202.90, deductible $283, Part A $1,736) and Medicare & You (run-year handbook)
IRC §§36B, 223, 4980B; IRS Publication 969 (run year)
Fidelity Investments, Retiree Health Care Cost Estimate (latest edition); EBRI Issue Brief on savings needed for health expenses in retirement (latest)
days.exam_map: Retirement Savings and Income Planning — Social Security and Medicare planning; Risk Management and Insurance Planning — Health insurance and health care cost management

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Pensions and annuities: lump sums, guarantees and the price of a lifetime
days.headline_hint: What a monthly check for life is actually worth — priced from a mortality table and a yield
days.focus: Defined-benefit pensions and commercial annuities done as pricing problems. The accrual formula and early-retirement reductions, the qualified joint-and-survivor annuity and spousal consent, the §417(e)(3) lump-sum conversion with the three segment rates and the applicable mortality table, the run-year PBGC guarantee, pension risk transfers and the multiemployer rescue. Then annuities: pricing a single-premium immediate annuity from the Society of Actuaries 2012 IAM table and a Treasury curve, the money's-worth ratio, deferred and qualifying longevity annuities, the exclusion ratio, indexed and registered-index-linked contracts, variable annuities with lifetime-withdrawal riders, §1035 exchanges and guaranty-association limits — and the annuity puzzle from Yaari onward. The reader can take a real lump-sum offer or annuity quote and say whether it is fairly priced.
parts: Defined benefits: the accrual formula, early-retirement reductions and the QJSA
The lump-sum conversion under §417(e)(3): segment rates, the mortality table and who wins when rates move
The PBGC guarantee, pension risk transfers and the multiemployer rescue
Pricing a life annuity: the 2012 IAM table, a discount curve and the money's-worth ratio
The product shelf: SPIA, DIA and QLAC, fixed-indexed, RILA, and the lifetime-withdrawal rider's true cost
Taxation and exchanges: the exclusion ratio, §1035, and the annuity puzzle
worked_examples: A frozen-plan participant at 60 offered $612,000 now or $3,150 a month single-life at 65: the lump sum rebuilt from the plan's stated segment rates and the 2026 applicable mortality table, the implied discount rate, and the spouse's joint-and-50% alternative.

A $250,000 SPIA for a 70-year-old man quoted at $1,660 a month: expected present value from the SOA 2012 IAM basic table with Scale G2 improvement at the current Treasury curve, a money's-worth ratio near 0.9, and how a 100-basis-point rate move changes the quote.
A $210,000 QLAC (the 2026 cap) bought at 65 with income from 85: the RMD it removes at 73 under the Uniform Lifetime divisor, and the monthly income it buys.

Verizon's 2012 transfer of $7.5 billion of pension obligations to Prudential and AT&T's 2023 $8.05 billion transfer to Athene, from the sponsors' own filings: what the participant lost (PBGC coverage) and gained (state guaranty coverage).
sources: IRC §§72, 401(a)(11), 417(e)(3), 430; ERISA Title IV; IRS notices on the applicable mortality table and monthly segment rates for the run year
Society of Actuaries, 2012 Individual Annuity Mortality Basic Table and Projection Scale G2
Mitchell, Poterba, Warshawsky and Brown, 'New Evidence on the Money's Worth of Individual Annuities', American Economic Review 89(5), 1999; Yaari, Review of Economic Studies 32(2), 1965
Milevsky, Pensionize Your Nest Egg (2nd ed., 2015); PBGC, Maximum Monthly Guarantee Tables (2026)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Decumulation: the withdrawal-rate literature and sequence risk
days.headline_hint: Four percent, three point seven, or none of the above: thirty years of arguing about how much to spend
days.focus: The research on turning a portfolio into income, read paper by paper and re-run on the data: Bengen's 1994 SAFEMAX, the Trinity study and its updates, Pfau's international evidence, Blanchett's spending smile and Morningstar's annual safe-withdrawal estimate, Guyton-Klinger guardrails and Kitces' ratchet, the Scott-Sharpe-Watson critique, Merton's 'crisis', Milevsky-Robinson's ruin probability in closed form, the Waring-Siegel annually-recalculated annuity, bucket, total-return and floor-and-upside architectures, and the RMD rule. Sequence risk shown on Shiller's data for the 1966 and 2000 retirees; Monte Carlo and its return assumptions; then the tax layer — withdrawal ordering after Cook-Meyer-Reichenstein, bracket-filling, conversions in the gap years, and home equity as the last reserve. The reader can build and defend a spending policy.
parts: Bengen, Trinity and the birth of the four percent rule — replicated on Shiller's data
Sequence risk in numbers: the 1966 and 2000 retirees, and why average return is the wrong statistic
Dynamic rules: Guyton-Klinger guardrails, Kitces' ratchet, Blanchett's smile and the RMD rule
The theorists' objection: Scott-Sharpe-Watson, Merton, Milevsky-Robinson and the ARVA
Architectures: buckets, total return and floor-and-upside, with the annuity as floor
The tax layer: withdrawal order, bracket-filling, conversions in the gap years, and home equity
worked_examples: A $1,500,000 60/40 portfolio drawn at 4% inflation-adjusted from January 1966 and from January 1982 on Shiller's monthly S&P and bond data: year-by-year balances, the year the 1966 retiree runs dry, and the 1982 retiree's terminal wealth.
Guyton-Klinger's 10% guardrails applied to a 5.2% initial rate through 2000–2012: each cut and raise triggered, and the spending path against the fixed rule.
Milevsky-Robinson's closed-form ruin probability for a 65-year-old spending 4.5% at 5% real return and 12% volatility, against the Monte Carlo answer from 10,000 paths.

A 63-year-old couple with $900,000 pre-tax, $300,000 Roth, $400,000 taxable and $70,000 of spending: the conventional order against the Cook-Meyer-Reichenstein order with conversions to the top of the 12% bracket ($100,800 MFJ in 2026) — lifetime tax and terminal wealth over 30 years.

connect_back.subject: Mathematics
connect_back.topic: Law of large numbers and the CLT

sources: Bengen, 'Determining Withdrawal Rates Using Historical Data', Journal of Financial Planning, October 1994; Cooley, Hubbard and Walz, 'Retirement Savings: Choosing a Withdrawal Rate That Is Sustainable', AAII Journal, February 1998

Guyton and Klinger, 'Decision Rules and Maximum Initial Withdrawal Rates', JFP, March 2006; Blanchett, 'Exploring the Retirement Consumption Puzzle', JFP, May 2014; Morningstar, The State of Retirement Income (2024 edition: 3.7%; and the latest edition)

Scott, Sharpe and Watson, 'The 4% Rule — At What Price?', Journal of Investment Management 7(3), 2009; Milevsky and Robinson, 'A Sustainable Spending Rate without Simulation', Financial Analysts Journal 61(6), 2005; Waring and Siegel, 'The Only Spending Rule Article You Will Ever Need', FAJ 71(1), 2015
Cook, Meyer and Reichenstein, 'Tax-Efficient Withdrawal Strategies', FAJ 71(2), 2015; Pfau, Retirement Planning Guidebook (2023 ed.); Shiller, online U.S. stock market data set

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Long-term care and the insurance ledger of retirement
days.headline_hint: The one-in-two risk nobody prices: paying for care when the market is not the problem
days.focus: The non-market risks of retirement, each with its probability and its price. Long-term care: the ASPE incidence and duration data, the CareScout cost-of-care medians for Pittsburgh and the nation, traditional policies and their pricing (elimination period, benefit period, inflation rider, §7702B tax treatment and the run-year §213(d)(10) deductibility bands), hybrid life/LTC contracts, Partnership policies, self-insurance done as a probability tree, and Medicaid in Pennsylvania — the asset limit, the sixty-month lookback, the community-spouse allowances and compliant annuities. Then the rest of the ledger: longevity risk from the SOA tables, life insurance in retirement and pension maximisation, umbrella liability and property, and the Society of Actuaries' post-retirement risk framework. The reader can write the risk page of a plan with numbers on every line.
parts: The incidence and cost of care: ASPE's 56% and CareScout's medians, Pittsburgh included
Traditional long-term care insurance: pricing the contract and the §7702B tax treatment
Hybrids, Partnership policies and the self-insurance probability tree
Medicaid as the insurer of last resort: Pennsylvania's limits, the lookback and the community spouse
Longevity, life insurance and pension maximisation: the SOA tables in the plan
Liability, property and the retirement risk matrix: the rest of the ledger
worked_examples: A 60-year-old couple choosing between a traditional $200-a-day, three-year, 3% compound policy each at roughly $3,800 a year, a $120,000 single-premium hybrid, and self-insuring: expected cost from ASPE's incidence and duration distribution at CareScout's 2024 medians ($127,750 private nursing room, $70,800 assisted living, $77,792 home health aide), inflated at 4%.

A Pennsylvania couple with $420,000 of countable assets when one spouse enters a nursing home: the run-year community spouse resource allowance (2025 maximum $157,920), the spend-down, and a Medicaid-compliant annuity's arithmetic.

Pension maximisation for a 64-year-old: single-life $4,100 a month against joint-and-100% $3,560, the $540 difference funding a $450,000 20-year term policy at a quoted premium — when it works and when it fails at 84.
The probability that at least one of a 65-year-old couple reaches 90 from the SOA RP-2014 tables with MP-2021 improvement, and the reserve that implies at a 3.5% withdrawal rate.
sources: IRC §§213(d)(10), 7702B; 42 U.S.C. §1396p (Medicaid transfers and estate recovery); 55 Pa. Code Chapter 178 (Pennsylvania resource eligibility)
ASPE, 'Long-Term Services and Supports for Older Americans: Risks and Financing' (2022 research brief); CareScout/Genworth, Cost of Care Survey (2024 and latest)
Society of Actuaries, Managing Post-Retirement Risks: Strategies for a Secure Retirement (2020 ed.); SOA RP-2014 and MP-2021 mortality tables
Brown and Finkelstein, 'The Interaction of Public and Private Insurance: Medicaid and the Long-Term Care Insurance Market', American Economic Review 98(3), 2008
days.exam_map: Risk Management and Insurance Planning — Long-term care insurance and long-term care planning; Retirement Savings and Income Planning — Eldercare and special needs planning

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Wills, probate, non-probate transfers and planning for incapacity
days.headline_hint: Most of your estate never sees a judge — and that is precisely the problem
days.focus: The documents and the process, under Pennsylvania's Probate, Estates and Fiduciaries Code with the national cases. What a will can and cannot control; execution and self-proving formalities; intestacy under §§2102–2104; the probate path through the Register of Wills — letters, notice, inventory, the family exemption, creditor advertising, accounting and the inheritance-tax return's nine-month clock; the non-probate estate (beneficiary designations, TOD and POD, joint tenancy and tenancy by the entireties) and the federal pre-emption cases that let a stale form override a will; the elective share; anti-lapse, ademption and abatement; digital assets. Then incapacity: the durable power of attorney under Act 95 of 2014 with its express 'hot powers', the health-care POA and living will, POLST, HIPAA releases, guardianship and the revocable trust as the incapacity instrument. The reader can audit a household's documents and titles and find the gaps.
parts: What a will governs and what it does not: the probate and non-probate estates
Dying without one: Pennsylvania intestacy on a blended-family balance sheet
Probate in Allegheny County: letters, notices, the inventory and the nine-month clock
Will substitutes and the pre-emption cases: Egelhoff, Kennedy and Sveen
The elective share, anti-lapse, ademption and the will's own failure modes
Incapacity: the durable power of attorney's hot powers, health-care directives and guardianship
worked_examples: A $1,800,000 Bridgeville estate, second spouse, two children from a first marriage, no will: 20 Pa.C.S. §2102 — one half to the spouse, one half split between the children — against what a will with a QTIP trust would have done.

Probate timeline and cost for that estate: the Allegheny County Register of Wills fee schedule, the Johnson Estate (1983) attorney-fee guideline, the $3,500 family exemption, and the 5% inheritance-tax discount for payment within three months.

Egelhoff v. Egelhoff, 532 U.S. 141 (2001) and Kennedy v. Plan Administrator for DuPont, 555 U.S. 285 (2009): the ex-spouse who collected because ERISA pre-empts the state's revocation-on-divorce statute — and the beneficiary-designation audit that prevents it.

Prince (died 2016 intestate; six years and an estate settled at $156 million) and Aretha Franklin (the 2023 Michigan verdict on the 2014 couch will): what each cost in fees and years against a modest estate plan.
sources: 20 Pa.C.S. (Probate, Estates and Fiduciaries Code) Chapters 21, 25, 31–33, 54, 55 and 56; Pennsylvania Act 95 of 2014 (powers of attorney); Act 169 of 2006 (advance directives)
Dukeminier and Sitkoff, Wills, Trusts, and Estates (11th ed., 2022)
Egelhoff v. Egelhoff, 532 U.S. 141 (2001); Kennedy v. Plan Administrator for DuPont Savings and Investment Plan, 555 U.S. 285 (2009); Sveen v. Melin, 584 U.S. 811 (2018)
Allegheny County Register of Wills, fee schedule and probate procedures (current)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Trusts: revocable, irrevocable, grantor and non-grantor
days.headline_hint: The legal machine that can own everything you have and still be invisible to the IRS
days.focus: Trusts as the estate planner's instrument, from anatomy to tax engine. Pennsylvania's Uniform Trust Act and trustee duties; the revocable living trust and what it does and does not do (probate, privacy, ancillary administration — not taxes); irrevocable trusts and the §2036/§2038 line that keeps them out of the estate; the grantor trust rules §§671–679 read power by power, including the §675(4)(C) swap power and the three revenue rulings that make the intentionally defective grantor trust work; non-grantor trust income tax with distributable net income, the run-year compressed brackets and the 65-day rule; state taxation after Kaestner; spendthrift and asset-protection limits; dynasty trusts after Pennsylvania's 2006 repeal of the rule against perpetuities; marital and credit-shelter trusts, Clayton QTIPs and the portability-versus-bypass trade; spousal lifetime access trusts and the reciprocal-trust doctrine; and the trust as IRA beneficiary. The reader can read a trust instrument and say who is taxed on what, and why.
parts: Anatomy and duties: settlor, trustee, beneficiary and the Uniform Trust Act
The revocable trust: what it avoids, what it does not, and how it is funded
Irrevocable trusts and the grantor trust rules, power by power (§§671–679)
The intentionally defective grantor trust: Rev. Ruls. 85-13, 2004-64 and 2023-2 in one machine
Non-grantor trusts and Form 1041: DNI, the 65-day rule, compressed brackets and Kaestner
Marital, bypass, dynasty and SLAT: choosing the trust for the estate's size
worked_examples: A $6,000,000 couple in 2026: a credit-shelter trust at the first death against portability with a full §1014 step-up at the second, grown at 6% for 15 years — estate tax, capital-gains tax and the state-tax line, side by side.

An accumulation trust with $90,000 of 2026 dividends and interest that distributes $40,000: DNI, the distribution deduction, tax at the 2026 trust brackets (37% above $16,000) plus the 3.8% NIIT, against the beneficiary's own 24% rate.

A grantor paying $85,000 a year of income tax on a $4,000,000 IDGT for 15 years: the untaxed transfer that Rev. Rul. 2004-64 blesses, compounded, and the Rev. Rul. 2023-2 cost — no basis step-up on the trust's $2,600,000 of gain.

North Carolina Dept. of Revenue v. Kimberley Rice Kaestner 1992 Family Trust, 588 U.S. 262 (2019): a beneficiary's residence alone could not support the state's tax — and the trust-situs decision it changed.
sources: IRC §§641–663, 671–679, 2036, 2038, 2056(b)(7); 20 Pa.C.S. Chapter 77 (Uniform Trust Act) and §6107.1 (rule against perpetuities repeal)
Rev. Rul. 85-13; Rev. Rul. 2004-64; Rev. Rul. 2023-2; United States v. Estate of Grace, 395 U.S. 316 (1969); North Carolina Dept. of Revenue v. Kaestner Trust, 588 U.S. 262 (2019)
Leimberg et al., The Tools and Techniques of Estate Planning (20th ed., 2023)
Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026 fiduciary brackets) and the run-year revenue procedure
