days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Gift, estate and GST tax: the unified credit, portability and basis
days.headline_hint: One tax, three doors: how the government counts what you give away, and what it forgets when you die
days.focus: The federal transfer-tax system computed on its own forms. The gift tax: annual exclusion, the present-interest requirement, tuition and medical exclusions, gift-splitting, Form 709 and the tax-exclusive base; the estate tax: the gross estate section by section (§2033 through §2044, with joint property, powers and life insurance), the deductions (§§2053–2058), adjusted taxable gifts, the tentative tax, the unified credit on the run-year basic exclusion ($15,000,000 for 2026 under the 2025 Act, indexed thereafter) and the anti-clawback regulations; portability and the deceased spousal unused exclusion with the five-year late election; the generation-skipping tax with inclusion ratios and automatic allocation; and basis — §1014 step-up, §1015 carryover, the one-year rule — which decides between giving and bequeathing. Valuation closes it, with Michael Jackson's estate as the case. The reader can fill in a Form 706 and choose between a lifetime gift and a bequest in dollars.
parts: The gift tax: exclusions, splitting, Form 709 and the tax-exclusive base
The gross estate, section by section: §2033 to §2044
Deductions, the tentative tax and the unified credit on the run-year exclusion
Portability and the DSUE: the election, the late election and the last-deceased-spouse rule
The generation-skipping tax: skip persons, inclusion ratios and automatic allocation
Basis decides: §1014, §1015, the one-year rule and the gift-versus-bequest arithmetic
worked_examples: Form 709 for a married couple giving $2,000,000 of stock to two children in 2026: two $19,000 exclusions each with splitting, $1,924,000 of taxable gifts against the $15,000,000 exclusion, and the adjusted-taxable-gift carry into the estate.

Form 706 for a $24,000,000 widow dying in 2026 whose husband died in 2022 with $8,000,000 of unused exclusion: DSUE plus her own $15,000,000, the tentative tax, the $5,945,800 unified credit plus the DSUE credit, and 40% on the remainder.

A $10,000,000 taxable gift above the exclusion against the same money left at death: $4,000,000 of tax-exclusive gift tax moves $10,000,000, while $14,000,000 at death pays $5,600,000 and moves $8,400,000 — and the §2035(b) three-year gross-up.
Estate of Michael J. Jackson, T.C. Memo 2021-48: the IRS's $161 million against the estate's $2,105 for name and likeness, the Tax Court's $4.15 million, and what a valuation report must show.
sources: IRC §§2001, 2010, 2031–2058, 2501–2524, 2601–2664; Treas. Reg. §20.2010-1 (anti-clawback); Rev. Proc. 2022-32 (late portability election); Public Law 119-21 §70106 (the 2026 basic exclusion)
Stephens, Maxfield, Lind, Calfee and Smith, Federal Estate and Gift Taxation (9th ed., Thomson Reuters, updated)
IRS Form 706 and Form 709 instructions (run year); Rev. Rul. 59-60; Estate of Michael J. Jackson v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo 2021-48
McNulty and McCouch, Federal Estate and Gift Taxation in a Nutshell (9th ed., 2020)
days.exam_map: Estate Planning — Gift, estate, and GST tax compliance and calculation

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: GRATs, IDGT sales, ILITs, SLATs, QPRTs and valuation discounts
days.headline_hint: Beating the hurdle rate: the estate freezes that turn the IRS's own interest rate into a gift
days.focus: The transfer techniques that exploit §7520 and the applicable federal rates, each built from its statute and priced at the current rate (5.40% for September 2026, re-fetched for the run month). Grantor retained annuity trusts after Walton — the zeroed-out annuity, the mortality risk, rolling two-year GRATs and the reported Adelson and Zuckerberg uses; the sale to an intentionally defective grantor trust with seed gift and AFR note, and self-cancelling notes; irrevocable life insurance trusts — incidents of ownership, the three-year rule, Crummey powers and the 5-and-5 lapse; spousal lifetime access trusts and reciprocity; qualified personal residence trusts; family limited partnerships, lack-of-control and marketability discounts, §2704 and Estate of Powell. Then the honest question at a $15,000,000 exclusion: who actually needs any of this. The reader can model a GRAT or IDGT sale and say what it saves.
parts: The hurdle: §7520, the AFRs and why every freeze is a bet against a published rate
The GRAT after Walton: zeroing out, mortality risk, rolling GRATs and the famous ones
The sale to an IDGT: seed gift, note at AFR, SCINs and the §2036 exposure
The ILIT: §2042, the three-year rule, Crummey powers and the 5-and-5 lapse
SLATs, QPRTs and the reciprocal-trust doctrine
Discounts and their limits: FLPs, §2704, Estate of Powell — and who needs a freeze at $15 million
worked_examples: A two-year zeroed-out GRAT funded with $5,000,000 of stock at a 5.40% §7520 rate: the annuity of about $2,704,000 a year from the Table B factor, a remainder near zero, and the roughly $540,000 that passes if the stock returns 12% — against nothing if it returns 4%.

A sale of $20,000,000 of LLC units (30% combined discount) to an IDGT for a nine-year note at the mid-term AFR: the 10% seed gift, the interest the grantor receives untaxed under Rev. Rul. 85-13, and the freeze's value at 7% growth over 15 years.

An ILIT holding a $4,000,000 survivorship policy for three children: annual Crummey notices covering $114,000 of premium ($19,000 × 3 beneficiaries × 2 spouses), the 5-and-5 lapse computation, and the §2035 three-year risk if an existing policy is transferred.
Estate of Powell, 148 T.C. 392 (2017): the $10 million cash partnership formed a week before death and pulled back under §2036(a)(2), against a properly built partnership with a business purpose.
sources: IRC §§2035, 2036, 2042, 2514(e), 2702, 2704, 7520; Treas. Reg. §25.2702-3; Rev. Rul. 2026-17 (September 2026 rates) and the run-month revenue ruling
Walton v. Commissioner, 115 T.C. 589 (2000); Crummey v. Commissioner, 397 F.2d 82 (9th Cir. 1968); Estate of Powell v. Commissioner, 148 T.C. 392 (2017)
IRS Publication 1457, Actuarial Valuations Version 4A (Table B annuity factors)
Leimberg et al., The Tools and Techniques of Estate Planning (20th ed., 2023)
days.exam_map: Estate Planning — Strategies to transfer property; Intra-family and other business transfer techniques; Sources for estate liquidity

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Charitable planning: §170, donor-advised funds, QCDs, CRTs and CLTs
days.headline_hint: Giving it away twice: the split-interest trusts that pay you first and the charity later
days.focus: Charitable planning as tax arithmetic and instrument design. The §170 architecture — public charity versus private foundation limits, the fair-market-value rule for appreciated property, the five-year carryover, appraisal and Form 8283 rules, and the 2026 changes from the 2025 Act (the 0.5%-of-AGI floor, the 35% benefit cap in the top bracket, the non-itemizer deduction); donor-advised funds and bunching; qualified charitable distributions at the run-year limit; charitable remainder annuity and unitrusts under §664 with the 10% remainder and 5% exhaustion tests, NIMCRUT and flip variants, the four-tier income rules and the remainder factor computed from the §7520 rate; charitable lead trusts, grantor and non-grantor, zeroed out; charitable gift annuities; private foundations and their excise rules; conservation easements after the 2022 reform; and the legacy-sequencing rule — pre-tax accounts to charity, Roth to children. The reader can compute a CRT deduction from the tables and choose the instrument.
parts: The §170 architecture and what changed in 2026: limits, floors, caps and the FMV rule
Donor-advised funds, bunching and the QCD at the run-year limit
The charitable remainder trust: §664, the 10% test, the four tiers and the remainder factor
The charitable lead trust and the zeroed-out CLAT
Gift annuities, private foundations and the easement rules
Legacy sequencing: which asset to give, which to leave, and to whom
worked_examples: A $1,000,000 CRUT paying 6% to a couple aged 65 and 63 at a 5.40% §7520 rate: the remainder factor from Publication 1458, the deduction it produces, the capital-gains tax avoided on $700,000 of gain, and the four-tier character of the first year's $60,000.

A 74-year-old giving $30,000: a QCD against the 2026 $111,000 cap versus an itemized deduction at 24% with the 2026 0.5%-of-AGI floor and the $32,200 standard deduction — after-tax cost of each route.
A 20-year zeroed-out CLAT of $5,000,000 at 5.40%: the annuity that produces a zero taxable gift, and the remainder to the children if the assets earn 8%.
A founder with $10,000,000 of appreciated stock in a liquidity year: a DAF gift at the 30% AGI limit with carryover and the 2026 top-bracket 35% cap, against selling and giving cash at 60%.
sources: IRC §§170, 408(d)(8), 642(c), 664, 2055, 2522, 4940–4945; Treas. Reg. §§1.664-1 through 1.664-4; Public Law 119-21 (2025) charitable provisions effective 2026
IRS Publications 526, 561, 1457 and 1458 (actuarial tables); Rev. Rul. 77-374; Rev. Proc. 2016-42
Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026 QCD limit $111,000; one-time split-interest limit $55,000) and the run-year procedure
Leimberg et al., The Tools and Techniques of Charitable Planning (current ed.)
days.exam_map: Tax Planning — Charitable/philanthropic contributions and deductions; Estate Planning — Strategies to transfer property

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: State estate and inheritance taxes, and domicile: Pennsylvania in depth
days.headline_hint: The 4.5% that hits a Bridgeville estate at a hundred dollars, not fifteen million
days.focus: The state layer, which for a Pennsylvanian matters more than the federal one. The map for the run year: the estate-tax states with their thresholds and cliffs (New York's cliff, Massachusetts, Oregon, Washington's top rate), the inheritance-tax states, and the §2058 deduction. Then Pennsylvania's Inheritance and Estate Tax Act to the bottom: the four rates by relationship, what is exempt (spouse, charity, life insurance, retirement accounts of the under-59½, the family farm and family business exemptions), the one-year gift lookback with its $3,000 per-donee allowance, joint property, sole-use trusts, the 5% prepayment discount, REV-1500 and the nine-month deadline, and how the tax interacts with revocable trusts (it does not avoid it) and beneficiary designations. Then domicile as a plan: the factors courts use, the Pennsylvania-to-Florida move, state income tax on retirement income (Pennsylvania's exemption, the flat 3.07% and the local earned-income tax), and the residency audit. The reader can compute a Pennsylvania inheritance-tax return and advise on a change of domicile.
parts: The map: estate-tax states, inheritance-tax states, cliffs and the §2058 deduction
Pennsylvania's Inheritance Tax Act: rates, exemptions and the one-year lookback
REV-1500 in practice: joint property, retirement accounts, sole-use trusts and the 5% discount
Family farms and family businesses: the exemptions and their seven-year strings
Domicile as a plan: the factors, the Florida move and the residency audit
Retirement income across state lines: Pennsylvania's exemption, the flat 3.07% and the local EIT
worked_examples: A $3,000,000 Bridgeville estate — house, IRA, brokerage account, life insurance — passing to two children and a sibling: REV-1500 line by line at 4.5% and 12%, the insurance exclusion and the under-59½ retirement-account rule, and the 5% discount if paid by month three.

The same $3,000,000 estate in New York (the cliff above 105% of the run-year exclusion), Massachusetts ($2,000,000 threshold) and Washington (the post-2025 rate schedule): three state bills against Pennsylvania's.

A $6,000,000 family-owned machine shop with 22 employees: Pennsylvania's qualified family-owned business exemption under 72 P.S. §9111(t) — the tests, the seven-year continuation, and the recapture if it is sold in year four.

A retired couple with $140,000 of pension and IRA income choosing between Pennsylvania (retirement income exempt) and Florida or North Carolina: the full state and local income-tax line and the death-tax line over twenty years.
sources: 72 P.S. §9101 et seq. (Pennsylvania Inheritance and Estate Tax Act), especially §§9111, 9116 and 9142; Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, REV-1500 instructions and inheritance-tax informational notices (current)
IRC §2058; New York Tax Law §952; Massachusetts G.L. c. 65C; Washington RCW 83.100 (current rates)
Tax Foundation, 'Estate and Inheritance Taxes by State' (run-year edition)
Pennsylvania Bar Institute, Pennsylvania Inheritance Tax (current edition)
days.exam_map: Estate Planning — Gift, estate, and GST tax compliance and calculation; Tax Planning — Fundamental and current tax law

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Closely held businesses: valuation, buy-sell agreements and succession
days.headline_hint: After Connelly, the life-insurance policy that was supposed to pay the estate tax is now part of the estate
days.focus: The owner's estate as a business problem. Valuation under Rev. Rul. 59-60 and the discounts; buy-sell agreements — cross-purchase, entity-purchase and wait-and-see — and their funding with life insurance after Connelly v. United States; §2703 and whether the agreement fixes value; estate liquidity through §303 redemptions and §6166 installment deferral; §2032A special-use valuation; transfers within the family by gift of minority interests, installment sale and the IDGT; ESOPs and the §1042 rollover; qualified small business stock under §1202 as expanded in 2025; the S corporation and §199A in the owner's income plan; nonqualified deferred compensation and key-person coverage for the successor team; and the exit to a third party, priced. The reader can design a funded buy-sell and a liquidity plan for a real-size company.
parts: What the business is worth: Rev. Rul. 59-60, discounts and §2703
Buy-sell agreements: cross-purchase, entity, wait-and-see — and Connelly's reversal
Liquidity at death: §303 redemptions, §6166 deferral and §2032A
Keeping it in the family: minority-interest gifts, installment sales and the IDGT revisited
Selling it: ESOPs and §1042, §1202 after 2025, and the third-party exit
The owner's own retirement: cash balance plans, §199A, nonqualified deferred compensation and key-person cover
worked_examples: Connelly v. United States, 602 U.S. 257 (2024): Crown C Supply, Michael Connelly's 77.18%, the $3,500,000 policies, the $3,000,000 redemption, the estate's $3,860,000 company value against the IRS's $6,860,000, and the $889,914 of additional tax — then the cross-purchase or insurance-LLC structure that would have avoided it.

Two 50% owners of a $12,000,000 S corporation: a cross-purchase funded with $6,000,000 of insurance on each — premiums by age, the survivor's basis step-up, and the entity-purchase alternative's lost basis.

A $20,000,000 estate that is 45% closely held stock: the §6166 test, the run-year 2-percent portion (2025: $1,900,000), the interest schedule and the ten equal instalments over years five to fourteen.
A founder's $8,000,000 of §1202 stock issued in August 2025 and sold after four years: the 75% tier under the 2025 Act, the $15,000,000 cap, and the tax against an ordinary sale.
sources: Connelly v. United States, 602 U.S. 257 (2024), slip opinion at supremecourt.gov
Pratt, Valuing a Business (6th ed., 2022); Leimberg et al., The Tools and Techniques of Estate Planning (20th ed., 2023), buy-sell chapters
IRS Form 706 instructions on §6166 elections (run year)
days.exam_map: Retirement Savings and Income Planning — Business succession planning; Estate Planning — Intra-family and other business transfer techniques; Risk Management and Insurance Planning — Business owner insurance solutions

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Divorce and blended families
days.headline_hint: The QDRO, the QTIP and the ex-spouse on the beneficiary form: money when a family splits or merges
days.focus: Planning when the household changes shape. Divorce: equitable distribution in Pennsylvania, qualified domestic relations orders under §414(p) and the tax-free IRA transfer under §408(d)(6), §1041 transfers and the basis that travels with them, alimony after the 2017 Act, the §121 home-sale exclusion, retirement-benefit valuation for offset, and Social Security divorced-spouse and survivor benefits. Blended families: the elective share, prenuptial and postnuptial agreements, QTIP trusts as the instrument that provides for the second spouse and preserves the first family's inheritance, the beneficiary-designation audit, life insurance as an equaliser, and the Pennsylvania inheritance-tax rates that treat stepchildren as lineal but the spouse's relatives as strangers. The reader can build the property settlement and the blended-family estate plan side by side.
parts: Dividing retirement assets: the QDRO, §408(d)(6) and the valuation-versus-offset choice
Property, basis and the home: §1041, §121 and what the recipient really gets
Alimony, support and Social Security after divorce
The blended family's balance sheet: elective share, prenups and the second marriage
The QTIP as peace treaty: providing for the spouse, preserving the children's share
Beneficiary designations, life insurance and the Pennsylvania rate table for stepchildren
worked_examples: A $700,000 401(k) and a $300,000 pension split 50% by QDRO: the alternate payee's immediate rollover, shared-payment against separate-interest orders for the pension, and the tax if the alternate payee takes cash (no 10% penalty under §72(t)(2)(C)).
A couple with $500,000 of home equity and a $500,000 brokerage account with $150,000 of basis: the after-tax value of each side of an 'equal' split at the 2026 capital-gains brackets.
A 62-year-old divorced after a 14-year marriage whose ex-spouse's PIA is $3,200: her divorced-spouse benefit at 62 against 67 versus her own $1,100 PIA, and the survivor benefit if he dies first.

A second marriage with $2,500,000 and two children from a first marriage: a QTIP trust with the spouse's income for life and remainder to the children, the marital-deduction election, the Pennsylvania inheritance tax on the remainder at 4.5%, and the one-third elective share the spouse could claim without it.
sources: IRC §§121, 408(d)(6), 414(p), 1041, 2056(b)(7) (and §71 as repealed for post-2018 agreements); 23 Pa.C.S. §3502 (equitable distribution); 20 Pa.C.S. §2203 (elective share)
Social Security Act §202(b), (e); POMS RS 00202 and RS 00207
IRS Publication 504, Divorced or Separated Individuals (run year)
Woodhouse and Pinkerton, Divorce and Money (Nolo, current ed.); ACTEC commentaries on blended-family planning
days.exam_map: Tax Planning — Tax implications of special circumstances (divorce); Estate Planning — Estate planning for non-traditional relationships; Marital deduction

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Disability and special-needs planning
days.headline_hint: Two thousand dollars: the asset line that decides whether an inheritance helps or harms
days.focus: Planning for a household member who cannot work or who depends on means-tested programs. The benefit programs and their tests — SSDI and its insured-status rules, SSI's $2,000 resource limit and in-kind support rules, Medicaid and its waivers, and substantial gainful activity; disability-income insurance for the earner (own-occupation definitions, elimination and benefit periods, group versus individual, taxation by who paid the premium); special-needs trusts — first-party (d)(4)(A) with Medicaid payback, third-party, and pooled — and how a trust distribution is treated by SSI; ABLE accounts under §529A with the run-year contribution limit and the 2026 age-46 expansion; the letter of intent, guardianship and supported decision-making; and the estate plan that leaves the disabled child's share to the trust, not the child. The reader can structure an inheritance so that it adds to benefits rather than replacing them.
parts: The programs and their tests: SSDI, SSI, Medicaid and the $2,000 line
Insuring the earner: disability-income contracts read clause by clause
Special-needs trusts: first-party, third-party and pooled, and what SSI counts
ABLE accounts: §529A, the run-year limit, the age-46 expansion and the 529 rollover
Guardianship, supported decision-making and the letter of intent
The estate plan around a disabled child: shares, trustees, and the retirement-account beneficiary
worked_examples: A $300,000 inheritance left outright to an SSI recipient against the same sum left to a third-party special-needs trust: the month benefits stop, the spend-down, and trust distributions for housing (in-kind support reduction of up to one-third) against distributions for everything else.

A 45-year-old engineer earning $160,000 with employer-paid 60% group LTD (taxable) against an individual own-occupation policy with a 90-day elimination period: the after-tax monthly benefit under each, the premium, and the gap at 2026 brackets.
An ABLE account funded at the 2026 limit of $19,000 a year from age 25, plus a $35,000 lifetime 529-to-ABLE rollover: growth at 5%, and when the $100,000 SSI-disregard threshold is crossed.

A disabled child as beneficiary of a $600,000 IRA through an applicable multi-beneficiary trust: SECURE's eligible-designated-beneficiary stretch on the Single Life Table against the ten-year rule for a sibling.

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Sudden wealth, equity compensation and the expatriate
days.headline_hint: When the money arrives all at once — or leaves the country with you
days.focus: Three circumstances that break the ordinary plan. Sudden wealth from a liquidity event, inheritance or windfall: the behavioural evidence, the decision-free period, concentration and its unwinding through 10b5-1 plans, exchange funds, collars and charitable vehicles. Equity compensation to the bottom: incentive and nonqualified options, restricted stock and RSUs, the §83(b) election, the alternative minimum tax on ISO exercise at the run-year exemption, the disqualifying disposition, and employee stock purchase plans. The expatriate in both senses: the American abroad (the §911 exclusion and housing amount, foreign tax credits, FBAR and FATCA reporting, totalization agreements, PFICs, Medicare's non-coverage and Social Security's payability abroad) and the renouncing citizen or long-term resident (the §877A covered-expatriate tests, the mark-to-market exit tax with the run-year exclusion, deferred-compensation and IRA treatment, and the §2801 tax on gifts from covered expatriates). The reader can plan a founder's exit year and an expatriation.
parts: The windfall: what the evidence says people do, and the decision-free period
Concentration and its unwinding: 10b5-1 plans, exchange funds, collars and charity
Options, RSUs and the §83(b) election: taxed when, on what, at which rate
The AMT trap on incentive stock options, worked at the run-year exemption
The American abroad: §911, foreign tax credits, FBAR, FATCA, PFICs and totalization
Leaving for good: §877A's covered-expatriate tests, the exit tax and §2801
worked_examples: A founder with 400,000 ISOs at a $2 strike exercised at $40 and held: the $15,200,000 AMT preference, tentative minimum tax at the 2026 exemption and phase-out, the AMT credit carryforward, and the same exercise-and-sell as a disqualifying disposition.

A 10b5-1 plan for $6,000,000 of post-IPO stock: the cooling-off period under the 2022 Rule 10b5-1 amendments, a 24-month sale schedule, the tax by lot, and the exchange-fund alternative's seven-year lock.

An engineer in Munich earning €140,000: the 2026 §911 exclusion, the housing amount, German tax and foreign-tax-credit stacking, FBAR on €60,000 of accounts, and the totalization agreement's effect on Social Security credits.

A green-card holder of 12 years with $4,000,000 of net worth surrendering it: the covered-expatriate tests (net worth $2,000,000; the run-year average-tax threshold), mark-to-market gain of $1,800,000 less the run-year exclusion ($910,000 for 2026), and the IRA's deemed distribution.
sources: 31 U.S.C. §5314 and FinCEN Form 114; IRC §6038D and Form 8938; IRS Form 8854 instructions (run year)
IRS Publications 54 and 525 (run year); Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026 §911 and §877A amounts) and the run-year procedure
Brunel, Goals-Based Wealth Management (2015)

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: Ethics, fiduciary duty and the regulation of advice
days.headline_hint: Whose side is the adviser on? The rules that answer, and the data on who breaks them
days.focus: The professional-conduct layer, from the standards to the enforcement data. The CFP Board's Code of Ethics and Standards of Conduct in its current edition: the fiduciary duty at all times when giving financial advice, its three components, the fifteen duties, material-conflict disclosure and management, and the Practice Standards' seven-step process the capstone will follow. Then the law around it: the Investment Advisers Act after Capital Gains Research Bureau and the SEC's 2019 interpretation, Form ADV and Form CRS, the Marketing Rule, custody and Regulation S-P; Regulation Best Interest for broker-dealers and where it stops short of a fiduciary standard; ERISA's functional fiduciary and the Department of Labor's rule and its litigation; state registration; senior-protection rules; and the compensation models with their conflicts priced. Egan, Matvos and Seru's misconduct data and the share-class and cash-sweep enforcement cases close it. The reader can apply the standard to a real recommendation and read a Form ADV for what it does not say.
parts: The Code and Standards: fiduciary at all times, the fifteen duties and the seven steps
Conflicts: what must be disclosed, what must be managed, and what disclosure cannot cure
The Advisers Act: Capital Gains, the 2019 interpretation, Form ADV, marketing and custody
Regulation Best Interest and Form CRS: what 'best interest' means for a broker and what it does not
ERISA fiduciaries, the Department of Labor's rule and the courts
The evidence: Egan-Matvos-Seru, the enforcement cases and pricing the conflict
worked_examples: A recommendation to convert $400,000 of IRA to Roth and fund a fixed-indexed annuity paying a 6% commission: the Code's duty analysis step by step, the alternatives a fiduciary must consider, and the disclosure Reg BI would have required instead.

Reading a real Form ADV Part 2A fee schedule (a 1.0% tier on $2,000,000): thirty-year cost against a flat-fee planner at $8,000 a year at 6% growth — and the conflicts the brochure discloses in Items 5 and 12.

Egan, Matvos and Seru (JPE 2019): 7% of advisers with misconduct records, 38% repeat offenders, misconduct concentrated in counties with older and less-educated populations — the tables read directly.

The SEC's share-class selection disclosure initiative (2018–2020, over $139 million returned) and the 2024–2025 cash-sweep cases: what the conflict was, what the disclosure said, and what the client lost per $100,000 a year.
sources: CFP Board, Code of Ethics and Standards of Conduct (current edition) and Procedural Rules

Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§206, 208; SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, 375 U.S. 180 (1963); SEC Release IA-5248 (2019 fiduciary interpretation); Rule 206(4)-1 (marketing); Regulation Best Interest, Release 34-86031 (2019)

Egan, Matvos and Seru, 'The Market for Financial Adviser Misconduct', Journal of Political Economy 127(1), 2019; Bergstresser, Chalmers and Tufano, 'Assessing the Costs and Benefits of Brokers in the Mutual Fund Industry', Review of Financial Studies 22(10), 2009
ERISA §3(21); DOL Retirement Security Rule (89 Fed. Reg. 32122, April 2024, stayed July 2024) and PTE 2020-02, with the run-year litigation status

days.subject: Wealth Management
days.topic: The full plan: the Novak household of Bridgeville, end to end
days.headline_hint: One household, every number: a financial plan built in a morning and checked against the government's own tables
days.focus: The whole block applied to one named hypothetical household — Mark Novak (58, engineer, a 401(k) and a frozen cash-balance account) and Dana Novak (56, nurse, a 403(b) and a defined-benefit pension), two children (24 with student loans, 19 in college), Dana's mother (82, likely to need care), a $520,000 house in Bridgeville, $1,930,000 of investable assets across pre-tax, Roth, taxable and HSA, and a side LLC — carried through the seven-step process: engagement and data, the balance sheet and cash flow, the retirement projection with the Roth-conversion window and the claiming strategy, the income plan with guardrails and the health-care line, the risk page, the estate page with Pennsylvania's inheritance tax and the documents, and the monitoring plan. Every contribution limit, bracket, premium, bend point, exclusion and rate is the run-year figure, verified that morning against the IRS, SSA, CMS and Pennsylvania sources and printed with its year. The reader finishes able to produce a plan of this kind for a household of his own.
parts: The engagement and the data: scope, standards, and the Novaks' balance sheet and cash flow
Accumulation to 65: contributions at the run-year limits, the cash-balance payout and the conversion window
Income from 65: Social Security by the formula, the pension's lump-sum test, the withdrawal policy and the tax layer
Health and care: Medicare and IRMAA for two, Dana's mother and the long-term care decision
The estate page: wills, powers, trusts, beneficiary forms, the Pennsylvania inheritance-tax bill and the charitable line
The plan document and the monitoring calendar: what to revisit, when, and what would change the answer
worked_examples: The Novaks' contribution stack at the run-year limits (2026 reference: $24,500 plus the $8,000 catch-up in each plan, the $8,750 family HSA limit, after-tax overflow to the $72,000 ceiling) and the tax saved at their marginal bracket.

Both Social Security PIAs from indexed earnings records and the run-year bend points, Dana's pension at 62 against 65 against the lump sum under §417(e)(3), and the couple's claiming strategy at joint-life present value.
Ages 60 to 65: Roth conversions to the top of the 22% bracket each year, the COBRA or marketplace bridge and its MAGI cost, IRMAA two years later, and lifetime tax against no conversions — one table.

The estate page in numbers: Pennsylvania inheritance tax on $2,400,000 passing to the children at 4.5%, with and without the IRA-to-charity and Roth-to-children sequencing, the federal exclusion untouched, and the documents list with each Pennsylvania statute.
